title: 7.11.16 Capacity convergence and truncated measures
section: 7.11 Local energy moments
text:
In theorem 7.10.2 , a common bound for the densities forced the solutions to converge in capacity, and theorem 7.5.8 then identified the limiting equation. The canonical approximants $U_ j$ of proposition 7.11.5 have no such bound unless $\mu $ itself has a bounded density, since a bound $\mu _ j\leq M\, \mathrm dV$ for all $j$ would pass to the weak limit $\mu $; nor are the functions $U_ j$ uniformly bounded. We show that the convergence of the energy integrals in theorem 7.11.11 takes the place of the density bound once we pass to the uniformly bounded truncations $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $, whose Monge–Ampère measures differ from $\mu _ j$ by an error controlled by the energy (lemma 7.11.19 ). Thus a subsequence of canonical approximants that converges in $L^1(B)$ also converges locally in capacity, and the Monge–Ampère measures of the truncations of its limit approximate $\mu $ in total variation (theorem 7.11.24 ). Then 8748F8035D18 7.11.17  egin{equation}   egin{aligned}   igl \{ \max \{ f,-T\} >\max \{ g,-T\} +\delta  igr \} & \subset \{ f>g+\delta \} ,\   igl \{ \max \{ f,-T\} <\max \{ g,-T\} -\delta  igr \} & \subset \{ f<g-\delta \} . \end{aligned} \end{equation} Indeed, at a point of the first set we have $\max \{ f,-T\} >-T$, so $f=\max \{ f,-T\} >\max \{ g,-T\} +\delta \geq g+\delta $; the second inclusion is the first with $f$ and $g$ interchanged. Modifying a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on a compact set does not change its total Monge–Ampère mass. Lemma 7.11.18 . E1A777307E3D Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, and let $\varphi ,\psi $ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ which coincide outside a compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$ agree on $\Omega \setminus K$ and assign the same finite mass to $K$. In particular $\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, where both sides may be infinite. Proof. The two measures agree on the open set $\Omega \setminus K$, because the products are local (proposition 7.2.2 ). For $0\leq k\leq n-1$ put $S_ k=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}$. By the symmetry of the products (theorem 7.3.7 ) and definition 7.2.1 , \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^{k+1}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-k},  \] so the sum over $k$ telescopes and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R,\qquad R=(\varphi -\psi )\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}S_ k.  \] The coefficient measures of the current $R$ of order zero vanish on $\Omega \setminus K$, so $\operatorname{Supp}R\subset K$. By lemma 2.5.1 there is $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $K$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}R$, and therefore \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-\int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )=0,  \] where both integrals are finite. Since $\chi =1$ on $K$ and the two measures agree on $\Omega \setminus K$, it follows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n(K)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n(K)<\infty $, and adding the equal masses of $\Omega \setminus K$ gives the last assertion. $\square$ Lemma 7.11.19 . 546063653198 Let $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $T>0$, and put $\varphi _ T=\max \{ \varphi ,-T\} $. Then $\varphi _ T\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, and for every $p\geq 1$, \[  \int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n=\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n, \qquad e_ p(\varphi _ T)\leq e_ p(\varphi ),  \] B1ADA2B95634 7.11.20  egin{equation}  \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\| _{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 2e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation} Moreover, for every Borel set $E\subset B$, 92D8C50415C8 7.11.21  egin{equation}  \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}. \end{equation} Proof. Since $\varphi $ tends to zero uniformly at $\partial B$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ such that $\varphi >-T$ on $V\cap B$; there $\varphi _ T=\varphi $. Thus $\varphi _ T$ is bounded, nonpositive and plurisubharmonic, it has zero boundary values, and it coincides with $\varphi $ outside the compact set $\overline B\setminus V\subset B$. By lemma 7.11.18 , the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ have the same total mass, which is finite; in particular $\varphi _ T\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Put $F_ T=\{ \varphi \leq -T\} $. By maximum locality (proposition 7.3.10 ), the two measures agree on the complement $\{ \varphi >-T\} $. Since their total masses are equal and finite, they also assign the same mass $m_ T$ to $F_ T$, and Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  m_ T\leq T^{-p}\int _{F_ T}(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n\leq e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}.  \] As $\varphi _ T=-T$ on $F_ T$, we get \[  e_ p(\varphi _ T)=\int _{\{ \varphi >-T\} }(-\varphi )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n+T^ pm_ T \leq e_ p(\varphi ).  \] The two measures differ only on $F_ T$, where each has mass $m_ T$; this proves ( 7.11.20 ). Finally, $(\varphi _ T+T)/T$ is plurisubharmonic with values in $[0,1]$, so it is a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ (definition 7.4.2 ), and therefore $\int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n\leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)$. Since the two measures agree on $E\setminus F_ T$, we conclude \[  \int _ E(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n \leq \int _{E\setminus F_ T}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ T)^ n+m_ T \leq T^ n\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)+e_ p(\varphi )T^{-p}.  \] $\square$ Proposition 7.11.22 . 1036F9F7DDDA Let $p\geq 1$. For every $\varphi \in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and every $T>0$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ \varphi <-T\} ) \leq 2^{n+p}(n+1)!\, e_ p(\varphi )T^{-(n+p)}.  \] Let $\varphi _ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, let $u$ be the plurisubharmonic representative of the limit (theorem 5.10.4 ), and suppose that $E_ p=\sup _ je_ p(\varphi _ j)<\infty $. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is a constant $C_{K,p}$, depending only on $K$, $p$ and the ball $B$, such that 52F9E68B74CF 7.11.23  egin{equation}  \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ u<-T\} ) \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}T^{-p}\qquad (T>0). \end{equation} In particular, $\operatorname {Cap}^*_ B(K\cap \{ u=-\infty \} )=0$ for every compact set $K\subset B$. Proof. (1) Let $h$ be a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$, that is, $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ and $0\leq h\leq 1$. The set $\{ \varphi <-T\} $ is open, because $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, and it is relatively compact in $B$, because $\varphi $ has zero boundary values. Hence $
u =\mathbf1_{\{ \varphi <-T\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ is a finite measure, and it is dominated by $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. The tail estimate ( 7.11.3 ) of theorem 7.11.2 , applied to $
u $ and $w=h$, involves the constant $\kappa _{n,p}=2^{n+p}(n+1)!M^ n$, where $M\leq 1$ is the oscillation of $h$ on $B$, but not the mass of $
u $; it gives \[  \int _{\{ \varphi <-T\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n=
u (\{ \varphi <-T\} ) \leq 2^{n+p}(n+1)!\, e_ p(\varphi )T^{-(n+p)}.  \] Taking the supremum over $h$ proves (1). (2) Choose an open set $U$ and compact sets $L,L'\subset B$ with $K\subset U\Subset \operatorname{Int}L$ and $L\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$. By the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality (theorem 7.2.5 , with the base current $1$ and the pair $L\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$), there is a constant $C_ L$ with $\int _ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq C_ L$ for every competitor $h$, since $\| h\| _{L^\infty (L')}\leq 1$. The finite measure $\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ is dominated by $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$ and has mass at most $C_ L$, so the constant $A_ p$ of theorem 7.11.2 for this measure and $w=h$ is at most \[  C_{K,p}=\Bigl (1+ rac pn\Bigr ) igl (2^{n+p}(n+1)! igr )^{p/(n+p)}C_ L^{n/(n+p)}.  \] Hence the moment estimate ( 7.11.4 ), applied to $\varphi _ j$, gives \[  \int _ L(-\varphi _ j)^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}  \] for all $j$ and all competitors $h$. We pass this bound to the limit $u$. Since the $\varphi _ j$ are nonpositive, $u\leq 0$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by the submean inequality. Fix $S>0$. The truncations $\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} $ take values in $[-S,0]$ and converge to the plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u,-S\} $ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, since $t\mapsto \max \{ t,-S\} $ is $1$-Lipschitz. Since $\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$, lemma 7.11.9 shows that they also converge in $L^1(\mathbf1_ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n)$. As $t\mapsto t^ p$ is Lipschitz on $[0,S]$ and $(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p\leq (-\varphi _ j)^ p$, it follows that \[   egin{aligned}  \int _ L(-\max \{ u,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n & =\lim _{j	o \infty }\int _ L(-\max \{ \varphi _ j,-S\} )^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\ & \leq C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}. \end{aligned}  \] Letting $S	o \infty $, monotone convergence gives the same bound for $\int _ L(-u)^ p(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$. The set $U\cap \{ u<-T\} $ is open, because $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and it contains $K\cap \{ u<-T\} $. By Chebyshev's inequality its $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n$-measure is at most $C_{K,p}E_ p^{p/(n+p)}T^{-p}$. Taking the supremum over $h$ bounds $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(U\cap \{ u<-T\} )$, and hence the outer capacity in ( 7.11.23 ). Finally, $K\cap \{ u=-\infty \} $ is contained in $K\cap \{ u<-T\} $ for every $T$, so letting $T	o \infty $ shows that it has zero outer capacity. $\square$ Theorem 7.11.24 . D25577E2BC26 Under the hypotheses of theorem 7.11.11 , the relabeled subsequence $U_ j$ converges to $u$ locally in capacity. Moreover, let $E_2=\sup _ je_2(U_ j)$, which is finite by proposition 7.11.5 . For every $T>0$, the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ T=\max \{ u,-T\} $ has total mass at most $m$, and 8C2FAF9DC64B 7.11.25  egin{equation}  \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}. \end{equation} Proof. We estimate the capacities of the sets where the truncation $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ lies far below or far above $u_ T$ (Steps 1 and 2) and deduce convergence in capacity (Step 3). The estimate for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ then follows from the convergence of the truncated measures (Step 4). Fix $T>0$ and write $a_ j=\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ and $b=u_ T$. These plurisubharmonic functions take values in $[-T,0]$, and $a_ j	o b$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ because truncation is $1$-Lipschitz. By theorem 7.11.11 , $\varepsilon _ j=\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j	o 0$. Step 1. The sets where $a_ j<b-\delta $. Let $\delta >0$. The set $\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} $ is relatively compact in $B$, because $b\leq 0$ while $a_ j$ tends to zero at $\partial B$. Applying lemma 7.10.1 with $s=t=\delta /2$ and then Chebyshev's inequality, we obtain \[   egin{aligned}  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} ) & \leq \left( rac2\delta ight)^ n\int _{\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] The weight $(b-a_ j)_+$ takes values in $[0,T]$, and it is at most $|U_ j-u|$, since truncation does not increase distances. By ( 7.11.20 ) with $p=2$, $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\mu _ j\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$, where $\mu _ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n$. Hence \[  \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n \leq \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+T\cdot 2E_2T^{-2} \leq \varepsilon _ j+ rac{2E_2}T,  \] and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} )\leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}(\varepsilon _ j+2E_2/T)$. Step 2. The sets where $a_ j>b+\delta $. Let $L\subset B$ be compact. By theorem 7.5.2 , for every $\sigma >0$ there is an open set $G\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)<\sigma $ such that $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$. We claim that $L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} \subset G$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Let $z\in L\setminus G$. Since $b$ is upper semicontinuous, $b<b(z)+\delta /3$ on a closed ball $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset B$. Hartogs' lemma (theorem 5.10.4 ), applied to the sequence $a_ j$ with the constant majorant $b(z)+\delta /3$, gives $a_ j<b(z)+\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(z,r)}$ for all large $j$. Since $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$, after shrinking $r$ we also have $b>b(z)-\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$. Hence $a_ j-b<2\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$ for all large $j$. As $L\setminus G$ is compact, finitely many such balls cover it, which proves the claim. Consequently $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\leq \sigma $ for every $\sigma >0$, that is, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )	o 0$. Step 3. Convergence in capacity. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and apply Step 2 to a compact set $L\subset B$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. The bounded functions $a_ j-b$ are quasi-continuous by theorem 7.5.2 and the remark following definition 7.5.1 . Therefore lemma 7.5.4 , together with Steps 1 and 2 applied with $\delta /2$ in place of $\delta $, gives \[   egin{aligned} & \varlimsup _{j	o \infty }\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} )\ & \qquad \leq \varlimsup _{j	o \infty } igl (\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta /2\} ) +\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} ) igr )\ & \qquad \leq 2^{2n+3}\delta ^{-(n+1)} rac{E_2}T. \end{aligned}  \] It remains to remove the truncation. Outside $\{ U_ j<-T\} \cup \{ u<-T\} $ we have $a_ j=U_ j$ and $b=u$. Hence both sets $K\cap \{ U_ j>u+\delta \} $ and $K\cap \{ U_ j<u-\delta \} $ in definition 7.5.5 are contained in \[   igl (K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \}  igr )\cup \{ U_ j<-T\} \cup  igl (K\cap \{ u<-T\}  igr ).  \] By proposition 7.11.22 with $p=2$, applied in part (1) to $U_ j$, whose energy is at most $E_2$, and in part (2) to the sequence $(U_ j)$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ U_ j<-T\} )\leq  rac{2^{n+2}(n+1)!\, E_2}{T^{n+2}},\qquad \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ u<-T\} )\leq  rac{C_{K,2}E_2^{2/(n+2)}}{T^2},  \] and the capacity of the open set $\{ U_ j<-T\} $ equals its outer capacity. By subadditivity of the outer capacity, the upper limits as $j	o \infty $ of the outer capacities of the two sets in definition 7.5.5 are bounded by the sum of three terms, each of which tends to zero as $T	o \infty $. Since these upper limits do not depend on $T$, they vanish. Thus $U_ j	o u$ locally in capacity. Step 4. The truncated limit measure. Fix $T>0$ again. By Step 3 and ( 7.11.17 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_ j$ converge to $b$ locally in capacity, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n	o (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ weakly on $B$ by theorem 7.5.8 . By lemma 7.11.19 , each $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ has total mass $\mu _ j(B)=m$. Testing with functions $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, and letting $\chi $ increase to one, we see that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ has total mass at most $m$. Moreover, ( 7.11.20 ) gives \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm d\mu _ jight|\leq 2E_2T^{-2}  \] for every real $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $|\chi |\leq 1$. Since $\mu _ j	o \mu $ weakly by proposition 7.11.5 , letting $j	o \infty $ yields the same bound with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ and $\mu $ in place of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ and $\mu _ j$. Both limit measures are finite, so by the remark following the definition of the total variation distance, the supremum over such $\chi $ equals $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$. This proves ( 7.11.25 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 7.11.18
section: 7.11 Local energy moments
text: Lemma 7.11.18 . E1A777307E3D Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, and let $\varphi ,\psi $ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ which coincide outside a compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$ agree on $\Omega \setminus K$ and assign the same finite mass to $K$. In particular $\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n=\int _\Omega (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n$, where both sides may be infinite. Proof. The two measures agree on the open set $\Omega \setminus K$, because the products are local (proposition 7.2.2 ). For $0\leq k\leq n-1$ put $S_ k=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}$. By the symmetry of the products (theorem 7.3.7 ) and definition 7.2.1 , \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^{k+1}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-1-k}, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi S_ k)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^{n-k},  \] so the sum over $k$ telescopes and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R,\qquad R=(\varphi -\psi )\sum _{k=0}^{n-1}S_ k.  \] The coefficient measures of the current $R$ of order zero vanish on $\Omega \setminus K$, so $\operatorname{Supp}R\subset K$. By lemma 2.5.1 there is $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ which equals one on a neighborhood of $K$. Then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}R$, and therefore \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n-\int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=R(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )=0,  \] where both integrals are finite. Since $\chi =1$ on $K$ and the two measures agree on $\Omega \setminus K$, it follows that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi )^ n(K)=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n(K)<\infty $, and adding the equal masses of $\Omega \setminus K$ gives the last assertion. $\square$

Proposition 7.11.22 . 1036F9F7DDDA Let $p\geq 1$. The set $\{ \varphi <-T\} $ is open, because $\varphi $ is upper semicontinuous, and it is relatively compact in $B$, because $\varphi $ has zero boundary values. Hence $

By the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality (theorem 7.2.5 , with the base current $1$ and the pair $L\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$), there is a constant $C_ L$ with $\int _ L(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h)^ n\leq C_ L$ for every competitor $h$, since $\| h\| _{L^\infty (L')}\leq 1$. We pass this bound to the limit $u$. Since the $\varphi _ j$ are nonpositive, $u\leq 0$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by the submean inequality. Fix $S>0$. text: Theorem 7.11.24 . D25577E2BC26 Under the hypotheses of theorem 7.11.11 , the relabeled subsequence $U_ j$ converges to $u$ locally in capacity. Moreover, let $E_2=\sup _ je_2(U_ j)$, which is finite by proposition 7.11.5 . For every $T>0$, the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ T=\max \{ u,-T\} $ has total mass at most $m$, and 8C2FAF9DC64B 7.11.25 \begin{equation}  \| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}. \end{equation} Proof. We estimate the capacities of the sets where the truncation $\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ lies far below or far above $u_ T$ (Steps 1 and 2) and deduce convergence in capacity (Step 3). The estimate for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ then follows from the convergence of the truncated measures (Step 4). Fix $T>0$ and write $a_ j=\max \{ U_ j,-T\} $ and $b=u_ T$. These plurisubharmonic functions take values in $[-T,0]$, and $a_ j\to b$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$ because truncation is $1$-Lipschitz. By theorem 7.11.11 , $\varepsilon _ j=\int _ B|U_ j-u|\, \mathrm d\mu _ j\to 0$. Step 1. The sets where $a_ j<b-\delta $. Let $\delta >0$. The set $\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} $ is relatively compact in $B$, because $b\leq 0$ while $a_ j$ tends to zero at $\partial B$. Applying lemma 7.10.1 with $s=t=\delta /2$ and then Chebyshev's inequality, we obtain \[  \begin{aligned}  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} ) & \leq \left(\frac2\delta \right)^ n\int _{\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\\ & \leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] The weight $(b-a_ j)_+$ takes values in $[0,T]$, and it is at most $|U_ j-u|$, since truncation does not increase distances. By ( 7.11.20 ) with $p=2$, $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\mu _ j\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\leq 2E_2T^{-2}$, where $\mu _ j=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ j)^ n$. Hence \[  \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n \leq \int _ B(b-a_ j)_+\, \mathrm d\mu _ j+T\cdot 2E_2T^{-2} \leq \varepsilon _ j+\frac{2E_2}T,  \] and therefore $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta \} )\leq 2^{n+1}\delta ^{-(n+1)}(\varepsilon _ j+2E_2/T)$. Step 2. The sets where $a_ j>b+\delta $. Let $L\subset B$ be compact. By theorem 7.5.2 , for every $\sigma >0$ there is an open set $G\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)<\sigma $ such that $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$. We claim that $L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} \subset G$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Let $z\in L\setminus G$. Since $b$ is upper semicontinuous, $b<b(z)+\delta /3$ on a closed ball $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset B$. Hartogs' lemma (theorem 5.10.4 ), applied to the sequence $a_ j$ with the constant majorant $b(z)+\delta /3$, gives $a_ j<b(z)+\delta /3$ on $\overline{B(z,r)}$ for all large $j$. Since $b$ is continuous on $B\setminus G$, after shrinking $r$ we also have $b>b(z)-\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$. Hence $a_ j-b<2\delta /3$ on $(L\setminus G)\cap B(z,r)$ for all large $j$. As $L\setminus G$ is compact, finitely many such balls cover it, which proves the claim. Consequently $\varlimsup _ j\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\leq \sigma $ for every $\sigma >0$, that is, $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta \} )\to 0$. Step 3. Convergence in capacity. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and apply Step 2 to a compact set $L\subset B$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. The bounded functions $a_ j-b$ are quasi-continuous by theorem 7.5.2 and the remark following definition 7.5.1 . Therefore lemma 7.5.4 , together with Steps 1 and 2 applied with $\delta /2$ in place of $\delta $, gives \[  \begin{aligned} & \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} )\\ & \qquad \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\bigl (\operatorname {Cap}_ B(L\cap \{ a_ j>b+\delta /2\} ) +\operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ a_ j<b-\delta /2\} )\bigr )\\ & \qquad \leq 2^{2n+3}\delta ^{-(n+1)}\frac{E_2}T. \end{aligned}  \] It remains to remove the truncation. Outside $\{ U_ j<-T\} \cup \{ u<-T\} $ we have $a_ j=U_ j$ and $b=u$. Hence both sets $K\cap \{ U_ j>u+\delta \} $ and $K\cap \{ U_ j<u-\delta \} $ in definition 7.5.5 are contained in \[  \bigl (K\cap \{ |a_ j-b|>\delta \} \bigr )\cup \{ U_ j<-T\} \cup \bigl (K\cap \{ u<-T\} \bigr ).  \] By proposition 7.11.22 with $p=2$, applied in part (1) to $U_ j$, whose energy is at most $E_2$, and in part (2) to the sequence $(U_ j)$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ B(\{ U_ j<-T\} )\leq \frac{2^{n+2}(n+1)!\, E_2}{T^{n+2}},\qquad \operatorname {Cap}_ B^*(K\cap \{ u<-T\} )\leq \frac{C_{K,2}E_2^{2/(n+2)}}{T^2},  \] and the capacity of the open set $\{ U_ j<-T\} $ equals its outer capacity. By subadditivity of the outer capacity, the upper limits as $j\to \infty $ of the outer capacities of the two sets in definition 7.5.5 are bounded by the sum of three terms, each of which tends to zero as $T\to \infty $. Since these upper limits do not depend on $T$, they vanish. Thus $U_ j\to u$ locally in capacity. Step 4. The truncated limit measure. Fix $T>0$ again. By Step 3 and ( 7.11.17 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_ j$ converge to $b$ locally in capacity, so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ weakly on $B$ by theorem 7.5.8 . By lemma 7.11.19 , each $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ has total mass $\mu _ j(B)=m$. Testing with functions $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, $0\leq \chi \leq 1$, and letting $\chi $ increase to one, we see that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ has total mass at most $m$. Moreover, ( 7.11.20 ) gives \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm d\mu _ j\right|\leq 2E_2T^{-2}  \] for every real $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $|\chi |\leq 1$. Since $\mu _ j\to \mu $ weakly by proposition 7.11.5 , letting $j\to \infty $ yields the same bound with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n$ and $\mu $ in place of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j)^ n$ and $\mu _ j$. Both limit measures are finite, so by the remark following the definition of the total variation distance, the supremum over such $\chi $ equals $\| (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ T)^ n-\mu \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$. This proves ( 7.11.25 ). $\square$

title: 7.11.32 Mixed energy and truncation
section: 7.11 Local energy moments
text: In the next section we approximate several potentials at once by canonical approximants and pass to the limit in their mixed Monge–Ampère products. The approximants converge in capacity and have bounded energies, but we have no uniform bound for them, so theorem 7.5.8 does not apply to them directly. We therefore compare the mixed products with those of the truncated potentials, and for this we need to know that the sets where one of the potentials is very negative carry little mass of a mixed product. This follows from the mixed energy inequality of theorem 7.11.33 , which bounds a mixed energy by a constant multiple of the geometric mean of the energies $e_1$ of definition 7.11.1 . Theorem 7.11.33 . A26D05A19EF5 Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Then 802CC6F04E1F 7.11.34 \begin{equation}  \int _ B(-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \leq C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ n e_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}, \qquad C_ n=2^{n+2}. \end{equation} In particular the integral is finite, and it vanishes if one of the energies $e_1(u_ l)$ vanishes. Proof. Write $B=B(a,R)$ and $\rho (z)=|z-a|^2-R^2$. We say that $v\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ has a quadratic collar if $v=c\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$ for some constant $c>0$. We first prove the inequality with constant one for potentials with quadratic collars (Steps 1 and 2), and then approximate arbitrary elements of $\mathcal E_0(B)$ by such potentials while keeping their energies under control (Steps 3 and 4). For functions $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ which either all have quadratic collars, or are smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic, put \[  I(b_0,\ldots ,b_ n) =\int _ B(-b_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n.  \] The integral is finite: in the first case every mixed product of the $b_ l$ is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$, and in the second the integrand is a smooth form on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Step 1. Smooth functions. Let $b_0,\ldots ,b_ n$ be smooth real functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, with $b_2,\ldots ,b_ n$ plurisubharmonic and $b_0=0$ on $\partial B$, and put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ n$, with $S=1$ if $n=1$. Let $u_0,\ldots ,u_ n$ have quadratic collars, say $u_ l=c_ l\rho $ near $\partial B$. We first show that the assertions of Step 1 persist for them. Extend each $u_ l$ by $c_ l\rho $ to a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. In particular $I(u_0,\ldots ,u_ n)\leq 1$, which is the inequality with constant one. Step 3. Approximation with controlled energy. Let $u\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, put $m_\rho =\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho )^ n$, and for $j\geq 1$ let \[  \delta _ j=j^{-n-1},\qquad v_ j=\max \{ u-\delta _ j,j\rho \} .  \] Since $u-\delta _ j\leq -\delta _ j$ while $j\rho >-\delta _ j$ near $\partial B$, the function $v_ j$ equals $j\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\partial B$ in $B$. Since $v_ j$ and $j\rho $ coincide outside a compact subset of $B$, lemma 7.11.18 gives $\int _ B(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n=j^ nm_\rho $, and hence $v_ j\in \mathcal E_0(B)$. Moreover, $v_ j\to u$ uniformly on $B$. Indeed, let $s>0$, and choose a neighborhood $V$ of $\partial B$ with $u>-s$ on $V\cap B$. Since $u-\delta _ j\leq v_ j\leq 0$, we have $|v_ j-u|\leq s+\delta _ j$ on $V\cap B$. On the set $B\setminus V$, whose closure is a compact subset of $B$, the function $\rho $ is bounded away from zero and $u$ is bounded, so $j\rho <u-\delta _ j$, and hence $v_ j=u-\delta _ j$, there for all large $j$. Next we estimate $e_1(v_ j)$. Let $t>4\delta _ j$. Since $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j$ and $v_ j\leq 0$, \[  \{ v_ j<-t\} \subset \{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\}  \subset \{ u<-t/4\} ;  \] for the first inclusion note that on $\{ v_ j<-t\} $ we have $v_ j/2<-t/2<-t/4-\delta _ j$, hence $u\leq v_ j+\delta _ j<v_ j/2-t/4$. As $u$ tends to $0$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ tends to $-t/4$ at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 7.3.11 ) applies to $u$ and $v_ j/2-t/4$ and gives \[  \int _{\{ v_ j<-t\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j)^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<v_ j/2-t/4\} }\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ j/2)\bigr )^ n \leq 2^ n\int _{\{ u<-t/4\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n.  \] For $0<t\leq 4\delta _ j$ we use the total mass $j^ nm_\rho $ instead. Integrating over $t$ by the layer-cake formula $e_1(v)=\int _0^\infty (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n(\{ v<-t\} )\, \mathrm dt$, we obtain 77DC238179EB 7.11.37 \begin{equation}  e_1(v_ j)\leq 4\delta _ j j^ n m_\rho +2^{n+2}e_1(u) =\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u). \end{equation} Step 4. The general case. Apply the construction of Step 3 to each $u_ l$, obtaining functions $v_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ which equal $j\rho $ near $\partial B$. They are uniformly bounded, since $u_ l-1\leq v_{l,j}\leq 0$, and they converge uniformly, hence locally in capacity, to $u_ l$. Let $\chi \in C_ c(B)$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$. The weight $-u_0$ is bounded and quasi-continuous (theorem 7.5.2 ), so the weighted form of theorem 7.5.8 and Step 2 give \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ B\chi (-u_0)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n & =\lim _{j\to \infty }\int _ B\chi (-v_{0,j})\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{n,j}\\ & \leq \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(v_{l,j})^{1/(n+1)}. \end{aligned}  \] By ( 7.11.37 ), the right side is at most \[  \lim _{j\to \infty }\prod _{l=0}^ n\left(\frac{4m_\rho }j+C_ ne_1(u_ l)\right)^{1/(n+1)} =C_ n\prod _{l=0}^ ne_1(u_ l)^{1/(n+1)}.  \] Letting $\chi $ increase to one proves ( 7.11.34 ). Vanishing energies need no separate treatment, since the energies of the $v_{l,j}$ are positive. $\square$

text: Corollary 7.11.38 . 11945FC061EC Let $E\geq 0$, and for $1\leq l\leq n$ and $j\geq 1$ let $u_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with $e_1(u_{l,j})\leq E$. Suppose that, for each $l$, $u_{l,j}\to u_ l$ locally in capacity as $j\to \infty $, where $u_ l$ is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $B$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j} \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n  \] weakly on $B$. Proof. We compare the products with those of the truncations at a level $-T$: the latter converge by theorem 7.5.8 , and by theorem 7.11.33 the two differ by a term of order $1/T$. For $T>0$ put $a_{l,j}=\max \{ u_{l,j},-T\} $, and write \[  R_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},\qquad R_{j,T}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{n,j}.  \] By lemma 7.11.19 , $a_{l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ and $e_1(a_{l,j})\leq E$. For each $l$, theorem 7.11.33 with $u_0=u_{l,j}$, respectively $u_0=a_{l,j}$, gives \[  \int _ B(-u_{l,j})\, R_ j\leq C_ nE,\qquad \int _ B(-a_{l,j})\, R_{j,T}\leq C_ nE.  \] Let $D_{j,T}=\bigcup _{l=1}^ n\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $. On $\{ u_{l,j}\leq -T\} $ both $-u_{l,j}$ and $-a_{l,j}$ are at least $T$, so Chebyshev's inequality gives \[  R_ j(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T,\qquad R_{j,T}(D_{j,T})\leq nC_ nE/T.  \] On the complement of $D_{j,T}$, every $u_{l,j}$ is greater than $-T$. For $0\leq k\leq n$ put \[  P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{n,j},  \] so that $P_0=R_ j$ and $P_ n=R_{j,T}$. By the symmetry of the products, $P_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ and $P_{k-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k,j}\wedge \Theta _ k$ with the same closed positive current $\Theta _ k$ formed by the other $n-1$ factors, and maximum locality (proposition 7.3.10 with $p=1$, $u=u_{k,j}$, $v=-T$ and base current $\Theta _ k$) gives $P_ k=P_{k-1}$ on $\{ u_{k,j}>-T\} $. Hence $R_ j=R_{j,T}$ on the complement of $D_{j,T}$, and for every $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, \[  \left|\int _ B\chi \, (R_ j-R_{j,T})\right| \leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T.  \] Now fix $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, choose an open set $B'\Subset B$ containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and let $T>\max _ l\sup _{B'}|u_ l|$. By ( 7.11.17 ), the uniformly bounded functions $a_{l,j}$ converge to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ locally in capacity, and theorem 7.5.8 shows that $R_{j,T}\to \bigwedge _ l\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ l,-T\} $ weakly on $B$. On $B'$ we have $\max \{ u_ l,-T\} =u_ l$, so by locality (proposition 7.2.2 ) this limit equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$ there. Consequently \[  \varlimsup _{j\to \infty }\left|\int _ B\chi \, R_ j-\int _ B\chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n\right|\leq 2nC_ nE\| \chi \| _\infty /T  \] for all large $T$, and letting $T\to \infty $ completes the proof. $\square$

Corollary 7.8.8 bounds a mixed Monge–Ampère product from below when the pure Monge–Ampère measures of the factors have continuous lower densities with respect to Lebesgue measure. For non-pluripolar products in section 13.1 we need the same inequality relative to an arbitrary positive Radon measure $\mu $, which may be singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. Instead of regularizing the potentials by convolution, as in the proof of that corollary, we restrict each pure Monge–Ampère measure to a compact set and replace it by its cube averages, as in proposition 7.11.5 . The averaged measures have piecewise constant densities, so the case of Lebesgue measure applies on each cube, and Hölder's inequality compares the resulting bound with the cube averages of the expected lower bound. The convergence results of section 7.11 then allow us to pass to the limit. Theorem 7.12.1 . AAD1BC0CC6C4 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $. Let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ n$ be nonnegative Borel functions on $\Omega $. If \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mu \qquad (1\leq i\leq n),  \] then 67F72EC709B4 7.12.2  egin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n \geq \left(\prod _{i=1}^ nf_ i^{1/n}ight)\mu . \end{equation} For $n=1$ the assertion is the hypothesis. Proof. Let $n\geq 2$, and put $\lambda =(\prod _ if_ i^{1/n})\mu $. We first prove the theorem when $\Omega $ is a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ and all $u_ i$ belong to $\mathcal E_0(B)$ (Steps 1 and 2), and then reduce the general case to this one by modifying the potentials near the boundary of a ball (Step 3). For a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ we write $ho (z)=|z-a_0|^2-R^2$. We use the generalized Hölder inequality 85B06455E0FF 7.12.3  egin{equation}  \int _ A\prod _{i=1}^ ng_ i^{1/n}\, \mathrm d
u \leq \prod _{i=1}^ n\Bigl (\int _ Ag_ i\, \mathrm d
u \Bigr )^{1/n} \end{equation} for a positive measure $
u $, a measurable set $A$ and nonnegative measurable functions $g_ i$. If one of the integrals $c_ i=\int _ Ag_ i\, \mathrm d
u $ vanishes, then $g_ i=0$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $A$ and both sides vanish, with the convention $0\cdot \infty =0$; if none vanishes and one is infinite, the right side is infinite. Otherwise, integrating the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality $\prod _ i(g_ i/c_ i)^{1/n}\leq  rac1n\sum _ ig_ i/c_ i$ over $A$ gives $\int _ A\prod _ i(g_ i/c_ i)^{1/n}\, \mathrm d
u \leq 1$, which is ( 7.12.3 ). For every compact $K\subset \Omega $ we have $\int _ Kf_ i\, \mathrm d\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n(K)<\infty $ by hypothesis, so ( 7.12.3 ) shows that $\lambda $ is a positive Radon measure. Step 1. Exhaustion by compactly supported measures. Choose closed balls $K_ l\subset B$ concentric with $B$, increasing with $l$ and exhausting $B$, and set \[  \alpha _{i,l}=\mathbf1_{K_ l}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] These measures are finite since $u_ i\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, they have compact support in $B$, and they are dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ i$. The function $u_ i$ has these properties for every $l$, and so has $A_{i,l+1}$, because $\alpha _{i,l+1}\geq \alpha _{i,l}$. Therefore \[  u_ i\leq A_{i,l+1}\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0.  \] We claim that $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ as $l	o \infty $. The decreasing limit $A_{i,\infty }$ satisfies $u_ i\leq A_{i,\infty }\leq 0$, so it is a bounded plurisubharmonic function (theorem 5.10.1 ) with zero boundary values. By theorem 7.3.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,\infty })^ n$ is the weak limit of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,\infty })^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$, and this measure has finite total mass. Let $\varepsilon >0$ and $S=\{ u_ i<A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $. Since $u_ i-(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho )$ tends to zero at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 7.3.11 ) applies. Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ))^ n$ and dropping the mixed terms, which are positive, we obtain \[  \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n \leq \int _ S igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ) igr )^ n \leq \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] The integrals of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$ are finite, so $S$ is Lebesgue null. Hence $u_ i\geq A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho $ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere on $B$, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 5.9.1 applied to $\max \{ u_ i,A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $ and $u_ i$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $A_{i,\infty }=u_ i$, as claimed. Step 2. A common grid. Fix $l$. Choose a sequence of partitions of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ into half-open cubes whose side lengths decrease to zero, the same for all $i$. Let $\alpha _{i,l,j}$ be the corresponding cube averages of $\alpha _{i,l}$, as in proposition 7.11.5 , and let $A_{i,l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ be the corresponding canonical approximants of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, the zero-boundary solutions of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$; they are defined for all large $j$. Discarding finitely many indices $j$, we may assume that they are defined for all $j$ and all $i$, and that every cube meeting $K_ l$ has its closure in $B$. By theorem 7.11.30 , $A_{i,l,j}	o A_{i,l}$ locally in capacity as $j	o \infty $. By proposition 7.11.5 , applied with the bounded subsolution $u_ i$, the energies $e_1(A_{i,l,j})$ are bounded uniformly in $j$; since there are only finitely many indices $i$, they have a common bound. (If $\alpha _{i,l}=0$, all these solutions vanish.) Therefore corollary 7.11.38 gives EF405F42095E 7.12.4  egin{equation}   igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \longrightarrow  igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l} \end{equation} weakly on $B$. Let $\lambda _ l=\mathbf1_{K_ l}\lambda $, a finite measure, and let $\lambda _{l,j}$ be its cube averages. For every cube $Q$, the hypothesis gives $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)\geq \int _{Q\cap K_ l}f_ i\, \mathrm d\mu $, and ( 7.12.3 ) then gives E7114DA296F9 7.12.5  egin{equation}  \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n} \geq  rac1{|Q|}\int _{Q\cap K_ l}\prod _{i=1}^ nf_ i^{1/n}\, \mathrm d\mu = rac{\lambda _ l(Q)}{|Q|}. \end{equation} Let $Q$ be a cube with $\lambda _ l(Q)>0$; it meets $K_ l$, so its interior lies in $B$. Recall that $\eta ^ n=c_ n\, \mathrm dV$ with $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and $c_ n=n!\pi ^{-n}$, by ( 7.2.4 ). Applying corollary 7.8.8 on the open set $\operatorname{Int}Q$ to the constant densities $c_ n^{-1}\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to $\eta ^ n$, and using ( 7.12.5 ), we obtain on $\operatorname{Int}Q$ \[   igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{c_ n|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\eta ^ n =\prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\mathrm dV \geq \lambda _{l,j}.  \] The factor $c_ n$ cancels because the $n$ exponents $1/n$ sum to one. Since the mixed product is positive, we conclude that $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j}\geq \lambda _{l,j}$ on $B$. As $j	o \infty $, $\lambda _{l,j}	o \lambda _ l$ weakly. Indeed, for $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, replacing the values of $\chi $ by its cube averages changes $\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _ l$ by at most $\lambda _ l(B)$ times the modulus of continuity of $\chi $ at the cube diameter. Letting $j	o \infty $ and using ( 7.12.4 ), we obtain $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}\geq \lambda _ l$. Finally let $l	o \infty $. By Step 1, $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ with $u_ i\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0$, so theorem 7.3.7 gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}	o  igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ weakly, while $\lambda _ l$ increases to $\lambda $. Testing with nonnegative functions in $C_ c(B)$ and using monotone convergence on the right, we obtain ( 7.12.2 ) for potentials in $\mathcal E_0(B)$. Step 3. Localization. Now let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded on $\Omega $. Choose a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a compact set $K\subset B$. Since adding constants does not change the products, we may assume that $u_ i\leq -1$ on $B$. With constants $C_ i>0$ so large that $C_ iho <\inf _ Bu_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, put \[  \widetilde u_ i=\max \{ u_ i,C_ iho \} .  \] Then $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, and $\widetilde u_ i=C_ iho $ near $\partial B$, because $C_ iho 	o 0$ at $\partial B$ while $u_ i\leq -1$. By locality of the products on the open neighborhood of $K$ where $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$, we have $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mathbf1_ K\mu $ on $B$. A Borel set $E\subset \Omega $ is the disjoint union of the Borel sets $E_ m=(E\cap L_ m)\setminus  igcup _{m'<m}L_{m'}$, and therefore $P(E)=\sum _ mP(E_ m)\geq \sum _ m\lambda (E_ m)=\lambda (E)$. $\square$ Corollary 7.12.6 . 0B504335901F Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $. If $f,g$ are nonnegative Borel functions on $\Omega $ and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq f\mu ,\qquad (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq g\mu ,  \] then, for each integer $1\leq k\leq n-1$, D13F44EA144A 7.12.7  egin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k} \geq f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\mu . \end{equation} For $k=0$ and $k=n$ the corresponding inequalities are the hypotheses; for $n=1$ only these occur. Proof. Apply theorem 7.12.1 to $k$ copies of $u$ with density $f$ and $n-k$ copies of $v$ with density $g$. $\square$ Corollary 7.12.8 . 7071C55A0E4E Under the hypotheses of corollary 7.12.6 , \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n\geq (f^{1/n}+g^{1/n})^ n\mu .  \] Proof. By additivity and symmetry of the products, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n=\sum _{k=0}^ n inom nk(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}$. Bound the terms with $1\leq k\leq n-1$ by corollary 7.12.6 and the terms with $k=0,n$ by the hypotheses; the binomial formula then gives the assertion. The density on the right is locally $\mu $-integrable, since $f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\leq f+g$ by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and $f$ and $g$ are locally $\mu $-integrable because $f\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ and $g\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. $\square$

For every compact $K\subset \Omega $ we have $\int _ Kf_ i\, \mathrm d\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n(K)<\infty $ by hypothesis, so ( 7.12.3 ) shows that $\lambda $ is a positive Radon measure. Choose closed balls $K_ l\subset B$ concentric with $B$, increasing with $l$ and exhausting $B$, and set \[  \alpha _{i,l}=\mathbf1_{K_ l}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] These measures are finite since $u_ i\in \mathcal E_0(B)$, they have compact support in $B$, and they are dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ i$. By theorem 7.11.30 , the equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A)^ n=\alpha _{i,l}$ has a bounded solution $A_{i,l}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ with zero boundary values, and $A_{i,l}$ is the largest bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq \alpha _{i,l}$ and upper boundary limits at most zero. The function $u_ i$ has these properties for every $l$, and so has $A_{i,l+1}$, because $\alpha _{i,l+1}\geq \alpha _{i,l}$. Therefore \[  u_ i\leq A_{i,l+1}\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0.  \] We claim that $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ as $l	o \infty $. The decreasing limit $A_{i,\infty }$ satisfies $u_ i\leq A_{i,\infty }\leq 0$, so it is a bounded plurisubharmonic function (theorem 5.10.1 ) with zero boundary values. By theorem 7.3.7 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,\infty })^ n$ is the weak limit of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,\infty })^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$, and this measure has finite total mass. Let $\varepsilon >0$ and $S=\{ u_ i<A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $. Since $u_ i-(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho )$ tends to zero at $\partial B$, the comparison theorem (theorem 7.3.11 ) applies. Expanding $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ))^ n$ and dropping the mixed terms, which are positive, we obtain \[  \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n+\varepsilon ^ n\int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho )^ n \leq \int _ S igl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho ) igr )^ n \leq \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n.  \] The integrals of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n$ are finite, so $S$ is Lebesgue null. Hence $u_ i\geq A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho $ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere on $B$, by the uniqueness assertion of theorem 5.9.1 applied to $\max \{ u_ i,A_{i,\infty }+\varepsilon ho \} $ and $u_ i$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $A_{i,\infty }=u_ i$, as claimed. Step 2. A common grid. Fix $l$. Choose a sequence of partitions of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ into half-open cubes whose side lengths decrease to zero, the same for all $i$. Let $\alpha _{i,l,j}$ be the corresponding cube averages of $\alpha _{i,l}$, as in proposition 7.11.5 , and let $A_{i,l,j}\in \mathcal E_0(B)$ be the corresponding canonical approximants of $\alpha _{i,l}$, that is, the zero-boundary solutions of $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$; they are defined for all large $j$. Discarding finitely many indices $j$, we may assume that they are defined for all $j$ and all $i$, and that every cube meeting $K_ l$ has its closure in $B$. By theorem 7.11.30 , $A_{i,l,j}	o A_{i,l}$ locally in capacity as $j	o \infty $. By proposition 7.11.5 , applied with the bounded subsolution $u_ i$, the energies $e_1(A_{i,l,j})$ are bounded uniformly in $j$; since there are only finitely many indices $i$, they have a common bound. (If $\alpha _{i,l}=0$, all these solutions vanish.) Therefore corollary 7.11.38 gives EF405F42095E 7.12.4  egin{equation}   igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \longrightarrow  igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l} \end{equation} weakly on $B$. Let $\lambda _ l=\mathbf1_{K_ l}\lambda $, a finite measure, and let $\lambda _{l,j}$ be its cube averages. For every cube $Q$, the hypothesis gives $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)\geq \int _{Q\cap K_ l}f_ i\, \mathrm d\mu $, and ( 7.12.3 ) then gives E7114DA296F9 7.12.5  egin{equation}  \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n} \geq  rac1{|Q|}\int _{Q\cap K_ l}\prod _{i=1}^ nf_ i^{1/n}\, \mathrm d\mu = rac{\lambda _ l(Q)}{|Q|}. \end{equation} Let $Q$ be a cube with $\lambda _ l(Q)>0$; it meets $K_ l$, so its interior lies in $B$. There the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j})^ n=\alpha _{i,l,j}$ have the constant densities $\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV$. Recall that $\eta ^ n=c_ n\, \mathrm dV$ with $\eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ and $c_ n=n!\pi ^{-n}$, by ( 7.2.4 ). Applying corollary 7.8.8 on the open set $\operatorname{Int}Q$ to the constant densities $c_ n^{-1}\alpha _{i,l}(Q)/|Q|$ with respect to $\eta ^ n$, and using ( 7.12.5 ), we obtain on $\operatorname{Int}Q$ \[   igwedge _{i=1}^ n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j} \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{c_ n|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\eta ^ n =\prod _{i=1}^ n\left( rac{\alpha _{i,l}(Q)}{|Q|}ight)^{1/n}\mathrm dV \geq \lambda _{l,j}.  \] The factor $c_ n$ cancels because the $n$ exponents $1/n$ sum to one. The measure $\lambda _{l,j}$ vanishes on the cubes with $\lambda _ l(Q)=0$ and does not charge the cube boundaries, which are Lebesgue null. Since the mixed product is positive, we conclude that $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l,j}\geq \lambda _{l,j}$ on $B$. As $j	o \infty $, $\lambda _{l,j}	o \lambda _ l$ weakly. Indeed, for $\chi \in C_ c(B)$, replacing the values of $\chi $ by its cube averages changes $\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _ l$ by at most $\lambda _ l(B)$ times the modulus of continuity of $\chi $ at the cube diameter. Letting $j	o \infty $ and using ( 7.12.4 ), we obtain $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}\geq \lambda _ l$. Finally let $l	o \infty $. By Step 1, $A_{i,l}\downarrow u_ i$ with $u_ i\leq A_{i,l}\leq 0$, so theorem 7.3.7 gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}A_{i,l}	o  igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ weakly, while $\lambda _ l$ increases to $\lambda $. Testing with nonnegative functions in $C_ c(B)$ and using monotone convergence on the right, we obtain ( 7.12.2 ) for potentials in $\mathcal E_0(B)$. Step 3. Localization. Now let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ n$ be locally bounded on $\Omega $. Choose a ball $B=B(a_0,R)$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a compact set $K\subset B$. Since adding constants does not change the products, we may assume that $u_ i\leq -1$ on $B$. With constants $C_ i>0$ so large that $C_ iho <\inf _ Bu_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, put \[  \widetilde u_ i=\max \{ u_ i,C_ iho \} .  \] Then $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$ on a neighborhood of $K$, and $\widetilde u_ i=C_ iho $ near $\partial B$, because $C_ iho 	o 0$ at $\partial B$ while $u_ i\leq -1$. Thus $\widetilde u_ i\in \mathcal E_0(B)$: its Monge–Ampère measure is smooth near $\partial B$ and locally finite on the rest of $B$. By locality of the products on the open neighborhood of $K$ where $\widetilde u_ i=u_ i$, we have $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mathbf1_ K\mu $ on $B$. The case already proved, applied to the measure $\mathbf1_ K\mu $, gives $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u_ i\geq \mathbf1_ K\lambda $, and on a neighborhood of $K$ the left side equals $ igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ by locality. Thus $P= igwedge _ i\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i$ satisfies $P(E)\geq \lambda (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset K$. The interiors of such compact sets $K$ cover $\Omega $, and since $\Omega $ has a countable basis, countably many of them, say $\operatorname{Int}L_1,\operatorname{Int}L_2,\ldots $, already cover $\Omega $. A Borel set $E\subset \Omega $ is the disjoint union of the Borel sets $E_ m=(E\cap L_ m)\setminus  igcup _{m'<m}L_{m'}$, and therefore $P(E)=\sum _ mP(E_ m)\geq \sum _ m\lambda (E_ m)=\lambda (E)$. $\square$

text: Corollary 7.12.6 . 0B504335901F Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and let $\mu $ be a positive Radon measure on $\Omega $. If $f,g$ are nonnegative Borel functions on $\Omega $ and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\geq f\mu ,\qquad (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\geq g\mu ,  \] then, for each integer $1\leq k\leq n-1$, D13F44EA144A 7.12.7 \begin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k} \geq f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\mu . \end{equation} For $k=0$ and $k=n$ the corresponding inequalities are the hypotheses; for $n=1$ only these occur. By additivity and symmetry of the products, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u+v))^ n=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}$. The density on the right is locally $\mu $-integrable, since $f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\leq f+g$ by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and $f$ and $g$ are locally $\mu $-integrable because $f\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ and $g\mu \leq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. $\square$

section: 7.13 Bounded complex Hessians and contact sets
text:
Monge–Ampère measures of envelopes are computed on contact sets: if a potential $u$ lies below an obstacle $f$ and $u=f$ on a set $E$, one expects the Monge–Ampère measure of $u$ on $E$ to be determined by the Hessian of $f$. A contact set may have empty interior, and then the locality of the products on open sets (proposition 7.2.2 ) says nothing about it. We show that weak derivatives are local on arbitrary measurable sets: two functions whose weak derivatives up to order two are locally integrable have the same such derivatives almost everywhere on the set where they agree. For potentials with bounded complex Hessians this yields a formula for the Bedford–Taylor product restricted to a contact set (proposition 7.13.4 ), which is used for envelopes in section 16.10 . We use the Sobolev spaces $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ of subsection 2.9.9 , for open sets $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$, integers $k\ge 0$ and $p\in \{ 1,2\} $; thus a function belongs to $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ if it and its distributional derivatives of order at most $k$ belong to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Since $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\subset L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, we have $W^{k,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)\subset W^{k,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Lemma 7.13.1 . 8736729F21D9 Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open and let $g\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ be real. Then $
abla g=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. If moreover $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then all first and second weak derivatives of $g$ vanish almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Here $\{ g=0\} $ may be formed with any measurable representative of $g$, since changing $g$ on a null set changes this set only by a null set. Proof. We first prove the chain rule \[  \partial _ a\Phi (g)=\Phi '(g)\, \partial _ a g\qquad (1\le a\le d)  \] for a $C^1$ function $\Phi \colon \mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ with bounded derivative; note that $\Phi (g)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, since $|\Phi (g)|\leq |\Phi (0)|+\| \Phi '\| _\infty |g|$. Let $V\Subset D$ be open. The mollifications $g_\varepsilon =g*ho _\varepsilon $ converge to $g$ in $L^1(V)$, together with their first derivatives $\partial _ ag_\varepsilon =(\partial _ ag)*ho _\varepsilon $, by the remark preceding lemma 2.9.14 ; passing to a sequence $\varepsilon _ k	o 0$, we may also assume that $g_{\varepsilon _ k}	o g$ almost everywhere on $V$. Since $\Phi $ is Lipschitz, $\Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})	o \Phi (g)$ in $L^1(V)$. Moreover, \[  \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\Phi '(g)\partial _ ag =\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})(\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag) + igl (\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})-\Phi '(g) igr )\partial _ ag  \] tends to zero in $L^1(V)$: the first term is bounded by $\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag|$, and the second tends to zero by dominated convergence, since it tends to zero almost everywhere, $\Phi '$ being continuous, and is bounded by $2\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag|$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(V)$ the classical chain rule gives $\int \Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}\, \psi $, and letting $k	o \infty $ we obtain $\int \Phi (g)\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g)\partial _ ag\, \psi $. As $V$ was arbitrary, this proves the chain rule. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ supported in $(-2,2)$, with $0\le \chi \le 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $[-1,1]$, and put $\Phi _\varepsilon (t)=\int _0^ t\chi (s/\varepsilon )\, \mathrm ds$ for $\varepsilon >0$. Then $\Phi _\varepsilon $ is smooth with $0\leq \Phi _\varepsilon '\leq 1$, $|\Phi _\varepsilon |\le 2\varepsilon $, and by the chain rule \[  
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)=\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g \longrightarrow \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g \quad 	ext{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)  \] as $\varepsilon 	o 0$, by dominated convergence, since $\chi (g/\varepsilon )	o \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }$ pointwise and $|\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g|\leq |
abla g|$. On the other hand, $\Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ uniformly, so $
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ in the sense of distributions. Since convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ implies convergence in the sense of distributions, the locally integrable function $\mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g$ defines the zero distribution, and hence vanishes almost everywhere (proposition 2.5.3 ). This is the first assertion. If $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then each $\partial _ ag$ belongs to $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ and, by the first assertion, vanishes almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Applying the first assertion to $\partial _ ag$, formed with any measurable representative, shows that $
abla \partial _ ag=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \partial _ ag=0\} $, a set which contains $\{ g=0\} $ up to a null set. Since there are finitely many derivatives, the union of the exceptional null sets is null. $\square$ Lemma 7.13.2 . D57C89462C1B Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $f\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. If the distributional Laplacian $\Delta f$ belongs to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. In particular, this holds if $f$ is continuous and $\Delta f$ is a locally bounded measurable function. Proof. Considering real and imaginary parts separately, we may assume that $f$ is real. Let $f_\varepsilon =f*ho _\varepsilon $ be the mollifications of $f$. For every compact set $L\subset D$ they are smooth on a neighborhood of $L$ for small $\varepsilon $, and by proposition 2.5.3 and lemma 2.5.1 , $f_\varepsilon 	o f$ and $\Delta f_\varepsilon =(\Delta f)*ho _\varepsilon 	o \Delta f$ in $L^2(L)$ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. We first show that the gradients converge. Let $\chi $ be a real test function, and let $h$ be a real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Since $\int \partial _ a(\chi ^2h\, \partial _ ah)=0$ for each $a$, by Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have \[   egin{aligned}  \int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2& =-\int \chi ^2h\Delta h-2\int \chi h
abla \chi \cdot 
abla h\ & \le 	frac 12\int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2 +\int \chi ^2|h\Delta h|+2\int h^2|
abla \chi |^2, \end{aligned}  \] where we used $2xy\le x^2/2+2y^2$. Hence \[  \int \chi ^2|
abla h|^2\leq 2\| \chi \| _\infty ^2\| h\| _{L^2(S)}\| \Delta h\| _{L^2(S)}+4\| 
abla \chi \| _\infty ^2\| h\| _{L^2(S)}^2, \qquad S=\operatorname{Supp}\chi .  \] Let $L\subset D$ be compact, and choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equal to one on $L$ (lemma 2.5.1 ). Apply the last inequality to $h=f_\varepsilon -f_\delta $. As $\varepsilon ,\delta 	o 0$, the norms $\| f_\varepsilon -f_\delta \| _{L^2(\operatorname{Supp}\chi )}$ tend to zero, while the norms $\| \Delta f_\varepsilon -\Delta f_\delta \| _{L^2(\operatorname{Supp}\chi )}$ stay bounded. Hence the gradients $
abla f_\varepsilon $ form a Cauchy family in $L^2(L)$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(\operatorname{Int}L)$ we have $\int \partial _ af_\varepsilon \, \psi =-\int f_\varepsilon \, \partial _ a\psi 	o -\int f\, \partial _ a\psi $, so the $L^2$ limits are the distributional first derivatives of $f$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$. Since $L$ was arbitrary, the first derivatives of $f$ belong to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, and $
abla f_\varepsilon 	o 
abla f$ in $L^2(L)$ for every compact $L\subset D$. For the second derivatives, let $L\subset D$ be compact, choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equal to one on a neighborhood $N$ of $L$, and for small $\varepsilon $ put $v_\varepsilon =\chi f_\varepsilon $, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$. These are smooth functions with compact support, and \[  \Delta v_\varepsilon =\chi \Delta f_\varepsilon +2
abla \chi \cdot 
abla f_\varepsilon +f_\varepsilon \Delta \chi  \] is a Cauchy family in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$, by the first part applied on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. For every real $v\in C^\infty _ c(\mathbb R^ d)$, integrating by parts twice gives \[  \sum _{a,b=1}^ d\| \partial _ a\partial _ b v\| _2^2 =\sum _{a,b=1}^ d\int (\partial _ a^2v)(\partial _ b^2v) =\| \Delta v\| _2^2.  \] Applying this identity to $v_\varepsilon -v_\delta $, we see that all second derivatives of $v_\varepsilon $ form Cauchy families in $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions identifies their limits with the distributional second derivatives of $\chi f$, which agree with those of $f$ on $N$, where $\chi f=f$. Thus the second derivatives of $f$ are square-integrable on $L$. Since $L$ was arbitrary, $f\in W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. The last assertion holds because continuous functions and locally bounded measurable functions are locally square-integrable. $\square$ Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. We say that a continuous function $f$ on $\Omega $ has a bounded complex Hessian if its distributional derivatives $f_{j ar k}=\partial ^2 f/\partial z_ j\partial  ar z_ k$ are locally bounded measurable functions. Since the Laplacian of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ is $4\sum _ j\partial ^2/\partial z_ j\partial  ar z_ j$ by ( 5.2.9 ), such a function belongs to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ by lemma 7.13.2 . Proposition 7.13.3 . C006456D2AFC Let $f,g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ be real, and put $E=\{ f=g\} $, formed with any measurable representatives of $f$ and $g$. Then the real weak first and second derivatives of $f$ and $g$ agree almost everywhere on $E$. In particular, \[  \mathbf1_ E f_{j ar k}=\mathbf1_ E g_{j ar k} \quad 	ext{almost everywhere, for all }j,k.  \] Proof. Apply lemma 7.13.1 to $f-g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, whose zero set, formed with the chosen representatives, is $E$. The complex derivatives $f_{j ar k}$ and $g_{j ar k}$ are fixed linear combinations of the real second derivatives, which gives the second assertion. $\square$ As in subsection 7.8.5 , $D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ denotes the mixed discriminant of Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices (section 5.3 ); in dimension zero we put $D()=1$. Proposition 7.13.4 . 1466731348C1 Let $u_1,\dots ,u_ n$ be continuous plurisubharmonic functions with bounded complex Hessians on $\Omega $, and let $A_ j=((u_ j)_{a ar b})$ be their complex Hessian matrices. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n = rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] If $v_1,\dots ,v_ n\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ are real, with weak complex Hessian matrices $B_ j=((v_ j)_{a ar b})$, and $E= igcap _ j\{ u_ j=v_ j\} $, formed with any Borel representatives of the $v_ j$, then \[  \mathbf1_ E\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n = rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\mathbf1_ E D(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] In particular, the density $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)$ is locally bounded. (In dimension zero, where $\mathbb C^0$ is a point and $\mathrm dV_0$ is the unit point mass, both sides of each identity equal $\mathrm dV_0$.) Proof. For smooth $u_ j$ we polarize ( 7.2.4 ), as in the proof of corollary 7.8.8 . Applied to the smooth function $\sum _ jt_ ju_ j$ with $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n\in \mathbb R$, it gives the identity \[  \Bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\sum _ jt_ ju_ j\Bigr )^ n= rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det \Bigl (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j\Bigr )\, \mathrm dV_{2n}  \] between exterior powers of smooth forms, and both sides are polynomials in $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$. We compare the coefficients of $t_1\cdots t_ n$. Since $2$-forms commute, on the left this coefficient is $n!$ times the exterior product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n$, which is the Bedford–Taylor product by proposition 7.2.2 (1); on the right it is $(n!)^2\pi ^{-n}D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, by the definition of the mixed discriminant. This proves the first formula for smooth $u_ j$. For continuous $u_ j$, let $u_{j,\varepsilon }=u_ j*ho _\varepsilon $ be their radial mollifications, which are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 5.9.2 ). They converge to $u_ j$ uniformly on compact sets (lemma 2.5.1 ), so their products converge weakly by proposition 7.2.6 . By proposition 2.5.3 , the complex Hessian matrix of $u_{j,\varepsilon }$ is the mollification $A_{j,\varepsilon }$ of the matrix $A_ j$ of locally bounded functions. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. For small $\varepsilon $, the entries of $A_{j,\varepsilon }$ are bounded on $K$ by the bounds of the entries of $A_ j$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, and by lemma 2.5.1 they converge to those of $A_ j$ in $L^1(K)$. Products of functions which are bounded on $K$ uniformly in $\varepsilon $ and converge in $L^1(K)$ converge in $L^1(K)$, because $|ab-a'b'|\leq |a||b-b'|+|b'||a-a'|$. Since $D$ is a polynomial in the matrix entries, it follows that $D(A_{1,\varepsilon },\dots ,A_{n,\varepsilon })	o D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ in $L^1(K)$. By the first part, $(n!/\pi ^ n)D(A_{1,\varepsilon },\dots ,A_{n,\varepsilon })\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ is the product of the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j,\varepsilon }$, so the weak limit of these products is $(n!/\pi ^ n)D(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. This proves the first formula in general. By lemma 7.13.2 , each $u_ j$ belongs to $W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )\subset W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so proposition 7.13.3 , applied to $u_ j$ and the chosen representative of $v_ j$, gives $A_ j=B_ j$ almost everywhere on $\{ u_ j=v_ j\} $, hence on $E$. Substituting into the first formula proves the second, and also shows that $\mathbf1_ ED(B_1,\dots ,B_ n)=\mathbf1_ ED(A_1,\dots ,A_ n)$ is locally bounded. $\square$ On a complex manifold, the second identity is applied in holomorphic charts to functions $u_ j$ which become plurisubharmonic after the addition of a smooth local potential $g_ j$ of a closed real $(1,1)$-form. If $g_ j+u_ j$ is plurisubharmonic with bounded complex Hessian, we apply proposition 7.13.4 to $g_ j+u_ j$ and $g_ j+v_ j$: adding the same smooth function to $u_ j$ and $v_ j$ does not change the contact set, and $g_ j+v_ j\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ whenever $v_ j\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

title: Lemma 7.13.1
section: 7.13 Bounded complex Hessians and contact sets
text:
Lemma 7.13.1 . 8736729F21D9 Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open and let $g\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ be real. Then $
abla g=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. If moreover $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then all first and second weak derivatives of $g$ vanish almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Here $\{ g=0\} $ may be formed with any measurable representative of $g$, since changing $g$ on a null set changes this set only by a null set. Proof. We first prove the chain rule \[  \partial _ a\Phi (g)=\Phi '(g)\, \partial _ a g\qquad (1\le a\le d)  \] for a $C^1$ function $\Phi \colon \mathbb R	o \mathbb R$ with bounded derivative; note that $\Phi (g)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, since $|\Phi (g)|\leq |\Phi (0)|+\| \Phi '\| _\infty |g|$. Let $V\Subset D$ be open. The mollifications $g_\varepsilon =g*ho _\varepsilon $ converge to $g$ in $L^1(V)$, together with their first derivatives $\partial _ ag_\varepsilon =(\partial _ ag)*ho _\varepsilon $, by the remark preceding lemma 2.9.14 ; passing to a sequence $\varepsilon _ k	o 0$, we may also assume that $g_{\varepsilon _ k}	o g$ almost everywhere on $V$. Since $\Phi $ is Lipschitz, $\Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})	o \Phi (g)$ in $L^1(V)$. Moreover, \[  \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\Phi '(g)\partial _ ag =\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})(\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag) + igl (\Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})-\Phi '(g) igr )\partial _ ag  \] tends to zero in $L^1(V)$: the first term is bounded by $\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}-\partial _ ag|$, and the second tends to zero by dominated convergence, since it tends to zero almost everywhere, $\Phi '$ being continuous, and is bounded by $2\| \Phi '\| _\infty |\partial _ ag|$. For $\psi \in C^\infty _ c(V)$ the classical chain rule gives $\int \Phi (g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g_{\varepsilon _ k})\partial _ ag_{\varepsilon _ k}\, \psi $, and letting $k	o \infty $ we obtain $\int \Phi (g)\partial _ a\psi =-\int \Phi '(g)\partial _ ag\, \psi $. As $V$ was arbitrary, this proves the chain rule. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ on $\mathbb R$ supported in $(-2,2)$, with $0\le \chi \le 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $[-1,1]$, and put $\Phi _\varepsilon (t)=\int _0^ t\chi (s/\varepsilon )\, \mathrm ds$ for $\varepsilon >0$. Then $\Phi _\varepsilon $ is smooth with $0\leq \Phi _\varepsilon '\leq 1$, $|\Phi _\varepsilon |\le 2\varepsilon $, and by the chain rule \[  
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)=\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g \longrightarrow \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g \quad 	ext{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)  \] as $\varepsilon 	o 0$, by dominated convergence, since $\chi (g/\varepsilon )	o \mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }$ pointwise and $|\chi (g/\varepsilon )
abla g|\leq |
abla g|$. On the other hand, $\Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ uniformly, so $
abla \Phi _\varepsilon (g)	o 0$ in the sense of distributions. Since convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ implies convergence in the sense of distributions, the locally integrable function $\mathbf1_{\{ g=0\} }
abla g$ defines the zero distribution, and hence vanishes almost everywhere (proposition 2.5.3 ). This is the first assertion. If $g\in W^{2,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$, then each $\partial _ ag$ belongs to $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$ and, by the first assertion, vanishes almost everywhere on $\{ g=0\} $. Applying the first assertion to $\partial _ ag$, formed with any measurable representative, shows that $
