text: Lemma 6.2.3 . 0C82C2C21EE7 Let $T$ be a densely defined operator from $H_0$ to $H_1$. Then $T^*$ is closed and $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. If $T$ is also closed, then $T^*$ is densely defined and $T^{**}=T$. Proof. If $y_ j\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, $y_ j\to y$ and $T^*y_ j\to w$, then for every $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ \[  \langle Tx,y\rangle =\lim _ j\langle Tx,y_ j\rangle =\lim _ j\langle x,T^*y_ j\rangle =\langle x,w\rangle ;  \] hence $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=w$, so $T^*$ is closed. A vector $y\in H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Ran}T$ exactly when the functional $x\mapsto \langle Tx,y\rangle $ vanishes, that is, when $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*y=0$. This proves $\ker T^*=(\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp $. In the same way, $(a,b)\in H_0\oplus H_1$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname {Gr}T$ if and only if $\langle Tx,b\rangle =\langle x,-a\rangle $ for all $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$, so \[  (\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =\{ (-T^*y,y):y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\} .  \] Now let $T$ be closed, and let $v\in H_1$ be orthogonal to $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Since $\operatorname {Gr}T$ is closed, proposition 6.2.1 and the description of $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp $ decompose $(0,v)$ as $(x,Tx)+(-T^*y,y)$ with $x\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus $x=T^*y$ and $v=Tx+y$. Since $v$ is orthogonal to $y\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, we obtain \[  0=\langle v,y\rangle =\langle Tx,y\rangle +\| y\| ^2=\langle x,T^*y\rangle +\| y\| ^2=\| x\| ^2+\| y\| ^2,  \] so $x=y=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$ is dense, and $T^{**}$ is defined. Let $J\colon H_1\oplus H_0\to H_0\oplus H_1$ and $J'\colon H_0\oplus H_1\to H_1\oplus H_0$ be the unitary maps $J(b,a)=(-a,b)$ and $J'(a,b)=(-b,a)$. The description of the orthogonal complement of a graph, applied to $T$ and to the densely defined operator $T^*$, reads $(\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp =J(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)$ and $(\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp =J'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})$. For a closed subspace $M$ we have $(M^\perp )^\perp =M$ by proposition 6.2.1 , and unitary maps carry orthogonal complements to orthogonal complements. Therefore \[  \operatorname {Gr}T=\bigl ((\operatorname {Gr}T)^\perp \bigr )^\perp =J\bigl ((\operatorname {Gr}T^*)^\perp \bigr ) =JJ'(\operatorname {Gr}T^{**})=\operatorname {Gr}T^{**},  \] because $JJ'=-\mathrm{id}$ and graphs are linear subspaces. Thus $T^{**}=T$. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.2.4
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.2 Hilbert spaces and closed operator complexes
text: Theorem 6.2.4 . FDE87BE964C7 Let $H_0,H_1,H_2$ be Hilbert spaces, let $T$ from $H_0$ to $H_1$ be a closed densely defined operator, and let $S$ from $H_1$ to $H_2$ be a closed operator with $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$. Let $g\in \ker S$ and $0\le M<\infty $, and assume that \[  |\langle g,f\rangle |^2\le M\bigl (\| T^*f\| ^2+\| Sf\| ^2\bigr ) \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S).  \] Then the equation $Tu=g$ has a solution $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ with $\| u\| ^2\le M$. Among all solutions there is a unique one of smallest norm, and it is orthogonal to $\ker T$. Proof. Since $S$ is closed, $\ker S$ is a closed subspace, and $H_1=\ker S\oplus (\ker S)^\perp $ by proposition 6.2.1 . Since $\operatorname {Ran}T\subset \ker S$, lemma 6.2.3 gives $(\ker S)^\perp \subset (\operatorname {Ran}T)^\perp =\ker T^*$. Let $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$, and write $f=f_0+f_1$ with $f_0\in \ker S$ and $f_1\in (\ker S)^\perp $. Then $f_1\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$ and $T^*f_1=0$, so $f_0\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$, $T^*f_0=T^*f$ and $Sf_0=0$. Moreover $\langle g,f\rangle =\langle g,f_0\rangle $, because $g\in \ker S$. The hypothesis applied to $f_0$ therefore gives \[  |\langle g,f\rangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*f\| \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Consequently the map $\lambda \colon T^*f\mapsto \langle g,f\rangle $ is well defined on $\operatorname {Ran}T^*$: if $T^*f=T^*f'$, then $|\langle g,f-f'\rangle |\le \sqrt M\, \| T^*(f-f')\| =0$. It is conjugate-linear and bounded by $\sqrt M$, hence uniformly continuous, so it extends uniquely to a conjugate-linear functional $\tilde\lambda $ on the closed subspace $W=\overline{\operatorname {Ran}T^*}$, again bounded by $\sqrt M$. If $P_ W$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$, then $x\mapsto \tilde\lambda (P_ Wx)$ is a conjugate-linear functional on $H_0$ of norm at most $\sqrt M$, because $\| P_ Wx\| \le \| x\| $. By the representation of conjugate-linear functionals in proposition 6.2.1 , there is $u\in H_0$ with $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$ and \[  \langle u,T^*f\rangle =\langle g,f\rangle \qquad (f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*).  \] Taking complex conjugates, we get $\langle T^*f,u\rangle =\langle f,g\rangle $ for all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*$. Thus the functional $f\mapsto \langle T^*f,u\rangle $ is bounded on $\operatorname{Dom}T^*$, so $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T^{**}$ and $T^{**}u=g$. Since $T^{**}=T$ by lemma 6.2.3 , we conclude that $u\in \operatorname{Dom}T$ and $Tu=g$. The solutions of $Tu=g$ form the affine subspace $u+\ker T$, which is closed because $\ker T$ is closed. If $P$ denotes the orthogonal projection onto $\ker T$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u-Pu\| ^2+\| Pu+k\| ^2$ for $k\in \ker T$. Hence $u-Pu$ is the unique solution of smallest norm; it is orthogonal to $\ker T$, and its norm is at most $\| u\| \le \sqrt M$. $\square$

title: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
text:
We shall prove Hörmander's estimate on open sets that are exhausted by the compact sublevel sets of a continuous plurisubharmonic function. These pseudoconvex open sets are characterized by the plurisubharmonicity of minus the logarithm of the boundary distance, and they carry smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions, which section 6.4 uses to localize the estimate. For $r>0$ we write $\Delta _ r=\{ t\in \mathbb C:|t|<r\} $ for the open disc of radius $r$ in $\mathbb C$, and $\Delta =\Delta _1$ for the unit disc; in this chapter the letter $\Delta $ always denotes a disc, never the Laplacian. Definition 6.3.1 . 10E4AE8BC531 Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. An exhaustion function of $\Omega $ is a function $ho \colon \Omega 	o \mathbb R$ such that the sublevel set $\{ z\in \Omega :ho (z)\le c\} $ is compact for every $c\in \mathbb R$. The open set $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex if it has a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. A continuous exhaustion function attains its minimum on each nonempty sublevel set, so it is bounded below; adding a constant, we may take it nonnegative. An open set $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex if and only if each of its connected components is. Indeed, the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to a component is a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of that component, because the component is open and closed in $\Omega $. Conversely, the components of $\Omega $ are open, and each of them contains a point with rational real coordinates, so there are at most countably many of them, say $\Omega _1,\Omega _2,\ldots $. If $ho _ k\ge 0$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega _ k$, then the function equal to $ho _ k+k$ on $\Omega _ k$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $: it is continuous and plurisubharmonic because the components are open, and its sublevel set $\{ \le c\} $ is the finite union of the compact sets $\{ ho _ k\le c-k\} $, $k\le c$. Recall from proposition 5.9.2 that a real function $u$ of class $C^2$ on an open set is plurisubharmonic if and only if its complex Hessian matrix $(u_{j ar k})$ is positive semidefinite at every point. Here, as in section 5.9 , a function on an open set is plurisubharmonic if it is plurisubharmonic on each connected component. Recall also, from the discussion following proposition 5.9.2 , that a function $u$ is strictly plurisubharmonic if every point has a neighborhood on which $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic for some $\varepsilon >0$. For smooth $u$ this means that $(u_{j ar k})$ is positive definite at every point, and then its smallest eigenvalue is a positive continuous function. To recognize plurisubharmonic functions we use the following criterion, in which the harmonic majorants in the submean inequality are restricted to real parts of polynomials. Lemma 6.3.2 . 5898ED42C26F Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ N$ be open and let $v\colon U	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be upper semicontinuous. Assume that for all $z_0\in U$ and $a\in \mathbb C^ N$ with $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset U$, and for every polynomial $P$ in one complex variable with $v(z_0+ta)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ whenever $|t|=1$, we have $v(z_0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. Then \[  v(z_0)\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta  \] for all such $z_0$ and $a$. Proof. Fix $z_0$ and $a$, and put $g(	heta )=v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)$, an upper semicontinuous function on the circle. By lemma 3.4.4 there are continuous real functions $g_ m$ decreasing to $g$ whose integrals decrease to the integral of $g$, which may be $-\infty $. Fix $m$ and $\delta >0$. We approximate $g_ m$ uniformly by real trigonometric polynomials, using the Fejér kernel \[  F_ N(	heta )= rac1N\Bigl |\sum _{k=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik	heta }\Bigr |^2=\sum _{|k|<N}\Bigl (1- rac{|k|}N\Bigr )\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik	heta },\qquad N\ge 1.  \] The two expressions agree because the product $\sum _{k,l=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(k-l)	heta }$ contains exactly $N-|h|$ pairs $(k,l)$ with $k-l=h$, for each integer $h$ with $|h|<N$. By the first expression $F_ N\ge 0$, and summing the geometric series gives $F_ N(	heta )=\sin ^2(N	heta /2)/(N\sin ^2(	heta /2))\le 1/(N\sin ^2(	heta /2))$ for $0<|	heta |\le \pi $; by the second, $F_ N$ has integral one with respect to the normalized measure $\mathrm d	heta /(2\pi )$ on $[-\pi ,\pi ]$. Let $q_ N=g_ m*F_ N$ be the convolution with respect to $\mathrm d	heta /(2\pi )$, that is, $q_ N(	heta )= rac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(	heta -	au )F_ N(	au )\, \mathrm d	au $. For $0<\delta '\le \pi $ let $\omega (\delta ')$ be the largest oscillation of $g_ m$ over arcs of length at most $\delta '$, which tends to zero with $\delta '$ by uniform continuity. Splitting the integral at $|	au |=\delta '$, we obtain \[  |q_ N(	heta )-g_ m(	heta )|\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }|g_ m(	heta -	au )-g_ m(	heta )|F_ N(	au )\, \mathrm d	au \le \omega (\delta ')+ rac{2\max |g_ m|}{N\sin ^2(\delta '/2)},  \] so $q_ N	o g_ m$ uniformly as $N	o \infty $. Inserting the second expression for $F_ N$ and substituting $\sigma =	heta -	au $, we see that $q_ N(	heta )=\sum _{|k|<N}c_ k\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik	heta }$ with $c_ k=(1-|k|/N) rac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(\sigma )\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\sigma }\, \mathrm d\sigma $. Since $g_ m$ is real, $c_{-k}= ar c_ k$, so $q_ N(	heta )=\operatorname{Re}P(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })$ for the polynomial $P(t)=c_0+2\sum _{0<k<N}c_ kt^ k$, and $\operatorname{Re}P(0)=c_0$ is the mean of $g_ m$. Choose $N$ with $|q_ N-g_ m|<\delta $. Then $\operatorname{Re}(P(t)+\delta )\ge g_ m\ge g$ on the circle, and the hypothesis gives \[  v(z_0)\le c_0+\delta = rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }g_ m\, \mathrm d	heta +\delta .  \] Letting $\delta 	o 0$ and then $m	o \infty $, we obtain the asserted inequality. $\square$ Richberg's lemma approximates a continuous strictly plurisubharmonic function from above by smooth strictly plurisubharmonic functions, at the cost of half of the lower bound for the complex Hessian. Convolution does this locally; the local pieces are glued by a regularized maximum. Lemma 6.3.3 (Richberg) . 52930869627B Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $u$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $, and let $a>0$ be such that $u-a|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then for every continuous function $\varepsilon \colon \Omega 	o (0,\infty )$ there is a smooth function $v$ on $\Omega $ with \[  u\le v\le u+\varepsilon ,\qquad v-	frac a2|z|^2\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] Proof. Step 1: local approximations. Let $(K_ m)_{m\ge 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 2.2 ), so that $K_ m\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}$ and $ igcup _ m\operatorname{Int}K_ m=\Omega $, and put $K_0=K_{-1}=\varnothing $. For each $m\ge 1$, the compact set $K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(c,r/3)$ with $c\in K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ and $B(c,r)\Subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}\setminus K_{m-2}$. Collecting these balls for all $m$, we obtain a sequence of balls $B_ i=B(c_ i,r_ i)\Subset \Omega $ whose inner balls $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$ cover $\Omega $. The family $(B_ i)$ is locally finite: a compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, and a ball chosen at a stage $m'\ge m+2$ lies in the complement of $K_{m'-2}\supset K_ m$, so the compact set meets only the finitely many balls chosen at the stages $m'\le m+1$. The function $u=(u-a|z|^2)+a|z|^2$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 . Let $ho _ h$, $h>0$, be the radial mollifiers of section 2.5 . By proposition 5.9.2 (2), we have $u*ho _ h\ge u$, and $(u-a|z|^2)*ho _ h=u*ho _ h-a|z|^2*ho _ h$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, hence has positive semidefinite complex Hessian by proposition 5.9.2 (1); by lemma 2.5.1 , $u*ho _ h	o u$ locally uniformly as $h	o 0$. Since $ho _ h$ is radial, $\int yho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)=0$, and expanding $|z-y|^2=|z|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle z,yangle +|y|^2$ gives $|z|^2*ho _ h=|z|^2+\int |y|^2ho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$, whose complex Hessian matrix is $I$. Hence the complex Hessian matrix of $u*ho _ h$ is at least $aI$. For each $i$ choose $\delta _ i$ with $0<\delta _ i<a/2$ and $\delta _ ir_ i^2<\min _{\overline B_ i}\varepsilon $, put $\eta _ i=\delta _ ir_ i^2/6$, and choose $h_ i>0$ so small that $u*ho _{h_ i}$ is defined near $\overline B_ i$ and satisfies $0\le u*ho _{h_ i}-u<\eta _ i$ there. Define \[  u_ i=u*ho _{h_ i}+\delta _ i igl ((2r_ i/3)^2-|z-c_ i|^2 igr ) \quad 	ext{on }B_ i.  \] The quadratic term is at least $\delta _ ir_ i^2/3=2\eta _ i$ on the inner ball $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$, is less than $-2\eta _ i$ where $|z-c_ i|>\sqrt7\, r_ i/3$, and is at most $4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9$ everywhere. Therefore \[   egin{aligned} & u_ i>u+\eta _ i& & 	ext{on }B(c_ i,r_ i/3),\ & u_ i<u-\eta _ i& & 	ext{where }\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i,\ & u_ i+\eta _ i<u+\varepsilon & & 	ext{on }B_ i, \end{aligned}  \] the last because $2\eta _ i+4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9=7\delta _ ir_ i^2/9<\varepsilon $ on $B_ i$. The complex Hessian matrix of $u_ i$ is at least $(a-\delta _ i)I\ge (a/2)I$. Step 2: a regularized maximum. Fix an even smooth function $	heta \ge 0$ on $\mathbb R$ with support in $(-1,1)$ and integral one, for instance the mollifier $ho _{1/2}$ of section 2.5 in dimension $d=1$. For an integer $p\ge 1$, positive numbers $\eta _1,\ldots ,\eta _ p$ and $t=(t_1,\ldots ,t_ p)\in \mathbb R^ p$, define \[  M_\eta (t)=\int _{\mathbb R^ p}\max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i x_ i) \prod _ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx.  \] The substitution $y_ i=\eta _ ix_ i$ and the evenness of $	heta $ show that $M_\eta $ is the convolution of the continuous function $t\mapsto \max _ it_ i$ with the smooth compactly supported function $y\mapsto \prod _ i\eta _ i^{-1}	heta (y_ i/\eta _ i)$, so $M_\eta $ is smooth by differentiation under the integral sign (section 2.5 ). It has the following properties. $M_\eta $ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable, since for fixed $x$ the function $t\mapsto \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i)$ is. $\max _ it_ i\le M_\eta (t)\le \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i)$. The upper bound holds because $|x_ i|<1$ on the support of the integrand. For the lower bound, integrate $\max _ j(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)\ge t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i$ and use $\int x_ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx_ i=0$. $M_\eta (t_1+c,\ldots ,t_ p+c)=M_\eta (t)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. Differentiating in $c$, together with the first property, gives $\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i\ge 0$ and $\sum _ i\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i=1$. If $t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)$ for some $i$, then deleting the variable $t_ i$ and the parameter $\eta _ i$ does not change the value of $M_\eta $. Indeed, for $|x_ j|<1$ we have $t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i<t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)<\max _{j
e i}(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)$, so the $i$-th term never realizes the maximum, and integrating out $x_ i$ removes it. For smooth real functions $w_1,\ldots ,w_ p$, the chain rule gives \[  \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}M_\eta (w)=\sum _ i rac{\partial M_\eta }{\partial t_ i}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}w_ i+\sum _{i,l} rac{\partial ^2M_\eta }{\partial t_ i\partial t_ l}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}w_ l}.  \] The real Hessian matrix $G=(\partial ^2M_\eta /\partial t_ i\partial t_ l)$ is positive semidefinite, because the second derivative of the convex function $s\mapsto M_\eta (t+s	au )$ is nonnegative for every $	au \in \mathbb R^ p$. Hence the matrix given by the second sum is positive semidefinite: for $b\in \mathbb C^ n$ its quadratic form equals $\sum _{i,l}G_{il}\zeta _ i ar\zeta _ l$ with $\zeta _ i=\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, b_ j$, and writing $\zeta =\xi +\mathrm i\xi '$ with $\xi ,\xi '\in \mathbb R^ p$, this is $\xi ^{\mathsf T}G\xi +\xi '^{\mathsf T}G\xi '\ge 0$ by the symmetry of $G$. Therefore, by the third property, if each $w_ i$ has complex Hessian matrix at least $(a/2)I$, so does $M_\eta (w_1,\ldots ,w_ p)$. Step 3: gluing. For $z\in \Omega $ let $I(z)=\{ i:z\in B_ i\} $, a finite nonempty set, and define $v(z)=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i(z))_{i\in I(z)} igr )$ with the parameters $(\eta _ i)_{i\in I(z)}$. We show that $v$ is smooth near a fixed point $z_0$. Let $I_0=\{ i:z_0\in B_ i\} $ and $I_1=\{ i:z_0\in \partial B_ i\} $, finite sets by local finiteness, and choose $j$ with $z_0\in B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$. There is a neighborhood $W$ of $z_0$ that is contained in $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$ and in $B_ i$ for $i\in I_0$, that meets $\overline B_ i$ only for $i\in I_0\cup I_1$, and whose intersection with $B_ i$, for $i\in I_1$, lies in the shell $\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i$. For $z\in W$ we have $I_0\subset I(z)\subset I_0\cup I_1$, $j\in I_0$, and every $i\in I(z)\cap I_1$ satisfies \[  u_ i(z)+\eta _ i<u(z)<u_ j(z)-\eta _ j.  \] By the fourth property of $M_\eta $, applied to these indices one at a time, $v=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i)_{i\in I_0} igr )$ on $W$, which is smooth. Thus $v$ is smooth on $\Omega $, and by Step 2 its complex Hessian matrix is at least $(a/2)I$; hence $v-	frac a2|z|^2$ is smooth with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, and so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1). Finally, every $z$ lies in some inner ball $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$, and the second property of $M_\eta $ gives $v(z)\ge u_ j(z)>u(z)$ and $v(z)\le \max _{i\in I(z)}(u_ i(z)+\eta _ i)<u(z)+\varepsilon (z)$. $\square$ Theorem 6.3.4 . EA195CC9592D Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set. If $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, then $-\log \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Conversely, if this function is plurisubharmonic, then $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex. Every pseudoconvex open set in $\mathbb C^ n$ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. Proof. Steps 1 and 2 deduce the plurisubharmonicity of $-\log \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ from a submean inequality for the distance to the boundary in a fixed direction; Step 3 uses this function to construct a continuous exhaustion function, which lemma 6.3.3 smooths. Step 1: distances in a fixed direction. Let $\Omega $ be pseudoconvex, with a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $ho $. For $z\in \Omega $ and $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ put \[  \delta (z,\xi )=\sup \{ r>0:z+\xi \Delta _ r\subset \Omega \} \in (0,\infty ],  \] so that $\delta (z,0)=\infty $. The function $\delta $ is lower semicontinuous on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$: if $r<\delta (z,\xi )$, then the compact disc $z+\xi \overline\Delta _ r$ lies in $\Omega $, hence so does $z'+\xi '\overline\Delta _ r$ for all $(z',\xi ')$ close to $(z,\xi )$, and $\delta (z',\xi ')\ge r$ for these points. Thus $V=-\log \delta $ is an upper semicontinuous function on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 6.3.2 for $V$ on the open set $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n\subset \mathbb C^{2n}$. Let $(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$, $|t|\le 1$, be a closed disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$, and let $P$ be a polynomial with $V(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ for $|t|=1$, that is, $\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\ge |\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|$. Consider the holomorphic map \[  h(t,w)=z_0+t a+w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}(\xi _0+t b),\qquad (t,w)\in \mathbb C^2.  \] We have $h(t,0)=z_0+ta\in \Omega $ for $|t|\le 1$; and $h(t,w)\in \Omega $ for $|t|=1$ and $|w|<1$, because then $|w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|<\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$. Let $R$ be the supremum of the numbers $r\ge 0$ with $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ r)\subset \Omega $. Since $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ 0\} )$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $ and $h$ is continuous, $R>0$. We show that $R\ge 1$. Suppose that $R<1$. Then $h(\partial \Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; let $c$ be the maximum of $ho $ on it. For $|w|<R$ we have $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ w\} )\subset \Omega $, because every radius smaller than an admissible one is admissible; since this set is compact and $h$ is continuous, there is $r'>1$ such that $t\mapsto h(t,w)$ maps the disc $\Delta _{r'}$ into $\Omega $, and hence into one connected component of $\Omega $. The function $t\mapsto ho (h(t,w))$ is finite, hence subharmonic on $\Delta _{r'}$ by proposition 5.9.3 , and it is at most $c$ on $\partial \Delta $. By upper semicontinuity, $\varlimsup _{t	o \zeta }(ho (h(t,w))-c)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Delta $, and the maximum principle of proposition 3.4.7 on the disc $\Delta $ gives $ho (h(t,w))\le c$ for $|t|<1$, hence for $|t|\le 1$. Thus $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \Delta _ R)$ lies in the compact set $\{ ho \le c\} $, and so does its closure $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$. This compact subset of $\Omega $ has positive distance from $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, and the uniform continuity of $h$ on compact sets gives $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _{R'})\subset \Omega $ for some $R'>R$, contradicting the definition of $R$. Hence $R\ge 1$. In particular $h(0,w)=z_0+w\mathrm e^{-P(0)}\xi _0\in \Omega $ for $|w|<1$, which means that $\delta (z_0,\xi _0)\ge \mathrm e^{-\operatorname{Re}P(0)}$, that is, $V(z_0,\xi _0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. By lemma 6.3.2 , $V$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed complex disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$. Step 2: the boundary distance. Now let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ and put $d(z)=\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. For a unit vector $\xi $ we have $\delta (z,\xi )\ge d(z)$, because $z+\xi \Delta _{d(z)}$ lies in the ball $B(z,d(z))\subset \Omega $. Equality holds if $\xi $ points from $z$ to a nearest point of the closed set $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, since that point, $z+d(z)\xi $, lies in $z+\xi \Delta _ r$ for every $r>d(z)$. Hence \[  -\log d(z)=\max _{|\xi |=1}V(z,\xi ).  \] For fixed $\xi $, the function $z\mapsto V(z,\xi )$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed disc $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset \Omega $, by Step 1 with $b=0$, and it is bounded above by $-\log d$. Therefore \[  V(z_0,\xi )\le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }V(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a,\xi )\, \mathrm d	heta \le  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }-\log d(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta ,  \] and taking the maximum over $\xi $ gives the submean inequality for $-\log d$. Since $d$ is positive and $1$-Lipschitz, $-\log d$ is continuous. Its restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is therefore subharmonic (definition 3.4.2 ): at a point $z_0+t_0a$ of such a section, the circle means over $\{ z_0+(t_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })a\} $ dominate the value for all small $r>0$. Hence $-\log d$, which is finite, is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ by definition 5.8.1 , that is, on $\Omega $. Step 3: smooth exhaustion functions. Let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set on which $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, and put \[  u(z)=|z|^2+\max \{ -\log d(z),0\} .  \] Then $u$ is continuous, $u-|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , and $u$ is an exhaustion function of $\Omega $: the set $\{ u\le c\} $ is contained in the ball $\{ |z|^2\le c\} $ and in $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, so it is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ contained in $\Omega $, hence compact. In particular, $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, which proves the converse statement. By lemma 6.3.3 with $a=1$ and $\varepsilon =1$, there is a smooth function $s$ with $u\le s\le u+1$ such that $s-|z|^2/2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then $s\ge u\ge 0$, and the complex Hessian matrix of $s$ is at least $I/2$ by proposition 5.9.2 (1) applied to $s-|z|^2/2$, so that $s$ is strictly plurisubharmonic. Moreover, since $s\ge u$, the sublevel set $\{ s\le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ u\le c\} $. Thus $s$ is a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. If $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ is pseudoconvex, Step 2 shows that $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, so this construction applies; for $\Omega =\mathbb C^ n$ we take $s=|z|^2$. $\square$ Corollary 6.3.5 . FFB7E3647C0B Products of pseudoconvex open sets are pseudoconvex. If $s$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, then each sublevel set $\{ s<c\} $, $c\in \mathbb R$, is pseudoconvex and relatively compact in $\Omega $. In particular, every pseudoconvex open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is the union of an increasing sequence of pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $. Proof. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $\Omega '\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be pseudoconvex, with nonnegative continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions $ho $ and $ho '$. The function $(z,w)\mapsto ho (z)+ho '(w)$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega 	imes \Omega '$, by proposition 5.9.3 applied to the two projections and by proposition 5.9.5 . Its sublevel set $\{ \le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ ho \le c\} 	imes \{ ho '\le c\} $, so $\Omega 	imes \Omega '$ is pseudoconvex. Next let $s$ be as in the statement and $c\in \mathbb R$. The function $x\mapsto 1/(c-x)$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,c)$, so the complex Hessian matrix of $1/(c-s)$ on the open set $\{ s<c\} $, namely $(c-s)^{-2}(s_{j ar k})+2(c-s)^{-3} igl (\partial _{z_ j}s\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}s} igr )$ by the chain rule, is positive semidefinite. Hence $|z|^2+1/(c-s)$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $\{ s<c\} $, by proposition 5.9.2 (1). For $C\le 0$ its sublevel set $\{ \le C\} $ is empty. For $C>0$ this sublevel set is closed in $\{ s<c\} $ and contained in the set $\{ s\le c-1/C\} $, which is a compact subset of $\{ s<c\} $; hence it is compact, and $\{ s<c\} $ is pseudoconvex. Moreover $\{ s<c\} $ is contained in the compact set $\{ s\le c\} $, so it is relatively compact in $\Omega $. Finally, if $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, theorem 6.3.4 provides a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $s$, and the sets $\Omega _ j=\{ s<j\} $, $j\ge 1$, are pseudoconvex, relatively compact in $\Omega $, increasing, and have union $\Omega $. (Some of them may be empty or disconnected; definition 6.3.1 allows arbitrary open sets.) $\square$ With the boundary distance at hand, the invariant exhaustion function required in Kiselman's minimum principle exists automatically on pseudoconvex domains. Corollary 6.3.6 . EC970F3402EB Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ m	imes \mathbb C^ k$ be a pseudoconvex domain that is invariant under imaginary translations and whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex, in the notation of section 5.12 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We construct a function $\psi $ with the properties required in theorem 5.12.1 ; the corollary then follows from that theorem. If $\Omega =\mathbb C^{m+k}$, let $\psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$. Otherwise let $d=\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )$ and put \[  \psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2+ \max \{ -\log d(z,w),0\} .  \] Imaginary translations are isometries of $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ that preserve $\Omega $ and its complement, so $d$ and $\psi $ are invariant under them. The function $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 : $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 6.3.4 , and $|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1), since its complex Hessian matrix is the diagonal matrix with entries $1$ in the $z$-directions and $ rac12$ in the $w$-directions, by the identity $(\operatorname{Re}w_ l)^2=	frac 12|w_ l|^2+	frac 12\operatorname{Re}(w_ l^2)$ for $1\le l\le k$. Finally, let $c\in \mathbb R$. Since $\psi $ is continuous, the set $\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $ is closed in $\Omega _{\mathbb R}$. It is contained in $\{ |z|^2+|t|^2\le c\} $ and, if $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^{m+k}$, in the set $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, which is closed in $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ and contained in $\Omega $; it is therefore a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ m	imes \mathbb R^ k$, hence compact. $\square$

title: Definition 6.3.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
text: Definition 6.3.1 . 10E4AE8BC531 Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. An exhaustion function of $\Omega $ is a function $\rho \colon \Omega \to \mathbb R$ such that the sublevel set $\{ z\in \Omega :\rho (z)\le c\} $ is compact for every $c\in \mathbb R$. The open set $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex if it has a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function.

title: Lemma 6.3.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
text: Lemma 6.3.2 . 5898ED42C26F Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ N$ be open and let $v\colon U\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be upper semicontinuous. Assume that for all $z_0\in U$ and $a\in \mathbb C^ N$ with $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset U$, and for every polynomial $P$ in one complex variable with $v(z_0+ta)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ whenever $|t|=1$, we have $v(z_0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. Then \[  v(z_0)\le \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)\, \mathrm d\theta  \] for all such $z_0$ and $a$. Proof. Fix $z_0$ and $a$, and put $g(\theta )=v(z_0+\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }a)$, an upper semicontinuous function on the circle. By lemma 3.4.4 there are continuous real functions $g_ m$ decreasing to $g$ whose integrals decrease to the integral of $g$, which may be $-\infty $. Fix $m$ and $\delta >0$. We approximate $g_ m$ uniformly by real trigonometric polynomials, using the Fejér kernel \[  F_ N(\theta )=\frac1N\Bigl |\sum _{k=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta }\Bigr |^2=\sum _{|k|<N}\Bigl (1-\frac{|k|}N\Bigr )\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta },\qquad N\ge 1.  \] The two expressions agree because the product $\sum _{k,l=0}^{N-1}\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(k-l)\theta }$ contains exactly $N-|h|$ pairs $(k,l)$ with $k-l=h$, for each integer $h$ with $|h|<N$. By the first expression $F_ N\ge 0$, and summing the geometric series gives $F_ N(\theta )=\sin ^2(N\theta /2)/(N\sin ^2(\theta /2))\le 1/(N\sin ^2(\theta /2))$ for $0<|\theta |\le \pi $; by the second, $F_ N$ has integral one with respect to the normalized measure $\mathrm d\theta /(2\pi )$ on $[-\pi ,\pi ]$. Let $q_ N=g_ m*F_ N$ be the convolution with respect to $\mathrm d\theta /(2\pi )$, that is, $q_ N(\theta )=\frac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(\theta -\tau )F_ N(\tau )\, \mathrm d\tau $. For $0<\delta '\le \pi $ let $\omega (\delta ')$ be the largest oscillation of $g_ m$ over arcs of length at most $\delta '$, which tends to zero with $\delta '$ by uniform continuity. Splitting the integral at $|\tau |=\delta '$, we obtain \[  |q_ N(\theta )-g_ m(\theta )|\le \frac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }|g_ m(\theta -\tau )-g_ m(\theta )|F_ N(\tau )\, \mathrm d\tau \le \omega (\delta ')+\frac{2\max |g_ m|}{N\sin ^2(\delta '/2)},  \] so $q_ N\to g_ m$ uniformly as $N\to \infty $. Inserting the second expression for $F_ N$ and substituting $\sigma =\theta -\tau $, we see that $q_ N(\theta )=\sum _{|k|<N}c_ k\mathrm e^{\mathrm ik\theta }$ with $c_ k=(1-|k|/N)\frac1{2\pi }\int _{-\pi }^{\pi }g_ m(\sigma )\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\sigma }\, \mathrm d\sigma $. Since $g_ m$ is real, $c_{-k}=\bar c_ k$, so $q_ N(\theta )=\operatorname{Re}P(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta })$ for the polynomial $P(t)=c_0+2\sum _{0<k<N}c_ kt^ k$, and $\operatorname{Re}P(0)=c_0$ is the mean of $g_ m$. Choose $N$ with $|q_ N-g_ m|<\delta $. Then $\operatorname{Re}(P(t)+\delta )\ge g_ m\ge g$ on the circle, and the hypothesis gives \[  v(z_0)\le c_0+\delta =\frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }g_ m\, \mathrm d\theta +\delta .  \] Letting $\delta \to 0$ and then $m\to \infty $, we obtain the asserted inequality. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.3.3 (Richberg)
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
text:
Lemma 6.3.3 (Richberg) . 52930869627B Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $u$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $, and let $a>0$ be such that $u-a|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic. Then for every continuous function $\varepsilon \colon \Omega 	o (0,\infty )$ there is a smooth function $v$ on $\Omega $ with \[  u\le v\le u+\varepsilon ,\qquad v-	frac a2|z|^2\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega ).  \] Proof. Step 1: local approximations. Let $(K_ m)_{m\ge 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 2.2 ), so that $K_ m\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}$ and $ igcup _ m\operatorname{Int}K_ m=\Omega $, and put $K_0=K_{-1}=\varnothing $. For each $m\ge 1$, the compact set $K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(c,r/3)$ with $c\in K_ m\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{m-1}$ and $B(c,r)\Subset \operatorname{Int}K_{m+1}\setminus K_{m-2}$. Collecting these balls for all $m$, we obtain a sequence of balls $B_ i=B(c_ i,r_ i)\Subset \Omega $ whose inner balls $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$ cover $\Omega $. The family $(B_ i)$ is locally finite: a compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, and a ball chosen at a stage $m'\ge m+2$ lies in the complement of $K_{m'-2}\supset K_ m$, so the compact set meets only the finitely many balls chosen at the stages $m'\le m+1$. The function $u=(u-a|z|^2)+a|z|^2$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 . Let $ho _ h$, $h>0$, be the radial mollifiers of section 2.5 . By proposition 5.9.2 (2), we have $u*ho _ h\ge u$, and $(u-a|z|^2)*ho _ h=u*ho _ h-a|z|^2*ho _ h$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, hence has positive semidefinite complex Hessian by proposition 5.9.2 (1); by lemma 2.5.1 , $u*ho _ h	o u$ locally uniformly as $h	o 0$. Since $ho _ h$ is radial, $\int yho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)=0$, and expanding $|z-y|^2=|z|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle z,yangle +|y|^2$ gives $|z|^2*ho _ h=|z|^2+\int |y|^2ho _ h(y)\, \mathrm dV(y)$, whose complex Hessian matrix is $I$. Hence the complex Hessian matrix of $u*ho _ h$ is at least $aI$. For each $i$ choose $\delta _ i$ with $0<\delta _ i<a/2$ and $\delta _ ir_ i^2<\min _{\overline B_ i}\varepsilon $, put $\eta _ i=\delta _ ir_ i^2/6$, and choose $h_ i>0$ so small that $u*ho _{h_ i}$ is defined near $\overline B_ i$ and satisfies $0\le u*ho _{h_ i}-u<\eta _ i$ there. Define \[  u_ i=u*ho _{h_ i}+\delta _ i igl ((2r_ i/3)^2-|z-c_ i|^2 igr ) \quad 	ext{on }B_ i.  \] The quadratic term is at least $\delta _ ir_ i^2/3=2\eta _ i$ on the inner ball $B(c_ i,r_ i/3)$, is less than $-2\eta _ i$ where $|z-c_ i|>\sqrt7\, r_ i/3$, and is at most $4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9$ everywhere. Therefore \[   egin{aligned} & u_ i>u+\eta _ i& & 	ext{on }B(c_ i,r_ i/3),\ & u_ i<u-\eta _ i& & 	ext{where }\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i,\ & u_ i+\eta _ i<u+\varepsilon & & 	ext{on }B_ i, \end{aligned}  \] the last because $2\eta _ i+4\delta _ ir_ i^2/9=7\delta _ ir_ i^2/9<\varepsilon $ on $B_ i$. The complex Hessian matrix of $u_ i$ is at least $(a-\delta _ i)I\ge (a/2)I$. Step 2: a regularized maximum. Fix an even smooth function $	heta \ge 0$ on $\mathbb R$ with support in $(-1,1)$ and integral one, for instance the mollifier $ho _{1/2}$ of section 2.5 in dimension $d=1$. For an integer $p\ge 1$, positive numbers $\eta _1,\ldots ,\eta _ p$ and $t=(t_1,\ldots ,t_ p)\in \mathbb R^ p$, define \[  M_\eta (t)=\int _{\mathbb R^ p}\max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i x_ i) \prod _ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx.  \] The substitution $y_ i=\eta _ ix_ i$ and the evenness of $	heta $ show that $M_\eta $ is the convolution of the continuous function $t\mapsto \max _ it_ i$ with the smooth compactly supported function $y\mapsto \prod _ i\eta _ i^{-1}	heta (y_ i/\eta _ i)$, so $M_\eta $ is smooth by differentiation under the integral sign (section 2.5 ). It has the following properties. $M_\eta $ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable, since for fixed $x$ the function $t\mapsto \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i)$ is. $\max _ it_ i\le M_\eta (t)\le \max _ i(t_ i+\eta _ i)$. The upper bound holds because $|x_ i|<1$ on the support of the integrand. For the lower bound, integrate $\max _ j(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)\ge t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i$ and use $\int x_ i	heta (x_ i)\, \mathrm dx_ i=0$. $M_\eta (t_1+c,\ldots ,t_ p+c)=M_\eta (t)+c$ for $c\in \mathbb R$. Differentiating in $c$, together with the first property, gives $\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i\ge 0$ and $\sum _ i\partial M_\eta /\partial t_ i=1$. If $t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)$ for some $i$, then deleting the variable $t_ i$ and the parameter $\eta _ i$ does not change the value of $M_\eta $. Indeed, for $|x_ j|<1$ we have $t_ i+\eta _ ix_ i<t_ i+\eta _ i\le \max _{j
e i}(t_ j-\eta _ j)<\max _{j
e i}(t_ j+\eta _ jx_ j)$, so the $i$-th term never realizes the maximum, and integrating out $x_ i$ removes it. For smooth real functions $w_1,\ldots ,w_ p$, the chain rule gives \[  \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}M_\eta (w)=\sum _ i rac{\partial M_\eta }{\partial t_ i}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}w_ i+\sum _{i,l} rac{\partial ^2M_\eta }{\partial t_ i\partial t_ l}(w)\, \partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}w_ l}.  \] The real Hessian matrix $G=(\partial ^2M_\eta /\partial t_ i\partial t_ l)$ is positive semidefinite, because the second derivative of the convex function $s\mapsto M_\eta (t+s	au )$ is nonnegative for every $	au \in \mathbb R^ p$. Hence the matrix given by the second sum is positive semidefinite: for $b\in \mathbb C^ n$ its quadratic form equals $\sum _{i,l}G_{il}\zeta _ i ar\zeta _ l$ with $\zeta _ i=\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}w_ i\, b_ j$, and writing $\zeta =\xi +\mathrm i\xi '$ with $\xi ,\xi '\in \mathbb R^ p$, this is $\xi ^{\mathsf T}G\xi +\xi '^{\mathsf T}G\xi '\ge 0$ by the symmetry of $G$. Therefore, by the third property, if each $w_ i$ has complex Hessian matrix at least $(a/2)I$, so does $M_\eta (w_1,\ldots ,w_ p)$. Step 3: gluing. For $z\in \Omega $ let $I(z)=\{ i:z\in B_ i\} $, a finite nonempty set, and define $v(z)=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i(z))_{i\in I(z)} igr )$ with the parameters $(\eta _ i)_{i\in I(z)}$. We show that $v$ is smooth near a fixed point $z_0$. Let $I_0=\{ i:z_0\in B_ i\} $ and $I_1=\{ i:z_0\in \partial B_ i\} $, finite sets by local finiteness, and choose $j$ with $z_0\in B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$. There is a neighborhood $W$ of $z_0$ that is contained in $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$ and in $B_ i$ for $i\in I_0$, that meets $\overline B_ i$ only for $i\in I_0\cup I_1$, and whose intersection with $B_ i$, for $i\in I_1$, lies in the shell $\sqrt7\, r_ i/3<|z-c_ i|<r_ i$. For $z\in W$ we have $I_0\subset I(z)\subset I_0\cup I_1$, $j\in I_0$, and every $i\in I(z)\cap I_1$ satisfies \[  u_ i(z)+\eta _ i<u(z)<u_ j(z)-\eta _ j.  \] By the fourth property of $M_\eta $, applied to these indices one at a time, $v=M_\eta  igl ((u_ i)_{i\in I_0} igr )$ on $W$, which is smooth. Thus $v$ is smooth on $\Omega $, and by Step 2 its complex Hessian matrix is at least $(a/2)I$; hence $v-	frac a2|z|^2$ is smooth with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, and so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1). Finally, every $z$ lies in some inner ball $B(c_ j,r_ j/3)$, and the second property of $M_\eta $ gives $v(z)\ge u_ j(z)>u(z)$ and $v(z)\le \max _{i\in I(z)}(u_ i(z)+\eta _ i)<u(z)+\varepsilon (z)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.3.4
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
text:
Theorem 6.3.4 . EA195CC9592D Let $n\ge 1$ and let $\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set. If $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, then $-\log \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ is a continuous plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Conversely, if this function is plurisubharmonic, then $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex. Every pseudoconvex open set in $\mathbb C^ n$ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. Proof. Steps 1 and 2 deduce the plurisubharmonicity of $-\log \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$ from a submean inequality for the distance to the boundary in a fixed direction; Step 3 uses this function to construct a continuous exhaustion function, which lemma 6.3.3 smooths. Step 1: distances in a fixed direction. Let $\Omega $ be pseudoconvex, with a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $ho $. For $z\in \Omega $ and $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$ put \[  \delta (z,\xi )=\sup \{ r>0:z+\xi \Delta _ r\subset \Omega \} \in (0,\infty ],  \] so that $\delta (z,0)=\infty $. The function $\delta $ is lower semicontinuous on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$: if $r<\delta (z,\xi )$, then the compact disc $z+\xi \overline\Delta _ r$ lies in $\Omega $, hence so does $z'+\xi '\overline\Delta _ r$ for all $(z',\xi ')$ close to $(z,\xi )$, and $\delta (z',\xi ')\ge r$ for these points. Thus $V=-\log \delta $ is an upper semicontinuous function on $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 6.3.2 for $V$ on the open set $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n\subset \mathbb C^{2n}$. Let $(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$, $|t|\le 1$, be a closed disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$, and let $P$ be a polynomial with $V(z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\le \operatorname{Re}P(t)$ for $|t|=1$, that is, $\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)\ge |\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|$. Consider the holomorphic map \[  h(t,w)=z_0+t a+w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}(\xi _0+t b),\qquad (t,w)\in \mathbb C^2.  \] We have $h(t,0)=z_0+ta\in \Omega $ for $|t|\le 1$; and $h(t,w)\in \Omega $ for $|t|=1$ and $|w|<1$, because then $|w\mathrm e^{-P(t)}|<\delta (z_0+ta,\xi _0+tb)$. Let $R$ be the supremum of the numbers $r\ge 0$ with $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ r)\subset \Omega $. Since $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ 0\} )$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $ and $h$ is continuous, $R>0$. We show that $R\ge 1$. Suppose that $R<1$. Then $h(\partial \Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; let $c$ be the maximum of $ho $ on it. For $|w|<R$ we have $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \{ w\} )\subset \Omega $, because every radius smaller than an admissible one is admissible; since this set is compact and $h$ is continuous, there is $r'>1$ such that $t\mapsto h(t,w)$ maps the disc $\Delta _{r'}$ into $\Omega $, and hence into one connected component of $\Omega $. The function $t\mapsto ho (h(t,w))$ is finite, hence subharmonic on $\Delta _{r'}$ by proposition 5.9.3 , and it is at most $c$ on $\partial \Delta $. By upper semicontinuity, $\varlimsup _{t	o \zeta }(ho (h(t,w))-c)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Delta $, and the maximum principle of proposition 3.4.7 on the disc $\Delta $ gives $ho (h(t,w))\le c$ for $|t|<1$, hence for $|t|\le 1$. Thus $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \Delta _ R)$ lies in the compact set $\{ ho \le c\} $, and so does its closure $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _ R)$. This compact subset of $\Omega $ has positive distance from $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, and the uniform continuity of $h$ on compact sets gives $h(\overline\Delta 	imes \overline\Delta _{R'})\subset \Omega $ for some $R'>R$, contradicting the definition of $R$. Hence $R\ge 1$. In particular $h(0,w)=z_0+w\mathrm e^{-P(0)}\xi _0\in \Omega $ for $|w|<1$, which means that $\delta (z_0,\xi _0)\ge \mathrm e^{-\operatorname{Re}P(0)}$, that is, $V(z_0,\xi _0)\le \operatorname{Re}P(0)$. By lemma 6.3.2 , $V$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed complex disc in $\Omega 	imes \mathbb C^ n$. Step 2: the boundary distance. Now let $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ and put $d(z)=\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. For a unit vector $\xi $ we have $\delta (z,\xi )\ge d(z)$, because $z+\xi \Delta _{d(z)}$ lies in the ball $B(z,d(z))\subset \Omega $. Equality holds if $\xi $ points from $z$ to a nearest point of the closed set $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, since that point, $z+d(z)\xi $, lies in $z+\xi \Delta _ r$ for every $r>d(z)$. Hence \[  -\log d(z)=\max _{|\xi |=1}V(z,\xi ).  \] For fixed $\xi $, the function $z\mapsto V(z,\xi )$ satisfies the circle submean inequality on every closed disc $\{ z_0+ta:|t|\le 1\} \subset \Omega $, by Step 1 with $b=0$, and it is bounded above by $-\log d$. Its restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is therefore subharmonic (definition 3.4.2 ): at a point $z_0+t_0a$ of such a section, the circle means over $\{ z_0+(t_0+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })a\} $ dominate the value for all small $r>0$. e \mathbb C^ n$ be an open set on which $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, and put \[  u(z)=|z|^2+\max \{ -\log d(z),0\} .  \] Then $u$ is continuous, $u-|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , and $u$ is an exhaustion function of $\Omega $: the set $\{ u\le c\} $ is contained in the ball $\{ |z|^2\le c\} $ and in $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, so it is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ contained in $\Omega $, hence compact. Moreover, since $s\ge u$, the sublevel set $\{ s\le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ u\le c\} $. Thus $s$ is a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function. If $\Omega 
e \mathbb C^ n$ is pseudoconvex, Step 2 shows that $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic, so this construction applies; for $\Omega =\mathbb C^ n$ we take $s=|z|^2$. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.3.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.3 Pseudoconvexity and boundary distance
text: Corollary 6.3.5 . FFB7E3647C0B Products of pseudoconvex open sets are pseudoconvex. If $s$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, then each sublevel set $\{ s<c\} $, $c\in \mathbb R$, is pseudoconvex and relatively compact in $\Omega $. In particular, every pseudoconvex open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is the union of an increasing sequence of pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $. Proof. Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $\Omega '\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be pseudoconvex, with nonnegative continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion functions $\rho $ and $\rho '$. The function $(z,w)\mapsto \rho (z)+\rho '(w)$ is continuous and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega \times \Omega '$, by proposition 5.9.3 applied to the two projections and by proposition 5.9.5 . Its sublevel set $\{ \le c\} $ is a closed subset of the compact set $\{ \rho \le c\} \times \{ \rho '\le c\} $, so $\Omega \times \Omega '$ is pseudoconvex. Next let $s$ be as in the statement and $c\in \mathbb R$. The function $x\mapsto 1/(c-x)$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,c)$, so the complex Hessian matrix of $1/(c-s)$ on the open set $\{ s<c\} $, namely $(c-s)^{-2}(s_{j\bar k})+2(c-s)^{-3}\bigl (\partial _{z_ j}s\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}s}\bigr )$ by the chain rule, is positive semidefinite. Hence $|z|^2+1/(c-s)$ is a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $\{ s<c\} $, by proposition 5.9.2 (1). For $C\le 0$ its sublevel set $\{ \le C\} $ is empty. For $C>0$ this sublevel set is closed in $\{ s<c\} $ and contained in the set $\{ s\le c-1/C\} $, which is a compact subset of $\{ s<c\} $; hence it is compact, and $\{ s<c\} $ is pseudoconvex. Moreover $\{ s<c\} $ is contained in the compact set $\{ s\le c\} $, so it is relatively compact in $\Omega $. Finally, if $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex, theorem 6.3.4 provides a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $s$, and the sets $\Omega _ j=\{ s<j\} $, $j\ge 1$, are pseudoconvex, relatively compact in $\Omega $, increasing, and have union $\Omega $. (Some of them may be empty or disconnected; definition 6.3.1 allows arbitrary open sets.) $\square$

text: Corollary 6.3.6 . EC970F3402EB Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ m\times \mathbb C^ k$ be a pseudoconvex domain that is invariant under imaginary translations and whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex, in the notation of section 5.12 . If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We construct a function $\psi $ with the properties required in theorem 5.12.1 ; the corollary then follows from that theorem. If $\Omega =\mathbb C^{m+k}$, let $\psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$. Otherwise let $d=\operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,\mathbb C^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )$ and put \[  \psi (z,w)=|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2+ \max \{ -\log d(z,w),0\} .  \] Imaginary translations are isometries of $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ that preserve $\Omega $ and its complement, so $d$ and $\psi $ are invariant under them. The function $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 : $-\log d$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 6.3.4 , and $|z|^2+|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1), since its complex Hessian matrix is the diagonal matrix with entries $1$ in the $z$-directions and $\frac12$ in the $w$-directions, by the identity $(\operatorname{Re}w_ l)^2=\tfrac 12|w_ l|^2+\tfrac 12\operatorname{Re}(w_ l^2)$ for $1\le l\le k$. Finally, let $c\in \mathbb R$. Since $\psi $ is continuous, the set $\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $ is closed in $\Omega _{\mathbb R}$. It is contained in $\{ |z|^2+|t|^2\le c\} $ and, if $\Omega \ne \mathbb C^{m+k}$, in the set $\{ d\ge \mathrm e^{-c}\} $, which is closed in $\mathbb C^{m+k}$ and contained in $\Omega $; it is therefore a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb C^ m\times \mathbb R^ k$, hence compact. $\square$

Let $\varphi \colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function that is bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. (1) The real and imaginary parts of $h$, given by $\operatorname{Re}\langle h,\chi angle $ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle h,\chi angle $ for real test functions $\chi $, are real distributions. Since derivatives of distributions commute, ( 5.2.9 ) shows that the Laplacian of $h$ is $4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}h=0$. As the Laplacian has real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of $h$ are harmonic distributions. By Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) they are given by smooth functions, and hence $h$ is given by a smooth function $g$. By integration by parts, the classical derivatives $\partial _{ ar z_ j}g$ represent the distributions $\partial _{ ar z_ j}h=0$, so they vanish almost everywhere by proposition 2.5.3 (4), and hence everywhere, being continuous functions. Proposition 6.4.4 . 866FA0174B79 Let $\varphi $ be a smooth real function on $\Omega $, and let $\delta _ j$ be the differential operator $\delta _ jg=-\partial _{z_ j}g+(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )g$, $1\le j\le n$. Then every smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-form $f=\sum _ jf_ j\, \mathrm d ar z_ j$ on $\Omega $ satisfies \[   egin{split} & \int \Bigl |\sum _ j\delta _ j f_ j\Bigr |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV +\int | ar\partial f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\ & \qquad =\int \sum _{j,k}\varphi _{j ar k}f_ j ar f_ k\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV +\int \sum _{j,k}|\partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV. \end{split}  \] Consequently, if $\psi $ is a smooth real function and $T$ and $S$ are the operators defined by the weights $\varphi _ k=\varphi +(k-3)\psi $ of lemma 6.4.2 , then for every $t>0$ 038AC5695B6F 6.4.5  egin{equation}  \int \sum _{j,k}\varphi _{j ar k}f_ j ar f_ k\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV \le (1+t^{-1})\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2 +(1+t)\int |f|^2| ar\partial \psi |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Proof. For smooth compactly supported functions $g$ and $w$, integration by parts (Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus on lines) gives \[  \langle \partial _{ ar z_ j}g,wangle _\varphi =-\int g\, \partial _{ ar z_ j} igl ( ar w\mathrm e^{-\varphi } igr )\, \mathrm dV=\int g\, \overline{ igl (-\partial _{z_ j}w+(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )w igr )}\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV=\langle g,\delta _ jwangle _\varphi ,  \] because $\varphi $ is real; thus $\delta _ j$ is the formal adjoint of $\partial _{ ar z_ j}$ for the inner product $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _\varphi $, and taking complex conjugates we also have $\langle \delta _ jw,gangle _\varphi =\langle w,\partial _{ ar z_ j}gangle _\varphi $. Since $\partial _{ ar z_ k} igl ((\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )g igr )=\varphi _{j ar k}g+(\partial _{z_ j}\varphi )\partial _{ ar z_ k}g$ and the derivatives $\partial _{z_ j}$ and $\partial _{ ar z_ k}$ commute, we obtain the commutation relation \[  \partial _{ ar z_ k}(\delta _ jg)-\delta _ j(\partial _{ ar z_ k}g)=\varphi _{j ar k}\, g.  \] By the adjoint relation, then the commutation relation, and then the conjugate adjoint relation, \[   egin{split}  \Bigl \| \sum _ j\delta _ jf_ j\Bigr \| _\varphi ^2& =\sum _{j,k}\langle \delta _ jf_ j,\delta _ kf_ kangle _\varphi =\sum _{j,k}\langle \partial _{ ar z_ k}\delta _ jf_ j,f_ kangle _\varphi \ & =\sum _{j,k}\langle \varphi _{j ar k}f_ j,f_ kangle _\varphi +\sum _{j,k}\langle \delta _ j\partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j,f_ kangle _\varphi \ & =\int \sum _{j,k}\varphi _{j ar k}f_ j ar f_ k\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV+\sum _{j,k}\langle \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j,\partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ kangle _\varphi . \end{split}  \] On the other hand, $ ar\partial f=\sum _{j<k}(\partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ k-\partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j)\, \mathrm d ar z_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ k$, and expanding the squares gives \[  \|  ar\partial f\| _\varphi ^2=\sum _{j
e k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2-\sum _{j
e k}\langle \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j,\partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ kangle _\varphi .  \] When we add the two identities, the terms with $j
e k$ in the last sums cancel, and the remaining terms $\| \partial _{ ar z_ j}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2$ combine with $\sum _{j
e k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2$ to give $\sum _{j,k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}f_ j\| _\varphi ^2$. This proves the identity. For the estimate, we have $\varphi _1-\varphi _2=-\psi $ and $\partial _{z_ j}\varphi _2=\partial _{z_ j}\varphi -\partial _{z_ j}\psi $, so ( 6.4.1 ) reads \[  \sum _ j\delta _ jf_ j=\mathrm e^\psi T^*f+\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\psi )f_ j.  \] By the elementary inequality $|x+y|^2\le (1+t^{-1})|x|^2+(1+t)|y|^2$ for $x,y\in \mathbb C$, \[  \Bigl \| \sum _ j\delta _ jf_ j\Bigr \| _\varphi ^2\le (1+t^{-1})\int |T^*f|^2\mathrm e^{2\psi -\varphi }\, \mathrm dV+(1+t)\int \Bigl |\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\psi )f_ j\Bigr |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV.  \] The first integral is $\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2$, because $\varphi _1=\varphi -2\psi $, and $|\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\psi )f_ j|^2\le | ar\partial \psi |^2|f|^2$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, since $|\partial _{z_ j}\psi |=|\partial _{ ar z_ j}\psi |$ for real $\psi $. Moreover $\|  ar\partial f\| _\varphi ^2=\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2$, because $\varphi _3=\varphi $. Inserting these bounds into the identity and dropping its last, nonnegative, term, we obtain ( 6.4.5 ). $\square$

Theorem 6.4.7 (Hörmander) . F85650C9CE6A Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, and let $\varphi $ be a smooth plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that \[  M=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{H_\varphi ^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty  \] and $ ar\partial \alpha =0$. Then there is $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ with $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ and $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le M$. Proof. The idea is to modify the weight far out in $\Omega $ so that lemma 6.4.2 applies and the error term in ( 6.4.5 ) is absorbed by additional convexity, and then to let the modification recede to the boundary. Step 1: auxiliary functions. The matrix $H_\varphi $ is positive semidefinite because $\varphi $ is plurisubharmonic, and by the discussion preceding the theorem, applied with $A=H_\varphi $, the finiteness of $M$ implies that $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$. By theorem 6.3.4 , $\Omega $ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $s$. Fix an integer $t\ge 1$. Let $\kappa _0$ be the function fixed at the beginning of this section, put $c_\kappa =\sup |\kappa _0'|$, and for integers $
u \ge 1$ put $\chi _
u =\kappa _0(s-t-1-
u )$. Then $0\le \chi _
u \le 1$, and $\chi _
u \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, because $\{ s\le t+2+
u \} $ is compact; $\chi _
u =1$ on $\{ s\le t+1+
u \} $, hence on a neighborhood of any given compact set for large $
u $; and $ ar\partial \chi _
u =\kappa _0'(s-t-1-
u )\,  ar\partial s$ vanishes on $\{ s<t+2\} $ and satisfies $| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\le c_\kappa ^2| ar\partial s|^2$. We put \[  \psi = igl (1-\kappa _0(s-t-1) igr )\log  igl (1+c_\kappa ^2| ar\partial s|^2 igr ).  \] Then $\psi $ is smooth and nonnegative; $\psi $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ vanish on $\{ s\le t+1\} $, since $1-\kappa _0(x-t-1)$ and its derivative vanish for $x\le t+1$; and $| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2\le \mathrm e^\psi $ for every $
u $, because $\mathrm e^\psi =1+c_\kappa ^2| ar\partial s|^2$ on $\{ s\ge t+2\} $ and $ ar\partial \chi _
u =0$ on $\{ s<t+2\} $. Next we choose a smooth convex nondecreasing function $\gamma \colon \mathbb R	o [0,\infty )$ with $\gamma =0$ on $(-\infty ,t]$ such that D557EE261608 6.4.8  egin{equation}  \gamma (s)\ge 2\psi ,\qquad H_{\gamma (s)}\ge (1+t)| ar\partial \psi |^2 I, \qquad \int _\Omega |\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi -\gamma (s)+\psi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty . \end{equation} For integers $l\ge 1$ the sets $K_ l=\{ t+l\le s\le t+l+1\} $ are compact. The smallest eigenvalue of $H_ s$ is a positive continuous function on $\Omega $ (see the discussion following proposition 5.9.2 ), so its minimum $\lambda _ l$ over $K_ l$ is positive (if $K_ l=\varnothing $, put $\lambda _ l=1$ and $m_ l=P_ l=I_ l=0$), and the numbers $m_ l=(1+t)\max _{K_ l}| ar\partial \psi |^2$, $P_ l=2\max _{K_ l}\psi $ and $I_ l=\int _{K_ l}|\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi +\psi }\, \mathrm dV$ are finite, since $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$. Choose a smooth nondecreasing function $g\colon \mathbb R	o [0,\infty )$ that vanishes on $(-\infty ,t]$ and satisfies, for every $l\ge 1$, \[  g\ge m_ l/\lambda _ l\  	ext{on }[t+l,t+l+1],\qquad \int _{t+l-1}^{t+l}g(x)\, \mathrm dx\ge \max  igl \{ P_ l,\log ^+(2^ lI_ l) igr \} .  \] For instance, let $\kappa _1(x)=1-\kappa _0(2x)$, a smooth nondecreasing function with $\kappa _1=0$ on $(-\infty ,0]$ and $\kappa _1=1$ on $[1/2,\infty )$, and put $g(x)=\sum _{l\ge 1}c_ l\kappa _1(x-t-l+1)$ with $c_ l=\max \{ m_ l/\lambda _ l,2P_ l,2\log ^+(2^ lI_ l)\} $. The sum is locally finite, since only the terms with $l<x-t+1$ are nonzero at $x$, and all its terms vanish for $x\le t$. The $l$-th term equals $c_ l$ on $[t+l-1/2,\infty )$, so $g\ge c_ l$ on $[t+l,t+l+1]$ and $\int _{t+l-1}^{t+l}g(x)\, \mathrm dx\ge c_ l/2$. Put $\gamma (x)=\int _{-\infty }^ xg(y)\, \mathrm dy$. Then $\gamma $ is smooth, nondecreasing and convex, because $\gamma '=g$ is nondecreasing, and $\gamma =0$ on $(-\infty ,t]$. Since $\Omega $ is the union of $\{ s\le t+1\} $ and the sets $K_ l$, we may check the first two conditions in ( 6.4.8 ) on each of these sets. On $\{ s\le t+1\} $ they hold because $\psi $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ vanish there while $\gamma \ge 0$ and $H_{\gamma (s)}\ge 0$. On $K_ l$ we have $\gamma (s)\ge \gamma (t+l)\ge P_ l\ge 2\psi $, and the chain rule \[  H_{\gamma (s)}=\gamma '(s)H_ s+\gamma ''(s) igl (\partial _{z_ j}s\, \overline{\partial _{z_ k}s} igr )_{j,k}\ge \gamma '(s)H_ s  \] gives $H_{\gamma (s)}\ge (m_ l/\lambda _ l)\lambda _ lI\ge (1+t)| ar\partial \psi |^2I$. Finally, the integral in ( 6.4.8 ) over the compact set $\{ s\le t+1\} $ is finite, and its integral over $K_ l$ is at most $\mathrm e^{-\gamma (t+l)}I_ l\le 2^{-l}$, because $\gamma (s)\ge \gamma (t+l)\ge \log ^+(2^ lI_ l)$ there; summing over $l$, we obtain the third condition. Step 2: the estimate. Put $\varphi _0=\varphi +\gamma (s)$ and $\varphi _ k=\varphi _0+(k-3)\psi $ for $k=1,2,3$, and let $T$ and $S$ be the corresponding operators. By the last condition in ( 6.4.8 ), $\alpha \in \mathcal H_1=L^2_{(0,1)}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2})$, and $\alpha \in \ker S$. Let $f$ be a smooth compactly supported $(0,1)$-form. We apply ( 6.4.5 ) with $\varphi _0$ in place of $\varphi $ and with the integer $t$ fixed in Step 1. Since $H_{\varphi _0}=H_\varphi +H_{\gamma (s)}$, the second condition in ( 6.4.8 ) absorbs the last term of ( 6.4.5 ), and we obtain \[  \int H_\varphi [f]\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi _0}\, \mathrm dV \le (1+t^{-1})\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2.  \] Moreover $\varphi -2\varphi _2=-\varphi _0-\gamma (s)+2\psi \le -\varphi _0$ by the first condition in ( 6.4.8 ). Since $M<\infty $, the dual energy of $\alpha $ is finite almost everywhere, and the inequality $|\sum _ j\alpha _ j ar f_ j|^2\le |\alpha |_{H_\varphi ^{-1}}^2H_\varphi [f]$ together with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \[   egin{split}  |\langle \alpha ,fangle _{\mathcal H_1}|^2 & \le \int |\alpha |_{H_\varphi ^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\cdot \int H_\varphi [f]\, \mathrm e^{\varphi -2\varphi _2}\, \mathrm dV \le M\int H_\varphi [f]\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi _0}\, \mathrm dV\ & \le M(1+t^{-1}) igl (\| T^*f\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2+\| Sf\| _{\mathcal H_2}^2 igr ). \end{split}  \] Both sides are continuous for the graph norm of lemma 6.4.2 , whose hypotheses hold by Step 1; hence the inequality extends to all $f\in \operatorname{Dom}T^*\cap \operatorname{Dom}S$. By theorem 6.2.4 there is $u_ t\in \mathcal H_0$ with $ ar\partial u_ t=\alpha $ and $\| u_ t\| _{\mathcal H_0}^2\le M(1+t^{-1})$. On $\{ s<t\} $ both $\gamma (s)$ and $\psi $ vanish, so $\varphi _1=\varphi $ there and \[  \int _{\{ s<t\} }|u_ t|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le M(1+t^{-1}).  \] Step 3: passage to the limit. For each integer $l\ge 1$ the functions $u_ t$ with $t\ge l$ have squared norms at most $2M$ in $L^2(\{ s<l\} ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. By proposition 6.2.2 and a diagonal argument, there is a sequence $t_ i	o \infty $ such that $u_{t_ i}$ converges weakly in $L^2(\{ s<l\} ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ for every $l$. The limits on different sublevel sets agree on their intersections, because restriction from $\{ s<l+1\} $ to $\{ s<l\} $ is a bounded linear map, and they define a function $u$ on $\Omega $. Weak convergence in these spaces implies convergence in the sense of distributions: a test function $\chi $ has support in some set $\{ s<l\} $, and $\int u_{t_ i}\chi \, \mathrm dV=\langle u_{t_ i}, ar\chi \mathrm e^\varphi angle _\varphi $ with $ ar\chi \mathrm e^\varphi \in L^2(\{ s<l\} ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. Hence $ ar\partial u=\alpha $. By the lower semicontinuity of the norm in proposition 6.2.2 , $\int _{\{ s<l\} }|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ iM(1+t_ i^{-1})=M$ for every $l$, and the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\le M$. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.4.9

text: Theorem 6.4.9 . 88735CB0C076 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $q$ be a smooth real function on $\Omega $ whose complex Hessian matrix $A=H_ q$ is positive semidefinite. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that \[  M=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV<\infty  \] and $\bar\partial \alpha =0$. Then the equation $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with $\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$. In particular, if $A\ge \lambda I$ for a positive continuous function $\lambda $ on $\Omega $, then $M$ may be replaced by $\int _\Omega \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV$. Proof. We regularize $p$ on relatively compact pseudoconvex subsets of $\Omega $, apply theorem 6.4.7 there, and pass to a weak limit. Since the weight $p+q$ is bounded above on compact sets, the discussion preceding theorem 6.4.7 shows that $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$, so that $\bar\partial \alpha $ is defined. By corollary 6.3.5 there are pseudoconvex open sets $\Omega _1\subset \Omega _2\subset \cdots $ with $\Omega _ j\Subset \Omega $ and $\bigcup _ j\Omega _ j=\Omega $. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be the radial mollifier of section 2.5 , and choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ j<\operatorname {dist}(\overline\Omega _ j,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )$. By proposition 5.9.2 (2), $p_ j=p*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$ is defined, smooth and plurisubharmonic on the open neighborhood $\{ z\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon _ j\} $ of $\overline\Omega _ j$, so its complex Hessian is positive semidefinite there, and $p_ j\downarrow p$ pointwise as $j\to \infty $. Put $\varphi _ j=p_ j+q$. Then $\varphi _ j$ is smooth with complex Hessian matrix $H_{\varphi _ j}\ge A\ge 0$ near $\overline\Omega _ j$, so it is plurisubharmonic there by proposition 5.9.2 (1), and $\varphi _ j\ge p+q$. Since the dual energy decreases when the matrix increases, \[  \int _{\Omega _ j}|\alpha |_{H_{\varphi _ j}^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV \le \int _{\Omega _ j}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] By theorem 6.4.7 there is $u_ j$ on $\Omega _ j$ with $\bar\partial u_ j=\alpha $ and $\int _{\Omega _ j}|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M$. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact. Then $K\subset \Omega _ k$ for some $k$, and for $j\ge k$ we have $\varphi _ j\le \varphi _ k$ on $K$, because $p_ j$ decreases. Hence $\int _ K|u_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{\max _ K\varphi _ k}M$ for $j\ge k$, so the sequence $(u_ j)$ is eventually bounded in $L^2(K)$ for every compact set $K$. Let $(K_ m)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ (section 2.2 ). By proposition 6.2.2 and a diagonal argument, we find a subsequence that converges weakly in $L^2(K_ m)$ for every $m$. The weak limits are compatible, because restriction from $K_{m+1}$ to $K_ m$ is a bounded linear map, and they define a function $u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$; since every compact subset of $\Omega $ lies in some $K_ m$, the subsequence converges weakly to $u$ in $L^2(K)$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Then $u_ j\to u$ in the sense of distributions, and $\bar\partial u=\alpha $. Now let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset \Omega _ k$. On $L^2(K)$ the norm with weight $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ is equivalent to the unweighted norm, so the subsequence also converges weakly for it, and the lower semicontinuity in proposition 6.2.2 gives \[  \int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV\le M.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ as $k\to \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\le M$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets proves the estimate. The last assertion follows from the pointwise inequality $|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\le \lambda ^{-1}|\alpha |^2$. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.4.10

text: Lemma 6.4.10 . 961105705CF9 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$. Every distribution $h$ on $\Omega $ with $\bar\partial h=0$ is a holomorphic function: there is $g\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $\langle h,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega g\chi \, \mathrm dV$ for every test function $\chi $. Let $\varphi \colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a measurable function that is bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Then the elements of $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ represented by holomorphic functions form a closed subspace $\mathcal K$. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form with distribution coefficients such that the equation $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. Then among these solutions there is exactly one of smallest norm, and a solution is of smallest norm if and only if it is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. Proof. (1) The real and imaginary parts of $h$, given by $\operatorname{Re}\langle h,\chi \rangle $ and $\operatorname{Im}\langle h,\chi \rangle $ for real test functions $\chi $, are real distributions. Since derivatives of distributions commute, ( 5.2.9 ) shows that the Laplacian of $h$ is $4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j}h=0$. As the Laplacian has real coefficients, the real and imaginary parts of $h$ are harmonic distributions. By Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) they are given by smooth functions, and hence $h$ is given by a smooth function $g$. By integration by parts, the classical derivatives $\partial _{\bar z_ j}g$ represent the distributions $\partial _{\bar z_ j}h=0$, so they vanish almost everywhere by proposition 2.5.3 (4), and hence everywhere, being continuous functions. Thus $g$ is holomorphic. (2) Let $L\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $m_ L$ be a real upper bound for $\varphi $ on $L$. For $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ we have $\int _ L|u|^2\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{m_ L}\int _ L|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. Hence $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })\subset L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, so that $\bar\partial u$ is defined in the sense of distributions, and convergence in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ implies convergence in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, hence in the sense of distributions. The space $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$ is a Hilbert space, by the completeness argument at the beginning of section 6.2 , applied to the positive measure $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV$. The set $\mathcal K$ is a linear subspace. It is closed: if $g_ j\in \mathcal K$ converge to $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$, then $g_ j\to g$ in the sense of distributions, so $\bar\partial g=\lim _ j\bar\partial g_ j=0$, and by (1) $g$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, that is, $g\in \mathcal K$. Let $u_0$ be a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi })$. By (1), an element $u$ of this space is a solution if and only if $\bar\partial (u-u_0)=0$, that is, $u-u_0\in \mathcal K$. Thus the solutions form the nonempty closed convex set $u_0+\mathcal K$, which by proposition 6.2.1 contains a unique element $u_{\min }$ of smallest norm. If a solution $u$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, then $\| u+k\| ^2=\| u\| ^2+\| k\| ^2\geq \| u\| ^2$ for every $k\in \mathcal K$, so $u$ has smallest norm, that is, $u=u_{\min }$. Conversely, if $P$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal K$ (proposition 6.2.1 ), then $u_{\min }-Pu_{\min }$ is a solution orthogonal to $\mathcal K$, hence equal to $u_{\min }$; so $u_{\min }$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal K$. $\square$

section: 6.5 Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane
text:
We now construct holomorphic functions with a prescribed value at a point, or a prescribed restriction to a hyperplane, and with controlled weighted norms. In both cases, a smooth function with the right values is corrected by a solution of a $ ar\partial $-equation whose weight has a singular term forcing the correction to vanish where the values are prescribed. Proposition 6.5.1 . 66BCDC65B27D Let $r,L>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L$, let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $B(a,2r)\subset \Omega $, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $h$ is holomorphic on $B(a,2r)$ and $\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=h(a),\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C(n,r,L) \int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV,  \] where the constant $C(n,r,L)$ depends only on $n$, $r$ and $L$, and not on $\Omega $, $p$, $h$ or $a$.
