u }$, which is positive semidefinite; so $|G|^2$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1), and hence subharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, $\delta >0$ and $K_\delta =\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \delta \} \subset \Omega $, then the mean value inequality over balls in theorem 3.4.5 , applied to $|F_ j|^2$, gives $|F_ j(z)|^2\le |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{K_\delta }|F_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV$ for $z\in K$ and large $j$, and the right side is bounded independently of $j$ by the preceding estimate applied to $K_\delta $. Next, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $\Omega $. For $z\in K'_0=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le \sqrt n\, r\} $, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 5.2.1 ) with $a=z$ gives $|\partial _{z_ l}F_ j(z)|\le r^{-1}\max _{K'}|F_ j|$ for $1\le l\le n$ and all large $j$ (those with $K'\subset D_ j$). Since $\mathrm dF_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}F_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, it follows that these $F_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence $(F_ j)$ is equicontinuous on $K$ from some index on. By proposition 2.7.4 on a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $\Omega $ to a continuous function $F$. Since $ ar\partial F_ j=0$ and $F_ j	o F$ in the sense of distributions, $ ar\partial F=0$, and $F$ is holomorphic by lemma 6.4.10 (1). Moreover $F(z',0)=\lim _ jF_ j(z',0)=f(z')$ for $z'\in \Omega _0$. Finally, let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $k$ be so large that $K\subset D_ k$. For $j\ge k$ we have $p_ j\le p_ k$ on $K$, so locally uniform convergence gives \[  \int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV=\lim _ j\int _ K|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ k}\, \mathrm dV\le \varliminf _ j\int _{D_ j}|F_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-p_ j}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I.  \] This holds for all large $k$, and $\mathrm e^{-p_ k}$ increases to $\mathrm e^{-p}$ as $k	o \infty $; so the monotone convergence theorem gives $\int _ K|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$, and exhausting $\Omega $ by compact sets gives $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C_0I$. $\square$ Applying the theorem once for each normal direction, we obtain extension from affine subspaces of any codimension, in particular from points. Corollary 6.5.8 . 33DEA3F4EDB8 Let $C$ be the constant of theorem 6.5.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L>0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then for every $a\in \Omega $ with $p(a)>-\infty $ there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=1,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV \le C^ n L^{2n}\mathrm e^{-p(a)}.  \] More generally, let $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an affine complex subspace of codimension $r$, $0\le r\le n$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega \cap V$ with finite slice norm $\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$, computed with Lebesgue measure on $V$. Then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $F|_{\Omega \cap V}=f$ and $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C^ rL^{2r}\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$. Proof. We prove the second assertion; the first is the case $V=\{ a\} $, $r=n$ and $f=1$, whose slice norm with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$ is $\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$. If $r=0$ we take $F=f$, and if $\Omega \cap V=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. Assume now that $r\ge 1$ and $\Omega \cap V
e \varnothing $. Choose $b\in \Omega \cap V$ and unitary affine coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ centered at $b$ with $V=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $, and put $\Omega _ k=\Omega \cap \{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $ for $0\le k\le r$, an open subset of a space isomorphic to $\mathbb C^{n-k}$. Unitary coordinates preserve Lebesgue measure. Each $\Omega _ k$ with $k<n$ is pseudoconvex: the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to the closed subset $\Omega _ k$ of $\Omega $ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.3 , applied to the linear embedding of $\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $, and its sublevel sets are compact. By the discussion following definition 6.3.1 , every connected component of $\Omega _ k$ is pseudoconvex as well. Since $\Omega $ is open and has diameter at most $L$, we have $|z-b|<L$ for $z\in \Omega $ (a point $z\in \Omega $ with $|z-b|=L$ could be moved slightly away from $b$ inside $\Omega $), so the coordinate $w_ k$ takes its values in $\Delta _ L$ on $\Omega _{k-1}$. Put $f_ r=f$, let $1\le k\le r$, and assume that $f_ k\in \mathcal O(\Omega _ k)$ has finite norm $\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}$. Let $W$ be a connected component of $\Omega _{k-1}$; ordering the coordinates as $(w_{k+1},\ldots ,w_ n,w_ k)$, we regard $W$ as an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-k}	imes \Delta _ L$ whose slice by $\{ w_ k=0\} $ is the open subset $W\cap \Omega _ k$ of $\Omega _ k$. By proposition 5.9.3 , the restriction of $p$ to $W$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the second case $\mathrm e^{-p}=\infty $ on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, so the finiteness of the norm of $f_ k$ forces $f_ k=0$ almost everywhere on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, hence everywhere there, since $f_ k$ is continuous, and we put $f_{k-1}=0$ on $W$. In the first case, theorem 6.5.4 , applied to $W$ with normal coordinate $w_ k$, gives a holomorphic function $f_{k-1}$ on $W$ extending the restriction of $f_ k$ to $W\cap \Omega _ k$, with \[  \int _ W|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{W\cap \Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] The components $W$ are open, disjoint and cover $\Omega _{k-1}$, and the sets $W\cap \Omega _ k$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega _ k$. Hence these functions define $f_{k-1}\in \mathcal O(\Omega _{k-1})$ extending $f_ k$, and summing over $W$ gives \[  \int _{\Omega _{k-1}}|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] Proceeding in this way for $k=r,r-1,\ldots ,1$ and multiplying the $r$ estimates, we see that $F=f_0$ has the required properties. $\square$ Corollary 6.5.9 . BFB355F9DDF9 Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a complex submanifold, let $a\in Y$, and let $p$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Let $f$ be a holomorphic germ on $Y$ at $a$ such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p|_ Y}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $Y$. Then there is a holomorphic germ $F$ on $X$ at $a$ with $F|_ Y=f$ such that $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Here integrability refers to smooth positive volume forms on $Y$ and $X$; since any two such forms are locally comparable, the notion does not depend on their choice. Proof. Let $k=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim X$ near $a$. By the definition of a complex submanifold (definition 5.2.3 ), there are holomorphic coordinates $w=(w',w'')\in \mathbb C^ k	imes \mathbb C^{n-k}$ centered at $a$ in which $Y=\{ w''=0\} $; by proposition 5.9.3 , $p$ is plurisubharmonic near $0$ in these coordinates. On a compact neighborhood of $a$, the densities of smooth positive volume forms with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure are bounded above and below by positive constants. Hence we may test integrability with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $Y=\mathbb C^ k	imes \{ 0\} $ and $\mathrm dV_{2n}$ in the coordinates $w$. Choose a ball $B$ around $0$ so small that $p$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, that $f$ is defined on $B\cap Y$, and that $\int _{B\cap Y}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2k}<\infty $. The ball $B$ is a bounded pseudoconvex domain, by corollary 6.3.5 applied to the exhaustion function $|w|^2$ of $\mathbb C^ n$, and $B\cap Y$ is its intersection with the linear subspace $\{ w''=0\} $ of codimension $n-k$. By corollary 6.5.8 there is $F\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $F|_{B\cap Y}=f$ and $\int _ B|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}<\infty $. (If $k=0$, the integral over $Y$ is the weighted value $|f(a)|^2\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$; if $p|_ Y$ is identically $-\infty $ near $a$, then $f=0$ and $F=0$, in accordance with the conventions of theorem 6.5.4 .) $\square$

title: Proposition 6.5.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.5 Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane
text: Proposition 6.5.1 . 66BCDC65B27D Let $r,L>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L$, let $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $B(a,2r)\subset \Omega $, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. If $h$ is holomorphic on $B(a,2r)$ and $\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $, then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=h(a),\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C(n,r,L) \int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV,  \] where the constant $C(n,r,L)$ depends only on $n$, $r$ and $L$, and not on $\Omega $, $p$, $h$ or $a$. Proof. Fix a smooth function $\kappa $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\le \kappa \le 1$, $\kappa =1$ on $(-\infty ,1]$ and $\kappa =0$ on $[3/2,\infty )$, for instance $\kappa (x)=\kappa _0(2x-2)$ with the function $\kappa _0$ fixed at the beginning of section 6.4 , and put $\chi (z)=\kappa (|z-a|/r)$. Then $\chi $ is smooth, because $\kappa $ is constant near $0$; it has compact support in $B(a,2r)$, equals one on $B(a,r)$, and satisfies $|\bar\partial \chi |\le c_0/r$ with $c_0=\sup |\kappa '|/2$, because $|\bar\partial |z-a||=1/2$ for $z\ne a$. Extend $\chi h$ by zero to $\Omega $. Then $\alpha =\bar\partial (\chi h)=h\, \bar\partial \chi $ is a smooth $\bar\partial $-closed form supported in the shell $r\le |z-a|\le 2r$. The function $p+n\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ by proposition 5.10.3 , proposition 5.9.5 . We apply theorem 6.4.9 with this function in place of $p$ and with $q=|z-a|^2$, for which $A=I$. Since $\mathrm e^{-|z-a|^2}\le 1$ and $|z-a|^{-2n}\le r^{-2n}$ on the support of $\alpha $, we obtain a solution of $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ with \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2|z-a|^{-2n}\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}\, \mathrm dV \le c_0^2r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] On $B(a,r)$ we have $\bar\partial u=\alpha =0$, so $u$ is holomorphic there, by lemma 6.4.10 (1). Since $p$ is bounded above on $B(a,r)$, the factor $\mathrm e^{-p-|z-a|^2}$ is bounded below there by a positive constant. If $u(a)$ were nonzero, then $|u|$ would be bounded below by a positive constant near $a$, and the integral on the left would diverge, because $\int _{B(a,\rho )}|z-a|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV$ is a positive multiple of $\int _0^\rho \tau ^{-2n}\tau ^{2n-1}\, \mathrm d\tau =\infty $ by integration in polar coordinates ( 3.1.2 ). Thus $u(a)=0$. The function $F=\chi h-u$ satisfies $\bar\partial F=0$, so it is holomorphic by the same lemma, and $F(a)=h(a)$. Since $|z-a|<L$ on $\Omega $, we have $|z-a|^{2n}\mathrm e^{|z-a|^2}\le L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}$, and therefore \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}\int _{B(a,2r)}|h|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] Finally, $|F|^2\le 2|\chi h|^2+2|u|^2$ and $|\chi h|\le |h|\mathbf1_{B(a,2r)}$ give the assertion with $C(n,r,L)=2+2c_0^2L^{2n}\mathrm e^{L^2}r^{-2n-2}$. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.5.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.5 Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane
text:
Lemma 6.5.2 . 0822DB927561 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a pseudoconvex open set, $n\ge 1$, let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$, and let $\psi $ be a smooth bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Put $A=H_\psi $ and $h=| ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2$, where $ ar\partial \psi $ is identified with the vector $(\partial _{ ar z_ j}\psi )_ j$, and assume that $h<1$ almost everywhere. Let $\alpha $ be a $(0,1)$-form on $\Omega $ with measurable coefficients such that $E=\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $ and $ ar\partial \alpha =0$, let $0\le a<1$, and assume that $h\le a$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $. Then $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution with \[  \int _\Omega (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le  rac{1+\sqrt a}{1-\sqrt a}\, E.  \] Proof. The idea is that, if $u$ is the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, then $u\mathrm e^\psi $ is the minimal solution of a twisted equation in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, to which we apply Hörmander's estimate. Put $m=\sup _\Omega |\psi |<\infty $. Since $\mathrm e^{-m}\le \mathrm e^{\pm \psi }\le \mathrm e^ m$, the spaces $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$ and $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ consist of the same functions, with equivalent norms, and so contain the same holomorphic functions. By the discussion preceding theorem 6.4.7 , applied with the weight $p-\psi $, which is bounded above on compact sets, $\alpha \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$; so $ ar\partial \alpha $ is defined. Since $\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\le \mathrm e^{2m}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$, we have $\int _\Omega |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV\le \mathrm e^{2m}E<\infty $. Hence theorem 6.4.9 , applied with the plurisubharmonic function $p$ and the smooth function $q=\psi $, whose complex Hessian matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite, shows that the equation $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ has a solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })=L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$. Let $u$ be the minimal solution in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$, given by lemma 6.4.10 (2). The function $v=u\mathrm e^\psi $ belongs to $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ and solves \[   ar\partial v= eta =(\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi )\mathrm e^\psi .  \] For every holomorphic $g$ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ we have $\int v ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int u ar g\, \mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV=0$, so $v$ is the minimal solution of $ ar\partial v= eta $ in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$, by lemma 6.4.10 (2). We now estimate $v$ by theorem 6.4.9 , applied again with $p$ and $q=\psi $. The form $ eta = ar\partial v$ is $ ar\partial $-closed, and it lies in $L^2_{\mathrm{loc},(0,1)}(\Omega )$ because $\alpha $ and $u$ are locally square integrable and $\psi $ is smooth. Since $E<\infty $ and $h<1$, the dual energies of $\alpha $ and $ ar\partial \psi $ are finite almost everywhere, and at such points both vectors lie in the subspace on which the dual energy is a Hermitian quadratic form. The triangle inequality $|\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}+|u|h^{1/2}$ therefore gives \[  \int | eta |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV\le 2E+2\sup _\Omega \mathrm e^\psi \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] So theorem 6.4.9 yields a solution of $ ar\partial w= eta $ whose squared norm in $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p-\psi })$ is at most this integral, and the minimal solution $v$ has no larger norm. As $\int |v|^2\mathrm e^{-p-\psi }\, \mathrm dV=\int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, we obtain \[  \int |u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV \le \int |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] At almost every point, let $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _{A^{-1}}$ be the Hermitian inner product associated with the dual energy on the subspace where it is finite; by the polarization identity $\langle x,yangle _{A^{-1}}= rac14\sum _{k=0}^3\mathrm i^ k|x+\mathrm i^ ky|_{A^{-1}}^2$, the function $\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}$ is measurable. We expand \[  |\alpha +u\,  ar\partial \psi |_{A^{-1}}^2=|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2+2\operatorname{Re} igl ( ar u\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}} igr )+h|u|^2, \qquad |\langle \alpha , ar\partial \psi angle _{A^{-1}}|\le |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2},  \] the second inequality being the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The function $h|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}$ is integrable, since $h<1$ almost everywhere and $u\in L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-p})$; moving its integral to the left, we find that $J=\int (1-h)|u|^2\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV$, which is finite, satisfies \[  J\le E+2\int |u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\mathrm e^{\psi -p}\, \mathrm dV.  \] If $a=0$, then $h=0$ almost everywhere on $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, the last integral vanishes, and $J\le E$, as claimed. Let $a>0$. The last integrand vanishes outside $\{ \alpha 
e 0\} $, where $h\le a$ and hence $h/(1-h)\le a/(1-a)$. For $t>1$, the inequality $2xy\le t^{-1}x^2+ty^2$ with $x=(1-h)^{1/2}|u|$ and $y=(h/(1-h))^{1/2}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}$ gives there \[  2|u|\, |\alpha |_{A^{-1}}h^{1/2}\le t^{-1}(1-h)|u|^2+ rac{ta}{1-a}|\alpha |_{A^{-1}}^2.  \] Integrating, we obtain \[  J\le \left(1+ rac{ta}{1-a}ight)E+t^{-1}J.  \] Since $J$ is finite, this gives $J\le  rac t{t-1} igl (1+ rac{ta}{1-a} igr )E$. Choose $t=1+a^{-1/2}$. Then $1+ta/(1-a)=(1+\sqrt a)/(1-a)=1/(1-\sqrt a)$ and $t/(t-1)=1+\sqrt a$, so $J\le (1+\sqrt a)E/(1-\sqrt a)$. $\square$

Lemma 6.5.3 . EE99921A3F33 Let $0<\varepsilon <1/4$. For $\zeta \in \mathbb C$ with $|\zeta |<1/4$ put \[  s=-\log (|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2),\qquad \eta =s+\log s,\qquad \psi _\varepsilon =-\log \eta .  \] Then $\psi _\varepsilon $ is a smooth, bounded, strictly subharmonic function on the disc $\Delta _{1/4}$. Let $h=|\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon |^2/(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }$. Then \[   egin{split}  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }& \ge (6s^2)^{-1},\  h& \le  rac{2}{-\log (2\varepsilon ^2)}\quad 	ext{for }|\zeta |\le \varepsilon ,\   rac{\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }}{|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }} & \le 25/4\quad 	ext{for }\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon . \end{split}  \] In particular $h<1$ everywhere, and the bound for $h$ on the disc $|\zeta |\le \varepsilon $ tends to zero as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. Proof. Since $|\zeta |^2+\varepsilon ^2<1/8$, we have $s>\log 8>2$, so $\eta >s>2$ and $\psi _\varepsilon <0$ is well defined. For fixed $\varepsilon $, $s$ ranges in a bounded interval, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is bounded; and $\psi _\varepsilon =G(|\zeta |^2)$ for a function $G$ that is smooth near $[0,1/16)$, so $\psi _\varepsilon $ is smooth. For $\zeta 
e 0$ put $x=|\zeta |^2$, $t=\log x$ and $b=x/(x+\varepsilon ^2)\in (0,1)$, and denote derivatives with respect to $t$ by primes. Then $s'=-b$ and $b'=b(1-b)$, so $s''=-b(1-b)$. With $D=1+1/s$ we have $\eta '=s'+s'/s=-bD$ and $D'=-s'/s^2=b/s^2$. Hence $\psi _\varepsilon '=-\eta '/\eta =bD/\eta $ and $\psi _\varepsilon ''=(b'D+bD')/\eta -bD\eta '/\eta ^2$, that is, \[  \psi _\varepsilon '= rac{bD}{\eta },\qquad \psi _\varepsilon ''=A+B,\quad A= rac{b^2D^2}{\eta ^2},\quad B= rac{b(1-b)D}{\eta }+ rac{b^2}{\eta s^2}>0.  \] For a function $g$ of $t=\log |\zeta |^2$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g'/ ar\zeta $ and $\partial _\zeta \partial _{ ar\zeta }g=g''/|\zeta |^2$. Hence $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=\psi _\varepsilon ''/x>0$ and $h=(\psi _\varepsilon ')^2/\psi _\varepsilon ''=A/(A+B)<1$ for $\zeta 
e 0$. In general $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =G'(|\zeta |^2)\zeta $ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G''(|\zeta |^2)|\zeta |^2+G'(|\zeta |^2)$, so at $\zeta =0$ we have $\partial _{ ar\zeta }\psi _\varepsilon =0$ and $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }=G'(0)$, where $G'(x)=\psi _\varepsilon '/x=D/(\eta (x+\varepsilon ^2))>0$; so $(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta }>0$ and $h=0$ there. Thus $\psi _\varepsilon $ is strictly subharmonic, and $h<1$ everywhere. For the first estimate let $\zeta 
e 0$. Since $B\ge b^2/(\eta s^2)$, we have $A/B\le D^2s^2/\eta =(s+1)^2/\eta $, and therefore \[  (1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }= rac{B}{\eta (A+B)} \ge  rac1{\eta +(s+1)^2}\ge  rac1{6s^2},  \] because $\eta \le 2s\le 2s^2$ and $(s+1)^2\le 4s^2$ for $s\ge 1$. At $\zeta =0$ we have $(1-h)\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }=1/\eta \ge 1/(6s^2)$ as well. For the second estimate let $0<x\le \varepsilon ^2$. Then $b\le 1/2$, and $B\ge b(1-b)D/\eta $ gives \[  h\le  rac AB\le  rac{bD}{\eta (1-b)}\le  rac D\eta = rac{s+1}{s\eta }\le  rac2s,  \] since $s+1\le 2s\le 2\eta $; moreover $s\ge -\log (2\varepsilon ^2)$, because $x+\varepsilon ^2\le 2\varepsilon ^2$. Together with $h(0)=0$, this proves the second estimate. For the third, let $\varepsilon /2\le |\zeta |\le \varepsilon $. Then $1/5\le b\le 1/2$, so $\eta \psi _\varepsilon ''\ge \eta B\ge b(1-b)D\ge b(1-b)\ge 4/25$, and $\mathrm e^{\psi _\varepsilon }/(|\zeta |^2(\psi _\varepsilon )_{\zeta  ar\zeta })=1/(\eta \psi _\varepsilon '')\le 25/4$. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.5.4 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi)
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.5 Interpolation and extension across a hyperplane
text:
Theorem 6.5.4 (Ohsawa–Takegoshi) . D315377B239D There is an absolute constant $C$ with the following property. Let $n\ge 1$ and $R>0$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^{n-1}	imes \Delta _ R$ be a pseudoconvex open set, where $\Delta _ R\subset \mathbb C$ is the disc of radius $R$ centered at $0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Put $\Omega _0=\Omega \cap \{ z_ n=0\} $, which we identify with an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Then every holomorphic function $f$ on $\Omega _0$ with \[  I=\int _{\Omega _0}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}<\infty  \] has an extension $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F|_{\Omega _0}=f,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}\le C R^2 I.  \] Here, for $n=1$, $\Omega _0$ is a point or empty, and $I$ is the weighted value of $|f|^2$ at that point, the integral with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$. If $\Omega _0=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. On a connected component of $\Omega _0$ on which the restriction of $p$ is identically $-\infty $, finiteness of $I$ forces $f=0$, and this component contributes zero to $I$. Proof. text: Corollary 6.5.8 . 33DEA3F4EDB8 Let $C$ be the constant of theorem 6.5.4 . Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\ge 1$, be a pseudoconvex open set of diameter at most $L>0$, and let $p\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then for every $a\in \Omega $ with $p(a)>-\infty $ there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ such that \[  F(a)=1,\qquad \int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV \le C^ n L^{2n}\mathrm e^{-p(a)}.  \] More generally, let $V\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be an affine complex subspace of codimension $r$, $0\le r\le n$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on $\Omega \cap V$ with finite slice norm $\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$, computed with Lebesgue measure on $V$. Then there is $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $F|_{\Omega \cap V}=f$ and $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV\le C^ rL^{2r}\int _{\Omega \cap V}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2r}$. Proof. We prove the second assertion; the first is the case $V=\{ a\} $, $r=n$ and $f=1$, whose slice norm with respect to the counting measure $\mathrm dV_0$ is $\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$. If $r=0$ we take $F=f$, and if $\Omega \cap V=\varnothing $ we take $F=0$. Assume now that $r\ge 1$ and $\Omega \cap V\ne \varnothing $. Choose $b\in \Omega \cap V$ and unitary affine coordinates $w=(w_1,\ldots ,w_ n)$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ centered at $b$ with $V=\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ r=0\} $, and put $\Omega _ k=\Omega \cap \{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $ for $0\le k\le r$, an open subset of a space isomorphic to $\mathbb C^{n-k}$. Unitary coordinates preserve Lebesgue measure. Each $\Omega _ k$ with $k<n$ is pseudoconvex: the restriction of a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function of $\Omega $ to the closed subset $\Omega _ k$ of $\Omega $ is continuous and plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.3 , applied to the linear embedding of $\{ w_1=\cdots =w_ k=0\} $, and its sublevel sets are compact. By the discussion following definition 6.3.1 , every connected component of $\Omega _ k$ is pseudoconvex as well. Since $\Omega $ is open and has diameter at most $L$, we have $|z-b|<L$ for $z\in \Omega $ (a point $z\in \Omega $ with $|z-b|=L$ could be moved slightly away from $b$ inside $\Omega $), so the coordinate $w_ k$ takes its values in $\Delta _ L$ on $\Omega _{k-1}$. Put $f_ r=f$, let $1\le k\le r$, and assume that $f_ k\in \mathcal O(\Omega _ k)$ has finite norm $\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}$. Let $W$ be a connected component of $\Omega _{k-1}$; ordering the coordinates as $(w_{k+1},\ldots ,w_ n,w_ k)$, we regard $W$ as an open subset of $\mathbb C^{n-k}\times \Delta _ L$ whose slice by $\{ w_ k=0\} $ is the open subset $W\cap \Omega _ k$ of $\Omega _ k$. By proposition 5.9.3 , the restriction of $p$ to $W$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. In the second case $\mathrm e^{-p}=\infty $ on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, so the finiteness of the norm of $f_ k$ forces $f_ k=0$ almost everywhere on $W\cap \Omega _ k$, hence everywhere there, since $f_ k$ is continuous, and we put $f_{k-1}=0$ on $W$. In the first case, theorem 6.5.4 , applied to $W$ with normal coordinate $w_ k$, gives a holomorphic function $f_{k-1}$ on $W$ extending the restriction of $f_ k$ to $W\cap \Omega _ k$, with \[  \int _ W|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{W\cap \Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] The components $W$ are open, disjoint and cover $\Omega _{k-1}$, and the sets $W\cap \Omega _ k$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega _ k$. Hence these functions define $f_{k-1}\in \mathcal O(\Omega _{k-1})$ extending $f_ k$, and summing over $W$ gives \[  \int _{\Omega _{k-1}}|f_{k-1}|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k+2}\le CL^2\int _{\Omega _ k}|f_ k|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2k}.  \] Proceeding in this way for $k=r,r-1,\ldots ,1$ and multiplying the $r$ estimates, we see that $F=f_0$ has the required properties. $\square$

text: Corollary 6.5.9 . BFB355F9DDF9 Let $X$ be a complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a complex submanifold, let $a\in Y$, and let $p$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Let $f$ be a holomorphic germ on $Y$ at $a$ such that $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p|_ Y}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $Y$. Then there is a holomorphic germ $F$ on $X$ at $a$ with $F|_ Y=f$ such that $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}$ is integrable on some neighborhood of $a$ in $X$. Here integrability refers to smooth positive volume forms on $Y$ and $X$; since any two such forms are locally comparable, the notion does not depend on their choice. Proof. Let $k=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim X$ near $a$. By the definition of a complex submanifold (definition 5.2.3 ), there are holomorphic coordinates $w=(w',w'')\in \mathbb C^ k\times \mathbb C^{n-k}$ centered at $a$ in which $Y=\{ w''=0\} $; by proposition 5.9.3 , $p$ is plurisubharmonic near $0$ in these coordinates. On a compact neighborhood of $a$, the densities of smooth positive volume forms with respect to coordinate Lebesgue measure are bounded above and below by positive constants. Hence we may test integrability with Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $Y=\mathbb C^ k\times \{ 0\} $ and $\mathrm dV_{2n}$ in the coordinates $w$. Choose a ball $B$ around $0$ so small that $p$ is plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, that $f$ is defined on $B\cap Y$, and that $\int _{B\cap Y}|f|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2k}<\infty $. The ball $B$ is a bounded pseudoconvex domain, by corollary 6.3.5 applied to the exhaustion function $|w|^2$ of $\mathbb C^ n$, and $B\cap Y$ is its intersection with the linear subspace $\{ w''=0\} $ of codimension $n-k$. By corollary 6.5.8 there is $F\in \mathcal O(B)$ with $F|_{B\cap Y}=f$ and $\int _ B|F|^2\mathrm e^{-p}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}<\infty $. (If $k=0$, the integral over $Y$ is the weighted value $|f(a)|^2\mathrm e^{-p(a)}$; if $p|_ Y$ is identically $-\infty $ near $a$, then $f=0$ and $F=0$, in accordance with the conventions of theorem 6.5.4 .) $\square$

title: 6.6 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.6 Lelong numbers and multiplier ideals
text:
A plurisubharmonic function can have a complicated pole set, but near each point its growth is governed by a single logarithmic rate. The Lelong number $
u (u,a)$ of a plurisubharmonic function $u$ at a point $a$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ such that $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; with this normalization $
u (\log |z|^2,0)=1$. By the Jensen–Lelong formula, $
u (u,a)$ is also the limiting density at $a$ of the positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, which links the pointwise growth of $u$ with the measures studied in the preceding chapters. Lelong numbers do not, however, determine the integrability properties of a singular weight $\varphi $ (example 6.9.4 ). These are recorded by the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, which consists of the holomorphic germs $f$ for which $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is locally integrable. The $L^2$ estimates and extension theorems of section 6.1 make multiplier ideals accessible. Solving a $ ar\partial $-equation with a weight that has a logarithmic pole at a point, we approximate every germ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, to arbitrarily high order, by holomorphic functions on a polydisc that are square integrable against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$; with the Krull intersection theorem and the strong Noetherian property, this shows that $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is a coherent sheaf (theorem 6.8.9 ). Comparing the vanishing orders of the generators of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ with the growth of $\varphi $ (lemma 6.9.1 ), we prove Siu's theorem that the sets where the Lelong number is at least $c>0$ are analytic. The same comparison shows that $\mathrm e^{-t\varphi }$ is integrable near a point $x$ for every $t>0$ if $
u (\varphi ,x)=0$, a fact used in section 13.1 for an example on the projective line. The Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem gives the restriction and subadditivity properties of multiplier ideals. Since its constant does not depend on the weight, it can be applied along a moving family of hyperplanes; comparing the resulting extensions on one fixed holomorphic curve, we prove that multiplier ideals are stable under increasing limits of weights and deduce the strong openness theorem $\mathcal I(\varphi )= igcup _{\varepsilon >0}\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )$ (corollary 6.11.6 ). The last section studies integrability on modifications. For a weight with analytic singularities, the change of variables formula on a log resolution reduces membership in the multiplier ideal to explicit one-variable integrals (theorem 6.12.8 ). For a general weight, the ideals $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ recover the generic Lelong numbers of $\varphi $ along all prime divisors over the ambient manifold, and strong openness gives a valuative criterion for membership in $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ in which one positive parameter serves for all divisors (theorem 6.12.16 ). These results are the local foundation for comparing singularities through their multiplier ideals in later chapters. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.12 .

Proposition 6.7.1 . C79BAEA70FC1 Let $n\geq 1$ and let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$. For sufficiently negative $t$ put \[  N(t)=\sup _{|z-a|<\exp (t/2)}u(z).  \] Then $N$ is finite, nondecreasing and convex, $N(t)$ is also the supremum of $u$ over the sphere $|z-a|=\exp (t/2)$, and the limit A6BF25586D16 6.7.2  egin{equation}  
u (u,a)=\lim _{t	o -\infty } rac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation} exists in $[0,\infty )$; it is zero if $u(a)>-\infty $. For every $r_0>0$ such that $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$ lies in the domain of $u$, EC4655061F9F 6.7.3  egin{equation}  u(z)\leq 
u (u,a)\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation} Consequently $
u (u,a)$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ for which $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; moreover, if $c\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+C$ for all $z$ outside a Lebesgue null set in some neighborhood of $a$, then $
u (u,a)\geq c$. The Lelong number does not change under a holomorphic change of coordinates, nor under the addition of a bounded function, provided the resulting function is plurisubharmonic. Proof. We may assume $a=0$. Let $R_*\in (0,\infty ]$ be the supremum of the radii $r$ for which $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$; since closed balls are compact, $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain exactly when $0<r<R_*$. For such $r$ put $S(r)=\sup _{|z|=r}u(z)$. This number is less than $+\infty $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous and hence bounded above on the compact sphere. It is also greater than $-\infty $. Otherwise, for every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)$, which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, would be $-\infty $ on the circle $|\zeta |=r$ and hence, by upper semicontinuity, have upper limits $-\infty $ there; the maximum principle (proposition 3.4.7 ), applied to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)+k$ for every $k>0$, would give $u=-\infty $ on the disc. Proposition 6.7.1 . C79BAEA70FC1 Let $n\geq 1$ and let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $a\in \mathbb C^ n$. For sufficiently negative $t$ put \[  N(t)=\sup _{|z-a|<\exp (t/2)}u(z).  \] Then $N$ is finite, nondecreasing and convex, $N(t)$ is also the supremum of $u$ over the sphere $|z-a|=\exp (t/2)$, and the limit A6BF25586D16 6.7.2  egin{equation}  
u (u,a)=\lim _{t	o -\infty } rac{N(t)}{t} \end{equation} exists in $[0,\infty )$; it is zero if $u(a)>-\infty $. For every $r_0>0$ such that $\overline{B(a,r_0)}$ lies in the domain of $u$, EC4655061F9F 6.7.3  egin{equation}  u(z)\leq 
u (u,a)\log  rac{|z-a|^2}{r_0^2} +\sup _{B(a,r_0)}u,\qquad 0<|z-a|<r_0. \end{equation} Consequently $
u (u,a)$ is the largest $c\geq 0$ for which $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+O(1)$ near $a$; moreover, if $c\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c\log |z-a|^2+C$ for all $z$ outside a Lebesgue null set in some neighborhood of $a$, then $
u (u,a)\geq c$. The Lelong number does not change under a holomorphic change of coordinates, nor under the addition of a bounded function, provided the resulting function is plurisubharmonic. Proof. We may assume $a=0$. Let $R_*\in (0,\infty ]$ be the supremum of the radii $r$ for which $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$; since closed balls are compact, $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain exactly when $0<r<R_*$. For such $r$ put $S(r)=\sup _{|z|=r}u(z)$. This number is less than $+\infty $ because $u$ is upper semicontinuous and hence bounded above on the compact sphere. It is also greater than $-\infty $. Otherwise, for every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)$, which is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, would be $-\infty $ on the circle $|\zeta |=r$ and hence, by upper semicontinuity, have upper limits $-\infty $ there; the maximum principle (proposition 3.4.7 ), applied to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)+k$ for every $k>0$, would give $u=-\infty $ on the disc. Thus $u$ would be identically $-\infty $ on $B(0,r)$, which is impossible because $u$ is locally integrable (theorem 5.9.1 ). Let $0<r_1<r_2<r_3<R_*$, and let $h(\zeta )=A+B\log |\zeta |^2$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb C\setminus \{ 0\} $ equal to $S(r_1)$ on $|\zeta |=r_1$ and to $S(r_3)$ on $|\zeta |=r_3$. For every unit vector $e$, the function $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-h(\zeta )$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ near the closed annulus $r_1\leq |\zeta |\leq r_3$, and by upper semicontinuity its upper limits at the two boundary circles are at most $0$; by the maximum principle (proposition 3.4.7 ) it is at most $0$ on the annulus. Taking the supremum over $e$ on the circle $|\zeta |=r_2$ gives $S(r_2)\leq h(r_2)$. Since $h(r_2)$ is the value at $\log r_2^2$ of the affine function of $\log r^2$ that equals $S(r_1)$ and $S(r_3)$ at $\log r_1^2$ and $\log r_3^2$, this says that $S$ is a convex function of $\log r^2$ on $(0,R_*)$. Applying the maximum principle in the same way to $\zeta \mapsto u(\zeta e)-S(r)$ on the disc $|\zeta |\leq r$, we obtain $u(\zeta e)\leq S(r)$ for $|\zeta |\leq r$; hence $S$ is nondecreasing and $u(0)\leq S(r)$. A finite convex function on an open interval is continuous, since on a compact subinterval its difference quotients are bounded between two fixed difference quotients taken outside the subinterval. Hence $\sup _{B(0,r)}u=\sup _{ho <r}S(ho )=S(r)$, so that $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})$ for $t<\log R_*^2$; this proves the assertions about $N$. Fix $r_0$ as in the statement and put $t_0=\log r_0^2$. Since $N$ is convex and nondecreasing on $(-\infty ,t_0]$, the difference quotients $(N(t_0)-N(t))/(t_0-t)$ are nonnegative and decrease as $t\downarrow -\infty $; let $c\in [0,\infty )$ be their limit. Writing $N(t)=N(t_0)-(t_0-t)\cdot  rac{N(t_0)-N(t)}{t_0-t}$ and dividing by $t$, we obtain $N(t)/t	o c$ as $t	o -\infty $. In particular $c$ does not depend on $t_0$, so for every fixed $s\leq t_0$ the quotients $(N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$ also tend to $c$ as $s'	o -\infty $. If $s'<s<t\leq t_0$, convexity gives $(N(t)-N(s))/(t-s)\geq (N(s)-N(s'))/(s-s')$; letting $s'	o -\infty $, we see that every difference quotient of $N$ on $(-\infty ,t_0]$ is at least $c$. Hence $N(t)-ct$ is nondecreasing, and $N(t)\leq c(t-t_0)+N(t_0)$ for $t<t_0$. Since $u(z)\leq S(|z|)=N(\log |z|^2)$, this is ( 6.7.3 ). Since $u(0)\leq S(r)$ for all $r$, we have $N(t)\geq u(0)$, hence $N(t)/t\leq u(0)/t$ for $t<0$, and $c=0$ if $u(0)>-\infty $. Conversely, if $c'\geq 0$ and $u(z)\leq c'\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r'$, then $N(t)=S(\mathrm e^{t/2})\leq c't+C$ for all sufficiently negative $t$, and division by $t<0$ gives $c\geq c'$. This proves the characterization of $
u (u,a)$ as the largest admissible coefficient. Now let $c\geq 0$, and suppose that $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for all $z\in B(0,r)\setminus A$, where $\overline{B(0,r)}$ lies in the domain of $u$ and $A$ is a Lebesgue null set. Let $0<|z|<r/2$ and $0<\delta <|z|/2$. The function $u$ is subharmonic (theorem 5.9.1 ), so theorem 3.4.5 gives $u(z)\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}\int _{B(z,\delta )}u\, \mathrm dV$. Every $y\in B(z,\delta )\setminus A$ satisfies $u(y)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$, because $c\geq 0$ and $|y|\leq |z|+\delta $; since $A$ is a null set, we obtain $u(z)\leq c\log (|z|+\delta )^2+C$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$, we get $u(z)\leq c\log |z|^2+C$ for $0<|z|<r/2$, and the converse part of the characterization gives $

The maps $F$ and $F^{-1}$ are continuously differentiable, hence Lipschitz near $a$ and $F(a)$, so $\log |F(z)-F(a)|^2-\log |z-a|^2$ is bounded near $a$, $z

Theorem 6.7.6 (Jensen–Lelong) . BD2098F182CC Let $n\geq 1$, $R>0$, and let $u$ be plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \mathbb C^ n$. Then the spherical mean $M_ u(a,r)$ of $u$ over $\partial B(a,r)$ is finite for every $0<r<R$, the function $r\mapsto D_ u(a,r)$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$, and 2D5BD01BDC4D 6.7.7  egin{equation}  M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1) =\int _{\log r_1^2}^{\log r_2^2}D_ u(a,\exp (t/2))\, \mathrm dt, \qquad 0<r_1<r_2<R. \end{equation} In particular, 59A9BF2835E9 6.7.8  egin{equation}  
u (u,a)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r) =\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{M_ u(a,r)}{\log r^2}. \end{equation} Proof. Step 1: smooth functions. Suppose first that $u$ is smooth. By proposition 3.1.5 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the substitution $r=\mathrm e^{t/2}$, for which $\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt=r/2$, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}) = rac r2\cdot  rac{\mu (B(a,r))}{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1}} =D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2}),  \] and ( 6.7.7 ) follows by integration, since $\mu =\Delta u\, \mathrm dV$ has a continuous density, so that the right side is continuous in $t$. To see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing, we show that $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is a convex function on $(-\infty ,\log R^2)$; the derivative of a differentiable convex function is nondecreasing. For a unit vector $\omega \in S^{2n-1}$, the function $v_\omega (\zeta )=u(a+\zeta \omega )$ is smooth on a neighborhood of the closed disc $|\zeta |\leq R$ in $\mathbb C$, and by ( 5.2.9 ) its Laplacian is \[  \Delta v_\omega (\zeta )=4\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(a+\zeta \omega )\, \omega _ j ar\omega _ k\geq 0,  \] because the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $u$ is positive semidefinite (proposition 5.9.2 (1)). Let $m_\omega (r)=(2\pi )^{-1}\int _0^{2\pi }v_\omega (r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta })\, \mathrm d	heta $ be the circle means of $v_\omega $ about $0$; they are the spherical means of $v_\omega $ in $\mathbb R^2$, because surface measure on the unit circle is arc length (subsection 2.9.20 ). By proposition 3.1.5 in $\mathbb R^2$, where $s_1=2\pi $, and the same substitution, \[   rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})= rac1{4\pi }\int _{|\zeta |<\mathrm e^{t/2}}\Delta v_\omega \, \mathrm dV_2,  \] which is nondecreasing in $t$ because $\Delta v_\omega \geq 0$. By the mean value theorem, a differentiable function with nondecreasing derivative is convex; so $t\mapsto m_\omega (\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex. Surface measure on $S^{2n-1}$ is invariant under the orthogonal transformations $\omega \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega $ of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ (subsection 3.1.1 ), so $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(a+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega )$ for every $	heta $. Averaging over $	heta \in [0,2\pi ]$ and using Fubini's theorem for the continuous integrand, we obtain \[  M_ u(a,r)= rac1{s_{2n-1}}\int _{S^{2n-1}}m_\omega (r)\, \mathrm dS(\omega ),\qquad 0<r<R.  \] An average of convex functions is convex, so $t\mapsto M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ is convex, and $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on $(0,R)$. Step 2: approximation. For general $u$, let $u_\varepsilon =u*ho _\varepsilon $ be the regularizations of ( 3.4.13 ). For small $\varepsilon $ they are defined on a neighborhood of the compact set $\overline{B(a,R)}$, and by proposition 5.9.2 (2) they are smooth and plurisubharmonic there and decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Subtracting a constant, which changes neither side of ( 6.7.7 ), nor $D_ u$, nor the Lelong number, we may assume $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$ on $\overline{B(a,R)}$ for all small $\varepsilon $. For $0\leq \eta <1$ put $\kappa _\eta =(1-\eta )/(1+\eta )^{2n-1}$. If $0<r<R$ and $|x-a|\leq \eta r$, the explicit formula ( 3.1.17 ) shows that the Poisson kernel $P$ of $B(a,r)$ satisfies $P(x,\zeta )\geq \kappa _\eta P(a,\zeta )=\kappa _\eta /(s_{2n-1}r^{2n-1})$ for $\zeta \in \partial B(a,r)$. Fix $0<r<R$ and choose $b\in B(a,r)$ with $u(b)>-\infty $, which is possible since the pole set of $u$ has measure zero; let $\eta =|b-a|/r$. By the maximum principle (proposition 3.4.7 ), applied to $u_\varepsilon $ minus the Poisson integral of its boundary values (theorem 3.1.18 ), we have $u_\varepsilon (x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u_\varepsilon (\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. At $x=b$, since $u_\varepsilon \leq 0$, this gives \[  u(b)\leq u_\varepsilon (b)\leq \kappa _\eta M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r).  \] Thus the integrals of the nonnegative functions $-u_\varepsilon $ over the sphere are bounded independently of $\varepsilon $. As $-u_\varepsilon $ increases to $-u$, the monotone convergence theorem shows that $M_ u(a,r)$ is finite and $M_{u_\varepsilon }(a,r)	o M_ u(a,r)$. For fixed $x\in B(a,r)$ the kernel $P(x,\cdot )$ is positive and bounded on $\partial B(a,r)$, so the same argument, applied to the functions $-P(x,\cdot )u_\varepsilon $, lets us pass to the limit in the Poisson inequality, and we obtain $u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta )$ for $x\in B(a,r)$. Since the functions $u_\varepsilon $ decrease to the locally integrable function $u$, the monotone convergence theorem, applied to $u_{\varepsilon _0}-u_\varepsilon $ for a fixed $\varepsilon _0$, shows that $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; hence the positive measures $\Delta u_\varepsilon $ converge to $\mu $ in the sense of distributions, hence vaguely (proposition 2.6.1 ). By proposition 2.6.2 , $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r))	o \mu (B(a,r))$ for every radius $r$ with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$; since the spheres $\partial B(a,r)$, $0<r<R$, are disjoint and $\mu $ is finite on $B(a,R)$, only countably many radii are excluded (lemma 2.2.5 ). Moreover, if $r_2<R$ and $\chi \in C^\infty _ c$ is a cutoff function with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one on $B(a,r_2)$, with support in a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a,R)}$ on which all $u_\varepsilon $ with small $\varepsilon $ are defined, then $\Delta u_\varepsilon (B(a,r_2))\leq \int \chi \, \Delta u_\varepsilon 	o \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $, so these masses are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $. By Step 1 each $D_{u_\varepsilon }(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing; letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ is nondecreasing on the dense set of radii with $\mu (\partial B(a,r))=0$, and hence on $(0,R)$, because $r\mapsto \mu (B(a,r))$ is left continuous. Finally, ( 6.7.7 ) holds for each $u_\varepsilon $ by Step 1. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, its left side converges to $M_ u(a,r_2)-M_ u(a,r_1)$, while the integrands on the right converge for all but countably many $t$ and are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $; dominated convergence gives ( 6.7.7 ) for $u$. Step 3: the limits. The nondecreasing nonnegative function $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ has a limit $\ell =\lim _{r\downarrow 0}D_ u(a,r)\in [0,\infty )$. Put $g(t)=M_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t/2})$ and fix $t_0<\log R^2$. Given $\delta >0$, choose $s_\delta <\min \{ t_0,0\} $ with $D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{s/2})\leq \ell +\delta $ for $s\leq s_\delta $. For $t<s_\delta $, ( 6.7.7 ) and the monotonicity of $D_ u(a,\cdot )$ give \[  \ell (t_0-t)\leq g(t_0)-g(t)\leq (\ell +\delta )(s_\delta -t)+(t_0-s_\delta )D_ u(a,\mathrm e^{t_0/2}).  \] Dividing by $-t>0$ and letting $t	o -\infty $, we see that all limit points of $g(t)/t$ lie in $[\ell ,\ell +\delta ]$. Hence $M_ u(a,r)/\log r^2	o \ell $ as $r\downarrow 0$. It remains to show that $\ell =
u (u,a)$. Let $0<\eta <1$. For $x\in B(a,\eta r)$, the Poisson inequality of Step 2 and the kernel bound give, since $u\leq 0$, \[  u(x)\leq \int _{\partial B(a,r)}P(x,\zeta )u(\zeta )\, \mathrm dS(\zeta ) \leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r).  \] Together with $M_ u(a,r)\leq \sup _{\partial B(a,r)}u=N(\log r^2)$, where $N$ is as in proposition 6.7.1 , we obtain \[  N(\log (\eta ^2r^2))\leq \kappa _\eta M_ u(a,r), \qquad M_ u(a,r)\leq N(\log r^2).  \] We divide by $\log r^2<0$ and let $r\downarrow 0$. Since $\log (\eta ^2r^2)/\log r^2	o 1$, this gives $
u (u,a)\geq \kappa _\eta \ell $ and $\ell \geq

title: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text:
From now on $X$ denotes a complex manifold, and $n\geq 0$ its dimension at the point under consideration. We also narrow a term of section 6.1 : a weight on $X$ is now a plurisubharmonic function on $X$, a special case of the measurable weights of section 6.4 ; in particular, a weight is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. Restrictions of weights to submanifolds may be identically $-\infty $ on some components, and definition 6.8.5 allows this case. Local integrability on $X$ refers to Lebesgue measure in holomorphic charts, or equivalently to any smooth positive volume form, since the densities of two such measures with respect to each other are bounded above and below by positive constants on compact subsets of a chart. To pass from a Hilbert space of holomorphic functions to a coherent ideal sheaf we need two facts from local algebra, the Krull intersection theorem and the strong Noetherian property of coherent sheaves. We prove them first, the second by induction on the dimension with the help of Weierstrass polynomials. Lemma 6.8.1 . 8312218F0503 Let $x\in X$, let $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and let $E$ be a submodule of a finitely generated $R$-module $F$. Then \[   igcap _{k\geq 1}(E+\mathfrak m^ kF)=E.  \] In particular, if a sequence of holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of $x$ converges locally uniformly and the germs at $x$ of all its members belong to an ideal $J\subset R$, then the germ of the limit belongs to $J$. Proof. We derive the intersection formula from the Artin–Rees lemma, after collecting the facts about Noetherian rings that we need. A commutative ring $A$ is Noetherian if all its ideals are finitely generated. Let $A$ be Noetherian. (i) Every submodule $N$ of $A^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. For $r=1$ this is the definition. Let $r\geq 2$. If $\overline{B(y,\delta )}\subset D$, then 69805453021C 6.8.7  egin{equation}  |F(y)|^2\leq  rac1{|B(y,\delta )|}\int _{B(y,\delta )}|F|^2\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Let $x\in D$, suppose that the germ of $F$ at $x$ is not zero, and let $P_ k
eq 0$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of the expansion of $F$ at $x$. Then for all sufficiently small $t>0$ D76FBA2B036A 6.8.8  egin{equation}  \int _{S^{2n-1}}|F(x+t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )\geq t^{2k}\int _{S^{2n-1}}|P_ k|^2\, \mathrm dS, \qquad \int _{S^{2n-1}}|P_ k|^2\, \mathrm dS>0. \end{equation} Proof. (1) The function $F$ is smooth with $\Delta F=4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}F=0$, by ( 5.2.9 ); so its real and imaginary parts are harmonic and have the ball mean value property (proposition 3.1.5 ). Thus $F(y)$ is the mean of $F$ over $B(y,\delta )$, and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives ( 6.8.7 ). (2) Homogeneous polynomials $P_ l$, $P_{l'}$ of different degrees are orthogonal in $L^2$ of the unit sphere: $P_ l(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega )=\mathrm e^{\mathrm il	heta }P_ l(\omega )$, and surface measure is invariant under the orthogonal maps $\omega \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }\omega $ (subsection 3.1.1 ), so $\int _{S^{2n-1}}P_ l\overline{P_{l'}}\, \mathrm dS=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(l-l')	heta }\int _{S^{2n-1}}P_ l\overline{P_{l'}}\, \mathrm dS$ for every $	heta $. For small $t>0$ the homogeneous expansion $F(x+t\omega )=\sum _ lt^ lP_ l(\omega )$ converges uniformly in $\omega \in S^{2n-1}$, by ( 5.2.1 ); integrating term by term, we obtain $\int _{S^{2n-1}}|F(x+t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=\sum _{l\geq k}t^{2l}\int _{S^{2n-1}}|P_ l|^2\, \mathrm dS$, which implies the first inequality. The last integral is positive, because $P_ k$ does not vanish identically on the sphere, by homogeneity, and nonempty relatively open subsets of the sphere have positive surface measure. $\square$ Theorem 6.8.9 . FE623FA661C4 For every weight $\varphi $ on $X$, the sheaf $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is coherent. More precisely, let $\Omega \subset X$ be an open set that a holomorphic chart identifies with a bounded open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, pseudoconvex if $n\geq 1$; for instance, $\Omega $ may be a bounded polydisc in a chart (corollary 6.3.5 ). Let $\varrho $ be a measurable function on $\Omega $ with $c_\varrho \leq \varrho \leq C_\varrho $ for positive constants $c_\varrho $ and $C_\varrho $, and let \[  \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )=\Bigl \{ F\in \mathcal O(\Omega ): \| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }^2=\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV<\infty \Bigr \} ,  \] with the inner product $\langle F,Gangle _{\varphi ,\varrho }=\int _\Omega F ar G\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV$, where $\mathrm dV$ is Lebesgue measure in the chart (the counting measure if $n=0$). For $\varrho =1$ we write $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega )$, $\| \cdot \| _\varphi $ and $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _\varphi $. Then the following hold. For every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ there is a constant $C_ K$ such that $|F(z)|\leq C_ K\| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }$ for all $F\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ and $z\in K$. The space $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ is a separable Hilbert space. It has orthonormal bases, that is, orthonormal families whose linear span is dense, and each of them is finite or countable. If $(e_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ is an enumeration of an orthonormal basis and $F\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$, then the partial sums $\sum _{j\leq N}\langle F,e_ jangle _{\varphi ,\varrho }e_ j$ converge to $F$ in norm and locally uniformly on $\Omega $, and $\sum _ j|\langle F,e_ jangle _{\varphi ,\varrho }|^2=\| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }^2$. The sheaf $\mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega $ is generated by the germs of the elements of $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$. In fact, if $(e_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ is as in (2), then the functions $e_ j$ generate $\mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega $, and near each point of $\Omega $ already an initial segment $e_1,\ldots ,e_ k$ generates it. Proof. If $n=0$, then $\Omega $ is empty, and there is nothing to prove, or a point $x$; in the latter case $\varphi (x)$ is finite, $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )=\mathbb C$, and $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x=\mathbb C$ is generated by every nonzero element, so all assertions are immediate. Assume therefore $n\geq 1$, and write $\mathcal H$, $\| \cdot \| $ and $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $ for $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$, its norm and its inner product. In the chart, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ (section 5.9 ). We prove (1) and (2) by Hilbert space arguments, and (3) by solving a $ ar\partial $-equation with a weight that has a logarithmic pole. We first prove (1). Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, let $r>0$ be half the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, and let $M$ be the maximum of the upper semicontinuous function $\varphi $ on the compact set $K_ r=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq r\} \subset \Omega $. Since $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \geq c_\varrho \mathrm e^{-M}$ on $K_ r$, the inequality ( 6.8.7 ) on $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset K_ r$ gives, for $z\in K$ and $F\in \mathcal H$, \[  |F(z)|^2\leq  rac1{|B(z,r)|}\int _{B(z,r)}|F|^2\, \mathrm dV\leq  rac{\mathrm e^ M}{c_\varrho |B(z,r)|}\| F\| ^2.  \] This proves (1). Next we show that $\mathcal H$ is a separable Hilbert space. The measurable function $\varphi -\log \varrho $ is bounded above on compact subsets of $\Omega $, and $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi +\log \varrho })$ is the $L^2$ space of the measure $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV$. By lemma 6.4.10 (2), applied to this function, the elements of this space that are represented by holomorphic functions form a closed subspace. A holomorphic function is determined by its class, since continuous functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere; hence $\mathcal H$ is identified with this closed subspace and is a Hilbert space. Multiplication by $\mathrm e^{-\varphi /2}\varrho ^{1/2}$ maps $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi +\log \varrho })$ isometrically into $L^2(\Omega )$, since $\varphi $ is locally integrable (theorem 5.9.1 ) and hence finite almost everywhere. The space $L^2(\Omega )$ is separable: by lemma 2.5.1 (5), $C_ c(\Omega )$ is dense in it. Let $\mathcal S$ be the countable set of functions that take constant values in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ on finitely many half-open cubes $\prod _{i=1}^{2n}[m_ i2^{-k},(m_ i+1)2^{-k})$, $m_ i\in \mathbb Z$, $k\geq 1$, whose closures lie in $\Omega $, and vanish elsewhere. Let $g\in C_ c(\Omega )$. For large $k$, the cubes of side $2^{-k}$ of this form that meet $\operatorname{Supp}g$ lie in a fixed compact subset $K'$ of $\Omega $. Assigning to each of them a value in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ within $2^{-k}$ of the value of $g$ at one of its points, we obtain $s_ k\in \mathcal S$ vanishing outside $K'$ with $\sup |g-s_ k|\leq 2^{-k}+\sup \{ |g(y)-g(y')|:|y-y'|\leq \sqrt{2n}\, 2^{-k}\} $, which tends to zero by uniform continuity of $g$; hence $s_ k	o g$ in $L^2(\Omega )$, and $\mathcal S$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega )$. A subset of a separable metric space is separable, so $\mathcal H$ is separable. Orthonormal bases of $\mathcal H$ exist: applying the Gram–Schmidt process to a countable dense sequence and discarding the vectors that depend linearly on the preceding ones, we obtain an orthonormal family whose linear span contains the dense sequence. Every orthonormal family is finite or countable, because two of its members have distance $\sqrt2$, so that the balls of radius $1/2$ around them are disjoint, and each of these balls contains a member of a fixed countable dense set. Let $(e_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be an enumeration of an orthonormal basis, let $F\in \mathcal H$, and put $c_ j=\langle F,e_ jangle $ and $S_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}c_ je_ j$. Since $F-S_ N$ is orthogonal to the span $V_ N$ of $e_1,\ldots ,e_ N$, every $v\in V_ N$ satisfies $\| F-v\| ^2=\| F-S_ N\| ^2+\| S_ N-v\| ^2\geq \| F-S_ N\| ^2$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, there is $v$ in some $V_{N_0}$ with $\| F-v\| <\varepsilon $, and since $V_{N_0}\subset V_ N$ for $N\geq N_0$, we get $\| F-S_ N\| <\varepsilon $ for all $N\geq N_0$. Thus $S_ N	o F$ in $\mathcal H$, and hence locally uniformly on $\Omega $, by (1). Taking $v=0$ above gives $\| F\| ^2=\| F-S_ N\| ^2+\sum _{j\leq N}|c_ j|^2$, and letting $N	o \infty $ we obtain $\sum _ j|c_ j|^2=\| F\| ^2$. This proves (2). We turn to (3). Let $\mathcal J$ be the ideal sheaf on $\Omega $ generated by the $e_ j$. By lemma 6.8.4 it is coherent and near each point generated by an initial segment $e_1,\ldots ,e_ k$. Every $F\in \mathcal H$ is the locally uniform limit of the partial sums $S_ N$, whose germs lie in $\mathcal J$, so the germs of $F$ lie in $\mathcal J$ by lemma 6.8.1 . Thus $\mathcal J$ is the ideal generated by $\mathcal H$, independently of the basis, and $\mathcal J\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega $ because $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\leq c_\varrho ^{-1}\| F\| ^2$ for $F\in \mathcal H$. It remains to prove that $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x\subset \mathcal J_ x$ for $x\in \Omega $. Fix $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and an integer $s\geq 0$; we construct $F\in \mathcal H$ with $f-F\in \mathfrak m_ x^{s+1}$, where $\mathfrak m_ x$ is the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Choose a cutoff function $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, equal to one near $x$, such that $f$ is holomorphic and $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. The $(0,1)$-form $\alpha =f ar\partial \chi $, extended by zero, is smooth, $ ar\partial $-closed and vanishes near $x$. We apply theorem 6.4.9 on the pseudoconvex set $\Omega $ with the plurisubharmonic function $p=\varphi +(n+s)\log |z-x|^2$ (proposition 5.10.3 , proposition 5.9.5 ) and the smooth function $q=|z|^2$, whose complex Hessian is the identity matrix. Since $|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}$ and $| ar\partial \chi |$ are bounded on the support of $\alpha $, we have $\int _\Omega |\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\leq C\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\chi }|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Hence there is $u$ with $ ar\partial u=\alpha $ and \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi -|z|^2}|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] Since $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ is bounded below by a positive constant on compact sets, $u$ is locally square integrable. Near $x$ we have $ ar\partial u=0$, so, by lemma 6.4.10 (1), $u$ agrees almost everywhere near $x$ with a holomorphic function; we replace $u$ by this function near $x$. We claim that $u$ vanishes to order at least $s+1$ at $x$. Since $\varphi $ is bounded above near $x$, the last display gives $\int _{B(x,r)}|u|^2|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $ for small $r>0$. We may assume that the germ of $u$ at $x$ is not zero, and we let $P_{k_0}
eq 0$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of its expansion at $x$. Applying ( 6.8.8 ) of lemma 6.8.6 to $u$ and integrating in polar coordinates ( 3.1.2 ), we obtain \[  \int _{B(x,r)}|u|^2|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}\, \mathrm dV\geq c\int _0^ rt^{2k_0-2s-1}\, \mathrm dt  \] with $c>0$. This is finite only if $k_0\geq s+1$, which proves the claim. Since $\Omega $ is bounded, $\mathrm e^{-|z|^2}|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}$ is bounded below on $\Omega $ by a positive constant, so $|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable on $\Omega $. The function $\chi f-u$ satisfies $ ar\partial (\chi f-u)=\alpha -\alpha =0$, so it agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function $F$ on $\Omega $, by lemma 6.4.10 (1). Since $|F|^2\leq 2|\chi f|^2+2|u|^2$ almost everywhere, $|\chi f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable by the choice of $\chi $, and $\varrho \leq C_\varrho $, we have $F\in \mathcal H$. Near $x$ the continuous functions $f-F$ and $u$ agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere, so $f-F=u\in \mathfrak m_ x^{s+1}$ by section 9.2 . Thus $f\in \mathcal J_ x+\mathfrak m_ x^{s+1}$ for every $s$, and lemma 6.8.1 gives $f\in \mathcal J_ x$. Hence $\mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega =\mathcal J$, which proves (3). Finally, every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $\Omega $ of the kind considered, namely a bounded polydisc in a chart. If $n\geq 1$, such a polydisc is pseudoconvex by corollary 6.3.5 , being a product of discs, each of which is a sublevel set of the smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $|\zeta -\zeta _0|^2$ of $\mathbb C$, where $\zeta _0$ is its center. By (3), $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is generated near each point by finitely many holomorphic functions, so it is coherent by theorem 9.2.7 and the last assertion of lemma 9.2.6 . $\square$ Lemma 6.8.10 . 3B37857D5B64 Let $\varphi $, $\Omega $, $\varrho $ and $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ be as in theorem 6.8.9 , let $x\in \Omega $, and let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ be elements whose germs generate $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Then there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ and a constant $C$ such that every $F\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ can be written as $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V$ with $h_ i\in \mathcal O(V)$ and \[  \sup _ V|h_ i|\leq C\| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }.  \] Consequently, if $m>0$ is real and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ generate $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ on a neighborhood of $x$, then there is a constant $C_ m$ such that 11D2B663BB36 6.8.11  egin{equation}  \varphi \leq  rac1m\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+C_ m \end{equation} on a neighborhood of $x$, with the convention $\log 0=-\infty $. Proof. We write $\mathcal H=\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ and $\| \cdot \| =\| \cdot \| _{\varphi ,\varrho }$. Choose balls $V_1\supset V_2\supset \cdots $ centered at $x$, with radii tending to zero, inside the neighborhood on which the $g_ i$ generate $\mathcal I(\varphi )$. For positive integers $j$ and $k$ let $S_{j,k}$ be the set of $F\in \mathcal H$ that can be written as $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V_ j$ with $h_ i\in \mathcal O(V_ j)$ and $\sup _{V_ j}|h_ i|\leq k$. These sets cover $\mathcal H$: by theorem 6.8.9 (3), the germ at $x$ of each $F\in \mathcal H$ lies in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$, so $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on some neighborhood of $x$ with holomorphic $h_ i$, and these coefficients are bounded on a smaller ball $V_ j$. We show that each $S_{j,k}$ is closed and then apply Baire's theorem. Let $F_ l\in S_{j,k}$ converge to $F$ in $\mathcal H$, with coefficients $h_{i,l}$. Then $F_ l	o F$ locally uniformly on $\Omega $, by theorem 6.8.9 (1). The coefficients are bounded by $k$ on $V_ j$. Let $K\subset V_ j$ be compact, and let $\varepsilon >0$ be such that the closed polydiscs of radius $2\varepsilon $ centered at points of $K$ lie in $V_ j$. For $y\in K$ and $y'\in B(y,\varepsilon )$, the closed polydisc of radius $\varepsilon $ centered at $y'$ then lies in $V_ j$, and the coefficient bound in ( 5.2.1 ) on this polydisc bounds all first partial derivatives of all $h_{i,l}$ at $y'$ by $k/\varepsilon $. So the $h_{i,l}$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on the balls of radius $\varepsilon $ centered at points of $K$, and they are equicontinuous on $K$. By proposition 2.7.4 , applied on a compact exhaustion of $V_ j$, and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $V_ j$ to continuous functions $h_ i$ with $|h_ i|\leq k$. Locally uniform convergence implies convergence in the sense of distributions, so $ ar\partial h_ i=0$, and the continuous functions $h_ i$ are holomorphic by lemma 6.4.10 (1) (if $n=0$, every function on $V_ j$ is holomorphic). Passing to the limit, we obtain $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V_ j$, that is, $F\in S_{j,k}$. By Baire's theorem, a complete metric space is not a countable union of closed subsets with empty interior. (If all the sets had empty interior, we could choose closed balls of radii at most $2^{-l}$, each contained in the interior of the previous one and disjoint from the $l$th set, since the interior of a ball minus a closed set with empty interior is a nonempty open set; their centers would form a Cauchy sequence whose limit lies in every ball but in none of the sets.) Hence some $S_{j,k}$ contains a ball $\{ F:\| F-F_0\| <\delta \} $. If $\| F\| <\delta $, then $F_0$ and $F_0+F$ both lie in $S_{j,k}$, and subtracting their representations writes $F$ on $V_ j$ with coefficients bounded by $2k$. For $F
eq 0$ we apply this to $\delta F/(2\| F\| )$ and obtain the first assertion with $V=V_ j$ and $C=4k/\delta $; for $F=0$ we take zero coefficients. For the second assertion, apply the first part with $\varrho =1$ to the weight $m\varphi $, and let $V$ and $C$ be the resulting neighborhood and constant. Let $a\in V$ with $\varphi (a)>-\infty $. By corollary 6.5.8 , applied on the pseudoconvex set $\Omega $ to the plurisubharmonic function $m\varphi $, there is $F\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ with $F(a)=1$ and $\| F\| _{m\varphi }^2\leq C_\Omega \mathrm e^{-m\varphi (a)}$, where $C_\Omega $ depends only on $n$ and the diameter of $\Omega $; if $n=0$, then $F=1$ has these properties with $C_\Omega =1$. Writing $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V$ and using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain \[  1=|F(a)|^2\leq rC^2\| F\| _{m\varphi }^2\sum _ i|g_ i(a)|^2 \leq rC^2C_\Omega \mathrm e^{-m\varphi (a)}\sum _ i|g_ i(a)|^2.  \] Taking logarithms gives ( 6.8.11 ) at $a$ with $C_ m=m^{-1}\log (rC^2C_\Omega )$. At points where $\varphi =-\infty $ the left side is $-\infty $; by the last display, these points include all common zeros of the $g_ i$. $\square$

Lemma 6.8.1 . 8312218F0503 Let $x\in X$, let $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and let $E$ be a submodule of a finitely generated $R$-module $F$. Then \[   igcap _{k\geq 1}(E+\mathfrak m^ kF)=E.  \] In particular, if a sequence of holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of $x$ converges locally uniformly and the germs at $x$ of all its members belong to an ideal $J\subset R$, then the germ of the limit belongs to $J$. Proof. We derive the intersection formula from the Artin–Rees lemma, after collecting the facts about Noetherian rings that we need. A commutative ring $A$ is Noetherian if all its ideals are finitely generated. Let $A$ be Noetherian. (i) Every submodule $N$ of $A^ r$, $r\geq 1$, is finitely generated. For $r=1$ this is the definition. Let $r\geq 2$. The last coordinates of the elements of $N$ form an ideal of $A$; choose $v_1,\ldots ,v_ q\in N$ whose last coordinates generate it, and, by induction on $r$, finitely many generators of the submodule $N\cap (A^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$, which is a submodule of $A^{r-1}$. If $v\in N$, subtracting from $v$ a combination of the $v_ i$ with the same last coordinate leaves an element of $N\cap (A^{r-1}	imes \{ 0\} )$; hence these finitely many elements generate $N$. (ii) Every submodule $N$ of a finitely generated $A$-module $M$ is finitely generated. Indeed, let $\pi \colon A^ r	o M$ map the standard basis to generators of $M$. By (i), the submodule $\pi ^{-1}(N)$ of $A^ r$ is finitely generated, and the images of its generators generate $N=\pi (\pi ^{-1}(N))$. (iii) The polynomial ring $A[t]$ is Noetherian (Hilbert's basis theorem). Let $I\subset A[t]$ be a nonzero ideal. The leading coefficients of the nonzero elements of $I$, together with $0$, form an ideal of $A$: if $f,g\in I$ have degrees $d\leq e$ and leading coefficients $a,b$ with $a+b
eq 0$, then $t^{e-d}f+g\in I$ has leading coefficient $a+b$, and if $c\in A$ with $ca
eq 0$, then $cf\in I$ has leading coefficient $ca$. Choose $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k\in I$ whose leading coefficients generate this ideal, and let $d_0$ be the largest of their degrees. If $f\in I$ has degree $d\geq d_0$, its leading coefficient is $\sum _ ia_ ic_ i$ for some $a_ i\in A$, where $c_ i$ is the leading coefficient of $p_ i$, and $f-\sum _ ia_ it^{d-\deg p_ i}p_ i$ is an element of $I$ of smaller degree. Repeating this, we see that $f$ differs from an element of $I\cap (A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1})$ by an element of the ideal generated by $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k$. The set $I\cap (A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1})$ is a submodule of the $A$-module $A+At+\cdots +At^{d_0-1}\cong A^{d_0}$, finitely generated by (i). Hence $I$ is generated by $p_1,\ldots ,p_ k$ and finitely many further elements. (iv) If $I\subset A$ is an ideal, then $A/I$ is Noetherian, since the ideals of $A/I$ are the images of the ideals of $A$ containing $I$. Hence, by (iii) and induction on the number of variables, every quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over $A$ is Noetherian. All this applies to $A=R$, which is Noetherian by proposition 9.2.4 , since a holomorphic chart at $x$ identifies $R$ with $\mathcal O_ n$. Next we prove the Artin–Rees lemma. If $\mathfrak m=0$, which happens only in dimension zero, the lemma is trivial; so let $\mathfrak m
eq 0$, and choose generators $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ p$ of $\mathfrak m$. Consider the subring $\mathcal R= igoplus _{k\geq 0}\mathfrak m^ kt^ k$ of $R[t]$, consisting of the polynomials whose coefficient of $t^ k$ lies in $\mathfrak m^ k$, where $\mathfrak m^0=R$. Since $\mathfrak m^ k$ is generated by the monomials of degree $k$ in $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ p$, the ring $\mathcal R$ is the image of the homomorphism $R[T_1,\ldots ,T_ p]	o R[t]$, $T_ i\mapsto \xi _ it$, and it is Noetherian by (iii) and (iv). In the $\mathcal R$-module of polynomials in $t$ with coefficients in $F$, consider the submodule $ igoplus _{k\geq 0}\mathfrak m^ kFt^ k$. It is generated over $\mathcal R$ by generators of $F$ placed in degree zero, and it contains the submodule $\mathcal E= igoplus _{k\geq 0}(E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF)t^ k$, because $\mathfrak m^ j(E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF)\subset E\cap \mathfrak m^{j+k}F$. By (ii), $\mathcal E$ is finitely generated. The homogeneous components of the elements of $\mathcal E$ again belong to $\mathcal E$, so the homogeneous components of finitely many generators generate $\mathcal E$; let these be $e_1t^{d_1},\ldots ,e_ lt^{d_ l}$ with $e_ i\in E\cap \mathfrak m^{d_ i}F$, and let $s=\max _ id_ i$. For $k\geq s$ this gives the Artin–Rees equality \[  E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF=\mathfrak m^{k-s}(E\cap \mathfrak m^ sF).  \] Indeed, let $y\in E\cap \mathfrak m^ kF$, and write $yt^ k=\sum _ iho _ ie_ it^{d_ i}$ with $ho _ i\in \mathcal R$. Comparing the coefficients of $t^ k$, we may replace each $ho _ i$ by its term of degree $k-d_ i$, which is $a_ it^{k-d_ i}$ with $a_ i\in \mathfrak m^{k-d_ i}$. Thus $y=\sum _ ia_ ie_ i$, where $a_ i\in \mathfrak m^{k-d_ i}=\mathfrak m^{k-s}\mathfrak m^{s-d_ i}$ and $\mathfrak m^{s-d_ i}e_ i\subset E\cap \mathfrak m^ sF$; hence $y\in \mathfrak m^{k-s}(E\cap \mathfrak m^ sF)$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Now let $Q$ be a finitely generated $R$-module and $G= igcap _ k\mathfrak m^ kQ$. By (ii), $G$ is finitely generated. Let $s$ be the index of the Artin–Rees equality for $G\subset Q$. Since $G\subset \mathfrak m^ kQ$ for all $k$, this equality with $k=s+1$ gives $G=G\cap \mathfrak m^{s+1}Q=\mathfrak m(G\cap \mathfrak m^ sQ)=\mathfrak mG$. If $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generate $G$, write $g_ i=\sum _ ja_{ij}g_ j$ with $a_{ij}\in \mathfrak m$. Multiplying this system of equations by the adjugate of the matrix $(\delta _{ij}-a_{ij})$ gives $\det (\delta _{ij}-a_{ij})\, g_ i=0$ for every $i$. Expanding the determinant, we see that it is congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak m$, hence a unit of the local ring $R$, and therefore $G=0$. Applied to $Q=F/E$, for which $\mathfrak m^ kQ=(E+\mathfrak m^ kF)/E$, this proves the intersection formula. For the last assertion, let $f_ l	o f$ locally uniformly near $x$, with germs $f_ l\in J$, and work in a holomorphic chart centered at $x$. By section 9.2 , a germ belongs to $\mathfrak m^ k$ if and only if its Taylor coefficients of order less than $k$ vanish; hence these coefficients identify $R/\mathfrak m^ k$ with a finite-dimensional vector space. By the integral formula for the coefficients in ( 5.2.1 ), the Taylor coefficients of $f_ l$ at $x$ converge to those of $f$, so the images of the $f_ l$ in $R/\mathfrak m^ k$ converge to the image of $f$. The image of $J$ there is a linear subspace of a finite-dimensional vector space, hence closed, so $f\in J+\mathfrak m^ k$ for every $k$. The intersection formula with $F=R$ and $E=J$ gives $f\in J$. $\square$
