text: Lemma 6.8.2 . 8DDA48CD81CB Let $\mathcal I$ be a locally finitely generated sheaf of ideals on a connected complex manifold $W$. If $\mathcal I_ y=0$ for some $y\in W$, then $\mathcal I_ z=0$ for every $z\in W$. Proof. The set of points $z$ with $\mathcal I_ z=0$ is open: near such a point, choose sections $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ generating all stalks of $\mathcal I$ on a neighborhood; their germs at $z$ vanish, so they vanish on a neighborhood $U'$ of $z$, and $\mathcal I$ has zero stalks on $U'$. The set of points with $\mathcal I_ z\neq 0$ is open as well: a section with nonzero germ at $z$, defined on a connected neighborhood of $z$, has nonzero germs at all points of this neighborhood, by the identity theorem. Since $W$ is connected, one of the two sets is empty. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.8.3
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text: Lemma 6.8.3 . 9B47698DCA71 Let $n\geq 1$, let $W'\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ be open, let $\Delta =\{ w\in \mathbb C:|w|<r\} $, and let \[  P(z',w)=w^\mu +a_1(z')w^{\mu -1}+\cdots +a_\mu (z'),\qquad \mu \geq 1,  \] with $a_1,\ldots ,a_\mu $ holomorphic on $W'$, such that for some $\rho <r$ all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in W'$, lie in the disc $|w|\leq \rho $. Put $D=W'\times \Delta $ and $Z=\{ P=0\} \subset D$, let $\pi \colon D\to W'$ be the projection, and let $P\mathcal O_ D$ be the ideal generated by $P$. Let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf of $\mathcal O_ D$-modules with $\mathcal G_ z=0$ for $z\in D\setminus Z$. Then for every $b\in W'$ the map \[  (\pi _*\mathcal G)_ b\to \bigoplus _{z\in Z\cap \pi ^{-1}(b)}\mathcal G_ z,  \] which sends the germ at $b$ of a section over $V'\times \Delta $ to its germs at the points of the fiber, is bijective. The morphism $\Phi \colon \mathcal O_{W'}^\mu \to \pi _*(\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D)$ that sends $(c_0,\ldots ,c_{\mu -1})$ to the class of $\sum _ kc_ kw^ k$ is an isomorphism. Let $\mathcal I\subset \mathcal O_ D$ be a coherent ideal with $P\in \mathcal I(D)$, and let $\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D$ denote its image in $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$. Then $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)=\Phi ^{-1}(\pi _*(\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D))$ is a coherent subsheaf of $\mathcal O_{W'}^\mu $. If $\mathcal I'$ is a second such ideal and $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)=\mathcal M(\mathcal I')$ on an open set $V'\subset W'$, then $\mathcal I=\mathcal I'$ on $V'\times \Delta $. Proof. For $z'\in W'$, the polynomial $P(z',\cdot )$ has at most $\mu $ roots, all in $\Delta $; so the fibers of $Z$ over $W'$ are finite. We first describe $Z$ near a fiber. Let $b\in W'$, let $w_1,\ldots ,w_ l$ be the distinct roots of $P(b,\cdot )$, and put $z_ i=(b,w_ i)$. Let $\delta >0$ be so small that the closed discs $|w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta $ are pairwise disjoint and contained in $\Delta $. The function $|P|$ is continuous and positive on the compact set $\{ b\} \times K$, where $K=\{ |w|\leq \rho \} \setminus \bigcup _ i\{ |w-w_ i|<\delta \} $; hence it is positive on $V_ b\times K$ for a neighborhood $V_ b$ of $b$, and for $z'\in V_ b$ all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ lie in $\bigcup _ i\{ |w-w_ i|<\delta \} $. Put $B_ i=V_ b\times \{ |w-w_ i|<2\delta \} $. These open sets are pairwise disjoint, and $Z\cap (V_ b\times \Delta )\subset \bigcup _ iB_ i$. Moreover, given neighborhoods $N_ i$ of the points $z_ i$, we can achieve $V_ b\times \{ |w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta \} \subset N_ i$ for all $i$: first decrease $\delta $ so that $\{ b\} \times \{ |w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta \} \subset N_ i$, and then decrease $V_ b$, using the compactness of these discs. We call such $\delta $ and $V_ b$ adapted to $b$; a smaller neighborhood of $b$ remains adapted. (1) Let $s$ be a section of $\mathcal G$ over $V'\times \Delta $ whose germs at all the $z_ i$ vanish. Then $s$ vanishes on neighborhoods $N_ i$ of the $z_ i$; choose $\delta $ and $V_ b\subset V'$ adapted to $b$ with $B_ i\subset N_ i$. The open sets $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ and $(V_ b\times \Delta )\setminus Z$ cover $V_ b\times \Delta $, and $s$ vanishes on each of them, on the last one because all stalks of $\mathcal G$ vanish there. Hence $s=0$ on $V_ b\times \Delta $, and the map is injective. Conversely, let $g_ i\in \mathcal G_{z_ i}$ be given, represented by sections $t_ i$ on neighborhoods $N_ i$ of the $z_ i$, and choose $\delta $ and $V_ b$ adapted to $b$ with $B_ i\subset N_ i$. On the open cover of $V_ b\times \Delta $ formed by the $B_ i$ and $(V_ b\times \Delta )\setminus Z$, consider the sections $t_ i|_{B_ i}$ and $0$. They agree on the overlaps: the $B_ i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $t_ i$ vanishes on $B_ i\setminus Z$, since $\mathcal G$ has zero stalks there. Gluing them, we obtain a section over $V_ b\times \Delta $ with germs $g_ i$ at the $z_ i$. Hence the map is surjective. (2) The map $\Phi $ is a morphism of sheaves of $\mathcal O_{W'}$-modules. It is injective on sections: suppose that the class of $R=\sum _{k<\mu }c_ kw^ k$ vanishes on $V'\times \Delta $, and let $z'\in V'$. If $w_0$ is a root of $P(z',\cdot )$ of multiplicity $m$, then $R=Pq$ near $(z',w_0)$ with $q$ holomorphic, so the polynomial $R(z',\cdot )=P(z',\cdot )q(z',\cdot )$ vanishes to order at least $m$ at $w_0$. Thus $R(z',\cdot )$, a polynomial of degree less than $\mu $, has at least $\mu $ zeros counted with multiplicity, and therefore vanishes; that is, $c_ k(z')=0$ for all $k$. To prove surjectivity on stalks, let $s$ be a section of $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$ over $V'\times \Delta $ and $b\in V'$. Near each $z_ i$, $s$ is the class of a holomorphic function $f_ i$ on a neighborhood $N_ i$ of $z_ i$. Choose $\delta $ and $V_ b\subset V'$ adapted to $b$ with $V_ b\times \{ |w-w_ i|\leq 2\delta \} \subset N_ i$. On the circles $|\zeta -w_ i|=2\delta $ the function $P(z',\zeta )$ does not vanish for $z'\in V_ b$, since these circles have distance at least $\delta $ from all roots. For $z'\in V_ b$ and $w\in \mathbb C$ put \[  R(z',w)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\sum _{i=1}^ l\int _{|\zeta -w_ i|=2\delta } \frac{f_ i(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )}\, \frac{P(z',\zeta )-P(z',w)}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta .  \] The difference quotient is a polynomial in $w$ of degree $\mu -1$ whose coefficients are polynomials in $\zeta $ and in the $a_ k(z')$; hence $R$ is a polynomial in $w$ of degree less than $\mu $ whose coefficients are holomorphic on $V_ b$, by differentiation under the integral sign. For $z'\in V_ b$ and $|w-w_ i|<2\delta $ put \[  q_ i(z',w)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\sum _{j=1}^ l\int _{|\zeta -w_ j|=2\delta }\frac{f_ j(z',\zeta )}{P(z',\zeta )(\zeta -w)}\, \mathrm d\zeta ,  \] a holomorphic function on $B_ i$. Adding the two integrals, we obtain \[  P(z',w)q_ i(z',w)+R(z',w)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\sum _{j=1}^ l\int _{|\zeta -w_ j|=2\delta }\frac{f_ j(z',\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, \mathrm d\zeta =f_ i(z',w),  \] since the term $j=i$ equals $f_ i(z',w)$ by Cauchy's formula, and the terms $j\neq i$ vanish by Cauchy's theorem, the point $w$ lying outside the closed disc $|\zeta -w_ j|\leq 2\delta $. Hence $f_ i\equiv R$ modulo $P$ on $B_ i$, so $s$ and the class of $R$ agree on each $B_ i$; on $(V_ b\times \Delta )\setminus Z$ both vanish, since $P$ is a unit there. Thus $s=\Phi (c)$ on $V_ b\times \Delta $, where $c$ is the tuple of coefficients of $R$. Being injective, and surjective on all stalks, $\Phi $ is an isomorphism. (3) The sheaf $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)$ is a subsheaf of $\mathcal O_{W'}$-modules of $\mathcal O_{W'}^\mu $. Since $\mathcal O_{W'}$ is coherent (theorem 9.2.7 ), the last assertion of lemma 9.2.6 shows that it suffices to prove that $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)$ is locally finitely generated. Note that $\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D$ has zero stalks off $Z$, because $P$ is a unit there; so (1) applies to it as well as to $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$. Fix $b\in W'$, with $z_ i$ as above. Since $\mathcal I$ is coherent, there are neighborhoods $N_ i$ of $z_ i$ and sections $f_{i1},\ldots ,f_{i\kappa }$ of $\mathcal I$ over $N_ i$ generating all stalks of $\mathcal I$ on $N_ i$. Choose $\delta $ and $V_ b$ adapted to $b$ with $B_ i\subset N_ i$. For $1\leq i\leq l$, $1\leq \lambda \leq \kappa $ and $0\leq m<\mu $, let $\sigma _{i\lambda m}$ be the section of $\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D$ over $V_ b\times \Delta $ that equals the class of $w^ mf_{i\lambda }$ on $B_ i$ and $0$ on the other $B_ j$ and on $(V_ b\times \Delta )\setminus Z$. As in (1), these local sections glue, since the $B_ j$ are pairwise disjoint and the class of $w^ mf_{i\lambda }$ vanishes on $B_ i\setminus Z$, where $P$ is a unit. We claim that the sections $\Phi ^{-1}(\sigma _{i\lambda m})$ of $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)$ over $V_ b$ generate all its stalks. Let $b'\in V_ b$, and let $y_1,\ldots ,y_ p$ be the points of $Z$ over $b'$; each of them lies in exactly one $B_ i$. By (1), every element of $\pi _*(\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D)_{b'}$ is a sum of elements $e$ whose germs vanish at all points of the fiber except one point $y_ q$, where the germ is some $g\in (\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D)_{y_ q}$. Let $y_ q\in B_ i$, and write $g$ as the class of $\sum _\lambda h_\lambda f_{i\lambda }$ with germs $h_\lambda $ at $y_ q$. By (1) for $\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D$ and by (2), for each $\lambda $ there is $c^{(\lambda )}\in \mathcal O_{W',b'}^\mu $ such that $R_\lambda =\sum _ mc^{(\lambda )}_ mw^ m$ is congruent to $h_\lambda $ modulo $P$ at $y_ q$ and to $0$ modulo $P$ at the other points of the fiber. Then the element $\sum _{\lambda ,m}c^{(\lambda )}_ m\sigma _{i\lambda m}$ of $\pi _*(\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D)_{b'}$ has the germ $g$ at $y_ q$ and the germ $0$ at every other point of the fiber: at the other points in $B_ i$ its germ is the class of $\sum _\lambda R_\lambda f_{i\lambda }\in P\mathcal O_ D$, and at the points outside $B_ i$ it vanishes by construction. By the injectivity in (1), it equals $e$. This proves the claim, and $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)$ is coherent. Finally, let $\mathcal M(\mathcal I)=\mathcal M(\mathcal I')$ on $V'$, and let $z\in V'\times \Delta $. If $z\notin Z$, then $\mathcal I_ z=\mathcal O_{D,z}=\mathcal I'_ z$, since $P$ is a unit at $z$. Let $z\in Z$, $b=\pi (z)$, and $f\in \mathcal I_ z$. By (1), there is an element of $\pi _*(\mathcal O_ D/P\mathcal O_ D)_ b$ whose germ at $z$ is the class of $f$ and whose germs at the other points of the fiber vanish. It belongs to $\pi _*(\mathcal I/P\mathcal O_ D)_ b=\Phi (\mathcal M(\mathcal I)_ b)=\Phi (\mathcal M(\mathcal I')_ b)=\pi _*(\mathcal I'/P\mathcal O_ D)_ b$, so its germ at $z$ belongs to $(\mathcal I'/P\mathcal O_ D)_ z$. Hence $f\in \mathcal I'_ z+P\mathcal O_{D,z}=\mathcal I'_ z$. By symmetry, $\mathcal I_ z=\mathcal I'_ z$. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.8.4 (Strong Noetherian property)
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text: Lemma 6.8.4 (Strong Noetherian property) . 4C0C502048AA Let $\mathcal F$ be a coherent analytic sheaf on $X$. Every increasing sequence $\mathcal F_1\subset \mathcal F_2\subset \cdots $ of coherent subsheaves of $\mathcal F$ is stationary near every point: each $x\in X$ has a neighborhood $U$ such that $\mathcal F_ j|_ U=\mathcal F_{j_0}|_ U$ for all $j\geq j_0$, for some index $j_0$. Consequently, on each compact subset of $X$ the sequence is stationary after one sufficiently large index. In particular, a sheaf of ideals generated by countably many holomorphic functions on $X$ is coherent, and near each point it is generated by finitely many of these functions, forming an initial segment of the sequence. Proof. The assertion on compact sets follows from the local one by covering a compact set with finitely many of the neighborhoods $U$ and taking the largest of the corresponding indices. To prove the local assertion at a point $x$, note that $\mathcal F$, being locally finitely generated, is near $x$ the image of a surjective morphism $\phi \colon \mathcal O^ r\to \mathcal F$ defined by finitely many generators. The inverse images $\phi ^{-1}(\mathcal F_ j)$ form an increasing sequence of subsheaves of $\mathcal O^ r$, and they are coherent by lemma 9.2.6 , being the kernels of the morphisms $\mathcal O^ r\to \mathcal F/\mathcal F_ j$ between coherent sheaves; here $\mathcal O^ r$ is coherent by theorem 9.2.7 . Since $\mathcal F_ j=\phi (\phi ^{-1}(\mathcal F_ j))$, the sequence $(\mathcal F_ j)$ is stationary wherever $(\phi ^{-1}(\mathcal F_ j))$ is. We may therefore assume that $\mathcal F=\mathcal O^ r$, and we reduce to the case of ideals, $r=1$, by induction on $r$. Let $p\colon \mathcal O^ r\to \mathcal O$ be the projection to the last coordinate. The images $p(\mathcal F_ j)$ form an increasing sequence of coherent ideals, and the kernels $\mathcal F_ j\cap (\mathcal O^{r-1}\oplus 0)$ of $p|_{\mathcal F_ j}$ form an increasing sequence of coherent subsheaves of $\mathcal O^{r-1}$, by lemma 9.2.6 . Suppose that both sequences are constant for $j\geq j_0$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $x$. If $\sigma $ is a germ of $\mathcal F_ j$ at a point of $U$, with $j\geq j_0$, choose a germ $\sigma '$ of $\mathcal F_{j_0}$ with $p(\sigma ')=p(\sigma )$; then $\sigma -\sigma '$ lies in the kernel for the index $j$, which equals the kernel for $j_0$, so $\sigma \in \mathcal F_{j_0}$. Thus $\mathcal F_ j=\mathcal F_{j_0}$ on $U$. For ideals $\mathcal I_1\subset \mathcal I_2\subset \cdots $ we argue by induction on the dimension $n$ of $X$ at $x$; by the reduction just made, the induction hypothesis applies to coherent subsheaves of $\mathcal O^\mu $ in dimension $n-1$. In dimension zero, $x$ is an open point of $X$ and the only ideals of $\mathcal O_{X,x}=\mathbb C$ are $0$ and $\mathbb C$, so the increasing sequence $(\mathcal I_{j,x})$ is eventually constant, and $U=\{ x\} $ has the required property. Let $n\geq 1$, and let $W$ be a connected coordinate neighborhood of $x$. If all stalks $\mathcal I_{j,x}$ vanish, then all $\mathcal I_ j$ vanish on $W$ by lemma 6.8.2 , and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise some $\mathcal I_{j_1}$ has a nonzero germ $g$ at $x$. After a linear change of coordinates $z=(z',w)$ centered at $x$, in which $g$ is distinguished in $w$ (section 9.2 ), the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 5.5.2 ) shows that $g$ is a unit times a Weierstrass polynomial $P(z',w)$ of some degree $\mu $, so that the germ of $P$ belongs to $\mathcal I_{j_1,x}$. If $\mu =0$, then $g$ is a unit, the section $1=g\cdot g^{-1}$ belongs to $\mathcal I_{j_1}$ near $x$, and $\mathcal I_ j$ is the unit ideal near $x$ for all $j\geq j_1$. Let $\mu \geq 1$. By ( 9.2.1 ) the roots of $P(z',\cdot )$ tend to $0$ as $z'\to 0$, so there is a product $D=W'\times \Delta \subset W$ of a polydisc $W'\subset \mathbb C^{n-1}$ centered at $0$ and a disc $\Delta =\{ |w|<r\} $ such that the coefficients of $P$ are holomorphic on $W'$, $P$ is a section of $\mathcal I_{j_1}$ over $D$, and all roots of $P(z',\cdot )$, $z'\in W'$, lie in $\{ |w|\leq \rho \} $ for some $\rho <r$. For $j\geq j_1$ the ideals $\mathcal I_ j|_ D$ contain $P$, and by lemma 6.8.3 (3) the sheaves $\mathcal M(\mathcal I_ j|_ D)$ form an increasing sequence of coherent subsheaves of $\mathcal O_{W'}^\mu $. By the induction hypothesis, they are constant for $j\geq j_0$ on a neighborhood $V'$ of $0$, for some $j_0\geq j_1$, and lemma 6.8.3 (3) gives $\mathcal I_ j=\mathcal I_{j_0}$ on the neighborhood $V'\times \Delta $ of $x$ for all $j\geq j_0$. This proves the local assertion. Finally, let $h_1,h_2,\ldots $ be holomorphic functions on $X$. The ideals $\mathcal J_ j$ generated by $h_1,\ldots ,h_ j$ are locally finitely generated subsheaves of $\mathcal O$, hence coherent by theorem 9.2.7 , lemma 9.2.6 , and the stalk at $y$ of the ideal $\mathcal J$ generated by all the $h_ l$ is the union of the stalks $\mathcal J_{j,y}$. By the local assertion, every point has a neighborhood $U$ and an index $j_0$ with $\mathcal J_ j=\mathcal J_{j_0}$ on $U$ for $j\geq j_0$; then $\mathcal J=\mathcal J_{j_0}$ on $U$. Hence $\mathcal J$ is coherent, and near each point it is generated by $h_1,\ldots ,h_{j_0}$. $\square$

title: Definition 6.8.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text: Definition 6.8.5 . 990C506B7D25 Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$. Its multiplier ideal is the subsheaf $\mathcal I(\varphi )\subset \mathcal O_ X$ with stalks \[  \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x =\{ f\in \mathcal O_{X,x}: |f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi } \text{ is integrable near }x\} .  \] Here $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is taken to be $0$ where $f=0$, so the zero germ always belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The same definition applies to a function $\varphi $ that is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component, as happens for restrictions of weights; where $\varphi $ is identically $-\infty $, the multiplier ideal is zero. Definition 6.8.5 . 990C506B7D25 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, the multiplier ideal sheaf $\mathcal{I}(\varphi )$  of $\varphi $ is by definition the ideal sheaf given by \[  \Gamma \left(U,\mathcal{I}(\varphi )\right)=\left\{  f\in \mathcal{O}_ X(U) : |f|^2\exp (-\varphi )\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U) \right\}   \] for any open subset $U\subseteq X$. Definition 6.8.5 . 990C506B7D25 Let $\mathcal O_ X$ denote the sheaf of holomorphic functions on $X$. For a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $X$, the multiplier ideal $\mathcal I(u)\subseteq \mathcal O_ X$ is the ideal sheaf whose sections over an open set $U$ are the holomorphic functions $g$ on $U$ for which $|g|^2\mathrm{e}^{-u}$ is locally integrable on $U$ with respect to a smooth positive volume form. Its stalk at $x$ is denoted by $\mathcal I(u)_ x$.

title: Lemma 6.8.6
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text: Lemma 6.8.6 . E20924A743CA Let $F$ be a holomorphic function on an open set $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$. If $\overline{B(y,\delta )}\subset D$, then 69805453021C 6.8.7 \begin{equation}  |F(y)|^2\leq \frac1{|B(y,\delta )|}\int _{B(y,\delta )}|F|^2\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Let $x\in D$, suppose that the germ of $F$ at $x$ is not zero, and let $P_ k\neq 0$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of the expansion of $F$ at $x$. Then for all sufficiently small $t>0$ D76FBA2B036A 6.8.8 \begin{equation}  \int _{S^{2n-1}}|F(x+t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )\geq t^{2k}\int _{S^{2n-1}}|P_ k|^2\, \mathrm dS, \qquad \int _{S^{2n-1}}|P_ k|^2\, \mathrm dS>0. \end{equation} Proof. (1) The function $F$ is smooth with $\Delta F=4\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j}F=0$, by ( 5.2.9 ); so its real and imaginary parts are harmonic and have the ball mean value property (proposition 3.1.5 ). Thus $F(y)$ is the mean of $F$ over $B(y,\delta )$, and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives ( 6.8.7 ). (2) Homogeneous polynomials $P_ l$, $P_{l'}$ of different degrees are orthogonal in $L^2$ of the unit sphere: $P_ l(\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\omega )=\mathrm e^{\mathrm il\theta }P_ l(\omega )$, and surface measure is invariant under the orthogonal maps $\omega \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\omega $ (subsection 3.1.1 ), so $\int _{S^{2n-1}}P_ l\overline{P_{l'}}\, \mathrm dS=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(l-l')\theta }\int _{S^{2n-1}}P_ l\overline{P_{l'}}\, \mathrm dS$ for every $\theta $. For small $t>0$ the homogeneous expansion $F(x+t\omega )=\sum _ lt^ lP_ l(\omega )$ converges uniformly in $\omega \in S^{2n-1}$, by ( 5.2.1 ); integrating term by term, we obtain $\int _{S^{2n-1}}|F(x+t\omega )|^2\, \mathrm dS(\omega )=\sum _{l\geq k}t^{2l}\int _{S^{2n-1}}|P_ l|^2\, \mathrm dS$, which implies the first inequality. The last integral is positive, because $P_ k$ does not vanish identically on the sphere, by homogeneity, and nonempty relatively open subsets of the sphere have positive surface measure. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.8.9
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.8 Coherent ideals from weighted integrability
text: Theorem 6.8.9 . FE623FA661C4 For every weight $\varphi $ on $X$, the sheaf $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is coherent. More precisely, let $\Omega \subset X$ be an open set that a holomorphic chart identifies with a bounded open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, pseudoconvex if $n\geq 1$; for instance, $\Omega $ may be a bounded polydisc in a chart (corollary 6.3.5 ). Let $\varrho $ be a measurable function on $\Omega $ with $c_\varrho \leq \varrho \leq C_\varrho $ for positive constants $c_\varrho $ and $C_\varrho $, and let \[  \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )=\Bigl \{ F\in \mathcal O(\Omega ): \| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }^2=\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV<\infty \Bigr \} ,  \] with the inner product $\langle F,G\rangle _{\varphi ,\varrho }=\int _\Omega F\bar G\, \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV$, where $\mathrm dV$ is Lebesgue measure in the chart (the counting measure if $n=0$). For $\varrho =1$ we write $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega )$, $\| \cdot \| _\varphi $ and $\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle _\varphi $. Then the following hold. For every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ there is a constant $C_ K$ such that $|F(z)|\leq C_ K\| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }$ for all $F\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ and $z\in K$. The space $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ is a separable Hilbert space. It has orthonormal bases, that is, orthonormal families whose linear span is dense, and each of them is finite or countable. If $(e_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ is an enumeration of an orthonormal basis and $F\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$, then the partial sums $\sum _{j\leq N}\langle F,e_ j\rangle _{\varphi ,\varrho }e_ j$ converge to $F$ in norm and locally uniformly on $\Omega $, and $\sum _ j|\langle F,e_ j\rangle _{\varphi ,\varrho }|^2=\| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }^2$. The sheaf $\mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega $ is generated by the germs of the elements of $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$. In fact, if $(e_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ is as in (2), then the functions $e_ j$ generate $\mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega $, and near each point of $\Omega $ already an initial segment $e_1,\ldots ,e_ k$ generates it. Proof. If $n=0$, then $\Omega $ is empty, and there is nothing to prove, or a point $x$; in the latter case $\varphi (x)$ is finite, $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )=\mathbb C$, and $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x=\mathbb C$ is generated by every nonzero element, so all assertions are immediate. Assume therefore $n\geq 1$, and write $\mathcal H$, $\| \cdot \| $ and $\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle $ for $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$, its norm and its inner product. In the chart, $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ (section 5.9 ). We prove (1) and (2) by Hilbert space arguments, and (3) by solving a $\bar\partial $-equation with a weight that has a logarithmic pole. We first prove (1). Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, let $r>0$ be half the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, and let $M$ be the maximum of the upper semicontinuous function $\varphi $ on the compact set $K_ r=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\leq r\} \subset \Omega $. Since $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \geq c_\varrho \mathrm e^{-M}$ on $K_ r$, the inequality ( 6.8.7 ) on $\overline{B(z,r)}\subset K_ r$ gives, for $z\in K$ and $F\in \mathcal H$, \[  |F(z)|^2\leq \frac1{|B(z,r)|}\int _{B(z,r)}|F|^2\, \mathrm dV\leq \frac{\mathrm e^ M}{c_\varrho |B(z,r)|}\| F\| ^2.  \] This proves (1). Next we show that $\mathcal H$ is a separable Hilbert space. The measurable function $\varphi -\log \varrho $ is bounded above on compact subsets of $\Omega $, and $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi +\log \varrho })$ is the $L^2$ space of the measure $\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\varrho \, \mathrm dV$. By lemma 6.4.10 (2), applied to this function, the elements of this space that are represented by holomorphic functions form a closed subspace. A holomorphic function is determined by its class, since continuous functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere; hence $\mathcal H$ is identified with this closed subspace and is a Hilbert space. Multiplication by $\mathrm e^{-\varphi /2}\varrho ^{1/2}$ maps $L^2(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\varphi +\log \varrho })$ isometrically into $L^2(\Omega )$, since $\varphi $ is locally integrable (theorem 5.9.1 ) and hence finite almost everywhere. The space $L^2(\Omega )$ is separable: by lemma 2.5.1 (5), $C_ c(\Omega )$ is dense in it. Let $\mathcal S$ be the countable set of functions that take constant values in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ on finitely many half-open cubes $\prod _{i=1}^{2n}[m_ i2^{-k},(m_ i+1)2^{-k})$, $m_ i\in \mathbb Z$, $k\geq 1$, whose closures lie in $\Omega $, and vanish elsewhere. Let $g\in C_ c(\Omega )$. For large $k$, the cubes of side $2^{-k}$ of this form that meet $\operatorname{Supp}g$ lie in a fixed compact subset $K'$ of $\Omega $. Assigning to each of them a value in $\mathbb Q+\mathrm i\mathbb Q$ within $2^{-k}$ of the value of $g$ at one of its points, we obtain $s_ k\in \mathcal S$ vanishing outside $K'$ with $\sup |g-s_ k|\leq 2^{-k}+\sup \{ |g(y)-g(y')|:|y-y'|\leq \sqrt{2n}\, 2^{-k}\} $, which tends to zero by uniform continuity of $g$; hence $s_ k\to g$ in $L^2(\Omega )$, and $\mathcal S$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega )$. A subset of a separable metric space is separable, so $\mathcal H$ is separable. Orthonormal bases of $\mathcal H$ exist: applying the Gram–Schmidt process to a countable dense sequence and discarding the vectors that depend linearly on the preceding ones, we obtain an orthonormal family whose linear span contains the dense sequence. Every orthonormal family is finite or countable, because two of its members have distance $\sqrt2$, so that the balls of radius $1/2$ around them are disjoint, and each of these balls contains a member of a fixed countable dense set. Let $(e_ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be an enumeration of an orthonormal basis, let $F\in \mathcal H$, and put $c_ j=\langle F,e_ j\rangle $ and $S_ N=\sum _{j\leq N}c_ je_ j$. Since $F-S_ N$ is orthogonal to the span $V_ N$ of $e_1,\ldots ,e_ N$, every $v\in V_ N$ satisfies $\| F-v\| ^2=\| F-S_ N\| ^2+\| S_ N-v\| ^2\geq \| F-S_ N\| ^2$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, there is $v$ in some $V_{N_0}$ with $\| F-v\| <\varepsilon $, and since $V_{N_0}\subset V_ N$ for $N\geq N_0$, we get $\| F-S_ N\| <\varepsilon $ for all $N\geq N_0$. Thus $S_ N\to F$ in $\mathcal H$, and hence locally uniformly on $\Omega $, by (1). Taking $v=0$ above gives $\| F\| ^2=\| F-S_ N\| ^2+\sum _{j\leq N}|c_ j|^2$, and letting $N\to \infty $ we obtain $\sum _ j|c_ j|^2=\| F\| ^2$. This proves (2). We turn to (3). Let $\mathcal J$ be the ideal sheaf on $\Omega $ generated by the $e_ j$. By lemma 6.8.4 it is coherent and near each point generated by an initial segment $e_1,\ldots ,e_ k$. Every $F\in \mathcal H$ is the locally uniform limit of the partial sums $S_ N$, whose germs lie in $\mathcal J$, so the germs of $F$ lie in $\mathcal J$ by lemma 6.8.1 . Thus $\mathcal J$ is the ideal generated by $\mathcal H$, independently of the basis, and $\mathcal J\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega $ because $\int _\Omega |F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV\leq c_\varrho ^{-1}\| F\| ^2$ for $F\in \mathcal H$. It remains to prove that $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x\subset \mathcal J_ x$ for $x\in \Omega $. Fix $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and an integer $s\geq 0$; we construct $F\in \mathcal H$ with $f-F\in \mathfrak m_ x^{s+1}$, where $\mathfrak m_ x$ is the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Choose a cutoff function $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, equal to one near $x$, such that $f$ is holomorphic and $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. The $(0,1)$-form $\alpha =f\bar\partial \chi $, extended by zero, is smooth, $\bar\partial $-closed and vanishes near $x$. We apply theorem 6.4.9 on the pseudoconvex set $\Omega $ with the plurisubharmonic function $p=\varphi +(n+s)\log |z-x|^2$ (proposition 5.10.3 , proposition 5.9.5 ) and the smooth function $q=|z|^2$, whose complex Hessian is the identity matrix. Since $|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}$ and $|\bar\partial \chi |$ are bounded on the support of $\alpha $, we have $\int _\Omega |\alpha |^2\mathrm e^{-p-q}\, \mathrm dV\leq C\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\chi }|f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Hence there is $u$ with $\bar\partial u=\alpha $ and \[  \int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi -|z|^2}|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}\, \mathrm dV<\infty .  \] Since $\mathrm e^{-p-q}$ is bounded below by a positive constant on compact sets, $u$ is locally square integrable. Near $x$ we have $\bar\partial u=0$, so, by lemma 6.4.10 (1), $u$ agrees almost everywhere near $x$ with a holomorphic function; we replace $u$ by this function near $x$. We claim that $u$ vanishes to order at least $s+1$ at $x$. Since $\varphi $ is bounded above near $x$, the last display gives $\int _{B(x,r)}|u|^2|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}\, \mathrm dV<\infty $ for small $r>0$. We may assume that the germ of $u$ at $x$ is not zero, and we let $P_{k_0}\neq 0$ be the first nonzero homogeneous term of its expansion at $x$. Applying ( 6.8.8 ) of lemma 6.8.6 to $u$ and integrating in polar coordinates ( 3.1.2 ), we obtain \[  \int _{B(x,r)}|u|^2|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}\, \mathrm dV\geq c\int _0^ rt^{2k_0-2s-1}\, \mathrm dt  \] with $c>0$. This is finite only if $k_0\geq s+1$, which proves the claim. Since $\Omega $ is bounded, $\mathrm e^{-|z|^2}|z-x|^{-2(n+s)}$ is bounded below on $\Omega $ by a positive constant, so $|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable on $\Omega $. The function $\chi f-u$ satisfies $\bar\partial (\chi f-u)=\alpha -\alpha =0$, so it agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function $F$ on $\Omega $, by lemma 6.4.10 (1). Since $|F|^2\leq 2|\chi f|^2+2|u|^2$ almost everywhere, $|\chi f|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ is integrable by the choice of $\chi $, and $\varrho \leq C_\varrho $, we have $F\in \mathcal H$. Near $x$ the continuous functions $f-F$ and $u$ agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere, so $f-F=u\in \mathfrak m_ x^{s+1}$ by section 9.2 . Thus $f\in \mathcal J_ x+\mathfrak m_ x^{s+1}$ for every $s$, and lemma 6.8.1 gives $f\in \mathcal J_ x$. Hence $\mathcal I(\varphi )|_\Omega =\mathcal J$, which proves (3). Finally, every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $\Omega $ of the kind considered, namely a bounded polydisc in a chart. If $n\geq 1$, such a polydisc is pseudoconvex by corollary 6.3.5 , being a product of discs, each of which is a sublevel set of the smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion function $|\zeta -\zeta _0|^2$ of $\mathbb C$, where $\zeta _0$ is its center. By (3), $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ is generated near each point by finitely many holomorphic functions, so it is coherent by theorem 9.2.7 and the last assertion of lemma 9.2.6 . $\square$

text: Lemma 6.8.10 . 3B37857D5B64 Let $\varphi $, $\Omega $, $\varrho $ and $\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ be as in theorem 6.8.9 , let $x\in \Omega $, and let $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ be elements whose germs generate $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Then there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x$ and a constant $C$ such that every $F\in \mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ can be written as $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V$ with $h_ i\in \mathcal O(V)$ and \[  \sup _ V|h_ i|\leq C\| F\| _{\varphi ,\varrho }.  \] Consequently, if $m>0$ is real and $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ generate $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ on a neighborhood of $x$, then there is a constant $C_ m$ such that 11D2B663BB36 6.8.11 \begin{equation}  \varphi \leq \frac1m\log \sum _ i|g_ i|^2+C_ m \end{equation} on a neighborhood of $x$, with the convention $\log 0=-\infty $. Proof. We write $\mathcal H=\mathcal H_\varphi (\Omega ,\varrho )$ and $\| \cdot \| =\| \cdot \| _{\varphi ,\varrho }$. Choose balls $V_1\supset V_2\supset \cdots $ centered at $x$, with radii tending to zero, inside the neighborhood on which the $g_ i$ generate $\mathcal I(\varphi )$. For positive integers $j$ and $k$ let $S_{j,k}$ be the set of $F\in \mathcal H$ that can be written as $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V_ j$ with $h_ i\in \mathcal O(V_ j)$ and $\sup _{V_ j}|h_ i|\leq k$. These sets cover $\mathcal H$: by theorem 6.8.9 (3), the germ at $x$ of each $F\in \mathcal H$ lies in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$, so $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on some neighborhood of $x$ with holomorphic $h_ i$, and these coefficients are bounded on a smaller ball $V_ j$. We show that each $S_{j,k}$ is closed and then apply Baire's theorem. Let $F_ l\in S_{j,k}$ converge to $F$ in $\mathcal H$, with coefficients $h_{i,l}$. Then $F_ l\to F$ locally uniformly on $\Omega $, by theorem 6.8.9 (1). The coefficients are bounded by $k$ on $V_ j$. Let $K\subset V_ j$ be compact, and let $\varepsilon >0$ be such that the closed polydiscs of radius $2\varepsilon $ centered at points of $K$ lie in $V_ j$. For $y\in K$ and $y'\in B(y,\varepsilon )$, the closed polydisc of radius $\varepsilon $ centered at $y'$ then lies in $V_ j$, and the coefficient bound in ( 5.2.1 ) on this polydisc bounds all first partial derivatives of all $h_{i,l}$ at $y'$ by $k/\varepsilon $. So the $h_{i,l}$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on the balls of radius $\varepsilon $ centered at points of $K$, and they are equicontinuous on $K$. By proposition 2.7.4 , applied on a compact exhaustion of $V_ j$, and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $V_ j$ to continuous functions $h_ i$ with $|h_ i|\leq k$. Locally uniform convergence implies convergence in the sense of distributions, so $\bar\partial h_ i=0$, and the continuous functions $h_ i$ are holomorphic by lemma 6.4.10 (1) (if $n=0$, every function on $V_ j$ is holomorphic). Passing to the limit, we obtain $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V_ j$, that is, $F\in S_{j,k}$. By Baire's theorem, a complete metric space is not a countable union of closed subsets with empty interior. (If all the sets had empty interior, we could choose closed balls of radii at most $2^{-l}$, each contained in the interior of the previous one and disjoint from the $l$th set, since the interior of a ball minus a closed set with empty interior is a nonempty open set; their centers would form a Cauchy sequence whose limit lies in every ball but in none of the sets.) Hence some $S_{j,k}$ contains a ball $\{ F:\| F-F_0\| <\delta \} $. If $\| F\| <\delta $, then $F_0$ and $F_0+F$ both lie in $S_{j,k}$, and subtracting their representations writes $F$ on $V_ j$ with coefficients bounded by $2k$. For $F\neq 0$ we apply this to $\delta F/(2\| F\| )$ and obtain the first assertion with $V=V_ j$ and $C=4k/\delta $; for $F=0$ we take zero coefficients. For the second assertion, apply the first part with $\varrho =1$ to the weight $m\varphi $, and let $V$ and $C$ be the resulting neighborhood and constant. Let $a\in V$ with $\varphi (a)>-\infty $. By corollary 6.5.8 , applied on the pseudoconvex set $\Omega $ to the plurisubharmonic function $m\varphi $, there is $F\in \mathcal H_{m\varphi }(\Omega )$ with $F(a)=1$ and $\| F\| _{m\varphi }^2\leq C_\Omega \mathrm e^{-m\varphi (a)}$, where $C_\Omega $ depends only on $n$ and the diameter of $\Omega $; if $n=0$, then $F=1$ has these properties with $C_\Omega =1$. Writing $F=\sum _ ig_ ih_ i$ on $V$ and using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain \[  1=|F(a)|^2\leq rC^2\| F\| _{m\varphi }^2\sum _ i|g_ i(a)|^2 \leq rC^2C_\Omega \mathrm e^{-m\varphi (a)}\sum _ i|g_ i(a)|^2.  \] Taking logarithms gives ( 6.8.11 ) at $a$ with $C_ m=m^{-1}\log (rC^2C_\Omega )$. At points where $\varphi =-\infty $ the left side is $-\infty $; by the last display, these points include all common zeros of the $g_ i$. $\square$

u (v,x)=
u (v',x)$ by proposition 6.7.1 . If $X$ has dimension zero at $x$, then $v(x)$ is finite and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise let $U$ be a connected neighborhood of $x$ on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic and $|h|\leq M$ for a constant $M$. Theorem 6.9.5 (Siu) . 946909269108 Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$ and let $c>0$. Then \[  E_ c(\varphi )=\{ x\in X:

Lelong numbers vanish on components of dimension zero, so we may assume that $X$ is connected of dimension $n\geq 1$. We describe $E_ c(\varphi )$ as an intersection of analytic sets defined by the orders of the ideals $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ and then show that such an intersection is analytic. Hence for $y\in W$ we have $\operatorname {ord}_ y\mathfrak a\geq k$ if and only if $\partial ^\alpha g_ i(y)=0$ for all $i$ and all $|\alpha |<k$: the condition is necessary because the $g_ i$ belong to $\mathfrak a_ y$, and sufficient because, by the Leibniz rule, every element $\sum _ ih_ ig_ i$ then vanishes to order at least $k$ at $y$. This is a finite system of holomorphic equations, and for $k\leq 0$ the set is all of $W$. u (\varphi ,x)<c$, the upper bound gives $\operatorname {ord}_ x\mathcal I(m\varphi )\leq m
u (\varphi ,x)\leq mc-n<\lfloor mc-nfloor +1$ as soon as $m(c-
u (\varphi ,x))\geq n$. Thus $E_ c(\varphi )$ is an intersection of analytic subsets of $X$. An arbitrary intersection $A= igcap _\lambda A_\lambda $ of analytic subsets of $X$ is analytic. Since $A$ is closed, it suffices to show that each $p\in A$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $A\cap W$ is the intersection of $W$ with finitely many of the $A_\lambda $. Let $I_\lambda \subset \mathcal O_{X,p}$ be the ideal generated by the germs at $p$ of local defining functions of $A_\lambda $. This neighborhood may depend on $\lambda $, and we now remove this dependence. The union of the other components meeting $N$ is closed and does not contain $p$, so there is an open neighborhood $W'\subset N$ of $p$ with $B\cap W'\subset B_1\cup \cdots \cup B_ l$. Fix $\lambda $ and $i$. The regular locus $(B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $B_ i$ (corollary 9.3.16 ), and its analytic subset $A_\lambda \cap (B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has nonempty interior in it, because $A_\lambda $ contains a neighborhood of $p$ in $B_ i$ and $p$ lies in the closure of $(B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By lemma 9.2.8 , $A_\lambda \cap (B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is therefore all of $(B_ i)_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and $B_ i\subset A_\lambda $ because $A_\lambda $ is closed. Therefore $B\cap W'\subset A_\lambda $ for every $\lambda $, and $A\cap W'=B\cap W'$. Applied to ( 6.9.6 ), this shows that $E_ c(\varphi )$ is analytic. By proposition 6.7.1 , $
u (\varphi ,x)=0$ at every point where $\varphi (x)>-\infty $. Thus $E_ c(\varphi )$ is contained in the pole set of $\varphi $, which has measure zero because $\varphi $ is locally integrable (theorem 5.9.1 ), and therefore has no interior points; so $E_ c(\varphi )
eq X$. Finally, let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. Every point of $X$ at which $X$ has positive dimension has a coordinate ball $U$ on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with $u$ plurisubharmonic, and $
u (T,y)=
u (u,y)$ for $y\in U$ (definition 6.7.4 ). By what we have proved, applied to the weight $u$ on $U$, the set $\{ y\in U:

u (\varphi ,x).  \] It is attained at every point of $Z$ outside a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$. Moreover, the complement in $Z$ of every countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$ is dense in $Z$; in particular, $
u (\varphi ,Z)$ is attained on a dense subset of $Z$. The same definition and conclusions apply to the Lelong numbers of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, and give the generic Lelong number $
u (T,Z)$. If $\pi \colon Y	o X$ is a smooth model of $X$ (section 9.8 ), that is, a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map from a complex manifold $Y$, and $E\subset Y$ is a prime divisor, that is, an irreducible hypersurface, we define \[  
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E).  \] This number depends only on the prime divisor over $X$ represented by $E$ (definition 9.8.4 ), not on the model. Proof. Put $\lambda =
u (\varphi ,Z)$. For every integer $j\geq 1$, theorem 6.9.5 shows that $Z\cap E_{\lambda +1/j}(\varphi )$ is an analytic subset of $Z$, and it is a proper subset by the definition of $\lambda $. At every point of $Z$ outside the union of these sets, $
u (\varphi ,x)<\lambda +1/j$ for all $j$, hence $
u (\varphi ,x)=\lambda $. We now show that the complement in $Z$ of an arbitrary countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$ is dense in $Z$; applied to the sets $Z\cap E_{\lambda +1/j}(\varphi )$, this shows that $
u (\varphi ,Z)$ is attained on a dense subset of $Z$. The density is clear if $Z$ is a point, for then the proper analytic subsets of $Z$ are empty. Let $\dim Z>0$. By corollary 9.3.16 , applied to the family consisting of $Z$ alone, $Z$ is an irreducible component of itself; so its regular locus $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a connected manifold, dense in $Z$. Let $B$ be a proper analytic subset of $Z$. Then $B\cap Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is an analytic subset of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it is proper, since otherwise the closed set $B$ would contain the closure $Z$ of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$. By lemma 9.2.8 , every point of $B\cap Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has a connected open neighborhood $U$ in $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ with a holomorphic function $g
ot\equiv 0$ on $U$ such that $B\cap U\subset \{ g=0\} $; shrinking $U$ to a coordinate ball, on which $g
ot\equiv 0$ by the identity theorem, we see from lemma 5.5.1 that $B\cap U$ is a null set in the chart. Covering a chart $N$ of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ by countably many such balls and by open sets disjoint from $B$, we see that $B\cap N$ is a null set. Consequently, a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $Z$ meets every chart of $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$ in a null set, which has no interior points. Its complement is therefore dense in $Z_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and hence in $Z$. For a closed positive $(1,1)$-current the same argument applies, since theorem 6.9.5 holds for its Lelong numbers. For the second assertion, note first that $\varphi \circ \pi $ is a weight on $Y$: by proposition 5.9.3 it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on each component of $Y$, and the second alternative is excluded. Indeed, since $\pi $ is bimeromorphic (section 9.4 ), there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $A\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is nowhere dense in $Y$ and $\pi $ maps $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ biholomorphically onto $X\setminus A$. If $\varphi \circ \pi $ were identically $-\infty $ on a component $Y_0$ of $Y$, then $\varphi $ would be $-\infty $ on the nonempty open set $\pi (Y_0\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A))$, which is impossible because $\varphi $ is locally integrable. Now let $E\subset Y$ and $E'\subset Y'$ be prime divisors on smooth models $\pi \colon Y	o X$ and $\pi '\colon Y'	o X$ that represent the same prime divisor over $X$, and let $ho \colon Y''	o Y$ and $ho '\colon Y''	o Y'$ be maps from a common smooth model on which the strict transforms of $E$ and $E'$ coincide, say with $E''$. By proposition 9.8.3 , $ho $ is biholomorphic over $Y\setminus S$ for an analytic subset $S\subset Y$ of codimension at least two, so it maps the nonempty open subset $E''\cap ho ^{-1}(Y\setminus S)$ of $E''$ onto the nonempty open subset $E\setminus S$ of $E$, and $
u (\varphi \circ \pi \circ ho ,q)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,ho (q))$ for $q$ in this set, because Lelong numbers are invariant under biholomorphisms (proposition 6.7.1 ). By the first part, the generic value along $E$ is attained on a dense subset of $E$, so it equals the infimum of the Lelong numbers over any nonempty open subset of $E$; the same holds for $E''$. Hence $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)=
u (\varphi \circ \pi \circ ho ,E'')$. The same argument for $ho '$ gives $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ',E')=
u (\varphi \circ \pi \circ ho ,E'')$, since $\pi \circ ho =\pi '\circ ho '$. $\square$

title: Proposition 6.9.8
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.9 Analytic Lelong level sets and generic values
text:
Proposition 6.9.8 . B720E73C2654 Let $\varphi $ be a weight on $X$, let $Z\subset X$ be a connected closed complex submanifold of positive codimension, which is an irreducible analytic subset by corollary 9.3.16 , and let $z=(z',z'')$ be local coordinates near a point of $Z$ in which $Z=\{ z'=0\} $. Then near that point \[  \varphi (z)\leq 
u (\varphi ,Z)\log |z'|^2+C,\qquad z'
eq 0,  \] for a constant $C$, and no bound of this form with a coefficient larger than $
u (\varphi ,Z)$ holds near any point of $Z$. If $\pi \colon Y	o X$ is the blowup of a point $x$ at which $X$ has positive dimension (proposition 9.6.3 ), and $E=\pi ^{-1}(x)$, then $
u (\varphi ,E)=
u (\varphi ,x)$. Proof. Let $p\in Z$ be the given point and $\lambda =
u (\varphi ,Z)$. Choose $r_0>0$, a constant $C$ and a neighborhood $W$ of $p$ in $Z$ such that for every $y\in W$ the closed ball $\overline{B(y,r_0)}$ lies in the coordinate domain and $\varphi \leq C$ on it. By ( 6.7.3 ) at $y$, we have $\varphi (z)\leq 
u (\varphi ,y)\log (|z-y|^2/r_0^2)+C$ for $0<|z-y|<r_0$. Take $z=(z',z'')$ with $y=(0,z'')\in W$ and $0<|z'|<r_0$. Then $|z-y|=|z'|$, the logarithm is negative and $
u (\varphi ,y)\geq \lambda $, so $\varphi (z)\leq \lambda \log |z'|^2-\lambda \log r_0^2+C$. This is the asserted bound, with a constant independent of $z''$. Conversely, suppose that $\varphi (z)\leq c\log |z'|^2+C'$ for $z'
eq 0$ near a point $q$ of $Z$, where we may assume $c\geq 0$. For $y\in Z$ near $q$ we have $|z'|\leq |z-y|$, so $\varphi (z)\leq c\log |z-y|^2+C'$ for $z
otin Z$ near $y$. Since $Z=\{ z'=0\} $ is a Lebesgue null set in the chart, proposition 6.7.1 gives $
u (\varphi ,y)\geq c$. By proposition 6.9.7 there are points $y$ arbitrarily close to $q$ with $
u (\varphi ,y)=\lambda $, so $c\leq \lambda $. Now let $\pi $ be the blowup of $x$, and let $n=\dim _ xX$. If $n=1$, then $\pi $ is the identity and $E=\{ x\} $, so there is nothing to prove. Let $n\geq 2$ and choose coordinates centered at $x$. The blowup is covered by $n$ charts; in the $k$th chart, $z_ k=w_ k$ and $z_ j=w_ kw_ j$ for $j
eq k$, so that \[  |z|^2=|w_ k|^2\Bigl (1+\sum _{j
eq k}|w_ j|^2\Bigr ),\qquad E=\{ w_ k=0\} .  \] By ( 6.7.3 ), $\varphi \leq 
u (\varphi ,x)\log |z|^2+C$ near $x$. Pulling back, we get $\varphi \circ \pi \leq 
u (\varphi ,x)\log |w_ k|^2+C'$ on compact subsets of the $k$th chart near $E$; since $|w_ k|$ is at most the distance to any point of $E$ in that chart, $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,q)\geq 
u (\varphi ,x)$ for every $q\in E$, and $
u (\varphi ,E)\geq 
u (\varphi ,x)$. Conversely, $E\cong \mathbb P^{n-1}$ is a compact connected submanifold of $Y$, so the first part of the proposition, applied to the weight $\varphi \circ \pi $ and $E$, gives $\varphi \circ \pi \leq 
u (\varphi ,E)\log |w_ k|^2+C$ near each point of $E$, in the coordinates of a chart containing it. Cover $E$ by finitely many such neighborhoods, on each of which $\log |w_ k|^2-\log |z|^2$ is bounded. Since $\pi $ is proper, the inverse image of a small neighborhood of $x$ lies in their union, so $\varphi (z)\leq 
u (\varphi ,E)\log |z|^2+C''$ near $x$, for $z
eq x$. Hence $
u (\varphi ,E)\leq 
u (\varphi ,x)$. $\square$

title: 6.10 Restriction, products and integral closure
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.10 Restriction, products and integral closure
text: The Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem and the Hilbert spaces of theorem 6.8.9 determine how multiplier ideals behave under restriction, products and holomorphic pullback; we also show that multiplier ideals are integrally closed. For a holomorphic map $f\colon X\to Y$ and a coherent ideal $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ Y$, we denote by $f^{-1}\mathfrak a\cdot \mathcal O_ X$ the ideal of $\mathcal O_ X$ generated by the compositions $g\circ f$ of local sections $g$ of $\mathfrak a$; it is locally generated by the compositions of local generators of $\mathfrak a$ with $f$. It is the ideal written $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_ X$ in section 9.6 ; we keep $f$ in the notation when several maps occur. For a complex submanifold $Z\subset X$ with ideal sheaf $\mathcal I_ Z$ and an ideal $\mathfrak a\subset \mathcal O_ X$, the restriction of $\mathfrak a$ to $Z$ is the image \[  \mathfrak a|_ Z^{\mathrm{im}} =\mathfrak a/(\mathfrak a\cap \mathcal I_ Z)\subset \mathcal O_ X/\mathcal I_ Z=\mathcal O_ Z,  \] that is, the ideal of restrictions $g|_ Z$ of local sections $g$ of $\mathfrak a$. Here $\mathcal O_ X/\mathcal I_ Z$ is identified with $\mathcal O_ Z$ through restriction: in local coordinates $(v,w)$ with $Z=\{ w=0\} $, every holomorphic function on $Z$ is the restriction of a function independent of $w$, and a function vanishing on $Z$ belongs to $\mathcal I_ Z$ by definition. We use the image rather than the tensor product $\mathfrak a\otimes _{\mathcal O_ X}\mathcal O_ Z$, whose natural map to $\mathcal O_ Z$ need not be injective. For instance, for $X=\mathbb C$, $Z=\{ 0\} $ and $\mathfrak a=(z)$, the element $z\otimes 1$ of the stalk at $0$ is mapped to $z|_ Z=0$, but it is not zero, since $(zf,g)\mapsto f(0)g(0)$ is a well-defined $\mathcal O_{X,0}$-balanced bilinear map $\mathfrak a_0\times \mathcal O_{Z,0}\to \mathbb C$ with value $1$ at $(z,1)$. Theorem 6.10.1 . DFD10C71D607 Let $Z\subset X$ be a complex submanifold and $\varphi $ a weight on $X$. Then 5BDE1812FA47 6.10.2 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )|_ Z^{\mathrm{im}}; \end{equation} on a connected component of $Z$ on which $\varphi |_ Z\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. If $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _2$ are weights on complex manifolds $X_1$ and $X_2$, and $p_ i\colon X_1\times X_2\to X_ i$ are the projections, then 01EC6A2D5998 6.10.3 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2) =(p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _1)\cdot \mathcal O) (p_2^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _2)\cdot \mathcal O). \end{equation} In particular, for weights $\varphi $ and $\psi $ on $X$, 0EA6BB9CDFD8 6.10.4 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi +\psi )\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi ). \end{equation} Proof. The inclusion ( 6.10.2 ) is a restatement of corollary 6.5.9 : if $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)_ x$, that corollary provides a holomorphic germ $F$ at $x$ with $F|_ Z=f$ and $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The product formula is local. Near a point $(x_1,x_2)$ we choose bounded polydiscs $\Omega _ i$ around $x_ i$ in charts of $X_ i$ on which $\varphi _ i$ is bounded above; subtracting constants, which changes none of the multiplier ideals, we may assume that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\leq 0$. We write $\Phi =\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2$, a nonpositive weight on the polydisc $\Omega _1\times \Omega _2$. Let $(e_ j)$ and $(g_ k)$ be orthonormal bases of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$ and $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, which exist by theorem 6.8.9 (2). By Fubini's theorem the functions $e_ j(z)g_ k(w)$ form an orthonormal family in $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. We show that its linear span is dense. Let $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. By Fubini's theorem, for almost every $w\in \Omega _2$ we have $\varphi _2(w)>-\infty $ and $F(\cdot ,w)\in \mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$, and for such $w$ we put \[  a_ j(w)=\int _{\Omega _1}F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)} \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}\, \mathrm dV_ z.  \] We claim that each $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with an element of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$ of norm at most $\| F\| _\Phi $. Choose compact sets $K_\ell \uparrow \Omega _1$ and put $E_\ell =K_\ell \cap \{ \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell \} $; these sets increase and exhaust $\Omega _1$ up to the pole set of $\varphi _1$, which has measure zero. The function $a_{j,\ell }$ obtained by integrating over $E_\ell $ instead of $\Omega _1$ is holomorphic on $\Omega _2$. Indeed, let $L\subset \Omega _2$ be compact. For $z\in E_\ell \subset K_\ell $ and $w\in L$, the integrand $F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)}\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}$ and all its partial derivatives in $w$ are bounded, because $F$ and its derivatives are continuous on $K_\ell \times L$, $e_ j$ is bounded on $K_\ell $, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell $ on $E_\ell $. Hence we may differentiate under the integral sign any number of times: $a_{j,\ell }$ is smooth, and $\partial a_{j,\ell }/\partial \bar w_ m=0$ for all $m$, because $F$ is holomorphic in $w$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $z$, followed by integration in $w$ against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$, \[  \| a_ j-a_{j,\ell }\| _{\varphi _2}^2 \leq \| F\| _\Phi ^2 \int _{\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell }|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\, \mathrm dV_ z \longrightarrow 0  \] by dominated convergence, since the sets $\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell $ decrease to a null set and $|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}$ is integrable. Since $\varphi _2\leq 0$, the holomorphic functions $a_{j,\ell }$ therefore converge to $a_ j$ in $L^2(\Omega _2)$, and hence in the sense of distributions; so $\bar\partial a_ j=0$, and $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, by lemma 6.4.10 (1). The same Cauchy–Schwarz estimate over all of $\Omega _1$ gives $\| a_ j\| _{\varphi _2}\leq \| F\| _\Phi $, which proves the claim. Now suppose that $F$ is orthogonal to all the products $e_ jg_ k$. By Fubini's theorem, whose use is justified by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\langle a_ j,g_ k\rangle _{\varphi _2}=\langle F,e_ jg_ k\rangle _\Phi =0$ for all $k$. Since the linear span of the $g_ k$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, the element $a_ j$ of this space is orthogonal to itself, so $a_ j=0$ almost everywhere, for every $j$. Hence for almost every $w$ all the coefficients $\langle F(\cdot ,w),e_ j\rangle _{\varphi _1}$ vanish, and $F(\cdot ,w)=0$, because $F(\cdot ,w)$ is the limit of the partial sums of its expansion (theorem 6.8.9 (2)). Thus $F=0$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, since $F$ is continuous. Consequently, the closure $M$ of the linear span of the products $e_ jg_ k$ satisfies $M^\perp =0$, and $M=\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ by proposition 6.2.1 . We can now prove ( 6.10.3 ). Denote its right side by $\mathfrak b$; it is the ideal generated by the products $(f_1\circ p_1)(f_2\circ p_2)$ of local sections $f_ i$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi _ i)$. Each product $e_ jg_ k$ is a section of $\mathfrak b$. Every $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ is the norm limit, hence by ( 6.8.7 ) the locally uniform limit, of a sequence of finite linear combinations of these products, so its germs lie in $\mathfrak b$ by lemma 6.8.1 . Since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is generated by the germs of the elements of $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ (theorem 6.8.9 (3)), we obtain $\mathcal I(\Phi )\subset \mathfrak b$. Conversely, if $|f_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ i}$ is integrable near $x_ i$ for $i=1,2$, then $|f_1(z)f_2(w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi (z,w)}$ is integrable near $(x_1,x_2)$ by Fubini's theorem; since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is an ideal, $\mathfrak b\subset \mathcal I(\Phi )$. Finally, let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be weights on $X$, and apply ( 6.10.2 ) to the weight $\varphi \circ p_1+\psi \circ p_2$ on $X\times X$ and the diagonal, which we identify with $X$. The restriction of the weight is $\varphi +\psi $, and by ( 6.10.3 ) the restriction of its multiplier ideal is generated by the products $f_1f_2$ of local sections $f_1$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ and $f_2$ of $\mathcal I(\psi )$, that is, it equals $\mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi )$. This proves ( 6.10.4 ). $\square$ Corollary 6.10.5 . 05791D2DFFAA Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a holomorphic map of complex manifolds and $\varphi $ a weight on $Y$. Then \[  \mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X,  \] with equality if $f$ is a submersion. On a connected component of $X$ on which $\varphi \circ f\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is a submersion, and let $a\in X$. Choose holomorphic coordinates $y$ on $Y$ centered at $f(a)$. Since the differential of $f$ at $a$ is surjective, the complex Jacobian matrix at $a$ of the components of $y\circ f$, computed in a chart of $X$, has rank $\dim _{f(a)}Y$. By the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 5.2.4 (3)), these components are the first coordinates of a holomorphic chart $(z,w)=(y\circ f,w)$ of $X$ near $a$. In these coordinates $f$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Thus $\varphi \circ f=\varphi \circ p_1+0\circ p_2$, and ( 6.10.3 ), together with $\mathcal I(0)=\mathcal O$, gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)=p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O=f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. In general, the graph $\Gamma =\{ (x,f(x))\} $ is a complex submanifold of $X\times Y$, since in local coordinates $(x,y)$ the functions $(x,y-f(x))$ are holomorphic coordinates in which $\Gamma =\{ y-f(x)=0\} $; and $\iota (x)=(x,f(x))$ is a biholomorphism of $X$ onto $\Gamma $. The projection $q\colon X\times Y\to Y$ is a submersion, so $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ q)=q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y}$ by the first case. Since $\varphi \circ q\circ \iota =\varphi \circ f$, ( 6.10.2 ) applied to $\Gamma $ gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset (q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y})|_\Gamma ^{\mathrm{im}}$ after transport by $\iota $. The right side is generated by the functions $g\circ q\circ \iota =g\circ f$ with $g$ a local section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, so it equals $f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. $\square$ Proposition 6.10.6 . 675539E4A76C Every multiplier ideal is integrally closed: if a germ $F\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$ satisfies an equation $F^ d+a_1F^{d-1}+\cdots +a_ d=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x^ j$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. More explicitly, if $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and a holomorphic germ $F$ satisfies $|F|\leq C(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$ near $x$ for a constant $C$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The second assertion is immediate, since $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq C^2\sum _ j|g_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ near $x$. For the first, choose generators $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ (theorem 6.8.9 ), representatives of the $g_ j$, of $F$ and of the $a_ j$ on a common neighborhood, and put $|g|=(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$. Each $a_ j$ is a finite sum of products of $j$ generators with holomorphic coefficients, which are bounded on a smaller neighborhood; hence $|a_ j|\leq C_ j|g|^ j$ there. At a point where $|g|>0$, put $\lambda =|F|/|g|$. Dividing the equation by $|g|^ d$ gives $\lambda ^ d\leq \sum _ jC_ j\lambda ^{d-j}$, which forces $\lambda \leq C$ with $C=\max \{ 1,\sum _ jC_ j\} $. At a point where $|g|=0$, all the $a_ j$ vanish, so $F^ d=0$ and $F=0$. Thus $|F|\leq C|g|$ near $x$, and the second assertion applies. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.10.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.10 Restriction, products and integral closure
text: Theorem 6.10.1 . DFD10C71D607 Let $Z\subset X$ be a complex submanifold and $\varphi $ a weight on $X$. Then 5BDE1812FA47 6.10.2 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )|_ Z^{\mathrm{im}}; \end{equation} on a connected component of $Z$ on which $\varphi |_ Z\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. If $\varphi _1$ and $\varphi _2$ are weights on complex manifolds $X_1$ and $X_2$, and $p_ i\colon X_1\times X_2\to X_ i$ are the projections, then 01EC6A2D5998 6.10.3 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2) =(p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _1)\cdot \mathcal O) (p_2^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi _2)\cdot \mathcal O). \end{equation} In particular, for weights $\varphi $ and $\psi $ on $X$, 0EA6BB9CDFD8 6.10.4 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi +\psi )\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi ). \end{equation} Proof. The inclusion ( 6.10.2 ) is a restatement of corollary 6.5.9 : if $f\in \mathcal I(\varphi |_ Z)_ x$, that corollary provides a holomorphic germ $F$ at $x$ with $F|_ Z=f$ and $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The product formula is local. Near a point $(x_1,x_2)$ we choose bounded polydiscs $\Omega _ i$ around $x_ i$ in charts of $X_ i$ on which $\varphi _ i$ is bounded above; subtracting constants, which changes none of the multiplier ideals, we may assume that $\varphi _1,\varphi _2\leq 0$. We write $\Phi =\varphi _1\circ p_1+\varphi _2\circ p_2$, a nonpositive weight on the polydisc $\Omega _1\times \Omega _2$. Let $(e_ j)$ and $(g_ k)$ be orthonormal bases of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$ and $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, which exist by theorem 6.8.9 (2). By Fubini's theorem the functions $e_ j(z)g_ k(w)$ form an orthonormal family in $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. We show that its linear span is dense. Let $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$. By Fubini's theorem, for almost every $w\in \Omega _2$ we have $\varphi _2(w)>-\infty $ and $F(\cdot ,w)\in \mathcal H_{\varphi _1}(\Omega _1)$, and for such $w$ we put \[  a_ j(w)=\int _{\Omega _1}F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)} \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}\, \mathrm dV_ z.  \] We claim that each $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with an element of $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$ of norm at most $\| F\| _\Phi $. Choose compact sets $K_\ell \uparrow \Omega _1$ and put $E_\ell =K_\ell \cap \{ \mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell \} $; these sets increase and exhaust $\Omega _1$ up to the pole set of $\varphi _1$, which has measure zero. The function $a_{j,\ell }$ obtained by integrating over $E_\ell $ instead of $\Omega _1$ is holomorphic on $\Omega _2$. Indeed, let $L\subset \Omega _2$ be compact. For $z\in E_\ell \subset K_\ell $ and $w\in L$, the integrand $F(z,w)\overline{e_ j(z)}\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1(z)}$ and all its partial derivatives in $w$ are bounded, because $F$ and its derivatives are continuous on $K_\ell \times L$, $e_ j$ is bounded on $K_\ell $, and $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\leq \ell $ on $E_\ell $. Hence we may differentiate under the integral sign any number of times: $a_{j,\ell }$ is smooth, and $\partial a_{j,\ell }/\partial \bar w_ m=0$ for all $m$, because $F$ is holomorphic in $w$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $z$, followed by integration in $w$ against $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _2}$, \[  \| a_ j-a_{j,\ell }\| _{\varphi _2}^2 \leq \| F\| _\Phi ^2 \int _{\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell }|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}\, \mathrm dV_ z \longrightarrow 0  \] by dominated convergence, since the sets $\Omega _1\setminus E_\ell $ decrease to a null set and $|e_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _1}$ is integrable. Since $\varphi _2\leq 0$, the holomorphic functions $a_{j,\ell }$ therefore converge to $a_ j$ in $L^2(\Omega _2)$, and hence in the sense of distributions; so $\bar\partial a_ j=0$, and $a_ j$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function, by lemma 6.4.10 (1). The same Cauchy–Schwarz estimate over all of $\Omega _1$ gives $\| a_ j\| _{\varphi _2}\leq \| F\| _\Phi $, which proves the claim. Now suppose that $F$ is orthogonal to all the products $e_ jg_ k$. By Fubini's theorem, whose use is justified by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\langle a_ j,g_ k\rangle _{\varphi _2}=\langle F,e_ jg_ k\rangle _\Phi =0$ for all $k$. Since the linear span of the $g_ k$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{\varphi _2}(\Omega _2)$, the element $a_ j$ of this space is orthogonal to itself, so $a_ j=0$ almost everywhere, for every $j$. Hence for almost every $w$ all the coefficients $\langle F(\cdot ,w),e_ j\rangle _{\varphi _1}$ vanish, and $F(\cdot ,w)=0$, because $F(\cdot ,w)$ is the limit of the partial sums of its expansion (theorem 6.8.9 (2)). Thus $F=0$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, since $F$ is continuous. Consequently, the closure $M$ of the linear span of the products $e_ jg_ k$ satisfies $M^\perp =0$, and $M=\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ by proposition 6.2.1 . We can now prove ( 6.10.3 ). Denote its right side by $\mathfrak b$; it is the ideal generated by the products $(f_1\circ p_1)(f_2\circ p_2)$ of local sections $f_ i$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi _ i)$. Each product $e_ jg_ k$ is a section of $\mathfrak b$. Every $F\in \mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ is the norm limit, hence by ( 6.8.7 ) the locally uniform limit, of a sequence of finite linear combinations of these products, so its germs lie in $\mathfrak b$ by lemma 6.8.1 . Since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is generated by the germs of the elements of $\mathcal H_\Phi (\Omega _1\times \Omega _2)$ (theorem 6.8.9 (3)), we obtain $\mathcal I(\Phi )\subset \mathfrak b$. Conversely, if $|f_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ i}$ is integrable near $x_ i$ for $i=1,2$, then $|f_1(z)f_2(w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi (z,w)}$ is integrable near $(x_1,x_2)$ by Fubini's theorem; since $\mathcal I(\Phi )$ is an ideal, $\mathfrak b\subset \mathcal I(\Phi )$. Finally, let $\varphi $ and $\psi $ be weights on $X$, and apply ( 6.10.2 ) to the weight $\varphi \circ p_1+\psi \circ p_2$ on $X\times X$ and the diagonal, which we identify with $X$. The restriction of the weight is $\varphi +\psi $, and by ( 6.10.3 ) the restriction of its multiplier ideal is generated by the products $f_1f_2$ of local sections $f_1$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$ and $f_2$ of $\mathcal I(\psi )$, that is, it equals $\mathcal I(\varphi )\mathcal I(\psi )$. This proves ( 6.10.4 ). $\square$

text: Corollary 6.10.5 . 05791D2DFFAA Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a holomorphic map of complex manifolds and $\varphi $ a weight on $Y$. Then \[  \mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X,  \] with equality if $f$ is a submersion. On a connected component of $X$ on which $\varphi \circ f\equiv -\infty $, the left side is zero. Proof. Suppose first that $f$ is a submersion, and let $a\in X$. Choose holomorphic coordinates $y$ on $Y$ centered at $f(a)$. Since the differential of $f$ at $a$ is surjective, the complex Jacobian matrix at $a$ of the components of $y\circ f$, computed in a chart of $X$, has rank $\dim _{f(a)}Y$. By the holomorphic inverse function theorem (proposition 5.2.4 (3)), these components are the first coordinates of a holomorphic chart $(z,w)=(y\circ f,w)$ of $X$ near $a$. In these coordinates $f$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Thus $\varphi \circ f=\varphi \circ p_1+0\circ p_2$, and ( 6.10.3 ), together with $\mathcal I(0)=\mathcal O$, gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)=p_1^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O=f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. In general, the graph $\Gamma =\{ (x,f(x))\} $ is a complex submanifold of $X\times Y$, since in local coordinates $(x,y)$ the functions $(x,y-f(x))$ are holomorphic coordinates in which $\Gamma =\{ y-f(x)=0\} $; and $\iota (x)=(x,f(x))$ is a biholomorphism of $X$ onto $\Gamma $. The projection $q\colon X\times Y\to Y$ is a submersion, so $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ q)=q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y}$ by the first case. Since $\varphi \circ q\circ \iota =\varphi \circ f$, ( 6.10.2 ) applied to $\Gamma $ gives $\mathcal I(\varphi \circ f)\subset (q^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_{X\times Y})|_\Gamma ^{\mathrm{im}}$ after transport by $\iota $. The right side is generated by the functions $g\circ q\circ \iota =g\circ f$ with $g$ a local section of $\mathcal I(\varphi )$, so it equals $f^{-1}\mathcal I(\varphi )\cdot \mathcal O_ X$. $\square$

text: Proposition 6.10.6 . 675539E4A76C Every multiplier ideal is integrally closed: if a germ $F\in \mathcal O_{X,x}$ satisfies an equation $F^ d+a_1F^{d-1}+\cdots +a_ d=0$ with $a_ j\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x^ j$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. More explicitly, if $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ and a holomorphic germ $F$ satisfies $|F|\leq C(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$ near $x$ for a constant $C$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. Proof. The second assertion is immediate, since $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq C^2\sum _ j|g_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ near $x$. For the first, choose generators $g_1,\ldots ,g_ r$ of $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ (theorem 6.8.9 ), representatives of the $g_ j$, of $F$ and of the $a_ j$ on a common neighborhood, and put $|g|=(\sum _ j|g_ j|^2)^{1/2}$. Each $a_ j$ is a finite sum of products of $j$ generators with holomorphic coefficients, which are bounded on a smaller neighborhood; hence $|a_ j|\leq C_ j|g|^ j$ there. At a point where $|g|>0$, put $\lambda =|F|/|g|$. Dividing the equation by $|g|^ d$ gives $\lambda ^ d\leq \sum _ jC_ j\lambda ^{d-j}$, which forces $\lambda \leq C$ with $C=\max \{ 1,\sum _ jC_ j\} $. At a point where $|g|=0$, all the $a_ j$ vanish, so $F^ d=0$ and $F=0$. Thus $|F|\leq C|g|$ near $x$, and the second assertion applies. $\square$

EA6067858516 Let $\varphi $ and $\chi $ be weights on $X$, and let $x\in X$. Then B5400B2F91DA 6.11.7  egin{equation}  \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x= igcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x \end{equation} and, more generally, \[  \mathcal I(\varphi )_ x= igcup _{\varepsilon >0} \mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x.  \] Moreover, there is a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I((1+\varepsilon )\varphi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$, and similarly a single $\varepsilon >0$ with $\mathcal I(\varphi +\varepsilon \chi )_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. On a relatively compact neighborhood of $x$ the weights are bounded above, and subtracting constants we may assume $\varphi \leq 0$ and $\chi \leq 0$ there; this changes $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ only by bounded amounts and hence changes none of the ideals. Then $(1+\varepsilon )\varphi $ and $\varphi +\varepsilon \chi $ decrease as $\varepsilon $ increases, so the corresponding ideals decrease with $\varepsilon $ and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. The sequences $(1+1/j)\varphi $ and $\varphi +\chi /j$ increase with $j$ and converge to $\varphi $ wherever $\varphi $ and $\chi $ are finite, hence almost everywhere. A germ of order $k$ at $0$ is $z^ k$ times a unit, so by polar coordinates it belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k-2c+1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, that is, $k+1>c$. Hence $\mathcal I(\varphi )=(z^{\lfloor cfloor })$. When $c$ is a positive integer, the germ $z^{c-1}$ just fails, because the radial integral diverges logarithmically. This strict threshold shows why theorem 6.11.4 concerns increasing sequences: on the unit disc, the weights $\varphi _ j=(1-1/j)\log |z|^2$, $j\geq 2$, decrease to $\log |z|^2$, yet $\mathcal I(\varphi _ j)=\mathcal O$ for every $j$, whereas $\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)=(z)$.

Theorem 6.11.4 . FF9DF4BE3CA8 Let $(\psi _ j)_{j\geq 1}$ be an increasing sequence of weights on $X$ that converges almost everywhere to a weight $\varphi $. Then at every $x\in X$, CF22C9DDEA36 6.11.5  egin{equation}   igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x, \end{equation} and $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x=\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ for all sufficiently large $j$; the required index may depend on $x$ and on the sequence. Proof. Since the $\psi _ j$ increase to $\varphi $ almost everywhere, $\psi _ j\leq \varphi $ almost everywhere. The plurisubharmonic functions $\max \{ \psi _ j,\varphi \} $ and $\varphi $ therefore agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by theorem 5.9.1 ; that is, $\psi _ j\leq \varphi $ everywhere. Consequently $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)\subset \mathcal I(\varphi )$ for every $j$, and the left side of ( 6.11.5 ) is contained in the right side. We prove the reverse inclusion by induction on the dimension $n$ of $X$ at $x$. If $n=0$, all the weights are finite at $x$ and all the ideals equal $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Let $n\geq 1$, assume the theorem in dimension $n-1$, and take $x=0$ in a coordinate chart. We argue by contradiction, extending a germ that is missing from $ igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_0$ from slices $\{ z_1=a_ i\} $ with $a_ i	o 0$, as outlined at the beginning of this section. Step 1: reduction to a curve. The union $J= igcup _ j\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_0$ is an ideal, because the ideals increase with $j$. By proposition 9.2.4 it is generated by finitely many germs $g_1,\ldots ,g_ k$, $k\geq 0$, and these all belong to $\mathcal I(\psi _{j_0})_0$ for some $j_0$. Suppose, to reach a contradiction, that some $F\in \mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ does not belong to $J$; in particular $F
eq 0$. Choose representatives of $F$ and of the $g_ l$ on a neighborhood $U$ of $0$ on which $|g_ l|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_0}}$ and $|F|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ are integrable. If $|F|\leq C|g|$, with $|g|=(\sum _ l|g_ l|^2)^{1/2}$, held on a neighborhood of $0$, then $F\in \mathcal I(\psi _{j_0})_0\subset J$ by proposition 6.10.6 ; so no such bound holds. Lemma 6.11.1 now provides linear coordinates and a curve $\gamma (t)=(t^ q,\gamma _2(t),\ldots ,\gamma _ n(t))$ such that $F\circ \gamma $ has no zeros for small $t
eq 0$ and each $(g_ l/F)\circ \gamma $ extends holomorphically with value $0$ at $t=0$. In these coordinates choose polydiscs $\Delta _{R_0}	imes P_0\Subset U$ and $\Omega =\Delta _ R	imes P\Subset \Delta _{R_0}	imes P_0$ centered at $0$, and let $r,c>0$ be the constants of lemma 6.11.2 for $\gamma $, $F$ and $\Omega $. Subtracting the same constant from $\varphi $ and all $\psi _ j$, we may assume that $\varphi \leq 0$ on $\Delta _{R_0}	imes P_0$; then also $\psi _ j\leq 0$ there. Step 2: choice of slices. By Fubini's theorem, the function \[  G(a)=\int _{P_0}|F(a,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (a,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w  \] is integrable on $\Delta _{R_0}$. Hence, given any null set $N\subset \Delta _{R_0}$, there is a sequence of points $a_ i
otin N$, $a_ i
eq 0$, with $a_ i	o 0$ and $|a_ i|^2G(a_ i)	o 0$; otherwise $G(a)\geq c'|a|^{-2}$ for almost every $a$ in some punctured disc around $0$, and $G$ would not be integrable. We take for $N$ the union of three sets: the set where $G=\infty $; the set of $a$ for which one of the countably many functions $\varphi (a,\cdot )$, $\psi _ j(a,\cdot )$ is identically $-\infty $ on $P_0$; and the set of $a$ for which $\psi _ j(a,\cdot )	o \varphi (a,\cdot )$ fails on a subset of $P_0$ of positive measure. The first set is null because $G$ is integrable, and the other two are null by Fubini's theorem, because pole sets of weights have measure zero and $\psi _ j	o \varphi $ almost everywhere. Then the functions $\psi _ j(a_ i,\cdot )$ and $\varphi (a_ i,\cdot )$ are weights on $P_0$ (proposition 5.9.3 ), and the former increase to the latter almost everywhere on $P_0$. Moreover $G(a_ i)>0$ for all large $i$, because $F(a_ i,\cdot )$ does not vanish identically on $P_0$: for small $|a_ i|$, the slice $\{ a_ i\} 	imes P_0$ contains the points $\gamma (b)$ with $b^ q=a_ i$, at which $F
eq 0$. Discarding finitely many terms, we assume that this holds for all $i$. Step 3: integrability on a fixed inner slice. Fix $i$. Since $G(a_ i)<\infty $, the germ of $F(a_ i,\cdot )$ at every point of $P_0$ belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi (a_ i,\cdot ))$. By the induction hypothesis, applied on $P_0$, each point of the compact set $\overline P\subset P_0$ has a neighborhood on which $|F(a_ i,\cdot )|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j(a_ i,\cdot )}$ is integrable for some $j$. Covering $\overline P$ by finitely many such neighborhoods and using that the $\psi _ j$ increase, we find one index $j$ for which $\int _ P|F(a_ i,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j(a_ i,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w<\infty $. For larger $j$ these integrands decrease and converge almost everywhere to $|F(a_ i,\cdot )|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi (a_ i,\cdot )}$, so by dominated convergence their integrals over $P$ converge to a number at most $G(a_ i)$. Since $G(a_ i)>0$, we can choose an index $j_ i$ with \[  \int _ P|F(a_ i,w)|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_ i}(a_ i,w)}\, \mathrm dV_ w \leq 2G(a_ i).  \] The polydisc $P$ does not depend on $i$; this is what makes the estimates of the next step uniform. Step 4: extension and contradiction. For large $i$ we have $|a_ i|<\min \{ r,R\} $, so that the normal coordinate $z_1-a_ i$ takes values in a disc of radius $2R$ on $\Omega $. The polydisc $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex by corollary 6.3.5 , being a product of discs, each of which is a sublevel set of a function $|\zeta -\zeta _0|^2$ on $\mathbb C$. Applying theorem 6.5.4 , after reordering the coordinates, with the normal coordinate $z_1-a_ i$, the radius $2R$ and the weight $\psi _{j_ i}$, and using the last display of Step 3, we obtain $H_ i\in \mathcal O(\Omega )$ with $H_ i(a_ i,\cdot )=F(a_ i,\cdot )$ on $P$ and \[  \int _\Omega |H_ i|^2\mathrm e^{-\psi _{j_ i}}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i),  \] where $C_0$ is the absolute constant of that theorem. In particular the germ of $H_ i$ at $0$ lies in $\mathcal I(\psi _{j_ i})_0\subset J$, so $H_ i=\sum _ lb_ lg_ l$ near $0$ with holomorphic $b_ l$, and $(H_ i/F)\circ \gamma =\sum _ l(b_ l\circ \gamma )\cdot (g_ l/F)\circ \gamma $ extends holomorphically across $t=0$ with value $0$. Since $\psi _{j_ i}\leq 0$, the last display also bounds $\int _\Omega |H_ i|^2\, \mathrm dV$. Now lemma 6.11.2 gives $c|a_ i|^{-2}\leq 8C_0R^2G(a_ i)$ for all large $i$, contradicting $|a_ i|^2G(a_ i)	o 0$. Hence $F\in J$, which proves ( 6.11.5 ). Finally, $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$ is generated by finitely many germs, which by ( 6.11.5 ) all lie in $\mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$ for one index $j$. Then $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x\subset \mathcal I(\psi _ j)_ x$, and equality holds for this and every later index, since the ideals increase and are contained in $\mathcal I(\varphi )_ x$. $\square$

A germ of order $k$ at $0$ is $z^ k$ times a unit, so by polar coordinates it belongs to $\mathcal I(\varphi )_0$ if and only if $\int _0^ rt^{2k-2c+1}\, \mathrm dt<\infty $, that is, $k+1>c$. This strict threshold shows why theorem 6.11.4 concerns increasing sequences: on the unit disc, the weights $\varphi _ j=(1-1/j)\log |z|^2$, $j\geq 2$, decrease to $\log |z|^2$, yet $\mathcal I(\varphi _ j)=\mathcal O$ for every $j$, whereas $\mathcal I(\log |z|^2)=(z)$.
