text: Corollary 10.2.19 . 5E8D4AB76812 Let $\theta $ be a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$ satisfies $\{ T\} =\{ \theta \} $ if and only if $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ for some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and then $\varphi $ is unique up to an additive constant. In particular, the class $\{ \theta \} $ contains a closed positive current if and only if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $. Proof. Let $T\geq 0$ be closed with $\{ T\} =\{ \theta \} $. Write $T=H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ as in ( 10.2.16 ); since $\{ T\} =\{ \theta \} $, also $\theta =H+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ with $g$ smooth. By theorem 10.2.15 , $f$ has a canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, and the difference $\varphi $ of this representative and $g$ satisfies $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $; thus $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Conversely, if $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a closed positive current, and it lies in $\{ \theta \} $ because adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution does not change the class. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi '$ with $\varphi ,\varphi '\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then $\varphi -\varphi '$ is constant almost everywhere by the uniqueness part of theorem 10.2.15 , say equal to $c$, and the quasi-plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi $ and $\varphi '+c$, which agree almost everywhere, agree everywhere by lemma 6.14.4 (1). $\square$

title: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text:
Fix a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta $ on $X$. A function $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is determined by its current $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ up to an additive constant, which we fix by normalizing the supremum. The local compactness and integrability theorems then become uniform statements for normalized potentials, and the upper envelope of the nonpositive potentials has minimal singularities. We also compare potentials on $X$ and on a modification of $X$. Integrals over $X$ are taken with respect to $\mathrm dV$, or equivalently $\omega ^ n$, unless stated otherwise. A $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function is integrable on the compact manifold $X$, being locally integrable. If $\varphi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and $\psi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic or continuous, an inequality between $\varphi $ and $\psi $ that holds almost everywhere holds everywhere. Indeed, by lemma 6.14.4 (1) the value of a quasi-plurisubharmonic function at a point is the limit of its averages over small coordinate balls centered at that point, a continuous function has the same property, and the inequality holds between these averages. In particular, a $	heta $-plurisubharmonic function is determined by its class in $L^1(X)$, and we regard $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ as a subset of $L^1(X)$. Proposition 10.3.1 . 2984F6438B4B Let $a\leq b$ be real numbers. The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$ is compact in $L^1(X)$, and the map $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X\varphi $ is continuous on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ for the $L^1$ topology. In particular, the functions $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi =0$ are uniformly bounded in $L^1(X)$. The same statements hold for a sequence of backgrounds: if smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $	heta _ j$ converge smoothly to $	heta $ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta _ j)$ satisfy $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(X)$ to some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ j	o \sup _ X\varphi $ whenever $\varphi _ j	o \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ in $L^1(X)$. The assertions for a fixed background hold more generally on every connected compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension, for every smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $	heta '$ on $X'$, with $L^1(X')$ taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$ covering $X$, smaller concentric balls $B'_ k$ still covering $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{B_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=	heta $ (lemma 6.14.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls). For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ the functions $\varphi +h_ k$ are plurisubharmonic on $B_ k$. Let $(\varphi _ j)$ be a sequence with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$. The plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on each $B_ k$. Since $\varphi _ j$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$, it attains its supremum at a point $x_ j$, and after passing to a subsequence $x_ j	o x$, since $X$ is compact and metrizable. Choose $k$ with $x\in B'_ k$. On $B_ k$ the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ cannot converge locally uniformly to $-\infty $, because their values at $x_ j$ are bounded below by $a+\inf _{B'_ k}h_ k$ for large $j$. By theorem 5.10.4 , a further subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$. If $B_ l$ meets $B_ k$, the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ l$ cannot tend to $-\infty $ locally uniformly on $B_ l$, since on the nonempty open set $B_ k\cap B_ l$ they differ by the smooth function $h_ l-h_ k$ from a sequence that converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; so again a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ l)$. Since $X$ is connected, every ball is joined to $B_ k$ by a finite chain of overlapping balls, and after finitely many extractions the sequence converges in $L^1(B'_ l)$ for every $l$, hence in $L^1(X)$, to some $\varphi $. The limit satisfies $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ as a distributional limit of positive currents, and its canonical representative belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Now let $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, all in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$; we show that $\sup _ X\varphi _ j	o \sup _ X\varphi $. The submean inequality for $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ on small balls shows that the $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Let $x_ j	o x$; we claim that $\varlimsup _ j\varphi _ j(x_ j)\leq \varphi (x)$. Indeed, choose $k$ with $x\in B_ k$, let $c>\varphi (x)$ be real, and use upper semicontinuity to choose a closed ball $K\subset B_ k$ around $x$ on which $\varphi <c$. The function $c+h_ k$ is continuous near $K$ and $\varphi +h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$, so the second part of theorem 5.10.4 gives $\varphi _ j+h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$ for large $j$; hence $\varphi _ j(x_ j)<c$ for large $j$. Choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and points $x_ j$ with $\varphi _ j(x_ j)=\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ converge to some $x$; the claim gives $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq \varphi (x)\leq \sup _ X\varphi $. Conversely, choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and $\sum _ j\| \varphi _ j-\varphi \| _{L^1}<\infty $; by monotone convergence $\sum _ j|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$ is integrable, hence finite almost everywhere, so $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ almost everywhere along it. We get $\varphi \leq \varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. The two inequalities prove that the supremum is continuous; in particular, the limit in the previous paragraph satisfies $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$. Thus the set in question is sequentially compact, hence compact, in the metric space $L^1(X)$. The continuous function $\| \cdot \| _{L^1}$ is bounded on the compact set of normalized functions. The arguments so far use only that $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that the volume form defining $L^1(X)$ is smooth and positive; hence they also prove the last assertion of the proposition. For smoothly convergent backgrounds, choose $C\geq 0$ with $	heta _ j\leq C\omega $ for all $j$. Then $C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq 0$, so all $\varphi _ j$ lie in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$, and the first part, applied to the closed form $C\omega $, gives an $L^1$-convergent subsequence and the convergence of the suprema. Since $	heta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j	o 	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as distributions, the limit belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. $\square$ Corollary 10.3.2 . 384717733620 For every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $M_ p$, depending only on $X$, $	heta $, $\omega $ and $p$, such that \[  \| u\| _{L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)}\leq M_ p \quad 	ext{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )	ext{ with }\sup _ Xu=0.  \] Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is empty, there is nothing to prove.) Choose finitely many coordinate polydiscs $D_ k$ such that the polydiscs $ rac14D_ k$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{D_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=	heta $. For $u$ as in the statement, $v_ k=u+h_ k-\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function on $D_ k$. By proposition 10.3.1 and the boundedness of the $h_ k$ and of the coordinate volume densities, the norms $\| v_ k\| _{L^1(D_ k)}$ are bounded independently of $u$. After rescaling $D_ k$ to the unit polydisc, ( 5.10.9 ) bounds $\| v_ k\| _{L^ p( rac14D_ k)}$ independently of $u$. Since $u=v_ k-h_ k+\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ on $D_ k$, the bounded functions $h_ k$ and the bounded volume densities give the assertion. $\square$ Corollary 10.3.3 . C7609FD8FC8C There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $	heta $ and $\omega $, such that 6B3D5F5D04A5 10.3.4  egin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\omega ^ n\leq C \quad 	ext{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )	ext{ with }\sup _ Xu=0. \end{equation} Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is empty, any $\alpha ,C>0$ will do.) Choose finitely many coordinate unit balls $B_ j$ such that the balls $ rac14B_ j$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $ho _ j$ near $\overline{B_ j}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho _ j=	heta $. For $u$ as in the statement put $v_ j=u+ho _ j-\sup _{B_ j}ho _ j$ on $B_ j$; then $v_ j$ is plurisubharmonic and $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$. By proposition 10.3.1 and comparison of the coordinate volume densities, $\| v_ j\| _{L^1(B_ j)}\leq M_ j$ for a constant $M_ j\geq 1$ independent of $u$. Applying proposition 5.10.12 to $v_ j/M_ j$, we see that $\int _{ rac14B_ j}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ is bounded independently of $u$, where $\alpha _ j=\alpha _ n/M_ j$. Put $\alpha =\min _ j\alpha _ j>0$. Since $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$ and $\alpha \leq \alpha _ j$, we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ ju}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ on $B_ j$. Summing over $j$ and comparing the coordinate volume densities with $\omega ^ n$ gives ( 10.3.4 ). $\square$ Recall from definition 5.47.2 that a subset of $X$ is pluripolar if it is locally contained in the pole set of a plurisubharmonic function. Corollary 10.3.5 . B2C28BB645D3 Let $K\subset X$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Then there is a constant $C$ such that \[  \sup _ X\varphi \leq \sup _ K\varphi +C\qquad 	ext{for all }\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ).  \] Consequently, every subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ on which $\sup _ K\varphi $ is bounded above and below is relatively compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. Suppose that no such constant exists. Since $\sup _ X\varphi -\sup _ K\varphi $ does not change when a constant is added to $\varphi $, there are $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=0$ and $\sup _ K\varphi _ j\leq -2^ j$. Choose $C\geq 0$ with $	heta \leq C\omega $ (lemma 6.14.1 ) and put $\psi _ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}\varphi _ j$. Since $\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\leq 1$, we have \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ N=\Bigl (1-\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\Bigr )C\omega +\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq \sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\psi _ N)$ is decreasing because $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, and $\| \psi _ N\| _{L^1}\leq \sup _ j\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1}<\infty $ by proposition 10.3.1 . By monotone convergence the limit $\psi $ is integrable, so it is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 5.10.1 , applied on coordinate balls after adding local potentials of $C\omega $, shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$. On $K$ every term $2^{-j}\varphi _ j$ is at most $-1$, so $\psi =-\infty $ on $K$. On every coordinate ball $U$ with a smooth function $h$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=C\omega $, the function $\psi +h$ is plurisubharmonic and equals $-\infty $ on $K\cap U$. Hence $K$ is pluripolar, a contradiction. The last assertion follows: bounds for $\sup _ K\varphi $ give bounds for $\sup _ X\varphi $, and proposition 10.3.1 applies. $\square$ Corollary 10.3.6 . 134C98DC2772 Let $(\varphi _ i)$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ whose suprema $\sup _ X\varphi _ i$ are bounded below. Then its pointwise infimum $\varphi $ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $\varphi _ i	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ i	o \sup _ X\varphi $. Proof. Fix an index $i_0$. For $i\geq i_0$ the suprema are bounded above by $\sup _ X\varphi _{i_0}$, so the tail of the net lies in a compact subset of $L^1(X)$ by proposition 10.3.1 , and a subnet converges in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. For each fixed $i$, the members of the subnet are eventually below $\varphi _ i$, so $\psi \leq \varphi _ i$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. Hence the pointwise infimum $\varphi $ is at least $\psi $ and is not identically $-\infty $. Applying theorem 5.10.1 on the coordinate balls of a finite cover, after adding local potentials of $	heta $, we find that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $\varphi _ i	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. The continuity of the supremum in proposition 10.3.1 gives the last assertion. $\square$ Definition 10.3.7 . 9499229CD425 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. Recall from section 6.18 that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $, written $\varphi \preceq \psi $, if $\varphi \leq \psi +C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$; we then also say that $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $. A potential $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ has minimal singularities if every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ is more singular than $\psi $. If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
e \varnothing $, put \[  V_	heta = igl (\sup \{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta ):\varphi \leq 0\}  igr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization. Lemma 10.3.8 . 5755B2D3C604 Suppose that $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
eq \varnothing $. Then $V_	heta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, $\sup _ XV_	heta =0$, and $\varphi \leq V_	heta +\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$; in particular, $V_	heta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities differ by a bounded function on the set where both are finite, and the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ 	heta \} $. Proof. The family whose upper envelope defines $V_	heta $ in definition 10.3.7 is nonempty, because $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ belongs to it for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and it is bounded above by $0$. Theorem 5.10.2 , applied on coordinate balls after adding smooth local potentials of $	heta $, therefore gives $V_	heta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and $V_	heta \leq 0$; and $\sup _ XV_	heta =0$, because $V_	heta \geq \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi $. The same inequality reads $\varphi \leq V_	heta +\sup _ X\varphi $, so $V_	heta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities are each more singular than the other, so their difference is bounded on the set where both are finite. Proposition 10.3.9 . 4C3B45D704A9 Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map from a complex manifold $Y$. Then $Y$ is compact and connected, and $\varphi \mapsto \varphi \circ \pi $ is a bijection from $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ onto $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$, which is continuous for convergence in $L^1(X)$ and $L^1(Y)$, the latter taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. By the definition of bimeromorphic maps (section 9.4 ), there is a nowhere dense analytic subset $E_0\subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ is nowhere dense and $\pi $ restricts to an isomorphism of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(E_0)$ onto $X\setminus E_0$. The set $X\setminus E_0$ is connected by lemma 9.2.9 , hence so is its dense preimage, and therefore $Y$ is connected. The image $\pi (Y)$ is closed, since proper maps are closed, and it contains the dense set $X\setminus E_0$; so $\pi $ is surjective. By proposition 9.8.3 there is an analytic subset $A\subset X$ of codimension at least two such that $\pi $ is an isomorphism over $X\setminus A$. Then $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is an analytic subset of $Y$ different from $Y$, because $\pi $ is surjective. Since $Y$ is connected, $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is locally contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function that does not vanish identically on a connected neighborhood (section 9.2 ), so it is nowhere dense and a null set (lemma 5.5.1 ). The same holds for $A$ in $X$. If $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, let $B$ be a coordinate ball and $h$ a smooth function on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ (lemma 6.14.2 ). On every connected coordinate neighborhood $W\subset \pi ^{-1}(B)$ the function $(\varphi +h)\circ \pi $ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $, by proposition 5.9.3 , and the second case is excluded because $\varphi +h$ is finite almost everywhere on the image under the biholomorphism $\pi $ of the nonempty open set $W\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Hence $\varphi \circ \pi =(\varphi +h)\circ \pi -h\circ \pi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, with $\pi ^*	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((\varphi +h)\circ \pi )\geq 0$ on $\pi ^{-1}(B)$. If $\varphi \circ \pi =\varphi '\circ \pi $, then $\varphi =\varphi '$ on $X\setminus A$, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section; this proves injectivity. Conversely, let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. Over $X\setminus A$ it descends to the function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}$, which is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic there. For continuity, we use proposition 10.3.1 on $X$ and on $Y$; by its last assertion, its assertions for a fixed background hold on $Y$. Let $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. There is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ with $\psi \geq \varphi $, $\psi =\varphi $ on $X\setminus B$, $\psi $ bounded near $\overline B$, and $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=0$ on $B$. Subtracting $h$ from the result on $B''$ and keeping $\varphi $ outside $B''$ gives $\psi $, since the result equals $\varphi +h$ on $B''\setminus B$; here $(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +h))^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi +h$. If $\psi '$ is another function with the stated properties, then by upper semicontinuity $\varlimsup _{z	o \zeta ,\, z\in B}\psi '(z)\leq \psi '(\zeta )=\varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. title: Proposition 10.3.1
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Proposition 10.3.1 . 2984F6438B4B Let $a\leq b$ be real numbers. The set of $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$ is compact in $L^1(X)$, and the map $\varphi \mapsto \sup _ X\varphi $ is continuous on $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for the $L^1$ topology. In particular, the functions $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi =0$ are uniformly bounded in $L^1(X)$. The same statements hold for a sequence of backgrounds: if smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ j$ converge smoothly to $\theta $ and $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ j)$ satisfy $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$, then a subsequence converges in $L^1(X)$ to some $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ j\to \sup _ X\varphi $ whenever $\varphi _ j\to \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ in $L^1(X)$. The assertions for a fixed background hold more generally on every connected compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension, for every smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta '$ on $X'$, with $L^1(X')$ taken with respect to any smooth positive volume form. Proof. Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$ covering $X$, smaller concentric balls $B'_ k$ still covering $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{B_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=\theta $ (lemma 6.14.2 , applied on slightly larger concentric balls). For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ the functions $\varphi +h_ k$ are plurisubharmonic on $B_ k$. Let $(\varphi _ j)$ be a sequence with $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq b$. The plurisubharmonic functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ are uniformly bounded above on each $B_ k$. Since $\varphi _ j$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $X$, it attains its supremum at a point $x_ j$, and after passing to a subsequence $x_ j\to x$, since $X$ is compact and metrizable. Choose $k$ with $x\in B'_ k$. On $B_ k$ the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ cannot converge locally uniformly to $-\infty $, because their values at $x_ j$ are bounded below by $a+\inf _{B'_ k}h_ k$ for large $j$. By theorem 5.10.4 , a further subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ k)$. If $B_ l$ meets $B_ k$, the functions $\varphi _ j+h_ l$ cannot tend to $-\infty $ locally uniformly on $B_ l$, since on the nonempty open set $B_ k\cap B_ l$ they differ by the smooth function $h_ l-h_ k$ from a sequence that converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; so again a subsequence converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(B_ l)$. Since $X$ is connected, every ball is joined to $B_ k$ by a finite chain of overlapping balls, and after finitely many extractions the sequence converges in $L^1(B'_ l)$ for every $l$, hence in $L^1(X)$, to some $\varphi $. The limit satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq 0$ as a distributional limit of positive currents, and its canonical representative belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Now let $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, all in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; we show that $\sup _ X\varphi _ j\to \sup _ X\varphi $. The submean inequality for $\varphi _ j+h_ k$ on small balls shows that the $\varphi _ j$ are uniformly bounded above. Let $x_ j\to x$; we claim that $\varlimsup _ j\varphi _ j(x_ j)\leq \varphi (x)$. Indeed, choose $k$ with $x\in B_ k$, let $c>\varphi (x)$ be real, and use upper semicontinuity to choose a closed ball $K\subset B_ k$ around $x$ on which $\varphi <c$. The function $c+h_ k$ is continuous near $K$ and $\varphi +h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$, so the second part of theorem 5.10.4 gives $\varphi _ j+h_ k<c+h_ k$ on $K$ for large $j$; hence $\varphi _ j(x_ j)<c$ for large $j$. Choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and points $x_ j$ with $\varphi _ j(x_ j)=\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ converge to some $x$; the claim gives $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j\leq \varphi (x)\leq \sup _ X\varphi $. Conversely, choose a subsequence along which $\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ tends to $\varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ and $\sum _ j\| \varphi _ j-\varphi \| _{L^1}<\infty $; by monotone convergence $\sum _ j|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$ is integrable, hence finite almost everywhere, so $\varphi _ j\to \varphi $ almost everywhere along it. We get $\varphi \leq \varliminf _ j\sup _ X\varphi _ j$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. The two inequalities prove that the supremum is continuous; in particular, the limit in the previous paragraph satisfies $a\leq \sup _ X\varphi \leq b$. Thus the set in question is sequentially compact, hence compact, in the metric space $L^1(X)$. The continuous function $\| \cdot \| _{L^1}$ is bounded on the compact set of normalized functions. The arguments so far use only that $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that the volume form defining $L^1(X)$ is smooth and positive; hence they also prove the last assertion of the proposition. For smoothly convergent backgrounds, choose $C\geq 0$ with $\theta _ j\leq C\omega $ for all $j$. Then $C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq 0$, so all $\varphi _ j$ lie in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$, and the first part, applied to the closed form $C\omega $, gives an $L^1$-convergent subsequence and the convergence of the suprema. Since $\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\to \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ as distributions, the limit belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.3.2
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Corollary 10.3.2 . 384717733620 For every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $M_ p$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $, $\omega $ and $p$, such that \[  \| u\| _{L^ p(X,\omega ^ n)}\leq M_ p \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0.  \] Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is empty, there is nothing to prove.) Choose finitely many coordinate polydiscs $D_ k$ such that the polydiscs $\frac14D_ k$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $h_ k$ near $\overline{D_ k}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h_ k=\theta $. For $u$ as in the statement, $v_ k=u+h_ k-\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function on $D_ k$. By proposition 10.3.1 and the boundedness of the $h_ k$ and of the coordinate volume densities, the norms $\| v_ k\| _{L^1(D_ k)}$ are bounded independently of $u$. After rescaling $D_ k$ to the unit polydisc, ( 5.10.9 ) bounds $\| v_ k\| _{L^ p(\frac14D_ k)}$ independently of $u$. Since $u=v_ k-h_ k+\sup _{D_ k}h_ k$ on $D_ k$, the bounded functions $h_ k$ and the bounded volume densities give the assertion. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.3.3
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Corollary 10.3.3 . C7609FD8FC8C There are $\alpha ,C>0$, depending only on $X$, $\theta $ and $\omega $, such that 6B3D5F5D04A5 10.3.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\omega ^ n\leq C \quad \text{for all }u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\text{ with }\sup _ Xu=0. \end{equation} Proof. (If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is empty, any $\alpha ,C>0$ will do.) Choose finitely many coordinate unit balls $B_ j$ such that the balls $\frac14B_ j$ with the same centers and a quarter of the radii cover $X$, and smooth functions $\rho _ j$ near $\overline{B_ j}$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _ j=\theta $. For $u$ as in the statement put $v_ j=u+\rho _ j-\sup _{B_ j}\rho _ j$ on $B_ j$; then $v_ j$ is plurisubharmonic and $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$. By proposition 10.3.1 and comparison of the coordinate volume densities, $\| v_ j\| _{L^1(B_ j)}\leq M_ j$ for a constant $M_ j\geq 1$ independent of $u$. Applying proposition 5.10.12 to $v_ j/M_ j$, we see that $\int _{\frac14B_ j}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ is bounded independently of $u$, where $\alpha _ j=\alpha _ n/M_ j$. Put $\alpha =\min _ j\alpha _ j>0$. Since $v_ j\leq u\leq 0$ and $\alpha \leq \alpha _ j$, we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ ju}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _ jv_ j}$ on $B_ j$. Summing over $j$ and comparing the coordinate volume densities with $\omega ^ n$ gives ( 10.3.4 ). $\square$

title: Corollary 10.3.5
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Corollary 10.3.5 . B2C28BB645D3 Let $K\subset X$ be a compact set that is not pluripolar. Then there is a constant $C$ such that \[  \sup _ X\varphi \leq \sup _ K\varphi +C\qquad \text{for all }\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ).  \] Consequently, every subset of $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ on which $\sup _ K\varphi $ is bounded above and below is relatively compact in $L^1(X)$. Proof. Suppose that no such constant exists. Since $\sup _ X\varphi -\sup _ K\varphi $ does not change when a constant is added to $\varphi $, there are $\varphi _ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=0$ and $\sup _ K\varphi _ j\leq -2^ j$. Choose $C\geq 0$ with $\theta \leq C\omega $ (lemma 6.14.1 ) and put $\psi _ N=\sum _{j=1}^ N2^{-j}\varphi _ j$. Since $\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\leq 1$, we have \[  C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ N=\Bigl (1-\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}\Bigr )C\omega +\sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(C\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq \sum _{j\leq N}2^{-j}(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j)\geq 0.  \] The sequence $(\psi _ N)$ is decreasing because $\varphi _ j\leq 0$, and $\| \psi _ N\| _{L^1}\leq \sup _ j\| \varphi _ j\| _{L^1}<\infty $ by proposition 10.3.1 . By monotone convergence the limit $\psi $ is integrable, so it is not identically $-\infty $, and theorem 5.10.1 , applied on coordinate balls after adding local potentials of $C\omega $, shows that $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,C\omega )$. On $K$ every term $2^{-j}\varphi _ j$ is at most $-1$, so $\psi =-\infty $ on $K$. On every coordinate ball $U$ with a smooth function $h$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=C\omega $, the function $\psi +h$ is plurisubharmonic and equals $-\infty $ on $K\cap U$. Hence $K$ is pluripolar, a contradiction. The last assertion follows: bounds for $\sup _ K\varphi $ give bounds for $\sup _ X\varphi $, and proposition 10.3.1 applies. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.3.6
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Corollary 10.3.6 . 134C98DC2772 Let $(\varphi _ i)$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ whose suprema $\sup _ X\varphi _ i$ are bounded below. Then its pointwise infimum $\varphi $ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$, and $\sup _ X\varphi _ i\to \sup _ X\varphi $. Proof. Fix an index $i_0$. For $i\geq i_0$ the suprema are bounded above by $\sup _ X\varphi _{i_0}$, so the tail of the net lies in a compact subset of $L^1(X)$ by proposition 10.3.1 , and a subnet converges in $L^1$ to some $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For each fixed $i$, the members of the subnet are eventually below $\varphi _ i$, so $\psi \leq \varphi _ i$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section. Hence the pointwise infimum $\varphi $ is at least $\psi $ and is not identically $-\infty $. Applying theorem 5.10.1 on the coordinate balls of a finite cover, after adding local potentials of $\theta $, we find that $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $\varphi _ i\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. The continuity of the supremum in proposition 10.3.1 gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Definition 10.3.7
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Definition 10.3.7 . 9499229CD425 Let $\varphi ,\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Recall from section 6.18 that $\varphi $ is more singular than $\psi $, written $\varphi \preceq \psi $, if $\varphi \leq \psi +C$ on $X$ for some constant $C$; we then also say that $\psi $ is less singular than $\varphi $. A potential $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has minimal singularities if every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ is more singular than $\psi $. If $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $, put \[  V_\theta =\bigl (\sup \{ \varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):\varphi \leq 0\} \bigr )^*,  \] where ${}^*$ denotes the upper semicontinuous regularization.

title: Lemma 10.3.8
section: 10.3 Normalized potentials and minimal singularities
text: Lemma 10.3.8 . 5755B2D3C604 Suppose that $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\neq \varnothing $. Then $V_\theta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\sup _ XV_\theta =0$, and $\varphi \leq V_\theta +\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; in particular, $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities differ by a bounded function on the set where both are finite, and the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ \theta \} $. Proof. The family whose upper envelope defines $V_\theta $ in definition 10.3.7 is nonempty, because $\varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ belongs to it for every $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and it is bounded above by $0$. Theorem 5.10.2 , applied on coordinate balls after adding smooth local potentials of $\theta $, therefore gives $V_\theta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $V_\theta \leq 0$; and $\sup _ XV_\theta =0$, because $V_\theta \geq \varphi -\sup _ X\varphi $ for every $\varphi $. The same inequality reads $\varphi \leq V_\theta +\sup _ X\varphi $, so $V_\theta $ has minimal singularities. Any two potentials with minimal singularities are each more singular than the other, so their difference is bounded on the set where both are finite. Replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ with $h$ smooth replaces $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )-h$; since $h$ is bounded, the notion of minimal singularities depends only on the class $\{ \theta \} $. $\square$

text:

Hence $\varphi \circ \pi =(\varphi +h)\circ \pi -h\circ \pi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, with $\pi ^*	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varphi \circ \pi )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((\varphi +h)\circ \pi )\geq 0$ on $\pi ^{-1}(B)$. Thus $\varphi \circ \pi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. If $\varphi \circ \pi =\varphi '\circ \pi $, then $\varphi =\varphi '$ on $X\setminus A$, hence almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere, as noted at the beginning of this section; this proves injectivity. Conversely, let $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. Over $X\setminus A$ it descends to the function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}$, which is $	heta $-plurisubharmonic there. It is bounded above, because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous on the compact manifold $Y$. On a coordinate ball $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $ on $B$, the plurisubharmonic function $\psi \circ \pi ^{-1}+h$ on $B\setminus A$ is therefore locally bounded above near $A$, and it extends to a plurisubharmonic function on $B$ by theorem 5.11.1 . The pullback $\varphi \circ \pi $ equals $\psi $ outside the null set $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, hence everywhere. This proves surjectivity. For continuity, we use proposition 10.3.1 on $X$ and on $Y$; by its last assertion, its assertions for a fixed background hold on $Y$. Let $\varphi _ j	o \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$. By the continuity of the supremum, it suffices to treat normalized functions, $\sup _ X\varphi _ j=\sup _ X\varphi =0$, since subtracting the suprema preserves $L^1$ convergence. The pullbacks have the same suprema, because $\pi $ is surjective, so they are relatively compact in $L^1(Y)$, and every cluster value lies in $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\pi ^*	heta )$. On compact subsets of $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$, a change of variables shows that every $L^1$ cluster value of $(\varphi _ j\circ \pi )$ coincides almost everywhere with $\varphi \circ \pi $; since $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ is a null set, every cluster value is $\varphi \circ \pi $. A relatively compact sequence in a metric space with a single cluster value converges to it; hence $\varphi _ j\circ \pi 	o \varphi \circ \pi $ in $L^1(Y)$. Finally, $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,E)$ is the infimum over $y\in E$ of the point Lelong numbers $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$. Near $y$ choose a smooth $g$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\pi ^*	heta $, so that the functions $\varphi \circ \pi +g$ are plurisubharmonic. By ( 6.7.10 ), applied to them, each $
u (\varphi \circ \pi ,y)$ is upper semicontinuous for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi \circ \pi $, hence, by the continuity just proved, for $L^1$ convergence of $\varphi $; and an infimum of upper semicontinuous functions is upper semicontinuous. Since Lelong numbers do not change when a constant is added, we may restrict to the normalized functions, which form a compact set by proposition 10.3.1 . An upper semicontinuous function with finite values attains its maximum on a compact set, which gives the uniform bound. $\square$

text: Corollary 10.3.10 . E6419D4591F9 Let $B'$ be a coordinate ball in $X$ and $B\Subset B'$ a ball in the same coordinates, and let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ be bounded near $\overline{B'}$. There is $\psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $\psi \geq \varphi $, $\psi =\varphi $ on $X\setminus B$, $\psi $ bounded near $\overline B$, and $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=0$ on $B$. It is the largest function in $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with these properties, and any two functions with these properties that are continuous on $\overline B$ coincide. Proof. Choose a ball $B''$ in the same coordinates with $\overline B\subset B''$ and $\overline{B''}\subset B'$. Write $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ on $B''$, with $h$ smooth (lemma 6.14.2 ), and apply corollary 7.7.5 to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\varphi +h$ on $B''$. Subtracting $h$ from the result on $B''$ and keeping $\varphi $ outside $B''$ gives $\psi $, since the result equals $\varphi +h$ on $B''\setminus B$; here $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi +h))^ n$ is the Bedford–Taylor product of the bounded plurisubharmonic function $\psi +h$. If $\psi '$ is another function with the stated properties, then by upper semicontinuity $\varlimsup _{z\to \zeta ,\, z\in B}\psi '(z)\leq \psi '(\zeta )=\varphi (\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B$. Hence $\psi '+h$ belongs to the family whose upper envelope is $\psi +h$ in corollary 7.7.5 , and $\psi '\leq \psi $ on $B$. If $\psi '$ is continuous on $\overline B$, then its boundary values $\varphi |_{\partial B}$ are continuous, and $\psi '+h$ is the solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem with the continuous boundary values $(\varphi +h)|_{\partial B}$; by the uniqueness in theorem 7.7.4 , any two such continuous functions coincide. $\square$

Let $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ and fix a smooth representative $	heta \in \alpha $. By theorem 10.2.15 , the closed currents in $\alpha $ are exactly the currents $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi $ a real distribution, so positivity properties of $\alpha $ become inequalities for $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $. Besides the positivity cones and the mixed Hodge index theorem, we prove Siu's decomposition of a closed positive current (theorem 10.4.8 ), which leads to modified nef classes. Definition 10.4.1 . CFDE52E42C6B A class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is pseudo-effective if it contains a closed positive current; Kähler if it contains a Kähler form; nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ it contains a smooth form $	heta _\varepsilon $ with $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $; big if it contains a closed current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. A closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$ is called a Kähler current . The cones of pseudo-effective, Kähler, nef and big classes are denoted $\mathcal E$, $\mathcal K$, $\mathcal N$ and $\mathcal B$. The zero class belongs to the pseudo-effective cone and to the nef cone. These notions do not depend on $\omega $, because any two Hermitian forms on the compact manifold $X$ are bounded by constant multiples of each other (lemma 6.14.1 ). By corollary 10.2.19 , $\alpha $ is pseudo-effective if and only if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )
e \varnothing $. Proposition 10.4.2 . 3B6E3B145113 The pseudo-effective cone $\mathcal E$ is closed and convex, and the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is open and convex. Moreover $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}\subset \mathcal E$, the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$, and the big cone $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. Proof. Sums and positive multiples of positive currents, Kähler forms or nef representatives are of the same kind, which proves convexity of all four cones. Let $\alpha _ j	o \alpha $ be pseudo-effective classes, with positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$. Since the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution pairs to zero with the closed form $\omega ^{n-1}$, the trace masses are \[  \int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\int _ X	heta _{\alpha _ j}\wedge \omega ^{n-1},  \] where $	heta _{\alpha _ j}$ are the representatives of ( 10.2.18 ); they are bounded because the classes converge. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart, $\chi $ a test function on the chart with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $K$, and $c'>0$ such that $ eta \leq c'\omega $ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 6.14.1 ), where $ eta $ is the Euclidean form ( 5.2.8 ) of the chart. By ( 10.2.10 ), applied with $\gamma _ j=c'\omega $ and $\gamma '_ j= eta $, the form $(c'\omega )^{n-1}- eta ^{n-1}$ is a sum of products of semipositive $(1,1)$-forms on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, hence strongly positive (proposition 5.3.2 ). Therefore $c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-\chi  eta ^{n-1}=(1-\chi )c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}+\chi  igl (c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}- eta ^{n-1} igr )$, with $\chi  eta ^{n-1}$ extended by zero outside the chart, is a smooth strongly positive form on $X$, so the trace measures satisfy $\mu _{T_ j}(K)\leq T_ j(\chi  eta ^{n-1})\leq c'^{n-1}\int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$, which is bounded independently of $j$. By the compactness assertion of theorem 5.3.7 , a subsequence of $(T_ j)$ converges weakly to a closed positive current $T$, and $\{ T\} =\alpha $ because the class map is weakly continuous. Hence $\mathcal E$ is closed. If $\omega _0\in \alpha $ is a Kähler form, then $\omega _0\geq c\omega $ for some $c>0$, and by ( 10.2.18 ) the form $\omega _0+	heta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is Kähler whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| <c$; hence $\mathcal K$ is open. If $\alpha $ is nef and $\varepsilon >0$, a representative $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ gives the Kähler form $	heta _\varepsilon +2\varepsilon \omega \in \alpha +2\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, so $\alpha \in \overline{\mathcal K}$. Conversely, let Kähler classes $\alpha _ j$ with Kähler forms $\omega _ j\in \alpha _ j$ converge to $\alpha $. Then $\omega _ j+	heta _{\alpha -\alpha _ j}\in \alpha $ is at least $-C\| \alpha -\alpha _ j\| \omega $, so $\alpha $ is nef; thus $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}$, and $\mathcal N\subset \mathcal E$ because $\mathcal K\subset \mathcal E$ and $\mathcal E$ is closed. Since $\mathcal K$ is open and contained in $\mathcal N$, it lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $\alpha $ is nef and $t>0$, then $\alpha +t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler: take a representative $	heta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ with $\varepsilon <t$. If $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$, then $\alpha -t\{ \omega \} $ is nef for small $t>0$, and therefore $\alpha =(\alpha -t\{ \omega \} )+t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler. Thus $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $T\in \alpha $ and $T\geq \delta \omega $, then $T+	heta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is positive whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| \leq \delta $, so a neighborhood of $\alpha $ lies in $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal E$, then $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} \in \mathcal E$ for some $\delta >0$, and adding $\delta \omega $ to a positive current in $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} $ gives a Kähler current in $\alpha $. Hence $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. $\square$ If $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ are smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms, Stokes' formula shows that $\int _ X	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$ is unchanged when one $	heta _ i$ is replaced by $	heta _ i+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth. We therefore write $\int _ X\alpha _1\cdots \alpha _ n=\int _ X	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$ for the intersection number of classes $\alpha _ i=\{ 	heta _ i\} $, and use the usual notation for powers, such as $\int _ X\alpha ^ n$. In the mixed Hodge index theorem below, the mixed scalar equation of lemma 10.2.9 turns a cohomological orthogonality condition into a pointwise one, to which the signature lemma for Hermitian matrices applies. Theorem 10.4.3 (The mixed Hodge index theorem) . 2AE132953DC7 Let $n\geq 2$, let $\omega _3,\ldots ,\omega _ n$ be Kähler forms on $X$, and put $\Omega =\omega _3\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n$, with $\Omega =1$ when $n=2$. The symmetric bilinear form \[  Q(\alpha , eta )=\int _ Xa\wedge b\wedge \Omega , \qquad a\in \alpha ,\quad b\in  eta ,  \] on $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ has signature $(1,\dim H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)-1)$. For every Kähler class $\gamma $, it is negative definite on the hyperplane $\{ \alpha :Q(\alpha ,\gamma )=0\} $. For Kähler classes $\alpha , eta $, A2FE7F1DA253 10.4.4  egin{equation}  Q(\alpha , eta )^2\geq Q(\alpha ,\alpha )Q( eta , eta ). \end{equation} Proof. Let $\gamma $ be a Kähler class with a Kähler form $h\in \gamma $, and let $\alpha $ satisfy $Q(\alpha ,\gamma )=0$. Choose a smooth closed real form $a\in \alpha $; then $\int _ Xa\wedge h\wedge \Omega =0$. Apply lemma 10.2.9 with $A=h\wedge \Omega $, a product of $n-1$ Kähler forms, and $\eta =-a\wedge h\wedge \Omega $. The resulting $f$ makes $a'=a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\in \alpha $ satisfy $a'\wedge h\wedge \Omega =0$ at every point. At a point, in holomorphic coordinates, the wedge products of real $(1,1)$-forms are expressed by mixed discriminants of their Hermitian matrices, so lemma 5.3.4 gives $a'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega \leq 0$, with equality only if $a'$ vanishes at that point. By Stokes' formula, \[  Q(\alpha ,\alpha )=\int _ Xa'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega \leq 0.  \] If this integral vanishes, the smooth nonpositive density $a'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega $ vanishes everywhere, so $a'=0$ and $\alpha =0$. Thus $Q$ is negative definite on the hyperplane $\{ Q(\cdot ,\gamma )=0\} $. Since $Q(\gamma ,\gamma )=\int _ Xh^2\wedge \Omega >0$, every class splits uniquely as a multiple of $\gamma $ plus a class in that hyperplane. The space $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is finite dimensional by theorem 10.2.15 , and $Q$ is positive on the line spanned by $\gamma $ and negative definite on its $Q$-orthogonal complement; this gives the signature. Finally, let $\alpha , eta $ be Kähler classes and write $ eta =c\alpha +\delta $ with $Q(\delta ,\alpha )=0$. Negative definiteness gives $Q( eta , eta )=c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )+Q(\delta ,\delta )\leq c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )$, while $Q(\alpha , eta )=cQ(\alpha ,\alpha )$. Since $Q(\alpha ,\alpha )>0$, we obtain $Q(\alpha , eta )^2=c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )^2\geq Q(\alpha ,\alpha )Q( eta , eta )$. $\square$ Corollary 10.4.5 . D52AB2ADBD8C Let $r\geq 1$, let $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ r$ be nef classes, and let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ r\geq 0$ be integers with $\sum _ i k_ i=n$. Then \[  \int _ X\alpha _1^{k_1}\cdots \alpha _ r^{k_ r} \geq \prod _{i:k_ i>0}\left(\int _ X\alpha _ i^ night)^{k_ i/n}.  \] In particular, for nef classes $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, \[  \int _ X\alpha _1\cdots \alpha _ n \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(\int _ X\alpha _ i^ night)^{1/n}.  \] Proof. Assume first that all $\alpha _ i$ are Kähler. Then all the intersection numbers $\int _ X\prod _ i\alpha _ i^{k_ i}$ are positive, and we put $b(k)=\log \int _ X\prod _ i\alpha _ i^{k_ i}$ for $k=(k_1,\ldots ,k_ r)$ with $\sum _ ik_ i=n$. If $n=1$, only one $k_ i$ is positive and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 2$. Let $i
eq j$ with $k_ i,k_ j\geq 1$, let $\Omega $ be the wedge product of Kähler representatives of the remaining $n-2$ factors, counted with multiplicity, and let $e_ i$ be the $i$th coordinate vector. Then ( 10.4.4 ) for $\alpha _ i,\alpha _ j$ reads \[  2b(k)\geq b(k+e_ i-e_ j)+b(k-e_ i+e_ j).  \] Fix the coordinates other than $i,j$ and put $s=k_ i+k_ j$. The inequality says that the finite sequence $l\mapsto b(\ldots ,l,\ldots ,s-l,\ldots )$, with $l$ in the $i$th and $s-l$ in the $j$th place, $0\leq l\leq s$, is concave: its consecutive differences decrease. A concave sequence lies above the linear interpolation between its endpoints, since the average of its first $l$ differences is at least the average of all $s$ differences. Consequently \[  b(k)\geq  rac{k_ i}{s}b(k^{(i)})+ rac{k_ j}{s}b(k^{(j)}),  \] where $k^{(i)}$ is obtained from $k$ by putting all $s$ factors in the $i$th place and $k^{(j)}$ by putting them in the $j$th place. We now prove $b(k)\geq \sum _ i(k_ i/n)\log \int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ by induction on the number of positive coordinates of $k$. If only one coordinate is positive, this is an equality. Otherwise choose $i
e j$ with $k_ i,k_ j\geq 1$. The vectors $k^{(i)}$ and $k^{(j)}$ have one positive coordinate fewer, and inserting the induction hypothesis for them into the last display gives the claim: for $m
e i,j$ the coefficient of $\log \int _ X\alpha _ m^ n$ is $(k_ i/s+k_ j/s)\, k_ m/n=k_ m/n$, and the coefficients of $\log \int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ and $\log \int _ X\alpha _ j^ n$ are $(k_ i/s)(s/n)=k_ i/n$ and $k_ j/n$. Exponentiating proves the corollary for Kähler classes. For nef classes, $\alpha _ i+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is Kähler for every $\varepsilon >0$ by proposition 10.4.2 , so the inequality holds for these classes. Each intersection number involved is a polynomial in $\varepsilon $ and tends to the corresponding number for the $\alpha _ i$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; in particular the limits $\int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ are nonnegative. Since $t\mapsto t^{k_ i/n}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty )$, the inequality passes to the limit. $\square$ The next proposition uses the cutoff-sum approximations $G_ m$ of lemma 6.17.1 : for $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and integers $m\geq 1$, $G_ m$ has gentle analytic singularities (definition 6.14.12 ) of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(m\varphi ))$ and satisfies $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(c/m)\omega $, where $c>0$ (the constant $c'$ of that lemma) depends only on $(X,\omega )$ and not on $	heta $, $\varphi $ or $m$. In particular $G_ m$ is smooth near every point where $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ is the unit ideal. Proposition 10.4.6 . 106B224C1E35 A class that contains a closed positive current with locally bounded potentials is nef. A class that contains a Kähler current with locally bounded potentials is Kähler. Every big class contains a Kähler current with gentle analytic singularities. Proof. Write the given current as $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. If $\varphi $ is bounded, then every $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ is the unit ideal, so the approximations $G_ m$ are smooth and satisfy $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(c/m)\omega $; hence the class is nef. If moreover $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $, then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta -\delta \omega )$, and the approximations for the background $	heta -\delta \omega $ satisfy $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq (\delta -c/m)\omega $; for large $m$ the smooth form $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ is a Kähler form in the class. For the last assertion, let $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $ be a Kähler current in a big class, with $\varphi $ not necessarily bounded. The same inequality shows that $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ is a Kähler current for large $m$, and $G_ m$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(m\varphi ))$ by lemma 6.17.1 . $\square$ Corollary 10.4.7 . 856BB9025ACA If a closed positive current with minimal singularities is a Kähler current, then its class is Kähler. Moreover, in a Kähler class every potential with minimal singularities is bounded. Proof. Write the current as $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $, where $\varphi $ has minimal singularities, and normalize $\varphi \leq 0$. Choose $C'\geq 0$ with $-	heta \leq C'\omega $ (lemma 6.14.1 ). For $0<t\leq \delta /(\delta +C')$ the current \[  (1-t)T+t	heta =	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}} igl ((1-t)\varphi  igr )\geq  igl ((1-t)\delta -tC' igr )\omega \geq 0  \] is positive, so $(1-t)\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$. By minimality, $(1-t)\varphi \leq \varphi +C$ for a constant $C$, so $\varphi \geq -C/t$ at every point where $\varphi $ is finite, hence almost everywhere. Since $\varphi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, the lower bound holds everywhere, as noted at the beginning of section 10.3 . Thus $\varphi $ is bounded, and proposition 10.4.6 shows that the class is Kähler. For the second assertion, suppose that the class contains a Kähler form $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Then $u$ is smooth and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, so a potential $\varphi $ with minimal singularities satisfies $u\leq \varphi +C$; hence $\varphi $ is bounded below, and it is bounded above as every quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. $\square$ Recall from definition 6.7.4 that the Lelong number $
u (T,x)$ of a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ at $x\in X$ is the Lelong number at $x$ of any local plurisubharmonic potential of $T$. If $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, then $\varphi +h$ is such a potential wherever $h$ is smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $, so $
u (T,x)=
u (\varphi ,x)$ in the sense recalled before proposition 10.3.9 ; in particular, these numbers do not depend on the background $	heta $. For a prime divisor $D\subset X$, the generic Lelong number of $T$ along $D$ (proposition 6.9.7 ) is therefore \[  
u (T,D)=\inf _{x\in D}
u (T,x)=\inf _{x\in D}
u (\varphi ,x)=
u (\varphi ,D),  \] and by that proposition the infimum is attained at every point of $D$ outside a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $D$. We write $[D]$ for the current of integration along $D$ (lemma 9.3.19 ); its coefficient measures are given by integration over $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and give no mass to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. Theorem 10.4.8 (Siu's divisorial decomposition) . D905BB5BE91D Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. Then $
u (T,D)>0$ for at most countably many prime divisors $D$, the series below converges weakly, and 383D7ED25D9E 10.4.9  egin{equation}  T=R+\sum _ D
u (T,D)[D], \end{equation} where $R$ is a closed positive current with $
u (R,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. In particular $T-
u (T,D)[D]\geq 0$ for every $D$. The decomposition is unique: if $T=R'+\sum _ Db_ D[D]$ for a weakly convergent series with coefficients $b_ D\geq 0$, at most countably many of them nonzero, and a closed positive current $R'$ with $
u (R',D)=0$ for every $D$, then $b_ D=
u (T,D)$ for every $D$ and $R'=R$. Proof. We first subtract one divisor, then show that only countably many divisors occur and that the series converges, and finally identify the residual current and prove uniqueness. Step 1: one divisor. Let $D$ be a prime divisor and $c=
u (T,D)$; we show that $T-c[D]\geq 0$. Near a regular point of $D$ choose coordinates with $D=\{ z_1=0\} $ on a coordinate polydisc $W$ with $|z_1|<1$, and a plurisubharmonic potential $u$ of $T$ on $W$. Since the Lelong numbers of $u$ at the points of $D\cap W$ are at least $c$, proposition 6.9.8 gives $u\leq c\log |z_1|^2+C$ near the point. Off $D$ the function $u-c\log |z_1|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and it is bounded above near $D$; by theorem 5.11.1 it extends to a plurisubharmonic function $v$. Since $v=u-c\log |z_1|^2$ almost everywhere and $[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z_1|^2$ near the point (theorem 5.5.6 ), we get $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=T-c[D]$ there. Hence $T-c[D]$ is positive on a neighborhood of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it equals $T$ on $X\setminus D$; so it is positive on the open set $X\setminus D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. To extend the positivity across $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, let $\phi $ be a strongly positive test form of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$. Since $T$ and $[D]$ have measure coefficients (theorem 5.3.7 ), there is a real measure $m_\phi $ on $X$, a combination of the coefficient measures with the coefficients of $\phi $ as densities, such that $(T-c[D])(\chi \phi )=\int \chi \, \mathrm dm_\phi $ for test functions $\chi $. The restriction of $m_\phi $ to the open set $X\setminus D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is a positive measure, because $(T-c[D])(\chi \phi )\geq 0$ for test functions $\chi \geq 0$ supported there; and its restriction to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is that of the positive measure $\chi \mapsto T(\chi \phi )$, because $[D]$ gives no mass to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. Hence $(T-c[D])(\phi )=m_\phi (X)\geq 0$, that is, $T-c[D]\geq 0$. Step 2: the series. By theorem 6.9.5 , each set $E_ j=\{ x:
u (T,x)\geq 1/j\} $ is an analytic subset of $X$ different from $X$. Being compact, $E_ j$ has finitely many irreducible components $Z$ by corollary 9.3.16 . We first show: 823C22786A3D 10.4.10  egin{equation}   egin{gathered} 	ext{a prime divisor $D$ contained in an analytic subset $E
eq X$}\ 	ext{is an irreducible component of $E$.} \end{gathered} \end{equation} An analytic subset of the connected manifold $X$ with an interior point is all of $X$, since the set of its interior points is open and, by the identity theorem applied to local defining functions, closed. Hence $E$ has no interior points, so its germs, and their branches, have dimension at most $n-1$, and $E_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension at most $n-2$ at every point (proposition 9.3.9 , corollary 9.3.13 ). At a point $y\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ the germ of $D$ has dimension $n-1$, so by monotonicity of dimension (see proposition 9.3.9 and the remarks following it) it is not contained in the germ of $E_{\mathrm{sing}}$; thus there are points $y'\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Near such a point $E$ is a complex submanifold of dimension at most $n-1$ containing the $(n-1)$-dimensional submanifold $D$, so $D$ and $E$ coincide near $y'$. Let $F$ be the connected component of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ containing $y'$. The analytic subset $D\cap F$ of the connected manifold $F$ has an interior point, so it is all of $F$, and $D$ contains the closure $Z$ of $F$, an irreducible component of $E$ (corollary 9.3.16 ). Since $D$ is compact and the components of $E$ form a locally finite family, $D$ meets only finitely many of them and is the union of its intersections with these. By induction on the number of sets, an irreducible set is not a finite union of analytic subsets different from itself; hence $D=D\cap Z'$ for a component $Z'$. Then $Z\subset D\subset Z'$, and since no component is contained in another, $D=Z$. This proves ( 10.4.10 ). In particular, two distinct prime divisors are not contained in one another, and every prime divisor $D$ with $
u (T,D)\geq 1/j$, being contained in $E_ j$, is one of its finitely many components. Therefore at most countably many prime divisors have $
u (T,D)>0$. Let $D_1,D_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration of them and put $S_ N=\sum _{k\leq N}
u (T,D_ k)[D_ k]$. We claim that $T-S_ N\geq 0$ for every $N$, and argue by induction; suppose that $T-S_{N-1}\geq 0$. Choose a point $x\in D_ N$ outside the proper analytic subsets $D_ N\cap D_ k$, $k<N$, and outside the exceptional sets of proposition 6.9.7 for $T$ and $T-S_{N-1}$ along $D_ N$. Such points exist, because by that proposition the complement in $D_ N$ of a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $D_ N$ is dense in $D_ N$. The currents $[D_ k]$, $k<N$, vanish near $x$, so $T-S_{N-1}=T$ near $x$, and therefore $
u (T-S_{N-1},D_ N)=

Consequently the trace measures of the $S_ N$ in every chart are bounded by that of $T$, and the masses $\int _ XS_ N\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ are bounded by $\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$. We now show that the sequence $(S_ N)$ converges weakly. Every test form is a finite linear combination of test forms $g\gamma $, where $g\geq 0$ is a test function supported in a chart and $\gamma $ is a strongly positive form with constant coefficients in that chart. To see this, use a partition of unity (proposition 5.2.6 ), the fact that strongly positive forms span the real forms (proposition 5.3.2 ), and write a real test function $g$ as $(g+M\psi )-M\psi $ with $\psi \geq 0$ a test function equal to one on $\operatorname{Supp}g$ and $M\geq \sup |g|$. Finally $R=T-S$ is closed and positive, as a weak limit of the closed positive currents $T-S_ N$. Step 3: properties of $R$ and uniqueness. Fix a prime divisor $D$ and write $T=R+
u (T,D)[D]+S_ D$, where $S_ D$ is the sum of the terms of the series for the other divisors. Lelong numbers are additive and nonnegative (proposition 6.7.9 ), and $

Hence $D\cap D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a null set for the surface measure of $D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$ (lemma 5.5.1 , in local coordinates of $D'_{\mathrm{reg}}$), and $[D']$ gives no mass to $D$. Now let $K\subset D$ be a compact subset of a chart, and for large $m$ let $\chi _ m$ be test functions with $0\leq \chi _ m\leq 1$, equal to one on $K$ and supported in the $1/m$-neighborhood of $K$ (lemma 2.5.1 ), all supported in a fixed compact subset of the chart, on which a test function $\psi $ equals one. For the trace measures in the chart, the weak convergence of the series gives $\mu _{S'_ D}(\chi _ m)=\sum _{D'}b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(\chi _ m)$. As $m	o \infty $, $\chi _ m	o \mathbf1_ K$ pointwise, and dominated convergence, applied to the measure $\mu _{S'_ D}$ and to the series, whose terms are bounded by $b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(\psi )$ with $\sum _{D'}b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(\psi )=\mu _{S'_ D}(\psi )<\infty $, gives $\mu _{S'_ D}(K)=\sum _{D'}b_{D'}\mu _{[D']}(K)=0$. Since $D$ is covered by countably many such compact sets, the trace measures of $S'_ D$, and hence its coefficient measures (theorem 5.3.7 ), vanish on $D$. By Step 1, $S'_ D-
u (S'_ D,D)[D]\geq 0$; comparing the trace measures of both sides on $D$, where $[D]$ has positive trace mass, forces $

u (T,D)$ for every $D$, and $R'=R$. $\square$ Definition 10.4.11 . A72955F9A4C1 A class $\alpha $ is modified nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a closed current $T_\varepsilon \in \alpha $ with $T_\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ and $
u (T_\varepsilon +\varepsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. We write $\mathcal{MN}$ for the cone of modified nef classes. A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $
u (T,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$ is called non-divisorial . The set $\mathcal{MN}$ is a convex cone. Indeed, multiplying $T_\varepsilon $ by $t>0$ shows that $t\alpha $ is modified nef, with $tT_{\varepsilon /t}$ for the allowance $\varepsilon $. If $\alpha ,\alpha '$ are modified nef, with currents $T_\varepsilon ,T'_\varepsilon $, then $T_{\varepsilon /2}+T'_{\varepsilon /2}\geq -\varepsilon \omega $ lies in $\alpha +\alpha '$. At a point of a prime divisor $D$ at which the Lelong numbers of the positive currents $T_{\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega /2$ and $T'_{\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega /2$ attain their generic values $0$ (proposition 6.9.7 ), the additivity of Lelong numbers (proposition 6.7.9 ) shows that their sum has Lelong number $0$; hence $
u (T_{\varepsilon /2}+T'_{\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega ,D)=0$. The cone $\mathcal{MN}$ contains $\mathcal N$, since smooth forms have zero Lelong numbers, and it is contained in $\mathcal E$: if $\alpha $ is modified nef, then $\alpha +\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ contains the positive current $T_\varepsilon +\varepsilon \omega $, and $\mathcal E$ is closed. It is also closed. Indeed, let $\alpha _ j	o \alpha $ with $\alpha _ j\in \mathcal{MN}$, and let $\varepsilon >0$. By ( 10.2.18 ) we may choose $j$ such that $\alpha -\alpha _ j$ has a smooth representative $\eta $ with $-\varepsilon \omega /2\leq \eta \leq \varepsilon \omega /2$. If $T'\in \alpha _ j$ satisfies $T'\geq -\varepsilon \omega /2$ and $
u (T'+\varepsilon \omega /2,D)=0$ for all $D$, then $T'+\eta \in \alpha $ satisfies $T'+\eta \geq -\varepsilon \omega $, and $
u (T'+\eta +\varepsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for all $D$, since adding smooth forms does not change Lelong numbers. As for the classes of definition 10.4.1 , the definition of modified nef classes does not depend on $\omega $. Indeed, let $\omega '$ be another Kähler form and $C\geq 1$ with $\omega \leq C\omega '$ (lemma 6.14.1 ). For every $\varepsilon >0$ the current $T=T_{\varepsilon /C}$ satisfies $T\geq -(\varepsilon /C)\omega \geq -\varepsilon \omega '$, and the positive currents $T+\varepsilon \omega '$ and $T+(\varepsilon /C)\omega $ differ by a smooth form, so that $
u (T+\varepsilon \omega ',D)=
u (T+(\varepsilon /C)\omega ,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. In the definition of modified nef classes we may take $T_\varepsilon $ with gentle analytic singularities whose pole set has codimension at least two. Indeed, write $T_{\varepsilon /2}=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +\varepsilon \omega /2)$ and apply lemma 6.17.1 to $\varphi $ with the background $	heta +\varepsilon \omega /2$, choosing $m$ with $c/m<\varepsilon /2$. Then $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -\varepsilon \omega $. Since $
u (\varphi ,D)=
u (T_{\varepsilon /2}+\varepsilon \omega /2,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$, at a point $x$ of $D$ where $
u (\varphi ,x)=
u (\varphi ,D)$ the ideal $\mathcal I(m\varphi )_ x$ is the unit ideal by corollary 6.9.3 . Hence the pole set of $G_ m$, which is the zero set of $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$, contains no prime divisor. It is not all of $X$, since $\mathcal I(m\varphi )_ x$ is the unit ideal at every point $x$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $, where $
u (\varphi ,x)=0$ (proposition 6.7.1 ); so its irreducible components have codimension at least one, those of codimension one would be prime divisors, and it has codimension at least two. Moreover $G_ m$ is smooth near such a point $x$, so the Lelong numbers of $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m+\varepsilon \omega $ vanish there, and $
u (	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m+\varepsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. Thus $T_\varepsilon =	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ has the required properties. Corollary 10.4.12 . B72607AB8B41 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ be distinct prime divisors and $a_1,\ldots ,a_ N>0$ real numbers, and put $D=\sum _ ia_ iD_ i$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has logarithmic singularities along $D$ with bounded remainder: near each point, $\varphi =\sum _ ia_ i\log |s_ i|^2+v$ with $v$ bounded, where $s_ i$ is a local equation of $D_ i$ (lemma 9.3.19 ), and $s_ i=1$ if the point does not lie on $D_ i$. Then $\{ 	heta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef, where $\{ D\} =\sum _ ia_ i\{ [D_ i]\} $. If $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current, then $\{ 	heta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. Proof. Near a point, let $h$ be smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=	heta $. Off the support of $D$ the function $v+h=(\varphi +h)-\sum _ ia_ i\log |s_ i|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, since $\log |s_ i|^2$ is pluriharmonic there, and it is bounded above. On a connected coordinate neighborhood of the point, the support of $D$ lies in the zero set of the holomorphic function $\prod _ is_ i
ot\equiv 0$, so theorem 5.11.1 extends $v+h$ to a plurisubharmonic function $\widetilde v$. The values of $\widetilde v$ on the support of $D$ are upper limits of values of $v+h$, so $\widetilde v$ is bounded, and $\widetilde v=v+h$ outside the null set $\operatorname{Supp}D$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ i|^2=[D_ i]$ (lemma 9.3.19 ), the current $T=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ satisfies $T-[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\geq 0$ near the point, where $[D]=\sum _ ia_ i[D_ i]$. title: Definition 10.4.1
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
text: Definition 10.4.1 . CFDE52E42C6B A class $\alpha \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is pseudo-effective if it contains a closed positive current; Kähler if it contains a Kähler form; nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ it contains a smooth form $\theta _\varepsilon $ with $\theta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $; big if it contains a closed current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. A closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$ is called a Kähler current . The cones of pseudo-effective, Kähler, nef and big classes are denoted $\mathcal E$, $\mathcal K$, $\mathcal N$ and $\mathcal B$. The zero class belongs to the pseudo-effective cone and to the nef cone.

title: Proposition 10.4.2
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
text: Proposition 10.4.2 . 3B6E3B145113 The pseudo-effective cone $\mathcal E$ is closed and convex, and the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is open and convex. Moreover $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}\subset \mathcal E$, the Kähler cone $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$, and the big cone $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. Proof. Sums and positive multiples of positive currents, Kähler forms or nef representatives are of the same kind, which proves convexity of all four cones. Let $\alpha _ j\to \alpha $ be pseudo-effective classes, with positive currents $T_ j\in \alpha _ j$. Since the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a distribution pairs to zero with the closed form $\omega ^{n-1}$, the trace masses are \[  \int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1} =\int _ X\theta _{\alpha _ j}\wedge \omega ^{n-1},  \] where $\theta _{\alpha _ j}$ are the representatives of ( 10.2.18 ); they are bounded because the classes converge. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart, $\chi $ a test function on the chart with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $K$, and $c'>0$ such that $\beta \leq c'\omega $ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 6.14.1 ), where $\beta $ is the Euclidean form ( 5.2.8 ) of the chart. By ( 10.2.10 ), applied with $\gamma _ j=c'\omega $ and $\gamma '_ j=\beta $, the form $(c'\omega )^{n-1}-\beta ^{n-1}$ is a sum of products of semipositive $(1,1)$-forms on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, hence strongly positive (proposition 5.3.2 ). Therefore $c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-\chi \beta ^{n-1}=(1-\chi )c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}+\chi \bigl (c'^{n-1}\omega ^{n-1}-\beta ^{n-1}\bigr )$, with $\chi \beta ^{n-1}$ extended by zero outside the chart, is a smooth strongly positive form on $X$, so the trace measures satisfy $\mu _{T_ j}(K)\leq T_ j(\chi \beta ^{n-1})\leq c'^{n-1}\int _ XT_ j\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$, which is bounded independently of $j$. By the compactness assertion of theorem 5.3.7 , a subsequence of $(T_ j)$ converges weakly to a closed positive current $T$, and $\{ T\} =\alpha $ because the class map is weakly continuous. Hence $\mathcal E$ is closed. If $\omega _0\in \alpha $ is a Kähler form, then $\omega _0\geq c\omega $ for some $c>0$, and by ( 10.2.18 ) the form $\omega _0+\theta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is Kähler whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| <c$; hence $\mathcal K$ is open. If $\alpha $ is nef and $\varepsilon >0$, a representative $\theta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ gives the Kähler form $\theta _\varepsilon +2\varepsilon \omega \in \alpha +2\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $, so $\alpha \in \overline{\mathcal K}$. Conversely, let Kähler classes $\alpha _ j$ with Kähler forms $\omega _ j\in \alpha _ j$ converge to $\alpha $. Then $\omega _ j+\theta _{\alpha -\alpha _ j}\in \alpha $ is at least $-C\| \alpha -\alpha _ j\| \omega $, so $\alpha $ is nef; thus $\mathcal N=\overline{\mathcal K}$, and $\mathcal N\subset \mathcal E$ because $\mathcal K\subset \mathcal E$ and $\mathcal E$ is closed. Since $\mathcal K$ is open and contained in $\mathcal N$, it lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $\alpha $ is nef and $t>0$, then $\alpha +t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler: take a representative $\theta _\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ with $\varepsilon <t$. If $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal N$, then $\alpha -t\{ \omega \} $ is nef for small $t>0$, and therefore $\alpha =(\alpha -t\{ \omega \} )+t\{ \omega \} $ is Kähler. Thus $\mathcal K$ is the interior of $\mathcal N$. If $T\in \alpha $ and $T\geq \delta \omega $, then $T+\theta _{\alpha '-\alpha }\in \alpha '$ is positive whenever $C\| \alpha '-\alpha \| \leq \delta $, so a neighborhood of $\alpha $ lies in $\mathcal E$. Conversely, if $\alpha $ lies in the interior of $\mathcal E$, then $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} \in \mathcal E$ for some $\delta >0$, and adding $\delta \omega $ to a positive current in $\alpha -\delta \{ \omega \} $ gives a Kähler current in $\alpha $. Hence $\mathcal B$ is the interior of $\mathcal E$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.4.3 (The mixed Hodge index theorem)
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
text: Theorem 10.4.3 (The mixed Hodge index theorem) . 2AE132953DC7 Let $n\geq 2$, let $\omega _3,\ldots ,\omega _ n$ be Kähler forms on $X$, and put $\Omega =\omega _3\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _ n$, with $\Omega =1$ when $n=2$. The symmetric bilinear form \[  Q(\alpha ,\beta )=\int _ Xa\wedge b\wedge \Omega , \qquad a\in \alpha ,\quad b\in \beta ,  \] on $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ has signature $(1,\dim H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)-1)$. For every Kähler class $\gamma $, it is negative definite on the hyperplane $\{ \alpha :Q(\alpha ,\gamma )=0\} $. For Kähler classes $\alpha ,\beta $, A2FE7F1DA253 10.4.4 \begin{equation}  Q(\alpha ,\beta )^2\geq Q(\alpha ,\alpha )Q(\beta ,\beta ). \end{equation} Proof. Let $\gamma $ be a Kähler class with a Kähler form $h\in \gamma $, and let $\alpha $ satisfy $Q(\alpha ,\gamma )=0$. Choose a smooth closed real form $a\in \alpha $; then $\int _ Xa\wedge h\wedge \Omega =0$. Apply lemma 10.2.9 with $A=h\wedge \Omega $, a product of $n-1$ Kähler forms, and $\eta =-a\wedge h\wedge \Omega $. The resulting $f$ makes $a'=a+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\in \alpha $ satisfy $a'\wedge h\wedge \Omega =0$ at every point. At a point, in holomorphic coordinates, the wedge products of real $(1,1)$-forms are expressed by mixed discriminants of their Hermitian matrices, so lemma 5.3.4 gives $a'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega \leq 0$, with equality only if $a'$ vanishes at that point. By Stokes' formula, \[  Q(\alpha ,\alpha )=\int _ Xa'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega \leq 0.  \] If this integral vanishes, the smooth nonpositive density $a'\wedge a'\wedge \Omega $ vanishes everywhere, so $a'=0$ and $\alpha =0$. Thus $Q$ is negative definite on the hyperplane $\{ Q(\cdot ,\gamma )=0\} $. Since $Q(\gamma ,\gamma )=\int _ Xh^2\wedge \Omega >0$, every class splits uniquely as a multiple of $\gamma $ plus a class in that hyperplane. The space $H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ is finite dimensional by theorem 10.2.15 , and $Q$ is positive on the line spanned by $\gamma $ and negative definite on its $Q$-orthogonal complement; this gives the signature. Finally, let $\alpha ,\beta $ be Kähler classes and write $\beta =c\alpha +\delta $ with $Q(\delta ,\alpha )=0$. Negative definiteness gives $Q(\beta ,\beta )=c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )+Q(\delta ,\delta )\leq c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )$, while $Q(\alpha ,\beta )=cQ(\alpha ,\alpha )$. Since $Q(\alpha ,\alpha )>0$, we obtain $Q(\alpha ,\beta )^2=c^2Q(\alpha ,\alpha )^2\geq Q(\alpha ,\alpha )Q(\beta ,\beta )$. $\square$
