title: Corollary 10.4.5
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
text:
Corollary 10.4.5 . D52AB2ADBD8C Let $r\geq 1$, let $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ r$ be nef classes, and let $k_1,\ldots ,k_ r\geq 0$ be integers with $\sum _ i k_ i=n$. Then \[  \int _ X\alpha _1^{k_1}\cdots \alpha _ r^{k_ r} \geq \prod _{i:k_ i>0}\left(\int _ X\alpha _ i^ night)^{k_ i/n}.  \] In particular, for nef classes $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, \[  \int _ X\alpha _1\cdots \alpha _ n \geq \prod _{i=1}^ n\left(\int _ X\alpha _ i^ night)^{1/n}.  \] Proof. Assume first that all $\alpha _ i$ are Kähler. Then all the intersection numbers $\int _ X\prod _ i\alpha _ i^{k_ i}$ are positive, and we put $b(k)=\log \int _ X\prod _ i\alpha _ i^{k_ i}$ for $k=(k_1,\ldots ,k_ r)$ with $\sum _ ik_ i=n$. If $n=1$, only one $k_ i$ is positive and there is nothing to prove; let $n\geq 2$. Let $i
eq j$ with $k_ i,k_ j\geq 1$, let $\Omega $ be the wedge product of Kähler representatives of the remaining $n-2$ factors, counted with multiplicity, and let $e_ i$ be the $i$th coordinate vector. Then ( 10.4.4 ) for $\alpha _ i,\alpha _ j$ reads \[  2b(k)\geq b(k+e_ i-e_ j)+b(k-e_ i+e_ j).  \] Fix the coordinates other than $i,j$ and put $s=k_ i+k_ j$. The inequality says that the finite sequence $l\mapsto b(\ldots ,l,\ldots ,s-l,\ldots )$, with $l$ in the $i$th and $s-l$ in the $j$th place, $0\leq l\leq s$, is concave: its consecutive differences decrease. A concave sequence lies above the linear interpolation between its endpoints, since the average of its first $l$ differences is at least the average of all $s$ differences. Consequently \[  b(k)\geq  rac{k_ i}{s}b(k^{(i)})+ rac{k_ j}{s}b(k^{(j)}),  \] where $k^{(i)}$ is obtained from $k$ by putting all $s$ factors in the $i$th place and $k^{(j)}$ by putting them in the $j$th place. We now prove $b(k)\geq \sum _ i(k_ i/n)\log \int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ by induction on the number of positive coordinates of $k$. If only one coordinate is positive, this is an equality. Otherwise choose $i
e j$ with $k_ i,k_ j\geq 1$. The vectors $k^{(i)}$ and $k^{(j)}$ have one positive coordinate fewer, and inserting the induction hypothesis for them into the last display gives the claim: for $m
e i,j$ the coefficient of $\log \int _ X\alpha _ m^ n$ is $(k_ i/s+k_ j/s)\, k_ m/n=k_ m/n$, and the coefficients of $\log \int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ and $\log \int _ X\alpha _ j^ n$ are $(k_ i/s)(s/n)=k_ i/n$ and $k_ j/n$. Exponentiating proves the corollary for Kähler classes. For nef classes, $\alpha _ i+\varepsilon \{ \omega \} $ is Kähler for every $\varepsilon >0$ by proposition 10.4.2 , so the inequality holds for these classes. Each intersection number involved is a polynomial in $\varepsilon $ and tends to the corresponding number for the $\alpha _ i$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; in particular the limits $\int _ X\alpha _ i^ n$ are nonnegative. Since $t\mapsto t^{k_ i/n}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty )$, the inequality passes to the limit. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.4.6
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
text: Proposition 10.4.6 . 106B224C1E35 A class that contains a closed positive current with locally bounded potentials is nef. A class that contains a Kähler current with locally bounded potentials is Kähler. Every big class contains a Kähler current with gentle analytic singularities. Proof. Write the given current as $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. If $\varphi $ is bounded, then every $\mathcal I(m\varphi )$ is the unit ideal, so the approximations $G_ m$ are smooth and satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq -(c/m)\omega $; hence the class is nef. If moreover $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $, then $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta -\delta \omega )$, and the approximations for the background $\theta -\delta \omega $ satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m\geq (\delta -c/m)\omega $; for large $m$ the smooth form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ is a Kähler form in the class. For the last assertion, let $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $ be a Kähler current in a big class, with $\varphi $ not necessarily bounded. The same inequality shows that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ m$ is a Kähler current for large $m$, and $G_ m$ has gentle analytic singularities of type $(m^{-1},\mathcal I(m\varphi ))$ by lemma 6.17.1 . $\square$

title: Corollary 10.4.7
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition
text: Corollary 10.4.7 . 856BB9025ACA If a closed positive current with minimal singularities is a Kähler current, then its class is Kähler. Moreover, in a Kähler class every potential with minimal singularities is bounded. Proof. Write the current as $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi \geq \delta \omega $, where $\varphi $ has minimal singularities, and normalize $\varphi \leq 0$. Choose $C'\geq 0$ with $-\theta \leq C'\omega $ (lemma 6.14.1 ). For $0<t\leq \delta /(\delta +C')$ the current \[  (1-t)T+t\theta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((1-t)\varphi \bigr )\geq \bigl ((1-t)\delta -tC'\bigr )\omega \geq 0  \] is positive, so $(1-t)\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. By minimality, $(1-t)\varphi \leq \varphi +C$ for a constant $C$, so $\varphi \geq -C/t$ at every point where $\varphi $ is finite, hence almost everywhere. Since $\varphi $ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, the lower bound holds everywhere, as noted at the beginning of section 10.3 . Thus $\varphi $ is bounded, and proposition 10.4.6 shows that the class is Kähler. For the second assertion, suppose that the class contains a Kähler form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Then $u$ is smooth and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, so a potential $\varphi $ with minimal singularities satisfies $u\leq \varphi +C$; hence $\varphi $ is bounded below, and it is bounded above as every quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $X$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.4.8 (Siu's divisorial decomposition)
section: 10.4 Positivity cones and divisorial decomposition

Theorem 10.4.8 (Siu's divisorial decomposition) . D905BB5BE91D Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $X$. Then $

u (T,D)$; we show that $T-c[D]\geq 0$. Near a regular point of $D$ choose coordinates with $D=\{ z_1=0\} $ on a coordinate polydisc $W$ with $|z_1|<1$, and a plurisubharmonic potential $u$ of $T$ on $W$. Since the Lelong numbers of $u$ at the points of $D\cap W$ are at least $c$, proposition 6.9.8 gives $u\leq c\log |z_1|^2+C$ near the point. Off $D$ the function $u-c\log |z_1|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, and it is bounded above near $D$; by theorem 5.11.1 it extends to a plurisubharmonic function $v$. Since $v=u-c\log |z_1|^2$ almost everywhere and $[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z_1|^2$ near the point (theorem 5.5.6 ), we get $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=T-c[D]$ there. Hence $T-c[D]$ is positive on a neighborhood of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$, and it equals $T$ on $X\setminus D$; so it is positive on the open set $X\setminus D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. To extend the positivity across $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, let $\phi $ be a strongly positive test form of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$. Since $T$ and $[D]$ have measure coefficients (theorem 5.3.7 ), there is a real measure $m_\phi $ on $X$, a combination of the coefficient measures with the coefficients of $\phi $ as densities, such that $(T-c[D])(\chi \phi )=\int \chi \, \mathrm dm_\phi $ for test functions $\chi $. The restriction of $m_\phi $ to the open set $X\setminus D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is a positive measure, because $(T-c[D])(\chi \phi )\geq 0$ for test functions $\chi \geq 0$ supported there; and its restriction to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is that of the positive measure $\chi \mapsto T(\chi \phi )$, because $[D]$ gives no mass to $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$. Hence $(T-c[D])(\phi )=m_\phi (X)\geq 0$, that is, $T-c[D]\geq 0$. Step 2: the series. By theorem 6.9.5 , each set $E_ j=\{ x:

eq X$}\ 	ext{is an irreducible component of $E$.} \end{gathered} \end{equation} An analytic subset of the connected manifold $X$ with an interior point is all of $X$, since the set of its interior points is open and, by the identity theorem applied to local defining functions, closed. Hence $E$ has no interior points, so its germs, and their branches, have dimension at most $n-1$, and $E_{\mathrm{sing}}$ has dimension at most $n-2$ at every point (proposition 9.3.9 , corollary 9.3.13 ). At a point $y\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ the germ of $D$ has dimension $n-1$, so by monotonicity of dimension (see proposition 9.3.9 and the remarks following it) it is not contained in the germ of $E_{\mathrm{sing}}$; thus there are points $y'\in D_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap E_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Near such a point $E$ is a complex submanifold of dimension at most $n-1$ containing the $(n-1)$-dimensional submanifold $D$, so $D$ and $E$ coincide near $y'$. Let $F$ be the connected component of $E_{\mathrm{reg}}$ containing $y'$. The analytic subset $D\cap F$ of the connected manifold $F$ has an interior point, so it is all of $F$, and $D$ contains the closure $Z$ of $F$, an irreducible component of $E$ (corollary 9.3.16 ). Since $D$ is compact and the components of $E$ form a locally finite family, $D$ meets only finitely many of them and is the union of its intersections with these. By induction on the number of sets, an irreducible set is not a finite union of analytic subsets different from itself; hence $D=D\cap Z'$ for a component $Z'$. Then $Z\subset D\subset Z'$, and since no component is contained in another, $D=Z$. This proves ( 10.4.10 ). In particular, two distinct prime divisors are not contained in one another, and every prime divisor $D$ with $

title: Definition 10.4.11

text: Definition 10.4.11 . A72955F9A4C1 A class $\alpha $ is modified nef if for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a closed current $T_\varepsilon \in \alpha $ with $T_\varepsilon \geq -\varepsilon \omega $ and $\nu (T_\varepsilon +\varepsilon \omega ,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$. We write $\mathcal{MN}$ for the cone of modified nef classes. A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ with $\nu (T,D)=0$ for every prime divisor $D$ is called non-divisorial .

B72607AB8B41 Let $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ N$ be distinct prime divisors and $a_1,\ldots ,a_ N>0$ real numbers, and put $D=\sum _ ia_ iD_ i$. Suppose that $\varphi $ has logarithmic singularities along $D$ with bounded remainder: near each point, $\varphi =\sum _ ia_ i\log |s_ i|^2+v$ with $v$ bounded, where $s_ i$ is a local equation of $D_ i$ (lemma 9.3.19 ), and $s_ i=1$ if the point does not lie on $D_ i$. Then $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is nef, where $\{ D\} =\sum _ ia_ i\{ [D_ i]\} $. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a Kähler current, then $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ is Kähler. Proof. Near a point, let $h$ be smooth with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\theta $. Off the support of $D$ the function $v+h=(\varphi +h)-\sum _ ia_ i\log |s_ i|^2$ is plurisubharmonic, since $\log |s_ i|^2$ is pluriharmonic there, and it is bounded above. On a connected coordinate neighborhood of the point, the support of $D$ lies in the zero set of the holomorphic function $\prod _ is_ i\not\equiv 0$, so theorem 5.11.1 extends $v+h$ to a plurisubharmonic function $\widetilde v$. The values of $\widetilde v$ on the support of $D$ are upper limits of values of $v+h$, so $\widetilde v$ is bounded, and $\widetilde v=v+h$ outside the null set $\operatorname{Supp}D$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s_ i|^2=[D_ i]$ (lemma 9.3.19 ), the current $T=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ satisfies $T-[D]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\geq 0$ near the point, where $[D]=\sum _ ia_ i[D_ i]$. Thus $T-[D]$ is a positive current in $\{ \theta \} -\{ D\} $ with locally bounded potentials. If $T\geq \delta \omega $, apply the same argument to $T-\delta \omega $, whose potential has the same logarithmic singularities; then $T-[D]\geq \delta \omega $. In both cases proposition 10.4.6 gives the assertion. $\square$

u (S,D')=0$. Hence $\pi _*S$ is non-divisorial. Let $ eta $ be a modified nef class on $Y$ and $t>0$. The class $ eta +t\{ \omega _ Y\} $ is big, and it is modified nef because $\mathcal{MN}$ is a convex cone containing the Kähler classes. By proposition 10.5.2 , a positive current with minimal singularities in this class is non-divisorial. Its pushforward is a non-divisorial positive current in $\pi _* eta +t\pi _*\{ \omega _ Y\} $, so this class is modified nef: the definition is satisfied with $T_\varepsilon $ equal to this current for every $\varepsilon $. These classes tend to $\pi _* eta $ as $t\downarrow 0$, and $\mathcal{MN}$ is closed, so $\pi _* eta $ is modified nef. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.5.7
section: 10.5 Minimal multiplicities and positivity loci
text:
Lemma 10.5.7 . C3C3386FA4FC Let $\pi \colon Y	o X$ be as above, and let $S$ be a non-divisorial closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $Y$. Then \[  \pi ^*\pi _*S=S+\sum _ E c_ E[E],\qquad c_ E\geq 0,  \] where $E$ ranges over the finitely many exceptional prime divisors of $\pi $. For every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $X$, $\pi _*\pi ^*T=T$. For a prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, $\pi _*[E]=0$ if $E$ is exceptional, and $\pi _*[E]=[\pi (E)]$ otherwise. Proof. Let $A$ be as above. The positive current $\pi ^*\pi _*S$, defined through local potentials as above, agrees with $S$ on $Y\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$. Their difference is a closed real current with measure coefficients supported on the proper analytic subset $\pi ^{-1}(A)$ of $Y$. By theorem 9.3.20 , it is a finite real linear combination of the currents of integration along the irreducible components of codimension one of the compact analytic set $\pi ^{-1}(A)$, which are exactly the exceptional prime divisors, as shown above; there are finitely many of them by corollary 9.3.16 . It remains to show that the coefficients $c_ E$ are nonnegative. Near a regular point of an exceptional prime divisor $E$ that lies on no other component, the difference is $c_ E[E]=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(c_ E\log |s_ E|^2)$, where $s_ E$ is a local equation of $E$ (lemma 9.3.19 ), so local potentials $u'$ of $\pi ^*\pi _*S$ and $u$ of $S$ satisfy $u'=u+c_ E\log |s_ E|^2+p$ with $p$ pluriharmonic. The additivity of Lelong numbers (proposition 6.7.9 ), applied to this identity if $c_ E\geq 0$ and to $u=u'+|c_ E|\log |s_ E|^2-p$ otherwise, together with $
u (\log |s_ E|^2,y)=1$, gives $
u (u',y)=
u (u,y)+c_ E$ at such points $y$. At points that are moreover generic for both currents, which exist because the points of $E$ excluded by these conditions form a countable union of proper analytic subsets of $E$ (proposition 6.9.7 ), this reads $
u (\pi ^*\pi _*S,E)=
u (S,E)+c_ E$; hence $c_ E=
u (\pi ^*\pi _*S,E)\geq 0$, since $S$ is non-divisorial. Since $\pi $ is a biholomorphism over $X\setminus A$, the positive current $\pi _*\pi ^*T$ agrees with $T$ on $X\setminus A$. Hence $\pi _*\pi ^*T-T$ is a closed real current with measure coefficients (theorem 5.3.7 ) supported on $A$, which has codimension at least two, so it vanishes by theorem 9.3.20 . For a prime divisor $E$ on $Y$, the current $\pi _*[E]$ is positive, closed and supported on the analytic set $\pi (E)$. If $E$ is exceptional, $\pi (E)$ has codimension at least two and $\pi _*[E]=0$ by the same theorem. Otherwise $\pi $ maps $E\setminus \pi ^{-1}(A)$ isomorphically onto $\pi (E)\setminus A$, so $\pi _*[E]=[\pi (E)]$ on $X\setminus A$, and the closed current $\pi _*[E]-[\pi (E)]$ of order zero is supported on $\pi (E)\cap A$, of codimension at least two in $X$; it vanishes by the same theorem. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.5.8
section: 10.5 Minimal multiplicities and positivity loci
text: Proposition 10.5.8 . 20DDDD0E7ECB Let $\pi \colon Y\to X$ be as above. Then $\pi ^*$ and $\pi _*$ map big classes to big classes. Proof. Choose $C$ with $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\omega _ Y$. Since $\pi _*$ preserves positivity, lemma 10.5.7 gives $\pi _*\omega _ Y\geq C^{-1}\pi _*\pi ^*\omega =C^{-1}\omega $. Hence a current $S\geq \delta \omega _ Y$ on $Y$ has $\pi _*S\geq \delta C^{-1}\omega $, which proves the assertion for $\pi _*$. Let $\alpha $ be big on $X$ and $T\in \alpha $ with $T\geq \delta \omega $. Choose a smooth closed representative $\eta $ of the class $\{ \pi _*\omega _ Y\} $, a constant $B>0$ with $\eta \leq B\omega $ (lemma 6.14.1 ), and $t>0$ with $tB\leq \delta $, so that $T-t\eta \geq 0$. The positive current $T-t\eta +t\pi _*\omega _ Y$ lies in $\alpha $. By lemma 10.5.7 , applied to the smooth, hence non-divisorial, current $\omega _ Y$, its pullback is \[  \pi ^*(T-t\eta )+t\omega _ Y+t\sum _ E c_ E[E]\geq t\omega _ Y.  \] This is a Kähler current in $\pi ^*\alpha $, so $\pi ^*\alpha $ is big. $\square$

title: Example 10.5.9
section: 10.5 Minimal multiplicities and positivity loci
text: Example 10.5.9 . A7A7F69130A0 The zero class $\alpha =0$ is nef, so $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(0)=\varnothing $ by theorem 10.5.4 . It is not big: a Kähler current $T\geq \delta \omega $ would have $\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}\geq \delta \int _ X\omega ^ n>0$, whereas this integral vanishes for every closed current in the zero class. Hence $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(0)=X$. More generally, $E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )=X$ for every class that is not big, while $E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )=\varnothing $ for every nef class; on the boundary of the pseudo-effective cone the two loci therefore detect different failures of positivity. This is also why the minimal multiplicities are defined with the allowances $\varepsilon \omega $ rather than through $V_\theta $: for a class that is not big, proposition 10.5.2 gives only the inequality $\nu (\alpha ,x)\leq \nu (V_\theta ,x)$, since the proof of equality uses a Kähler current in $\alpha $.

title: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
search_title: Curvature and metrics defined by sections
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text:
This section collects the notions for line bundles on $X$ used in the rest of the chapter, from the curvature class to the Fubini–Study metrics defined by holomorphic sections, and shows that spaces of global holomorphic sections are finite dimensional. Let $L	o X$ be a holomorphic line bundle, given as in definition 6.14.9 by frames $e_ i$ over an open cover $(V_ i)$ of $X$, and let $h_0$ be a smooth quadratic Hermitian metric on $L$. Its curvature form, which we denote by $c_1(L,h_0)$, equals $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e_ i|_{h_0}^2$ on $V_ i$. It also equals $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e|_{h_0}^2$ for every local holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$: on $V_ i$ we have $e=ge_ i$ with $g$ holomorphic and nowhere zero, so $\log |e|_{h_0}^2=\log |g|^2+\log |e_ i|_{h_0}^2$, and $\log |g|^2$ is pluriharmonic (section 5.4 ). Any other smooth metric is $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$ with $f$ smooth and real, and then $c_1(L,h_1)=c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ (lemma 6.14.10 (3)). Hence the class $c_1(L)=\{ c_1(L,h_0)\} \in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ does not depend on the metric. A holomorphic section of $L$ is given by holomorphic functions $f_ i$ on $V_ i$ with $f_ ie_ i=f_ je_ j$ on $V_ i\cap V_ j$. If $L$ and $L'$ are given by frames $e_ i$ and $e'_ i$ over a common cover, with transition functions $g_{ij}$ and $g'_{ij}$, their tensor product $L\otimes L'$ is given by the frames $e_ i\otimes e'_ i$ with the transition functions $g_{ij}g'_{ij}$, and the dual $L^{-1}$ of $L$ by the dual frames $e_ i^*$ with the transition functions $g_{ij}^{-1}$. Metrics on $L$ and $L'$ induce metrics with $|e_ i\otimes e'_ i|^2=|e_ i|^2|e'_ i|^2$ and $|e_ i^*|^2=|e_ i|^{-2}$. The curvature of a tensor product of metrics is the sum of the curvatures, and the curvature of a pullback metric is the pullback of the curvature, because the logarithms of the squared norms of local frames add, respectively compose. Line bundles are trivial over coordinate balls; we use this to work in a single frame on balls of a fixed size. Lemma 10.6.1 . DC3C9650BBBE Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on a complex manifold $M$, and let $B$ be a coordinate ball whose closure is contained in the domain of its chart. Then $L$ has a holomorphic frame over $B$, that is, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. Proof. We make the metric flat on $B$ and obtain the frame by parallel transport along the segments issuing from the center of $B$. Choose a smooth metric $h_0$ on $L$ (lemma 6.14.10 (1)). By lemma 6.14.2 there is a smooth real function $p$ on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=c_1(L,h_0)$, and the metric $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{p}$ on $L|_ B$ has curvature $c_1(L,h_0)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=0$, by lemma 6.14.10 (3). We call a holomorphic frame of $h_1$-length one over an open subset of $B$ a unit frame . Unit frames exist near every point of $B$. Indeed, every point of $B$ has a ball neighborhood $V\subset B$ over which $L$ has a holomorphic frame $e$, and $\log |e|_{h_1}^2$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e|_{h_1}^2=-c_1(L,h_1)=0$, so by lemma 6.14.2 it equals $\operatorname{Re}F$ for a holomorphic function $F$ on $V$, and $\mathrm e^{-F/2}e$ is a unit frame. Two unit frames on a connected open set differ by a holomorphic factor $g$ with $|g|=1$; then $ ar g=1/g$ is both holomorphic and antiholomorphic, so $\mathrm d ar g=0$ and $g$ is constant. Let $c$ be the center of $B$ and fix a unit vector $e_ c\in L_ c$. For $z\in B$, a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$ is a continuous map $t\mapsto \varepsilon (t)\in L_{c+t(z-c)}$, $t\in [0,1]$, with $\varepsilon (0)=e_ c$, which near every $t$ is a constant multiple of a unit frame. There is at most one flat lift: if $\varepsilon '$ is another one, then $\varepsilon '=g\varepsilon $ for a continuous function $g$ on $[0,1]$ which is locally constant, by the preceding paragraph, and equals $1$ at $t=0$, so $g=1$. It remains to show that flat lifts exist and that their values at $t=1$ depend holomorphically on $z$. Let $z_0\in B$, and choose $\delta _0>0$ with $\overline{B(z_0,\delta _0)}\subset B$. The set $\Gamma _0=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [0,1],\  |z-z_0|\leq \delta _0\} $ is a compact subset of the convex set $B$. Cover it by finitely many balls $V_ i\subset B$ carrying unit frames $e_ i$, let $\lambda >0$ be a Lebesgue number of this cover, choose $\delta \leq \delta _0$ with $2\delta <\lambda /2$, and choose $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots <t_ N=1$ with $(t_ k-t_{k-1})(|z_0-c|+\delta _0)<\lambda /2$. For $W=B(z_0,\delta )$, each set $\Gamma _ k=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k],\  z\in W\} $ has diameter less than $\lambda $, because $|(c+t(z-c))-(c+t'(z'-c))|\leq |t-t'|\, |z-c|+|z-z'|$; so $\Gamma _ k$ lies in some $V_{i_ k}$. The convex set $V_{i_ k}\cap V_{i_{k+1}}$ is connected and contains $c+t_ k(z_0-c)$, so $e_{i_ k}=\gamma _ ke_{i_{k+1}}$ there for a constant $\gamma _ k$. Let $a$ be the number with $e_ c=a\, e_{i_1}(c)$. For $z\in W$, the map equal to $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{k-1}e_{i_ k}(c+t(z-c))$ for $t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k]$ is well defined at the points $t_ k$ and is a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$. Hence, on $W$, the value $E(z)$ of the unique flat lift at $t=1$ is $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{N-1}e_{i_ N}(z)$, a constant multiple of the unit frame $e_{i_ N}$. Since $z_0$ was arbitrary, $E$ is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. $\square$ Families of holomorphic sections that are bounded in $L^2$ are relatively compact for uniform convergence. Lemma 10.6.2 . 94EC30DAF1A3 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$, and let $(f_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic functions on $U$ with $\sup _ j\int _ U|f_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a holomorphic function. Let $E$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ with a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$, and let $(s_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ with $\sup _ j\int _ X|s_ j|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$ to a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$, that is, $\sup _ X|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}	o 0$ along the subsequence. For every holomorphic line bundle $E$ on $X$, the space $H^0(X,E)$ of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ is finite dimensional. Assertions (2) and (3) hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$, with $\mathrm dV$ in (2) replaced by any smooth positive volume form on $X'$. Proof. (1) Let $M$ be the supremum in the statement. If $\overline{B(z,\delta )}\subset U$, then $|f_ j(z)|^2\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}M$ by ( 6.8.7 ). Hence the $f_ j$ are uniformly bounded on every compact subset of $U$: if $K\subset U$ is compact and $\delta >0$ is smaller than the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$ (any $\delta >0$ if $U=\mathbb C^ n$), then $|f_ j|^2\leq |B(0,\delta )|^{-1}M$ on $K$. We next show that the sequence is equicontinuous on compact sets. Let $K\subset U$ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $U$; let $M'$ be a bound for all $|f_ j|$ on $K'$. For $z$ at distance at most $\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 5.2.1 ) gives $|\partial _{z_ l}f_ j(z)|\leq M'/r$ for $1\leq l\leq n$. Since $\mathrm df_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}f_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, the $f_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence is equicontinuous on $K$. By proposition 2.7.4 , applied on the compact sets $K_ m=\{ z\in U:|z|\leq m,\  \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus U)\geq 1/m\} $, which exhaust $U$, and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a continuous function $f$. Then $ ar\partial f=0$ in the sense of distributions, as a limit of $ ar\partial f_ j=0$, so $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function by lemma 6.4.10 (1); both being continuous, $f$ is holomorphic. (2) Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$, with closures in the domains of their charts, such that the concentric balls $B'_ k$ of half the radius cover $X$, and let $B''_ k$ be the concentric balls of three quarters of the radius. By lemma 10.6.1 , $E$ has a holomorphic frame $e_ k$ over $B_ k$; write $s_ j=f_{j,k}e_ k$ on $B_ k$. On the compact set $\overline{B''_ k}$ the function $|e_ k|_{h_ E}^2$ is bounded below by a positive constant and $\mathrm dV$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of Lebesgue measure in the chart, so the integrals of $|f_{j,k}|^2$ over $B''_ k$ with respect to Lebesgue measure in the chart are bounded independently of $j$. Applying (1) successively for the finitely many $k$, we obtain a subsequence along which $f_{j,k}$ converges locally uniformly on $B''_ k$, hence uniformly on $\overline{B'_ k}$, to a holomorphic function $f_ k$, for every $k$. On $B''_ k\cap B''_ l$ the sections $f_ ke_ k$ and $f_ le_ l$ are both the pointwise limit of $s_ j$, so they define a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$ over $X$, and $\sup _{B'_ k}|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}\leq \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|e_ k|_{h_ E}\cdot \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|f_{j,k}-f_ k|	o 0$ for every $k$. (3) Fix a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$ on $E$ (lemma 6.14.10 (1)). The integral $\| s\| ^2=\int _ X|s|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV$ defines an inner product on $H^0(X,E)$: if $\| s\| =0$, then the continuous function $|s|_{h_ E}$ vanishes almost everywhere, hence everywhere. If $H^0(X,E)$ were infinite dimensional, the Gram–Schmidt process would give an orthonormal sequence $(s_ j)$. By (2), a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$, hence in $L^2$, since $X$ has finite volume; but $\| s_ i-s_ j\| ^2=2$ for $i
eq j$. This contradiction proves (3). The proofs of (2) and (3) use only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that $\mathrm dV$ is a smooth positive volume form; hence they also prove the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$ A line bundle is positive if it admits a smooth metric with positive definite curvature form. It is very ample if its full space of global holomorphic sections defines a holomorphic embedding into a projective space: this space is finite dimensional by lemma 10.6.2 (3), and for a basis $s_0,\ldots ,s_ N$ we require that the sections have no common zero and that $x\mapsto [s_0(x):\cdots :s_ N(x)]$ is a holomorphic embedding of $X$ into $\mathbb P^ N$. A compact complex manifold is projective if it admits a holomorphic embedding into a projective space. Definition 10.6.3 . A68F1B40919C A plurisubharmonic metric on $L$ is a quadratic metric of the form $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$. It assigns the value zero to the zero vector, also over the pole set of $\varphi $, and the value $+\infty $ to a nonzero vector over a pole of $\varphi $. Its Chern current is \[  c_1(L,h)=c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \] This definition uses the pointwise function $\varphi $, that is, the canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic representative; for an arbitrary measurable weight, the distributional curvature inequality would determine the metric only almost everywhere. If $h_0$ is replaced by $h_0\mathrm e^{-f}$, then $\varphi $ is replaced by $\varphi -f$, so the class of plurisubharmonic metrics and the pointwise metric $h$ do not depend on $h_0$. In particular, $L$ admits a plurisubharmonic metric if and only if $c_1(L)$ is pseudo-effective. The tensor product of two plurisubharmonic metrics is defined by adding their local weights; the norm of a nonzero vector is infinite over a pole of either factor. The pullback of a plurisubharmonic metric by a holomorphic map is a plurisubharmonic metric provided the pulled-back weights are not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component; the restriction to a submanifold is defined under the same condition. Proposition 10.6.4 . 95892535D04F For a nonzero holomorphic section $s$ of $L$ and a smooth metric $h_0$, A8F577E012B3 10.6.5  egin{equation}  c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_{h_0}^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $[Z(s)]$ is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $s$, counted with multiplicities. In particular $[Z(s)]$ represents $c_1(L)$. Proof. In a local frame write $s=fe$. Since $\log |s|_{h_0}^2=\log |f|^2+\log |e|_{h_0}^2$, the left side equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, which is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $f$ by theorem 5.5.6 . These local divisors agree on overlaps, because the transition functions have no zeros. $\square$ Example 10.6.6 . 01B4AD44BAC3 Let $N\geq 0$. The projective space $\mathbb P^ N$ is the quotient of $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the action of $\mathbb C^*$ by multiplication, with the quotient topology; we write $q$ for the quotient map and $[Z]=[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ N]$ for the class of $Z$. For $0\leq i\leq N$ the sets $U_ i=\{ [Z]:Z_ i
eq 0\} $ are open and cover $\mathbb P^ N$, and the map $\phi _ i\colon U_ i	o \mathbb C^ N$, $[Z]\mapsto (Z_ k/Z_ i)_{k
eq i}$, is a homeomorphism: it is continuous because $\phi _ i\circ q$ is, and its inverse is $q$ composed with the map inserting the coordinate $1$ in the $i$th place. On $\phi _ i(U_ i\cap U_ j)=\{ w_ j
eq 0\} $, where we put $w_ i=1$, the transition map $\phi _ j\circ \phi _ i^{-1}$ is $w\mapsto (w_ k/w_ j)_{k
eq j}$, which is holomorphic, and so is its inverse $\phi _ i\circ \phi _ j^{-1}$. The space $\mathbb P^ N$ is compact and connected, as the image under $q$ of the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$. It is Hausdorff, because the continuous map $[Z]\mapsto Z\overline Z^{\mathsf T}/|Z|^2$ to the space of complex matrices is injective, the matrix being the orthogonal projection onto the line $\mathbb CZ$; and being compact, it is paracompact. Thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $N$ (definition 5.2.3 ). The tautological line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$ has the fiber $\mathbb CZ$ over $[Z]$. In the sense of definition 6.14.9 it is given by the frames $e_ i([Z])=Z/Z_ i$ over $U_ i$, the points of the line with $i$th coordinate one. Since $e_ i=(Z_ j/Z_ i)e_ j$ on $U_ i\cap U_ j$, its transition functions are $g_{ij}=Z_ j/Z_ i$, which are holomorphic and nowhere zero on $U_ i\cap U_ j$ and satisfy $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. The Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ gives the smooth metric $|e_ i|^2=|Z|^2/|Z_ i|^2$, which satisfies $|e_ i|^2=|g_{ij}|^2|e_ j|^2$. The dual line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ has the dual frames $e_ i^*$, with $e_ i^*(e_ i)=1$ and transition functions $g_{ij}^{-1}$, and the dual metric $|e_ i^*|^2=|e_ i|^{-2}=|Z_ i|^2/|Z|^2$, the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$. A linear form $\ell $ on $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ defines a holomorphic section $s_\ell $ of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, the restriction of $\ell $ to the fibers of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$: on $U_ i$ it is $s_\ell =\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=(\ell (Z)/Z_ i)\, e_ i^*$, and these expressions agree on overlaps, because $\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=\ell (g_{ij}e_ j)\, g_{ij}^{-1}e_ j^*$. For the coordinate forms we write $X_ k=s_{Z_ k}$. Thus $X_ i=e_ i^*$ on $U_ i$, and \[  |X_ k|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2([Z])= rac{|Z_ k|^2}{|Z|^2}.  \] The tensor power $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)^{\otimes k}$, $k\geq 1$, has the frames $(e_ i^*)^{\otimes k}$, the transition functions $g_{ij}^{-k}$ and the metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}^ k$; products of $k$ sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, such as the monomials $X_0^{a_0}\cdots X_ N^{a_ N}$ with $a_0+\cdots +a_ N=k$, are holomorphic sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)$. Example 10.6.7 . 4CE1D9D7D803 Let $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ carry the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ of example 10.6.6 , dual to the Euclidean norm on the tautological line. On the chart $U_0=\{ [1:z_1:\cdots :z_ N]\} $ the tautological line is spanned by $(1,z)$, so the frame $X_0=e_0^*$ has squared norm $|X_0(1,z)|^2/|(1,z)|^2=(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$, and the curvature is \[  \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The matrix of $\partial _ j\partial _{ ar k}\log (1+|z|^2)$ is $ igl ((1+|z|^2)\delta _{jk}- ar z_ jz_ k igr )/(1+|z|^2)^2$, which is positive definite by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\sum _ j ar z_ j\xi _ j|^2\leq |z|^2|\xi |^2$. The same computation in the chart $U_ i$, with the frame $X_ i$, shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is a Kähler form on $\mathbb P^ N$; thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a compact Kähler manifold. On $\mathbb P^1$, integration in polar coordinates gives $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}= rac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}(1+|z|^2)^{-2}\, \mathrm dV=1$. The function $\log |X_1|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2=\log  igl (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2) igr )$, which vanishes at the point at infinity, is the weight of a singular plurisubharmonic metric whose Chern current is the Dirac current $[0]$ at the point $[1:0]$, by ( 10.6.5 ). Definition 10.6.8 . 9CC891317C85 A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with \[  \varphi = rac1m\max _{1\leq i\leq N}  igl (\log |s_ i|_{h_0^ m}^2+\lambda _ i igr ), \qquad m,N\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1},\quad \lambda _ i\in \mathbb Q,  \] where $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ are holomorphic sections of $L^ m$, not all zero. We denote the set of these metrics by $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest set of plurisubharmonic metrics that contains $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ and is closed under minima of metrics and under convex combinations of weights with rational coefficients. A convex combination of weights corresponds to the weighted geometric mean of the quadratic metrics, with value zero on the zero vector and the value $+\infty $ on a nonzero vector over a pole of a factor with positive coefficient. The classical Fubini–Study metric of example 10.6.7 , whose weight is the logarithm of a sum of squares rather than a maximum, does not belong to $\mathrm{FS}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1))$ when $N\geq 1$, since its curvature form $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is positive definite, whereas the curvature current of a metric in $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ vanishes on a nonempty open set. Indeed, one of the finitely many closed sets on which a single term attains the maximum has interior points. There, away from the zeros of the corresponding section $s_ i$, the induced metric on $L^ m$ gives $s_ i$ the constant norm $\mathrm e^{-\lambda _ i/2}$, so the curvature vanishes by proposition 10.6.4 . The classical metric differs, however, only by a bounded factor from a metric in $\mathrm{FS}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1))$: with $h_0=h_{\mathrm{FS}}$, the coordinate sections $X_0,\ldots ,X_ N$, $m=1$ and $\lambda _ i=0$ give the metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi =\max _ i\log |X_ i|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2$, and $1\leq \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\leq N+1$ because $|X_ i|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2([Z])=|Z_ i|^2/|Z|^2$. Proposition 10.6.9 . E5F620306821 Fubini–Study metrics do not depend on the choice of $h_0$, they have analytic singularities, and $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is closed under minima and rational convex combinations of weights. Consequently the generalized Fubini–Study metrics are exactly the metrics in $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is empty if no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero holomorphic section, even when $L$ admits plurisubharmonic metrics. Proof. In a local frame $e$ write $s_ i=f_ ie^ m$. The local weight $-\log |e|_ h^2=\varphi -\log |e|_{h_0}^2$ of the metric equals $m^{-1}\max _ i(\log |f_ i|^2+\lambda _ i)$, which does not involve $h_0$; it is plurisubharmonic and not identically $-\infty $, since $X$ is connected and some $s_ i
e 0$. It differs by a bounded function from $m^{-1}\log \sum _ i\mathrm e^{\lambda _ i}|f_ i|^2$, so it has analytic singularities with the rational coefficient $1/m$; the pole set is the common zero set of the $s_ i$. Consider two such metrics, given by sections $s_ i$ of $L^ m$ with constants $\lambda _ i$ and sections $r_ j$ of $L^ l$ with constants $\mu _ j$. Replacing $s_ i$ by $s_ i^{M/m}$ and $\lambda _ i$ by $(M/m)\lambda _ i$, and similarly for the $r_ j$, where $M$ is a common multiple of $m$ and $l$, does not change the potentials, so we may assume that both are given in degree $M$. The maximum of the two potentials, which corresponds to the minimum of the metrics, is then given by the union of the two lists. For a rational $t=a/b\in (0,1)$, the combination $t\varphi +(1-t)\psi $ of the two maxima is the maximum over all pairs $(i,j)$ of the corresponding combinations, that is, \[  t\varphi +(1-t)\psi = rac1{Mb}\max _{i,j}\Bigl (\log  igl |s_ i^ ar_ j^{b-a} igr |_{h_0^{Mb}}^2+a\lambda _ i+(b-a)\mu _ j\Bigr ),  \] where the sections $s_ i^ ar_ j^{b-a}$ of $L^{Mb}$ are not all zero and the constants are rational. Thus $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ is closed under both operations, and by induction under every finite sequence of them, so the generated set is $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ itself. If no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero section, no presentation as in definition 10.6.8 exists. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.6.1
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text: Lemma 10.6.1 . DC3C9650BBBE Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on a complex manifold $M$, and let $B$ be a coordinate ball whose closure is contained in the domain of its chart. Then $L$ has a holomorphic frame over $B$, that is, a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. Proof. We make the metric flat on $B$ and obtain the frame by parallel transport along the segments issuing from the center of $B$. Choose a smooth metric $h_0$ on $L$ (lemma 6.14.10 (1)). By lemma 6.14.2 there is a smooth real function $p$ on $B$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=c_1(L,h_0)$, and the metric $h_1=h_0\mathrm e^{p}$ on $L|_ B$ has curvature $c_1(L,h_0)-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}p=0$, by lemma 6.14.10 (3). We call a holomorphic frame of $h_1$-length one over an open subset of $B$ a unit frame . Unit frames exist near every point of $B$. Indeed, every point of $B$ has a ball neighborhood $V\subset B$ over which $L$ has a holomorphic frame $e$, and $\log |e|_{h_1}^2$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |e|_{h_1}^2=-c_1(L,h_1)=0$, so by lemma 6.14.2 it equals $\operatorname{Re}F$ for a holomorphic function $F$ on $V$, and $\mathrm e^{-F/2}e$ is a unit frame. Two unit frames on a connected open set differ by a holomorphic factor $g$ with $|g|=1$; then $\bar g=1/g$ is both holomorphic and antiholomorphic, so $\mathrm d\bar g=0$ and $g$ is constant. Let $c$ be the center of $B$ and fix a unit vector $e_ c\in L_ c$. For $z\in B$, a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$ is a continuous map $t\mapsto \varepsilon (t)\in L_{c+t(z-c)}$, $t\in [0,1]$, with $\varepsilon (0)=e_ c$, which near every $t$ is a constant multiple of a unit frame. There is at most one flat lift: if $\varepsilon '$ is another one, then $\varepsilon '=g\varepsilon $ for a continuous function $g$ on $[0,1]$ which is locally constant, by the preceding paragraph, and equals $1$ at $t=0$, so $g=1$. It remains to show that flat lifts exist and that their values at $t=1$ depend holomorphically on $z$. Let $z_0\in B$, and choose $\delta _0>0$ with $\overline{B(z_0,\delta _0)}\subset B$. The set $\Gamma _0=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [0,1],\  |z-z_0|\leq \delta _0\} $ is a compact subset of the convex set $B$. Cover it by finitely many balls $V_ i\subset B$ carrying unit frames $e_ i$, let $\lambda >0$ be a Lebesgue number of this cover, choose $\delta \leq \delta _0$ with $2\delta <\lambda /2$, and choose $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots <t_ N=1$ with $(t_ k-t_{k-1})(|z_0-c|+\delta _0)<\lambda /2$. For $W=B(z_0,\delta )$, each set $\Gamma _ k=\{ c+t(z-c):t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k],\  z\in W\} $ has diameter less than $\lambda $, because $|(c+t(z-c))-(c+t'(z'-c))|\leq |t-t'|\, |z-c|+|z-z'|$; so $\Gamma _ k$ lies in some $V_{i_ k}$. The convex set $V_{i_ k}\cap V_{i_{k+1}}$ is connected and contains $c+t_ k(z_0-c)$, so $e_{i_ k}=\gamma _ ke_{i_{k+1}}$ there for a constant $\gamma _ k$. Let $a$ be the number with $e_ c=a\, e_{i_1}(c)$. For $z\in W$, the map equal to $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{k-1}e_{i_ k}(c+t(z-c))$ for $t\in [t_{k-1},t_ k]$ is well defined at the points $t_ k$ and is a flat lift along the segment from $c$ to $z$. Hence, on $W$, the value $E(z)$ of the unique flat lift at $t=1$ is $a\gamma _1\cdots \gamma _{N-1}e_{i_ N}(z)$, a constant multiple of the unit frame $e_{i_ N}$. Since $z_0$ was arbitrary, $E$ is a nowhere vanishing holomorphic section of $L$ on $B$. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.6.2
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text: Lemma 10.6.2 . 94EC30DAF1A3 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$, and let $(f_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic functions on $U$ with $\sup _ j\int _ U|f_ j|^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a holomorphic function. Let $E$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ with a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$, and let $(s_ j)$ be a sequence of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ with $\sup _ j\int _ X|s_ j|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV<\infty $. Then a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$ to a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$, that is, $\sup _ X|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}\to 0$ along the subsequence. For every holomorphic line bundle $E$ on $X$, the space $H^0(X,E)$ of holomorphic sections of $E$ over $X$ is finite dimensional. Assertions (2) and (3) hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$, with $\mathrm dV$ in (2) replaced by any smooth positive volume form on $X'$. Proof. (1) Let $M$ be the supremum in the statement. If $\overline{B(z,\delta )}\subset U$, then $|f_ j(z)|^2\leq |B(z,\delta )|^{-1}M$ by ( 6.8.7 ). Hence the $f_ j$ are uniformly bounded on every compact subset of $U$: if $K\subset U$ is compact and $\delta >0$ is smaller than the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$ (any $\delta >0$ if $U=\mathbb C^ n$), then $|f_ j|^2\leq |B(0,\delta )|^{-1}M$ on $K$. We next show that the sequence is equicontinuous on compact sets. Let $K\subset U$ be compact, and choose $r>0$ such that the compact set $K'$ of points at distance at most $2\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$ lies in $U$; let $M'$ be a bound for all $|f_ j|$ on $K'$. For $z$ at distance at most $\sqrt n\, r$ from $K$, the closed polydisc of radius $r$ centered at $z$ lies in $K'$, and the coefficient bound in ( 5.2.1 ) gives $|\partial _{z_ l}f_ j(z)|\leq M'/r$ for $1\leq l\leq n$. Since $\mathrm df_ j=\sum _ l\partial _{z_ l}f_ j\, \mathrm dz_ l$, the $f_ j$ are Lipschitz with a common constant on every ball of radius $\sqrt n\, r$ centered at a point of $K$, so the sequence is equicontinuous on $K$. By proposition 2.7.4 , applied on the compact sets $K_ m=\{ z\in U:|z|\leq m,\  \operatorname {dist}(z,\mathbb C^ n\setminus U)\geq 1/m\} $, which exhaust $U$, and a diagonal argument, a subsequence converges locally uniformly on $U$ to a continuous function $f$. Then $\bar\partial f=0$ in the sense of distributions, as a limit of $\bar\partial f_ j=0$, so $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a holomorphic function by lemma 6.4.10 (1); both being continuous, $f$ is holomorphic. (2) Choose finitely many coordinate balls $B_ k$, with closures in the domains of their charts, such that the concentric balls $B'_ k$ of half the radius cover $X$, and let $B''_ k$ be the concentric balls of three quarters of the radius. By lemma 10.6.1 , $E$ has a holomorphic frame $e_ k$ over $B_ k$; write $s_ j=f_{j,k}e_ k$ on $B_ k$. On the compact set $\overline{B''_ k}$ the function $|e_ k|_{h_ E}^2$ is bounded below by a positive constant and $\mathrm dV$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of Lebesgue measure in the chart, so the integrals of $|f_{j,k}|^2$ over $B''_ k$ with respect to Lebesgue measure in the chart are bounded independently of $j$. Applying (1) successively for the finitely many $k$, we obtain a subsequence along which $f_{j,k}$ converges locally uniformly on $B''_ k$, hence uniformly on $\overline{B'_ k}$, to a holomorphic function $f_ k$, for every $k$. On $B''_ k\cap B''_ l$ the sections $f_ ke_ k$ and $f_ le_ l$ are both the pointwise limit of $s_ j$, so they define a holomorphic section $s$ of $E$ over $X$, and $\sup _{B'_ k}|s_ j-s|_{h_ E}\leq \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|e_ k|_{h_ E}\cdot \sup _{\overline{B'_ k}}|f_{j,k}-f_ k|\to 0$ for every $k$. (3) Fix a smooth quadratic metric $h_ E$ on $E$ (lemma 6.14.10 (1)). The integral $\| s\| ^2=\int _ X|s|_{h_ E}^2\, \mathrm dV$ defines an inner product on $H^0(X,E)$: if $\| s\| =0$, then the continuous function $|s|_{h_ E}$ vanishes almost everywhere, hence everywhere. If $H^0(X,E)$ were infinite dimensional, the Gram–Schmidt process would give an orthonormal sequence $(s_ j)$. By (2), a subsequence converges uniformly on $X$, hence in $L^2$, since $X$ has finite volume; but $\| s_ i-s_ j\| ^2=2$ for $i\neq j$. This contradiction proves (3). The proofs of (2) and (3) use only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension and that $\mathrm dV$ is a smooth positive volume form; hence they also prove the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$

title: Definition 10.6.3
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text: Definition 10.6.3 . A68F1B40919C A plurisubharmonic metric on $L$ is a quadratic metric of the form $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,c_1(L,h_0))$. It assigns the value zero to the zero vector, also over the pole set of $\varphi $, and the value $+\infty $ to a nonzero vector over a pole of $\varphi $. Its Chern current is \[  c_1(L,h)=c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi .  \]

title: Proposition 10.6.4
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text: Proposition 10.6.4 . 95892535D04F For a nonzero holomorphic section $s$ of $L$ and a smooth metric $h_0$, A8F577E012B3 10.6.5 \begin{equation}  c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_{h_0}^2=[Z(s)], \end{equation} where $[Z(s)]$ is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $s$, counted with multiplicities. In particular $[Z(s)]$ represents $c_1(L)$. Proof. In a local frame write $s=fe$. Since $\log |s|_{h_0}^2=\log |f|^2+\log |e|_{h_0}^2$, the left side equals $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, which is the current of integration along the zero divisor of $f$ by theorem 5.5.6 . These local divisors agree on overlaps, because the transition functions have no zeros. $\square$

title: Example 10.6.6
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text:
Example 10.6.6 . 01B4AD44BAC3 Let $N\geq 0$. The projective space $\mathbb P^ N$ is the quotient of $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ by the action of $\mathbb C^*$ by multiplication, with the quotient topology; we write $q$ for the quotient map and $[Z]=[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ N]$ for the class of $Z$. For $0\leq i\leq N$ the sets $U_ i=\{ [Z]:Z_ i
eq 0\} $ are open and cover $\mathbb P^ N$, and the map $\phi _ i\colon U_ i	o \mathbb C^ N$, $[Z]\mapsto (Z_ k/Z_ i)_{k
eq i}$, is a homeomorphism: it is continuous because $\phi _ i\circ q$ is, and its inverse is $q$ composed with the map inserting the coordinate $1$ in the $i$th place. On $\phi _ i(U_ i\cap U_ j)=\{ w_ j
eq 0\} $, where we put $w_ i=1$, the transition map $\phi _ j\circ \phi _ i^{-1}$ is $w\mapsto (w_ k/w_ j)_{k
eq j}$, which is holomorphic, and so is its inverse $\phi _ i\circ \phi _ j^{-1}$. The space $\mathbb P^ N$ is compact and connected, as the image under $q$ of the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$. It is Hausdorff, because the continuous map $[Z]\mapsto Z\overline Z^{\mathsf T}/|Z|^2$ to the space of complex matrices is injective, the matrix being the orthogonal projection onto the line $\mathbb CZ$; and being compact, it is paracompact. Thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $N$ (definition 5.2.3 ). The tautological line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$ has the fiber $\mathbb CZ$ over $[Z]$. In the sense of definition 6.14.9 it is given by the frames $e_ i([Z])=Z/Z_ i$ over $U_ i$, the points of the line with $i$th coordinate one. Since $e_ i=(Z_ j/Z_ i)e_ j$ on $U_ i\cap U_ j$, its transition functions are $g_{ij}=Z_ j/Z_ i$, which are holomorphic and nowhere zero on $U_ i\cap U_ j$ and satisfy $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$. The Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ gives the smooth metric $|e_ i|^2=|Z|^2/|Z_ i|^2$, which satisfies $|e_ i|^2=|g_{ij}|^2|e_ j|^2$. The dual line bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ has the dual frames $e_ i^*$, with $e_ i^*(e_ i)=1$ and transition functions $g_{ij}^{-1}$, and the dual metric $|e_ i^*|^2=|e_ i|^{-2}=|Z_ i|^2/|Z|^2$, the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$. A linear form $\ell $ on $\mathbb C^{N+1}$ defines a holomorphic section $s_\ell $ of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, the restriction of $\ell $ to the fibers of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(-1)$: on $U_ i$ it is $s_\ell =\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=(\ell (Z)/Z_ i)\, e_ i^*$, and these expressions agree on overlaps, because $\ell (e_ i)e_ i^*=\ell (g_{ij}e_ j)\, g_{ij}^{-1}e_ j^*$. For the coordinate forms we write $X_ k=s_{Z_ k}$. Thus $X_ i=e_ i^*$ on $U_ i$, and \[  |X_ k|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2([Z])= rac{|Z_ k|^2}{|Z|^2}.  \] The tensor power $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)^{\otimes k}$, $k\geq 1$, has the frames $(e_ i^*)^{\otimes k}$, the transition functions $g_{ij}^{-k}$ and the metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}^ k$; products of $k$ sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$, such as the monomials $X_0^{a_0}\cdots X_ N^{a_ N}$ with $a_0+\cdots +a_ N=k$, are holomorphic sections of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(k)$.

title: Example 10.6.7
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text: Example 10.6.7 . 4CE1D9D7D803 Let $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^ N}(1)$ carry the Fubini–Study metric $h_{\mathrm{FS}}$ of example 10.6.6 , dual to the Euclidean norm on the tautological line. On the chart $U_0=\{ [1:z_1:\cdots :z_ N]\} $ the tautological line is spanned by $(1,z)$, so the frame $X_0=e_0^*$ has squared norm $|X_0(1,z)|^2/|(1,z)|^2=(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$, and the curvature is \[  \omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2).  \] The matrix of $\partial _ j\partial _{\bar k}\log (1+|z|^2)$ is $\bigl ((1+|z|^2)\delta _{jk}-\bar z_ jz_ k\bigr )/(1+|z|^2)^2$, which is positive definite by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\sum _ j\bar z_ j\xi _ j|^2\leq |z|^2|\xi |^2$. The same computation in the chart $U_ i$, with the frame $X_ i$, shows that $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is a Kähler form on $\mathbb P^ N$; thus $\mathbb P^ N$ is a compact Kähler manifold. On $\mathbb P^1$, integration in polar coordinates gives $\int _{\mathbb P^1}\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}=\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}(1+|z|^2)^{-2}\, \mathrm dV=1$. The function $\log |X_1|_{\mathrm{FS}}^2=\log \bigl (|z|^2/(1+|z|^2)\bigr )$, which vanishes at the point at infinity, is the weight of a singular plurisubharmonic metric whose Chern current is the Dirac current $[0]$ at the point $[1:0]$, by ( 10.6.5 ).

title: Definition 10.6.8
section: 10.6 Curvature and metrics defined by sections
text: Definition 10.6.8 . 9CC891317C85 A Fubini–Study metric on $L$ is a metric $h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ with \[  \varphi =\frac1m\max _{1\leq i\leq N} \bigl (\log |s_ i|_{h_0^ m}^2+\lambda _ i\bigr ), \qquad m,N\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1},\quad \lambda _ i\in \mathbb Q,  \] where $s_1,\ldots ,s_ N$ are holomorphic sections of $L^ m$, not all zero. We denote the set of these metrics by $\mathrm{FS}(L)$. The set of generalized Fubini–Study metrics is the smallest set of plurisubharmonic metrics that contains $\mathrm{FS}(L)$ and is closed under minima of metrics and under convex combinations of weights with rational coefficients. A convex combination of weights corresponds to the weighted geometric mean of the quadratic metrics, with value zero on the zero vector and the value $+\infty $ on a nonzero vector over a pole of a factor with positive coefficient.

title: 10.7 Compact interpolation and global Bergman kernels
search_title: Compact interpolation and global Bergman kernels
section: 10.7 Compact interpolation and global Bergman kernels
text:
The local extension theorems of section 6.1 produce holomorphic functions with prescribed values on pseudoconvex domains. On the compact manifold $X$ we obtain global holomorphic sections in the same way, by cutting off a local solution and correcting it with an $L^2$ estimate for $ ar\partial $ on line bundles; the curvature must dominate the cost of a logarithmic pole at the interpolation point. Since the weights are singular, we prove the $L^2$ estimate (lemma 10.7.6 ) on complements of analytic subsets of $X$, starting from the Bochner–Kodaira identity. After the interpolation theorem at a point (theorem 10.7.9 ) we describe the weighted spaces of global sections and their Bergman kernels. All norms use the volume $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$. The canonical bundle $K_ X=\Lambda ^{n,0}T^*X$ is the holomorphic line bundle of $(n,0)$-forms; we give it the metric induced by $\omega $, and its dual $K_ X^{-1}$ the dual metric $h_{K^{-1},\omega }$. Recall that $H^0(X,L)$ denotes the vector space of global holomorphic sections of $L$ (lemma 10.6.2 ). We begin with the pointwise linear algebra behind the $L^2$ estimates of this chapter. Let $\sigma $ be a Hermitian form on a complex manifold $M$ of dimension $n\geq 1$. Forms on $M$ carry the pointwise inner product defined by the Riemannian metric $\sigma (\cdot ,J\cdot )$ as in section 10.2 ; for a holomorphic line bundle $F$ with a smooth quadratic metric $h$, $F$-valued forms carry the product of this inner product with $h$, written $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _{\sigma ,h}$ or $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle _\sigma $, and $\mathrm dV_\sigma =\sigma ^ n/n!$. Let $\Lambda _\sigma $ be the pointwise adjoint of the Lefschetz operator $u\mapsto \sigma \wedge u$, and for a real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ put $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]u=\gamma \wedge \Lambda _\sigma u-\Lambda _\sigma (\gamma \wedge u)$. A basis $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ of the $(1,0)$-covectors at a point $x$ is a $\sigma $-unitary coframe if $\sigma =\mathrm i\sum _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$. By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, for every real $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ there is a $\sigma $-unitary coframe at $x$ in which $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$, with real numbers $\lambda _ j$, the eigenvalues of $\gamma $ with respect to $\sigma $ at $x$. Lemma 10.7.1 . A0C109B78052 Let $\sigma $, $F$ and $h$ be as above, let $\gamma $ be a real $(1,1)$-form on $M$, let $x\in M$, and let $	heta _1,\ldots ,	heta _ n$ be a $\sigma $-unitary coframe at $x$ in which $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\lambda _ j	heta _ j\wedge  ar	heta _ j$. Put $e=	heta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge 	heta _ n$. For an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v=\sum _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ at $x$ we have $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v=\sum _ j\lambda _ jv_ j\, e\wedge  ar	heta _ j$ and $\langle [\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}=\sum _ j\lambda _ j|v_ j|_ h^2$. In particular, $[\gamma ,\Lambda _\sigma ]$ is positive semidefinite on $(n,1)$-covectors at $x$ if $\gamma \geq 0$ at $x$, and positive definite if $\gamma $ is positive definite at $x$. If $\alpha $ is a $(1,0)$-covector and $u$ an $F$-valued $(n,0)$-covector at $x$, then $|\langle  ar\alpha \wedge u,vangle _{\sigma ,h}|^2\leq |u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \langle [\mathrm i\alpha \wedge  ar\alpha ,\Lambda _\sigma ]v,vangle _{\sigma ,h}$ for every $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector $v$ at $x$. Let $\gamma $ be positive definite at $x$, and let $g$ be an $F$-valued $(n,1)$-covector at $x$. Finally, $|u|_{\sigma ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV_\sigma =|u|_{\omega ,h}^2\, \mathrm dV$ by lemma 10.7.1 (3), which gives exactly ( 10.7.7 ). $\square$ The sections obtained from this estimate are holomorphic only outside an analytic set; the following removable singularity theorem extends them. Lemma 10.7.8 . 189AC91F2DE3 Let $A$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset of a complex manifold $U$. A holomorphic function on $U\setminus A$ which, extended arbitrarily to $A$, belongs to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ extends holomorphically to $U$. The same holds for sections of a holomorphic line bundle. Proof. The question is local. We show that the given function $f$ satisfies $ ar\partial f=0$ in the sense of distributions near each point of $A$, by a one-variable argument on complex lines. Near a point of $A$, the set $A$ is the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions on a connected coordinate neighborhood, and one of them, $b$, does not vanish identically, since otherwise $A$ would contain a nonempty open set. The lowest-order nonzero homogeneous term $P$ of $b$ at the point is a nonzero polynomial, so its zero set is closed and nowhere dense; hence we may choose linearly independent vectors $v_1,\ldots ,v_ n$ with $P(v_ k)
eq 0$, choosing each $v_ k$ outside the union of this zero set and the span of $v_1,\ldots ,v_{k-1}$. We use linear coordinates centered at the point in which the $v_ k$ are the coordinate unit vectors. Then $t\mapsto b(tv_ k)$ has a zero of finite order at $t=0$, so by the Weierstrass preparation theorem (theorem 5.5.2 ), on a sufficiently small polydisc, $b$ is a unit times a monic polynomial in the $k$th coordinate with holomorphic coefficients in the others, for each $k$. Hence every complex line parallel to a coordinate axis meets the zero set of $b$ in this polydisc in finitely many points. By Fubini's theorem, $f$ is square integrable on almost every such line. On such a line, near each of the finitely many punctures, the Laurent expansion of $f$ has no terms of negative order: by orthogonality of the powers on circles, a term of order $-j$ with $j\geq 1$ would make the integral of $|f|^2$ diverge like $\int _0^ rt^{1-2j}\, \mathrm dt$. Hence the restriction of $f$ to almost every line extends holomorphically, and its $ ar\partial $-derivative along the line vanishes as a distribution. Integrating against compactly supported test functions and using Fubini's theorem, we find that every derivative $\partial f/\partial  ar z_ k$ vanishes as a distribution on the polydisc. A distribution with $ ar\partial f=0$ satisfies $\Delta f=4\sum _ k\partial _{z_ k}\partial _{ ar z_ k}f=0$, so it is smooth by Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) and therefore holomorphic. This holomorphic function agrees with $f$ on the complement of $A$, and the local extensions agree on overlaps. For sections of a line bundle, apply the result in local holomorphic frames. $\square$ Theorem 10.7.9 . 846B917F28CD There are constants $N,C>0$, depending only on $(X,\omega )$, with the following property. Let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth quadratic metric $h_0$ and a plurisubharmonic metric $h=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi }$ such that $c_1(L,h)\geq N\omega $. Let $x\in X$ with $\varphi (x)>-\infty $ and $v\in L_ x$. Then there is $s\in H^0(X,L)$ such that F28F18A2C23B 10.7.10  egin{equation}  s(x)=v,\qquad \int _ X|s|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C|v|_ h^2. \end{equation} Proof. If $v=0$, take $s=0$; assume $v
eq 0$. We cut off a local extension of $v$ and correct the error with lemma 10.7.6 outside $x$ and the poles of gentle approximations of $\varphi $; a logarithmic pole at $x$ in the weight makes the correction vanish at $x$. Step 1: data independent of $x$. Choose finitely many coordinate charts and, inside them, balls $B_ k$ of radii $\varrho _ k$, with closures in the charts, whose concentric balls of half the radius cover $X$. Put $r_0=\min _ k\varrho _ k/8$. Then for every $x\in X$ there is $k$ with $x\in  rac12B_ k$, and the coordinate ball $B$ of radius $4r_0$ centered at $x$ in the $k$th chart lies in $B_ k$. Let $\lambda $ be a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{2n}$ with values in $[0,1]$, equal to one on the ball of radius $2r_0$ and zero outside the ball of radius $3r_0$, and put \[  \psi _ x=\lambda (z-z(x))\, n\log  rac{|z-z(x)|^2}{16r_0^2}\  	ext{ on }B,\qquad \psi _ x=0\  	ext{ outside }B,  \] where $z$ are the chart coordinates. Then $\psi _ x\leq 0$, $\psi _ x$ is plurisubharmonic where $\lambda (z-z(x))=1$, and on the annulus where $\lambda (z-z(x))$ is not constant the logarithm and its first two derivatives are bounded independently of $x$. Hence there is $b_0\geq 0$, independent of $x$, with \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ x\geq -b_0\omega , \qquad \psi _ x=n\log |z-z(x)|^2+O(1)	ext{ near }x.  \] Choose $b_1\geq 0$ with $c_1(K_ X^{-1},h_{K^{-1},\omega })\geq -b_1\omega $ (lemma 6.14.1 ), and put $N=b_0+b_1+2$. Step 2: a local extension and its cutoff. By lemma 10.6.1 , $L$ has a holomorphic frame $e$ over $B$. With $|e|_{h_0}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_0}$, the local weight $p_0+\varphi $ of $h$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(p_0+\varphi )=c_1(L,h)\geq 0$. By corollary 6.5.8 , applied in this frame on the ball of radius $r_0$ around $x$, whose diameter $2r_0$ is fixed, there is a holomorphic section $f$ of $L$ over this ball with $f(x)=v$ and \[  \int _{|z-z(x)|<r_0}|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV\leq C_0|v|_ h^2;  \] here $C_0$ does not depend on $x$, because the volume densities are uniformly comparable on the finite cover. Let $\chi $ be a cutoff equal to one for $|z-z(x)|<r_0/2$ and zero for $|z-z(x)|>3r_0/4$, obtained by translating a fixed one. Put $G=\chi f$, extended by zero, and $g= ar\partial G=f\,  ar\partial \chi $. The form $g$ is supported in the annulus $r_0/2\leq |z-z(x)|\leq 3r_0/4$, on which $\psi _ x$ and $ ar\partial \chi $ are bounded independently of $x$. Step 3: global sections for the approximations of $\varphi $. Apply theorem 6.17.6 to $\varphi $ with the background $c_1(L,h_0)-N\omega $. It gives functions $\varphi _ j\downarrow \varphi $ with gentle analytic singularities, analytic pole sets $A_ j$, and $c_1(L,h_0)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ j\geq (N-\varepsilon _ j)\omega $ with $\varepsilon _ j	o 0$. Since $\varphi _ j(x)\geq \varphi (x)>-\infty $, no $A_ j$ contains $x$. Put \[  F=L\otimes K_ X^{-1},\qquad h_{F,j}=h_0\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\otimes h_{K^{-1},\omega }.  \] For $j$ so large that $\varepsilon _ j\leq 1$, this metric is smooth on $M_ j=X\setminus (A_ j\cup \{ x\} )$ and its curvature is at least $(N-\varepsilon _ j-b_0-b_1)\omega \geq \omega $. By lemma 10.7.5 , applied to $\varphi _ j+\psi _ x$, the manifold $M_ j$ carries a Kähler form $\sigma \geq \omega /2$ and cutoffs as required in lemma 10.7.6 . The canonical identification of $L$-valued $(0,q)$-forms with $F$-valued $(n,q)$-forms preserves the pointwise norms for $\omega $, because the $(n,0)$-covector and its dual cancel. Under this identification $g$ is $ ar\partial $-closed, and since $\varphi _ j\geq \varphi $, \[  \int _{M_ j}|g|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_1\int _{|z-z(x)|<r_0}|f|_ h^2\, \mathrm dV \leq C_1C_0|v|_ h^2,  \] with $C_1$ depending only on the fixed cutoffs and the bounds for $\psi _ x$ on the annulus. Lemma 10.7.6 , with $a=1$, gives $u_ j$ on $M_ j$ with $ ar\partial u_ j=g$ and \[  \int _{M_ j}|u_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\, \mathrm dV\leq  rac{C_1C_0}{2\pi }|v|_ h^2.  \] The section $s_ j=G-u_ j$ is holomorphic on $M_ j$. The weights $\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}$ are bounded below by a positive constant, since $\varphi _ j\leq \varphi _1$ is bounded above and $\psi _ x\leq 0$; hence $s_ j$ is square integrable for $h_0$ near $A_ j\cup \{ x\} $, and lemma 10.7.8 extends it to a global holomorphic section. Near $x$ we have $g=0$ and no point of $A_ j$, so $u_ j=G-s_ j$ is holomorphic near $x$. Moreover $|u_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\psi _ x}\geq c\, |u_ j|_{h_0}^2|z-z(x)|^{-2n}$ near $x$ for a constant $c>0$, by the upper bound for $\varphi _ j$ and since $\psi _ x=n\log |z-z(x)|^2+O(1)$. Since $\int _{|z-z(x)|<r}|z-z(x)|^{-2n}\, \mathrm dV=\infty $ for every $r>0$, by polar coordinates in $\mathbb R^{2n}$, the finiteness of the weighted integral of the continuous function $u_ j$ forces $u_ j(x)=0$. Hence $s_ j(x)=G(x)=v$. Since $\psi _ x\leq 0$, dropping the factor $\mathrm e^{-\psi _ x}$ only decreases the integrals, and with $|G|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\leq |f|_ h^2$ on the ball we obtain \[  \int _ X|s_ j|_{h_0}^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j}\, \mathrm dV \leq C_2|v|_ h^2,  \] where $C_2$ depends only on the fixed geometric cutoffs and on the constant of the local point estimate. Step 4: the limit. Since $\varphi _ j\leq \varphi _1\leq \sup _ X\varphi _1$, the sections $s_ j$ are bounded in $L^2$ for $h_0$, and by lemma 10.6.2 (2) a subsequence converges uniformly to a holomorphic section $s$ of $L$, which satisfies $s(x)=v$. Since $\varphi _ j\downarrow \varphi $, Fatou's lemma gives ( 10.7.10 ) with $C=C_2$. $\square$ Lemma 10.7.11 . F8C4EC9BBA24 Let $L$ and $T$ be holomorphic line bundles on $X$ with smooth quadratic metrics $h_0$ and $h_ T$, and let $\mathrm dV$ be a smooth positive volume form on $X$. For an integer $k\geq 1$ and a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\varphi $ on $X$, the space \[  \mathcal H_ k=\left\{ s\in H^0(X,L^ k\otimes T): \int _ X|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2\mathrm e^{-k\varphi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty ight\}   \] is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space for the displayed squared norm $\| s\| _ k^2$. If $\mathcal H_ k
e \{ 0\} $ and $s_1,\ldots ,s_{d_ k}$ is an orthonormal basis, then E4884F8C8C74 10.7.12  egin{equation}  \varphi _ k= rac1k\log \sup _{\| s\| _ k\leq 1}|s|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2 = rac1k\log \sum _{i=1}^{d_ k}|s_ i|_{h_0^ k\otimes h_ T}^2. \end{equation} Writing $	heta =c_1(L,h_0)$ and $	heta _ T=c_1(T,h_ T)$, the function $\varphi _ k$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +k^{-1}	heta _ T)$ and has gentle analytic singularities with coefficient $1/k$. Except for the gentle analytic singularities, which are defined only on compact Kähler manifolds (definition 6.14.12 ), these assertions hold more generally on every compact complex manifold $X'$ of positive dimension in place of $X$. Proof. By lemma 10.6.2 (3), $H^0(X,L^ k\otimes T)$ and its linear subspace $\mathcal H_ k$ are finite dimensional. The weighted integral defines an inner product on $\mathcal H_ k$: the function $\varphi $ is finite almost everywhere, so the weight is positive almost everywhere, and a section of norm zero vanishes almost everywhere and hence identically. A finite-dimensional inner product space is complete. At a point $y$, with the coefficients $c_ i$ of $s=\sum _ ic_ is_ i$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|s(y)|^2\leq \sum _ i|c_ i|^2\sum _ i|s_ i(y)|^2$, with equality when the $c_ i$ are proportional to the complex conjugates of the values of the $s_ i$ at $y$ in a local frame. This proves the equality in ( 10.7.12 ). In local frames with $|e|_{h_0}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_0}$ and $|e_ T|_{h_ T}^2=\mathrm e^{-p_ T}$, write $s_ i=f_ ie^ k\otimes e_ T$. Then \[  \varphi _ k= rac1k\log \sum _ i|f_ i|^2-p_0- rac{p_ T}k,  \] and $	heta +k^{-1}	heta _ T+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _ k=k^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _ i|f_ i|^2\geq 0$ by proposition 5.10.3 . Hence $\varphi _ k\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +k^{-1}	heta _ T)$, with analytic singularities of type $(1/k,\mathfrak b)$, where $\mathfrak b$ is the ideal sheaf generated locally by the $f_ i$. This ideal sheaf does not depend on the frames, because a change of frames multiplies all $f_ i$ by the same nowhere vanishing holomorphic function, and it is coherent by lemma 6.8.4 . Moreover $\mathrm e^{k\varphi _ k}=\sum _ i|s_ i|^2$ is smooth on $X$. The local expressions for $\varphi _ k$ above are presentations with the smooth remainders $-p_0-p_ T/k$, so proposition 6.14.8 shows that on every log resolution $\pi $ of $\mathfrak b$, with $\pi ^*\mathfrak b=\mathcal O(-D)$, locally $\varphi _ k\circ \pi $ is $k^{-1}\log |s_ D|^2$ plus a smooth function. These are the conditions of definition 6.14.12 . Apart from this appeal to definition 6.14.12 , the proof uses only that $X$ is a compact complex manifold of positive dimension, since the last assertion of lemma 10.6.2 gives its part (3) in this generality; hence it also proves the last assertion of the lemma. $\square$ Example 10.7.13 . E7DB735CB52F On $\mathbb P^1$ take $L=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, $T$ trivial, $\varphi =0$ and $\mathrm dV=\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$. A section of $L^ k$ is $f(z)X_0^ k$ on the chart $[1:z]$ with $f$ entire, and in the chart at infinity, with $\zeta =1/z$, it equals $\zeta ^ kf(1/\zeta )X_1^ k$; holomorphicity at $\zeta =0$ and Cauchy's estimates show that $f$ is a polynomial of degree at most $k$. Integration over circles makes the monomials orthogonal, and with $t=|z|^2$, \[  \| z^ j\| _ k^2=\int _0^\infty  rac{t^ j}{(1+t)^{k+2}}\, \mathrm dt = rac{j!(k-j)!}{(k+1)!},\qquad 0\leq j\leq k;  \] the last equality follows from the substitution $u=t/(1+t)$ and repeated integration by parts. Thus the sections $\sqrt{(k+1) inom {k}{j}}X_0^{k-j}X_1^ j$, $0\leq j\leq k$, form an orthonormal basis, and the sum of their squared norms is \[   rac{k+1}{(1+|z|^2)^ k}\sum _{j=0}^ k inom {k}{j}|z|^{2j}=k+1.  \] Consequently $\varphi _ k=k^{-1}\log (k+1)$, which tends to zero uniformly.
