title: Definition 13.2.4
section: 13.2 Truncation and plurifine locality
text: Definition 13.2.4 . D79952D7E272 If ( 13.2.3 ) holds, we say that the non-pluripolar product of $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite , and we call the limit $S$ of lemma 13.2.2 the non-pluripolar product \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle =S.  \] The angle brackets distinguish this construction from a product that retains mass on pluripolar sets. The empty product ($p=0$) is $1$.

title: Proposition 13.2.5
section: 13.2 Truncation and plurifine locality
text: Proposition 13.2.5 . 1FAE60CC76F9 Every locally finite non-pluripolar product $S$ is strongly positive: $S(\varphi )\geq 0$ for every compactly supported smooth weakly positive form $\varphi $ of bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$. Proof. First let all potentials be locally bounded. Near each point they are limits of decreasing sequences of smooth plurisubharmonic functions, for instance of their mollifications (proposition 5.9.2 (2)). The complex Hessians of these functions are semipositive $(1,1)$-forms (proposition 5.9.2 (1)), hence strongly positive, since the two notions of positivity coincide in bidegree $(1,1)$; by proposition 5.3.2 , their exterior products are strongly positive, and the product of such a product with a weakly positive form of complementary bidegree is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form. Thus the smooth products pair nonnegatively with every smooth compactly supported weakly positive form. By theorem 7.3.7 , the Bedford–Taylor product is their weak limit, and therefore it pairs nonnegatively with these forms as well. By lemma 13.2.1 , applied to the bounded products in the definition of $S_ k$, every $S_ k$ is strongly positive. Since $S_ k\to S$ weakly by lemma 13.2.2 , so is $S$. $\square$

title: Proposition 13.2.6
section: 13.2 Truncation and plurifine locality
text: Proposition 13.2.6 . 7F7123F92478 Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ and $v_1,\ldots ,v_ p$ be plurisubharmonic on $U$. If $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j$ for every $j$, then the non-pluripolar product of the $u_ j$ is locally finite if and only if that of the $v_ j$ is, and then the two products are equal; thus local finiteness and the product depend only on the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. The product is symmetric in its factors and local in the plurifine topology: if $u_ j=v_ j$ on a plurifine open set $O$ for every $j$ and both products are locally finite, then they have the same restriction to $O$. Finally, the product is multilinear: if $u_1'$ is plurisubharmonic on $U$, then the product of $u_1+u_1',u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite if and only if the products of $u_1,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ and of $u_1',u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ are, and in that case \[  \begin{aligned}  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1+u_1')\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle & =\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle \\ & \quad +\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1'\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle . \end{aligned}  \] Similarly, for real $c>0$ the product of $cu_1,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite if and only if that of $u_1,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ is, and then it is $c$ times the latter. Proof. In this proof we write $P^{(m)}(w_1,\ldots ,w_ p)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ w_1,-m\} \wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ w_ p,-m\} $ for plurisubharmonic $w_1,\ldots ,w_ p$ and an integer $m\geq 1$. Symmetry and locality. Each truncated product $S_ k$ is symmetric in its factors, hence so is the limit. Suppose that $u_ j=v_ j$ on the plurifine open set $O$ for every $j$, and that both products are locally finite. By lemma 13.2.2 , plurifine open subsets of $U$ are measurable for the completions of the total variations of the coefficient measures of both products, so the restrictions of the products to $O$ and to the plurifine open sets $W_ k=O\cap \bigcap _ j\{ u_ j>-k\} =O\cap \bigcap _ j\{ v_ j>-k\} $ are well defined; the sets $W_ k$ increase with $k$. On $W_ k$ the truncations $\max \{ u_ j,-k\} $ and $\max \{ v_ j,-k\} $ coincide, so the two level-$k$ products agree on $W_ k$ by theorem 5.47.22 . Since $W_ k$ is contained in the level-$k$ sets of both tuples, lemma 13.2.2 shows that the two non-pluripolar products also agree on $W_ k$. The union of the $W_ k$ is $O$ minus the union of the pole sets of the $u_ j$, a pluripolar set, which has outer measure zero for these total variations by the same lemma. Letting $k\to \infty $, we conclude that the two products have the same restriction to $O$. Dependence on the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$. Suppose that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j$ for every $j$. The distribution $v_ j-u_ j$ then has zero Laplacian, so by Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) it is a smooth function $w_ j$, and its complex Hessian vanishes: $w_ j$ is pluriharmonic. The plurisubharmonic functions $v_ j$ and $u_ j+w_ j$ agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere, since both are subharmonic (theorem 5.9.1 , theorem 3.4.12 ). Fix a relatively compact open set $V\subset U$ and an integer $C$ such that $|w_ j|\leq C$ on $V$ for all $j$. Write $O_ k(u),S_ k(u)$ and $O_ k(v),S_ k(v)$ for the level sets and truncated products of the two tuples. On $V\cap O_ k(v)$ we have $u_ j=v_ j-w_ j>-k-C$, hence \[  \max \{ v_ j,-k\} =v_ j=\max \{ u_ j,-k-C\} +w_ j .  \] The functions $\max \{ v_ j,-k\} $ and $\max \{ u_ j,-k-C\} +w_ j$ are bounded and plurisubharmonic on $V$ and coincide on $V\cap O_ k(v)$. Moreover, adding the pluriharmonic function $w_ j$ to a factor does not change Bedford–Taylor products. Indeed, by additivity (proposition 7.2.2 ) and symmetry (theorem 7.3.7 ), the difference is a sum of products having $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ as first factor; by proposition 7.2.2 (1), such a product is the exterior product of the remaining closed positive current with the smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j=0$. As $V\cap O_ k(v)\subset O_{k+C}(u)$, plurifine locality gives on $V$ \[  S_ k(v)=\mathbf1_{O_ k(v)}P^{(k+C)}(u_1,\ldots ,u_ p)=\mathbf1_{O_ k(v)}S_{k+C}(u)\leq S_{k+C}(u).  \] Thus ( 13.2.3 ) for the $u_ j$ implies ( 13.2.3 ) for the $v_ j$ on compact subsets of $V$, and exchanging the two tuples (that is, replacing $w_ j$ by $-w_ j$) gives the converse. If both products are locally finite, the display and lemma 13.2.2 give $\mathbf1_{O_ k(v)}\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ p\rangle =\mathbf1_{O_ k(v)}\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle $ on $V$ for every $k$. The sets $O_ k(v)$ exhaust the complement of the union of the pole sets, which are the same for the two tuples and carry no mass for either product. Hence the two products coincide. Additivity. Let $u_1'$ be plurisubharmonic and put \[  E_ k=\{ u_1>-k\} \cap \{ u_1'>-k\}  \cap \bigcap _{j=2}^ p\{ u_ j>-k\} .  \] These plurifine open sets increase with $k$ and exhaust the complement of the union of the pole sets of $u_1,u_1',u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$. On $E_ k$ we have $\max \{ u_1+u_1',-2k\} =u_1+u_1'=\max \{ u_1,-k\} +\max \{ u_1',-k\} $ and $\max \{ u_ j,-2k\} =\max \{ u_ j,-k\} $ for $j\geq 2$. Plurifine locality and the additivity of bounded products (proposition 7.2.2 ) therefore give 491D0E94E07A 13.2.7 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  \mathbf1_{E_ k}P^{(2k)}(u_1+u_1',u_2,\ldots ,u_ p) & =\mathbf1_{E_ k}P^{(k)}(u_1,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p)\\ & \quad +\mathbf1_{E_ k}P^{(k)}(u_1',u_2,\ldots ,u_ p). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Before local finiteness is known we argue with trace measures. By proposition 5.47.23 , for each of the three tuples the trace measures of the truncated products increase to a Borel measure, possibly infinite on compact sets, for which every pluripolar set has outer measure zero; for a locally finite product it is the trace measure of the product. The set $E_ k$ is contained in the level-$2k$ set of the first tuple and in the level-$k$ sets of the other two, so by the identity $\mathbf1_{O_ k}S_ l=S_ k$ of lemma 13.2.2 , the restriction of each limit measure to $E_ k$ is the restriction of the corresponding trace measure in ( 13.2.7 ). Hence, on $E_ k$, the limit measure of the first tuple is the sum of those of the other two. Letting $k\to \infty $, monotone convergence gives this equality on every Borel subset of $\bigcup _ kE_ k$, and hence everywhere, because the complement of $\bigcup _ kE_ k$ is pluripolar. Since all three measures are positive, the first is locally finite if and only if the other two are; this is the asserted equivalence of local finiteness. When the products are locally finite, ( 13.2.7 ) and lemma 13.2.2 give the additivity identity on each $E_ k$, and letting $k\to \infty $ proves it. For $c>0$ the same argument applies to the sets $\{ u_1>-k\} \cap \{ cu_1>-k\} \cap \bigcap _{j\geq 2}\{ u_ j>-k\} $, on which $\max \{ cu_1,-k\} =c\max \{ u_1,-k\} $, and proves the homogeneity assertion. $\square$

title: Example 13.2.9
section: 13.2 Truncation and plurifine locality
text: Example 13.2.9 . 6F4C920FEDCA Let $U=\{ (x,y)\in \mathbb C^2:|x|^2<1/2,\  |y|<\mathrm e^{-1}\} $, put $L=-\log |y|$, and define \[  u(x,y)=(|x|^2-1)\sqrt L\quad (y\ne 0),\qquad u(x,0)=-\infty .  \] On $U\setminus \{ y=0\} $ we have $L>1$, the function $u$ is smooth, and its complex second derivatives are \[  u_{x\bar x}=\sqrt L,\qquad u_{y\bar y}=\frac{1-|x|^2}{16|y|^2L^{3/2}},\qquad u_{x\bar y}=-\frac{\bar x}{4\bar y\sqrt L},\qquad \det (u_{j\bar k})=\frac{1-2|x|^2}{16|y|^2L}.  \] Since $u_{x\bar x}>0$ and $\det (u_{j\bar k})>0$, the complex Hessian is positive definite, so $u$ is plurisubharmonic off the axis $\{ y=0\} $ (proposition 5.9.2 (1)). Moreover $u<-\sqrt L/2$ is bounded above and tends to $-\infty $ at the axis. By theorem 5.11.1 , the plurisubharmonic extension across the axis takes the value $\varlimsup u=-\infty $ there, which is the displayed value; hence $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $U$. Off the axis, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2$ is the smooth measure with density a fixed positive multiple of $\det (u_{j\bar k})$, by ( 7.2.4 ). The sets $O_ k=\{ u>-k\} $ are open, since $u$ is continuous as an extended-real function, and they increase to $U\setminus \{ y=0\} $; on $O_ k$ the truncation $\max \{ u,-k\} $ equals $u$, so $S_ k=\mathbf1_{O_ k}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2$. Take $K=\{ |x|^2\leq 1/4,\  |y|\leq r\} $ with $0<r<\mathrm e^{-1}$. On $K$ we have $1-2|x|^2\geq 1/2$, and polar coordinates in $y$ give \[  \int _{|y|\leq r}\frac{\mathrm dA(y)}{|y|^2L}=2\pi \int _0^ r\frac{\mathrm dt}{t(-\log t)}=\infty .  \] Hence $\sup _ k\int _ KS_ k=\int _{K\setminus \{ y=0\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^2=\infty $, and ( 13.2.3 ) fails. Thus the non-pluripolar product of an arbitrary plurisubharmonic function need not be locally finite.

title: 13.3 Closedness and cutoff gradients
section: 13.3 Closedness and cutoff gradients
text: The indicators $\mathbf1_{O_ k}$ cannot be differentiated, so closedness of the non-pluripolar product does not follow directly from closedness of the truncated products. We replace the indicators by bounded plurisubharmonic cutoff functions and control the resulting error with the gradient estimates of section 7.14 . Here $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ is the real operator of ( 5.2.10 ), so that $\mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$. Theorem 13.3.1 . 8A125B338F90 Every locally finite non-pluripolar product is closed. Proof. Closedness is a local property, so we may shrink $U$ and subtract constants to assume that $u_ j\leq 0$ for every $j$. If $p=n$ the product has top degree and is closed for degree reasons, so let $p<n$. Fix a constant strongly positive $(n-p-1,n-p-1)$-form $\gamma $ and put \[  \Theta _ k=\gamma \wedge \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j,k},\qquad S_\gamma =\gamma \wedge \Bigl \langle \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\Bigr \rangle .  \] The $\Theta _ k$ are closed positive currents of bidimension $(1,1)$. By lemma 13.2.2 , $\mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k=\mathbf1_{O_ k}S_\gamma $ increases to $S_\gamma $, and in particular these restrictions have uniformly bounded mass on compact sets. We shall prove that $\mathrm dS_\gamma =0$. Cutoff functions. Put $u=\sum _ ju_ j\leq 0$ and $w_ k=\max \{ 1+u/k,0\} $. By proposition 5.9.5 , $w_ k$ is plurisubharmonic, and $0\leq w_ k\leq 1$. As $k\to \infty $, $w_ k$ increases to $1$ at every point where $u>-\infty $, because $u/k$ increases to $0$ there, while $w_ k=0$ on the pole set of $u$. Moreover $w_ k=0$ outside $O_ k$: if $u_ j\leq -k$ for some $j$, then $u\leq u_ j\leq -k$, since all $u_ i\leq 0$. Choose a smooth function $\zeta $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$, $\zeta =0$ on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and $\zeta =1$ near $1$. Then $\zeta (w_ k)$ and $\zeta '(w_ k)$ vanish outside $O_ k$, so that $\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k=\zeta (w_ k)S_\gamma $. At every point where $u>-\infty $ we have $\zeta (w_ k)\to 1$ and $\zeta '(w_ k)\to 0$, and $S_\gamma $ gives the pole set of $u$ zero mass. Dominated convergence therefore gives \[  \zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k\longrightarrow S_\gamma , \qquad \zeta '(w_ k)\longrightarrow 0 \quad S_\gamma \text{-almost everywhere}.  \] Gradient bound. Let $\eta $ be a compactly supported smooth real one-form, and let $\tau \geq 0$ be a smooth compactly supported function equal to one near $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $. By ( 7.14.4 ), the gradient measure of $w_ k$ with respect to $\Theta _ k$ is $E_{\Theta _ k}(w_ k)=\frac12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w_ k^2\Theta _ k)-w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k\wedge \Theta _ k$, and the last term is a positive measure because $w_ k\geq 0$. Hence \[  \int \tau E_{\Theta _ k}(w_ k) \leq \tfrac 12\int w_ k^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau \wedge \Theta _ k \leq C\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\tau } \mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k\wedge \beta \leq C'.  \] The second inequality uses $w_ k=0$ outside $O_ k$, $w_ k\leq 1$, and the bound of the coefficients of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau \wedge \Theta _ k$ by a constant times the trace measure (theorem 5.3.7 ). The constant $C'$ is independent of $k$ because $\mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k\leq S_\gamma $ and $S_\gamma $ is locally finite. Conclusion. By the chain rule ( 7.14.5 ), $\mathrm d(\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k)=\zeta '(w_ k)\, \mathrm dw_ k\wedge \Theta _ k$. We apply ( 7.14.6 ) with $a=\zeta '(w_ k)$. The constant $C_\eta $ there depends only on $\eta $, so it is the same for every $k$. The first factor on the right is bounded by the gradient bound, and the second tends to zero, since \[  |\zeta '(w_ k)|^2\Theta _ k\wedge \beta =|\zeta '(w_ k)|^2\mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k\wedge \beta \leq |\zeta '(w_ k)|^2 S_\gamma \wedge \beta  \] and the right side tends to zero on $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $ by dominated convergence. Hence the pairing of $\mathrm d(\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k)$ with $\eta $ tends to zero. Since $\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k\to S_\gamma $, the pairing of $\mathrm dS_\gamma $ with $\eta $ vanishes, so $\mathrm dS_\gamma =0$. Finally, $\gamma \wedge \mathrm d\langle \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\rangle =\mathrm dS_\gamma =0$ for every constant strongly positive $\gamma $. These forms span the constant real $(n-p-1,n-p-1)$-forms (proposition 5.3.2 ), and their products with smooth functions and the coordinate one-forms $\mathrm dz_ i,\mathrm d\bar z_ i$ span the test forms of the two bidegrees against which $\mathrm d\langle \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\rangle $ is evaluated. Therefore the non-pluripolar product is closed. $\square$

title: Theorem 13.3.1
section: 13.3 Closedness and cutoff gradients
text: Theorem 13.3.1 . 8A125B338F90 Every locally finite non-pluripolar product is closed. Proof. Closedness is a local property, so we may shrink $U$ and subtract constants to assume that $u_ j\leq 0$ for every $j$. If $p=n$ the product has top degree and is closed for degree reasons, so let $p<n$. Fix a constant strongly positive $(n-p-1,n-p-1)$-form $\gamma $ and put \[  \Theta _ k=\gamma \wedge \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j,k},\qquad S_\gamma =\gamma \wedge \Bigl \langle \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\Bigr \rangle .  \] The $\Theta _ k$ are closed positive currents of bidimension $(1,1)$. By lemma 13.2.2 , $\mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k=\mathbf1_{O_ k}S_\gamma $ increases to $S_\gamma $, and in particular these restrictions have uniformly bounded mass on compact sets. We shall prove that $\mathrm dS_\gamma =0$. Cutoff functions. Put $u=\sum _ ju_ j\leq 0$ and $w_ k=\max \{ 1+u/k,0\} $. By proposition 5.9.5 , $w_ k$ is plurisubharmonic, and $0\leq w_ k\leq 1$. As $k\to \infty $, $w_ k$ increases to $1$ at every point where $u>-\infty $, because $u/k$ increases to $0$ there, while $w_ k=0$ on the pole set of $u$. Moreover $w_ k=0$ outside $O_ k$: if $u_ j\leq -k$ for some $j$, then $u\leq u_ j\leq -k$, since all $u_ i\leq 0$. Choose a smooth function $\zeta $ on $\mathbb R$ with $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$, $\zeta =0$ on $(-\infty ,1/2]$ and $\zeta =1$ near $1$. Then $\zeta (w_ k)$ and $\zeta '(w_ k)$ vanish outside $O_ k$, so that $\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k=\zeta (w_ k)S_\gamma $. At every point where $u>-\infty $ we have $\zeta (w_ k)\to 1$ and $\zeta '(w_ k)\to 0$, and $S_\gamma $ gives the pole set of $u$ zero mass. Dominated convergence therefore gives \[  \zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k\longrightarrow S_\gamma , \qquad \zeta '(w_ k)\longrightarrow 0 \quad S_\gamma \text{-almost everywhere}.  \] Gradient bound. Let $\eta $ be a compactly supported smooth real one-form, and let $\tau \geq 0$ be a smooth compactly supported function equal to one near $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $. By ( 7.14.4 ), the gradient measure of $w_ k$ with respect to $\Theta _ k$ is $E_{\Theta _ k}(w_ k)=\frac12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(w_ k^2\Theta _ k)-w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k\wedge \Theta _ k$, and the last term is a positive measure because $w_ k\geq 0$. Hence \[  \int \tau E_{\Theta _ k}(w_ k) \leq \tfrac 12\int w_ k^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau \wedge \Theta _ k \leq C\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\tau } \mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k\wedge \beta \leq C'.  \] The second inequality uses $w_ k=0$ outside $O_ k$, $w_ k\leq 1$, and the bound of the coefficients of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\tau \wedge \Theta _ k$ by a constant times the trace measure (theorem 5.3.7 ). The constant $C'$ is independent of $k$ because $\mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k\leq S_\gamma $ and $S_\gamma $ is locally finite. Conclusion. By the chain rule ( 7.14.5 ), $\mathrm d(\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k)=\zeta '(w_ k)\, \mathrm dw_ k\wedge \Theta _ k$. We apply ( 7.14.6 ) with $a=\zeta '(w_ k)$. The constant $C_\eta $ there depends only on $\eta $, so it is the same for every $k$. The first factor on the right is bounded by the gradient bound, and the second tends to zero, since \[  |\zeta '(w_ k)|^2\Theta _ k\wedge \beta =|\zeta '(w_ k)|^2\mathbf1_{O_ k}\Theta _ k\wedge \beta \leq |\zeta '(w_ k)|^2 S_\gamma \wedge \beta  \] and the right side tends to zero on $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $ by dominated convergence. Hence the pairing of $\mathrm d(\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k)$ with $\eta $ tends to zero. Since $\zeta (w_ k)\Theta _ k\to S_\gamma $, the pairing of $\mathrm dS_\gamma $ with $\eta $ vanishes, so $\mathrm dS_\gamma =0$. Finally, $\gamma \wedge \mathrm d\langle \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\rangle =\mathrm dS_\gamma =0$ for every constant strongly positive $\gamma $. These forms span the constant real $(n-p-1,n-p-1)$-forms (proposition 5.3.2 ), and their products with smooth functions and the coordinate one-forms $\mathrm dz_ i,\mathrm d\bar z_ i$ span the test forms of the two bidegrees against which $\mathrm d\langle \bigwedge _ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\rangle $ is evaluated. Therefore the non-pluripolar product is closed. $\square$

title: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product

section: 13.4 Bounded factors and the first-degree product
text: Let $v$ be locally bounded and plurisubharmonic, and let $S=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle $ be locally finite. Since $S$ is closed and positive, the recursion of definition 7.2.1 defines $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge S$, and we expect this to be the non-pluripolar product of $v,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$. To prove it we must know that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge S$, like $S$, gives no mass to the pole sets of $u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$. This follows from a weighted form of the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality. We then identify the non-pluripolar product in degree one, which requires a measurable form of Fubini's theorem for Bedford–Taylor products. Lemma 13.4.1 . 263D0F5AEE0A Let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(r,r)$, $r\geq 1$, on a coordinate domain $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $K,L$ be compact sets with $K\Subset \operatorname{Int}L\subset L\Subset U$. Let $V\leq 0$ be plurisubharmonic on $U$, and let $v$ be locally bounded and plurisubharmonic on $U$. Then \[  \int _ K(-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1} \leq C_{K,L}\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)} \int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r,  \] where the right side may be infinite and the constant $C_{K,L}$ depends only on $K$, $L$ and the dimension, and not on $T$, $V$ or $v$. Proof. We treat $r\geq 2$ and smooth $V$ by an integration by parts on small balls, then general $V$ by monotone approximation, and reduce $r=1$ to $r=2$ by adding a variable. Step 1: $r\geq 2$ and $V$ smooth. Here $\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}=\sup _ L|v|$, as in theorem 7.2.5 . If it vanishes, then $v=0$ on $L$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=0$ on $\operatorname{Int}L\supset K$, and the left side vanishes. Otherwise both sides are homogeneous of degree one in $v$, and the left side does not change when a constant is added to $v$; replacing $v$ by $v/(2\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)})-3/2$, it therefore suffices to prove that $\int _ K(-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}\leq C\int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r$ for plurisubharmonic functions $v$ satisfying $-2\leq v\leq -1$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$. Cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(a,R_1)$ such that $\overline{B(a,R)}\subset \operatorname{Int}L$ for some $R>R_1$; it suffices to bound the integral over one ball $B(a,R_1)$. Put $B=B(a,R)$, $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$ and $b=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\beta /\pi $. Fix $R_1<R_2<R$, and let $\widetilde v=\max \{ v,A\psi \} $, with $A=2/(R^2-R_2^2)$, be the collar modification ( 7.3.2 ) of $v$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$, with $N=2$ and with $R^2-R_2^2$ in place of $\delta $. Thus $\widetilde v$ is plurisubharmonic on $\operatorname{Int}L$ and takes values in $[-2,0)$ on $B$; it equals $v$ on $B(a,R_2)$, and $A\psi $ on the collar $\{ R^2-1/A<|z-a|^2<R^2\} $. Choose $0<\delta <1/A$ and put $B_\delta =\{ \psi <-\delta \} $, so that $\widetilde v=A\psi $ on $B\setminus B_\delta $ and $B(a,R_1)\subset B_\delta $. Choose a smooth function $\kappa $ with $0\leq \kappa \leq R^2$, with compact support in $B$ and equal to $-\psi $ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B_\delta }$; this is possible because $0<-\psi \leq R^2$ on $B$. Put $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T$ and $Q=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\wedge T$; since $V$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, $Q$ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(r-1,r-1)$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa =-b$ near $\overline{B_\delta }$ and $S=Ab\wedge T$ on $B\setminus B_\delta $, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _{B_\delta }(-V)S\wedge b^{r-1} & =\int _ B VS\wedge b^{r-2}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa -A\int _{B\setminus B_\delta } VT\wedge b^{r-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa \\ & =\int _ B\kappa \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge Q\wedge b^{r-2} -A\int _{B\setminus B_\delta } VT\wedge b^{r-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa . \end{aligned}  \] For the second line we integrate by parts against the smooth compactly supported function $\kappa $: since $V$ is smooth and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T\wedge b^{r-2}$ is closed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(V\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T\wedge b^{r-2})=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde v\wedge T\wedge b^{r-2}$, and the Bedford–Taylor product is symmetric with respect to the smooth factor. We bound the two terms on the right. Choose a compact set $L'$ with $\overline B\subset \operatorname{Int}L'$ and $L'\subset \operatorname{Int}L$. Since $0\leq \kappa \leq R^2$, the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality (theorem 7.2.5 ) applied to $Q$ bounds the first term by a constant times the trace mass of $Q$ on $\overline B$. To bound this mass, test $Q$ against a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to one on $\overline B$ and supported in $L'$: \[  \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}=\int V\, T\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}\leq C\int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r,  \] since $V\leq 0$ and the coefficients of $T\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ are bounded by a fixed multiple of the trace measure. The collar term has the same bound, because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\kappa $ is a fixed smooth form. Finally, $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$ on $B(a,R_1)$ and $-V\geq 0$, so the left side of the display bounds $\pi ^{1-r}\int _{B(a,R_1)}(-V)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$. Summing over the finitely many balls proves the estimate, with a constant depending only on the chosen radii. Step 2: $r\geq 2$ and $V$ arbitrary. Choose a compact set $L_1$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L_1$ and $L_1\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, depending only on $K$ and $L$. The mollifications $V_ l=V*\rho _{\varepsilon _ l}$, with $\varepsilon _ l\downarrow 0$, are defined, smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $L_1$ for large $l$, and they decrease to $V$ (proposition 5.9.2 (2)); in particular $V\leq V_ l\leq 0$, so that $0\leq -V_ l\leq -V$. Step 1 only involves the weight on a neighborhood of the larger compact set, so it applies to $V_ l$ and the pair $(K,L_1)$ and gives \[  \int _ K(-V_ l)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}\leq C_{K,L_1}\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}\int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ^ r .  \] As $l\to \infty $, $-V_ l$ increases to $-V$, and monotone convergence against the positive measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ proves the estimate. Step 3: $r=1$. Let $t$ be the coordinate of $\mathbb C$, put $\beta _ t=\frac{\mathrm i}{2}\mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d\bar t$, let $D'\Subset D''\Subset D$ be the discs about $0$ of radii $1,2,3$, and let $P\colon U\times D\to U$ be the projection. By proposition 5.6.2 , $P^*T$ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(2,2)$ on $U\times D$. Moreover, by corollary 5.6.4 (1), the pullback of a current $R=\sum R_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ of order zero on $U$ is $P^*R=\sum (R_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ D)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$, where $\lambda _ D$ is Lebesgue measure on $D$. Since $v$ is a locally bounded Borel function, $P^*(vT)=(v\circ P)P^*T$ by corollary 5.6.4 (2), and since $P^*$ commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ P)\wedge P^*T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (P^*(vT)\bigr )=P^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T).  \] The functions $V\circ P\leq 0$ and $v\circ P$ are plurisubharmonic (proposition 5.9.3 ), and $\| v\circ P\| _{L^\infty (L\times \overline{D''})}=\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}$. We apply Step 2 with $r=2$ to these data, to the Euclidean form $\beta +\beta _ t$ and to the compact sets $K\times \overline{D'}\subset \operatorname{Int}L\times D''=\operatorname{Int}(L\times \overline{D''})$. Since $T\wedge \beta ^2=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta =0$ for bidegree reasons, the trace measures in Step 2 are \[  P^*T\wedge (\beta +\beta _ t)^2=2P^*(T\wedge \beta )\wedge \beta _ t, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ P)\wedge P^*T\wedge (\beta +\beta _ t)=P^*(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T)\wedge \beta _ t,  \] that is, the products of the measures $2T\wedge \beta $ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$ with Lebesgue measure on $D$. By Fubini's theorem (proposition 2.2.7 ), the inequality of Step 2 therefore reads \[  \pi \int _ K(-V)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\leq C\| v\| _{L^\infty (L)}\cdot 8\pi \int _ L(-V)T\wedge \beta ,  \] where $C$ is the constant of Step 2 for $K\times \overline{D'}$ and $L\times \overline{D''}$ in dimension $n+1$, which depends only on $K$, $L$ and $n$. This is the case $r=1$, with $C_{K,L}=8C$. $\square$ Lemma 13.4.2 . 5D93FCFBA57F Let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(r,r)$, $r\geq 1$, on a coordinate domain, whose trace measure gives zero mass to every pluripolar set. Then for every locally bounded plurisubharmonic $v$, the trace measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$ also gives zero mass to every pluripolar set. Consequently the same holds for every Bedford–Taylor product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge T$, $1\leq q\leq r$, of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions with base $T$. Proof. Let $E$ be a pluripolar subset of the coordinate domain $U$ on which $T$ lives. By definition 5.47.2 and since $U$ has a countable basis, $E$ is covered by countably many compact sets $K$, each having a compact neighborhood $L$ with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, together with an open neighborhood $W$ of $L$ and a function $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$ such that $E\cap K\subset \{ V=-\infty \} $; shrinking $W$ and subtracting a constant, we may assume $V\leq 0$. The set $\{ V=-\infty \} $ is a pluripolar Borel set, so it suffices to show that $K\cap \{ V=-\infty \} $ has measure zero for the trace measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$. Put $\mu =\mathbf1_ LT\wedge \beta ^ r$. This is a finite measure that does not charge $\{ V=-\infty \} $, so $V$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Hence $\min \{ -V/R,1\} \to 0$ $\mu $-almost everywhere as $R\to \infty $, and by dominated convergence we may choose numbers $R_ j\geq 2^ j$ such that \[  \int \min \{ -V/R_ j,1\} \, \mathrm d\mu \leq 2^{-j}\qquad (j\geq 1).  \] Put $\widetilde V=\sum _{j\geq 1}\max \{ V/R_ j,-1\} $. The partial sums are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , and they decrease, because every term is nonpositive. Their limit satisfies $\widetilde V\geq \sum _ jV/R_ j\geq V$, since $V\leq 0$ and $\sum _ j1/R_ j\leq 1$; hence it is not identically $-\infty $ on any component of $W$, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.1 . Moreover $\widetilde V\leq 0$, $\widetilde V=-\infty $ on $\{ V=-\infty \} $, where every term equals $-1$, and by monotone convergence \[  \int _ L(-\widetilde V)\, T\wedge \beta ^ r=\sum _{j\geq 1}\int \min \{ -V/R_ j,1\} \, \mathrm d\mu \leq 1.  \] By lemma 13.4.1 , applied on $W$, the function $-\widetilde V$ is integrable on $K$ for the trace measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge T$. Hence this measure gives zero mass to $K\cap \{ \widetilde V=-\infty \} \supset K\cap \{ V=-\infty \} $, which proves the first assertion. The second follows by induction on $q$, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge T)$, where the base current in parentheses is closed and positive of bidimension $(r-q+1,r-q+1)$. $\square$ Proposition 13.4.3 . 90E0E28D9A95 Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ be plurisubharmonic on a coordinate domain, $1\leq p\leq n$, and suppose that $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are locally bounded for some $0\leq q\leq p$. If $S=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle $ is locally finite, then the non-pluripolar product of $u_1,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite and \[  \langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge S,  \] where the right side is the Bedford–Taylor product of definition 7.2.1 with base $S$. Proof. For $q=0$ there is nothing to prove. Inserting the bounded factors $u_ q,u_{q-1},\ldots ,u_1$ one at a time, we reduce to the case $q=1$. So let $v=u_1$ be locally bounded and $S=\langle \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ p\rangle $ locally finite. By theorem 13.3.1 , $S$ is a closed positive current, so $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge S$ is defined; it is closed and positive, and by lemma 13.4.2 it gives zero mass to pluripolar sets, because $S$ does. If $p=1$, then $S=1$ and the assertion is that of bounded Bedford–Taylor theory. Let $p\geq 2$. The assertion is local, so we may assume $u_ j\leq 0$ for $j\geq 2$ and put \[  \begin{gathered} O_ k=\bigcap _{j\geq 2}\{ u_ j>-k\} ,\qquad \Theta _ k=\bigwedge _{j\geq 2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u_ j,-k\} ,\\ w_ k=\max \Bigl \{ 1+\frac1k\sum _{j\geq 2}u_ j,\, 0\Bigr \} . \end{gathered}  \] The functions $w_ k$ are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , and they take values in $[0,1]$ because all $u_ j\leq 0$. They vanish outside $O_ k$: if $u_ i\leq -k$ for some $i\geq 2$, then $\sum _{j\geq 2}u_ j\leq u_ i\leq -k$. The sets $\{ w_ k>0\} =\{ \sum _{j\geq 2}u_ j>-k\} $ increase to the set where all $u_ j$, $j\geq 2$, are finite. Take smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ l$ decreasing to $v$ near a given compact set. By lemma 13.2.2 , $S$ and $\Theta _ k$ have the same restriction to $O_ k$; since $w_ k$ vanishes outside $O_ k$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l$ is smooth, \[  w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\wedge S=w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l\wedge \Theta _ k.  \] The weighted form of theorem 7.3.7 , applied with the constant sequence of weights $w_ k$ and the fixed base currents $S$ on the left and $\Theta _ k$ on the right, gives $w_ kR=w_ k\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ k$ in the limit $l\to \infty $. Multiplying by the bounded Borel functions $\mathbf1_{\{ w_ k>\varepsilon \} }/w_ k$ and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we see that $R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ k$ have the same restriction to $\{ w_ k>0\} $. Now fix an integer $m\geq 1$. For $k\geq m$, the bounded functions $\max \{ u_ i,-k\} $ and $\max \{ u_ i,-m\} $ coincide on $O_ m$, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ m$ on $O_ m$ by theorem 5.47.22 . Since the sets $\{ w_ k>0\} \cap O_ m$, $k\geq m$, exhaust $O_ m$, we conclude that $\mathbf1_{O_ m}R=\mathbf1_{O_ m}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ m$. Consider finally the full tuple $v,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ on a relatively compact open set on which $|v|<m_0$. For $m\geq m_0$, its level-$m$ set is $O_ m$ and $v$ needs no truncation, so its truncated product at level $m$ is $\mathbf1_{O_ m}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \Theta _ m=\mathbf1_{O_ m}R$. These restrictions are bounded by $R$, hence have locally bounded mass, and they increase to $R$ because $R$ gives the pole sets of $u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ zero mass. Therefore the non-pluripolar product of $v,u_2,\ldots ,u_ p$ is locally finite and equals $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge S$. $\square$ To identify the first-degree product we shall integrate planar measures over almost every fiber of a coordinate projection. We first record the measure theory of such fiber integrals, and then prove the fiber formula for bounded potentials, with the Borel weights needed for truncation. Lemma 13.4.4 . CA3A887474EE Let $Q\subset \mathbb C^ r$ and $D\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open sets, $r,m\geq 1$, let $G\subset D$ be a Borel set, and for each $z\in G$ let $\mu _ z$ be a positive Radon measure on $Q$. Assume that $z\mapsto \int a\, \mathrm d\mu _ z$ is Borel on $G$ for every continuous function $a$ with compact support in $Q$. Then $z\mapsto \mu _ z(E_ z)$ is Borel on $G$ for every Borel set $E\subset Q\times D$, where $E_ z=\{ x:(x,z)\in E\} $. Moreover, for every nonnegative Borel function $f$ on $D$, \[  \lambda (E)=\int _ G\mu _ z(E_ z)f(z)\, \mathrm dV(z)  \] is a measure on the Borel sets of $Q\times D$, and \[  \int h\, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _ G\Bigl (\int _ Qh(x,z)\, \mathrm d\mu _ z(x)\Bigr )f(z)\, \mathrm dV(z)  \] for every nonnegative Borel function $h$ on $Q\times D$, the inner integral being a Borel function of $z\in G$. Proof. Fix open sets $Q''\Subset Q$ and $D''\Subset D$, so that $\mu _ z(Q'')<\infty $ for every $z$. If $A\subset Q''$ is open, the continuous functions $a_ l(x)=\min \{ 1,\max \{ l\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb C^ r\setminus A)-1,0\} \} $ have compact support in $A$ and increase to $\mathbf1_ A$, so $z\mapsto \mu _ z(A)$ is Borel by monotone convergence. Let $\mathcal D$ be the family of Borel sets $A\subset Q''$ for which $z\mapsto \mu _ z(A)$ is Borel on $G$. It contains the open subsets of $Q''$, which are closed under finite intersections and generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Q''$. It is closed under complements in $Q''$, because $\mu _ z(Q''\setminus A)=\mu _ z(Q'')-\mu _ z(A)$ with finite values, and under countable disjoint unions. By Dynkin's theorem (lemma 2.2.6 ), $\mathcal D$ contains every Borel subset of $Q''$. Next, let $\mathcal D'$ be the family of Borel sets $E\subset Q''\times D''$ for which $z\mapsto \mu _ z(E_ z)$ is Borel on $G$. It contains the products $A\times A'$ of Borel sets $A\subset Q''$ and $A'\subset D''$, since $\mu _ z((A\times A')_ z)=\mu _ z(A)\mathbf1_{A'}(z)$; these products are closed under finite intersections and generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Q''\times D''$, because every open subset of $Q''\times D''$ is a countable union of products of open balls. As before, $\mathcal D'$ is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions, so it contains every Borel subset of $Q''\times D''$. Exhausting $Q$ and $D$ by increasing sequences of such sets $Q''$ and $D''$, and using monotone convergence, we obtain the first assertion. By the first assertion, $\lambda (E)$ is defined, and $\lambda $ is countably additive by monotone convergence, applied first to the measures $\mu _ z$ and then to the integral over $G$. The formula for $\int h\, \mathrm d\lambda $ holds for indicator functions of Borel sets by definition, hence for nonnegative simple functions by linearity, and for nonnegative Borel functions by monotone convergence, applied in the same order; the inner integrals are Borel in $z$ as increasing limits of Borel functions. $\square$ Lemma 13.4.5 . 4AD0BFC1BFCD Let $r,m\geq 0$ be integers, let $Q\subset \mathbb C^ r$ and $D\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open sets with coordinates $x$ and $z$, and let $p_ D\colon Q\times D\to D$ be the projection. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ r$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $Q\times D$, and put \[  M=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ r,\qquad M_ z=\bigwedge _{j=1}^ r\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}_ x u_ j(\, \cdot \, ,z),  \] the Bedford–Taylor products on $Q\times D$ and on the fibers $Q\times \{ z\} $; here $u_ j(\, \cdot \, ,z)$ is locally bounded and plurisubharmonic on $Q$ by proposition 5.9.3 . For every smooth real $(m,m)$-form $\eta $ on $D$ and every bounded Borel function $h$ on $Q\times D$ with compact support, the fiber integral $z\mapsto \int _ Q h(x,z)\, M_ z(x)$ is Borel measurable and 7F078C7DCBDD 13.4.6 \begin{equation}  \int _{Q\times D}h\, p_ D^*\eta \wedge M =\int _ D\left(\int _ Q h(x,z)\, M_ z(x)\right)\eta (z). \end{equation} If $\eta \geq 0$, the identity holds for every nonnegative Borel function $h$, with possibly infinite values. Proof. If $r=0$ or $m=0$, one factor of $Q\times D$ is a point, carrying counting measure, and the corresponding product is the empty product $1$; then the two sides of ( 13.4.6 ) are the same integral. Let $r,m\geq 1$. For smooth potentials the formula is Fubini's theorem; we pass to the limit for continuous weights $h$, and then extend the formula to Borel weights by the uniqueness of measures. Approximation. Let $Q'\Subset Q$ and $D'\Subset D$ be open. Continuous weights. A finite smooth partition of unity (lemma 2.5.2 ), subordinate to a cover of $\operatorname{Supp}h$ by such products $Q'\times D'$, treats arbitrary continuous $h$ with compact support. Measurability. For a continuous function $a$ with compact support in $Q$, the function $z\mapsto \int a\, M_ z$ is Borel on $D$: if the support of $a$ lies in $Q'$, then on $D'$ it is the pointwise limit of the continuous functions $z\mapsto \int a\, M_ z^{(l)}$, and $D$ is covered by countably many such sets $D'$. Hence lemma 13.4.4 , applied with $G=D$ and $\mu _ z=M_ z$, shows that $z\mapsto \int _ Qh(x,z)\, M_ z(x)$ is Borel for every nonnegative Borel function $h$, and hence for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. Borel weights. Let $\eta =f\, \mathrm dV_ z\geq 0$ as before, and let $\lambda $ be the measure of lemma 13.4.4 for $\mu _ z=M_ z$ and this function $f$, so that \[  \lambda (E)=\int _ D M_ z(E_ z)\, \eta (z)  \] for Borel sets $E\subset Q\times D$. By the step on continuous weights, $\lambda $ and $p_ D^*\eta \wedge M$ therefore have the same integral against every test function, so they are equal by the uniqueness in theorem 2.5.6 . This proves the formula for nonnegative Borel $h$, and then for bounded real Borel $h$ with compact support, by splitting $h$ into its positive and negative parts. Finally, let $\eta =f\, \mathrm dV_ z$ be a smooth real form and $h$ a bounded Borel function supported in $K\times K_ D$, with $K\subset Q$ and $K_ D\subset D$ compact. Choose $\kappa \in C_ c^\infty (D)$ with $0\leq \kappa \leq 1$ and $\kappa =1$ on $K_ D$, and put $c=\sup _{\operatorname{Supp}\kappa }|f|$. Replacing $\eta $ by $\kappa \eta $ changes neither side of ( 13.4.6 ), and $\kappa \eta =\kappa (f+c)\, \mathrm dV_ z-c\kappa \, \mathrm dV_ z$ is the difference of two smooth nonnegative forms. This proves the formula for signed $\eta $. $\square$ Proposition 13.4.7 . 3553558C2E27 Let $u$ be plurisubharmonic on a coordinate domain.
